        return_counts=True,
    )
)

This matters because:

classes_

and:

global_majority_class_

are currently derived from different target arrays in feature-based CombinedClassifier mode.

docs.title: Inspect resolved data after fitting
docs.text:
GradientCOBRA:

print(
    model.X_k_.shape
)

print(
    model.X_l_.shape
)

MixCOBRA:

print(
    model.X_k_.shape
)

print(
    model.X_l_.shape
)

CombinedClassifier:

print(
    classifier.X_k_.shape
)

print(
    classifier.X_l_.shape
)

docs.title: Verify your explicit arrays were used
docs.text:
For NumPy arrays:

import numpy as np

print(
    np.array_equal(
        model.X_k_,
        X_train,
    )
)

print(
    np.array_equal(
        model.X_l_,
        X_cal,
    )
)

The resolver converts values with:

np.asarray()

so object identity is not the important check; compare values and shapes.

docs.title: Inspect calibration prediction space
docs.text:
GradientCOBRA:

P_cal = model._load_predictions(
    model.X_l_
)

print(
    P_cal.shape
)

CombinedClassifier:

print(
    classifier.pred_l_.shape
)

MixCOBRA:

P_cal = model._load_predictions(
    model.X_l_
)

print(
    P_cal.shape
)

docs.title: Inspect calibration CV folds
docs.text:
for fold in model.cv_folds_:
    print(
        fold.fold_id,
        len(
            fold.train_idx
        ),
        len(
            fold.eval_idx
        ),
    )

Those indices are relative to:

X_l_
y_l_

not to the original full dataset.

docs.title: Mapping CV rows back to your calibration set
docs.text:
fold = model.cv_folds_[0]

X_cal_train_fold = model.X_l_[
    fold.train_idx
]

X_cal_val_fold = model.X_l_[
    fold.eval_idx
]

This lets you inspect exactly which rows in your custom calibration set are used for one internal optimization fold.

docs.title: Random state and explicit aggregation data
docs.text:
Supplying X_l/y_l removes randomness from the first-level COBRA split because that split no longer occurs.

However, random_state can still affect:

base estimators
internal KFoldCV shuffling
optimizer-related components
other estimator-specific randomness.

So an explicit aggregation set does not make the entire model deterministic by itself.

docs.title: split_ratio is ignored for explicit data
docs.text:
This call:

model.fit(
    X_train,
    y_train,
    X_l=X_cal,
    y_l=y_cal,
    split_ratio=0.9,
)

still uses your supplied:

X_cal
y_cal.

The split_ratio value is never reached by the resolver's automatic-split branch.

docs.title: overlap is ignored for explicit data
docs.text:
Likewise:

overlap=0.2

does not cause rows to be copied between your explicit arrays.

If you want overlap between training and calibration data, you must construct that overlap yourself before calling fit().

docs.title: Intentional overlap
docs.text:
The source does not prevent the same observation from appearing in both:

X

and:

X_l.

For example:

X_l = X_train[
    -100:
]

y_l = y_train[
    -100:
]

is accepted structurally.

The package does not track row identity and does not warn about reused observations.

Any statistical consequences of that overlap are the caller's responsibility.

docs.title: No disjointness validation
docs.text:
The resolver validates shape consistency but does not test:

duplicate rows
shared row IDs
sample provenance
train/calibration disjointness.

So "custom aggregation data" means the package trusts the split you provide.

docs.title: Calibration size
docs.text:
The source does not impose a package-specific minimum calibration sample count before returning the explicit context.

However, later components can require enough rows for:

n_cv folds
distance calculations
optimization
class representation.

For example, n_cv=5 with a very small calibration set can produce empty or degenerate folds in the current custom KFold implementation.

docs.title: Check calibration size before fitting
docs.text:
print(
    len(
        X_cal
    )
)

print(
    model.n_cv
)

A calibration set should contain enough samples for the requested internal CV structure.

The current source does not automatically reduce n_cv to match a small calibration set.

docs.title: Regression fallback depends on calibration targets
docs.text:
Both GradientCOBRA and MixCOBRA compute:

global_mean_ = np.mean(
    y_l_
)

So changing the custom aggregation dataset changes not only:

distance geometry
CV objective
optimized parameters

but also the zero-weight fallback value.

docs.title: Classification fallback depends on calibration targets
docs.text:
CombinedClassifier computes:

global_majority_class_

from:

y_l_.

So a different calibration class distribution can change the fallback class used when a query has no positive kernel-weight mass.

docs.title: Calibration data affect optimization
docs.text:
The optimized parameters are selected from cross-validation performed on the calibration set.

Therefore changing:

X_l
y_l

can change:

bandwidth_
alpha / beta
optimization score
optimization history.

The source does not treat explicit aggregation data as a passive holdout; they actively define the aggregation model.

docs.title: Calibration data are part of the fitted estimator
docs.text:
Attributes such as:

X_l_
y_l_
prediction-space calibration arrays
distance matrices
CV folds

remain on the fitted estimator.

So the calibration data are not used only transiently during fit.

They define the reference set against which future query distances are computed.

docs.title: Prediction compares against calibration representation
docs.text:
For GradientCOBRA:

distance_matrix = self.distance_.matrix(
    Y_norm,
    self.Y_l_norm_,
)

For CombinedClassifier:

distance_matrix = self.distance_.matrix(
    preds_space,
    self.pred_l_,
)

For MixCOBRA, query representations are compared with the stored normalized calibration spaces.

Thus your explicit aggregation dataset becomes the model's prediction reference population.

docs.title: Difference from a conventional validation set
docs.text:
A conventional validation set is often used only for model selection and then discarded.

In the current COBRA implementation, the aggregation/calibration data also serve as the stored reference observations used by the final prediction mechanism.

So:

X_l/y_l

are more than a temporary evaluation set.

They are part of the fitted aggregation model.

docs.title: Saving custom split indices
docs.text:
For reproducibility, it is often useful to save the row indices that produced:

X_train/y_train
X_cal/y_cal.

For example:

np.save(
    "train_idx.npy",
    train_idx,
)

np.save(
    "cal_idx.npy",
    cal_idx,
)

Then the same explicit aggregation configuration can be reconstructed later.

The package does not save original full-dataset indices automatically.

docs.title: DataFrames
docs.text:
If you pass pandas DataFrames and Series, the resolver uses:

check_X_y()

and:

np.asarray()

so the fitted internal context is NumPy-based.

Index labels are not retained as sample identifiers.

If row identity matters, keep the original DataFrame index or split indices externally.

docs.title: Example: externally prepared holdout splitter
docs.text:
from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.splitters import (
    RandomHoldoutSplitter,
)

splitter = RandomHoldoutSplitter(
    calibration_size=0.3,
    random_state=42,
)

indices = splitter.split(
    X,
    y,
)

Then:

model.fit(
    X[
        indices.train_idx
    ],
    y[
        indices.train_idx
    ],
    X_l=X[
        indices.eval_idx
    ],
    y_l=y[
        indices.eval_idx
    ],
)

This is how you can use a splitter other than the high-level estimator's hard-coded default first-level path.

docs.title: Example: custom index logic
docs.text:
train_idx = np.arange(
    0,
    800,
)

cal_idx = np.arange(
    800,
    1000,
)

model.fit(
    X[
        train_idx
    ],
    y[
        train_idx
    ],
    X_l=X[
        cal_idx
    ],
    y_l=y[
        cal_idx
    ],
)

The package accepts the resulting arrays without needing to know how those indices were selected.

docs.title: Custom aggregation data with KFC Procedure
docs.text:
The top-level KFC Procedure does not currently expose:

X_l=
y_l=

through its public:

fit()

interface.

KFC performs its own internal split, then its C-Step receives the internal aggregation prediction matrix.

Therefore the custom aggregation-data interface documented here applies directly to the standalone COBRA estimators, not to the top-level KFCProcedure.fit() API.

docs.title: KFC C-Step wrappers
docs.text:
Inside KFC, wrappers such as:

GradientCOBRACombiner
MixCOBRACombiner
CobraClassifierCombiner

receive the already-created F-Step matrix and call the wrapped estimator with:

as_predictions=True.

That is a different advanced pathway from supplying raw feature-based X_l/y_l to standalone COBRA.

docs.title: Custom aggregation vs KFC internal split
docs.text:
Standalone COBRA:

you can provide X_l / y_l directly.

Top-level KFC:

KFCProcedure.fit() creates its own internal K/F vs C split.

If you need full control over the KFC internal split, the current public KFC fit interface does not expose that as X_l/y_l.

docs.title: Common mistake: using test data as aggregation data unintentionally
docs.text:
Because X_l/y_l become part of the fitted model and influence hyperparameter optimization, they are not untouched final-evaluation data.

If you need an independent test set, keep it separate and call:

predict(
    X_test
)

only after fitting.

docs.title: Common mistake: mismatched preprocessing
docs.text:
The base estimators are fitted on:

X

and asked to predict:

X_l.

If those arrays were produced with inconsistent external preprocessing, the package does not reconcile them.

Ensure they use the same feature schema and transformation conventions.

docs.title: Common mistake: different column order
docs.text:
Even if:

X.shape[1]
==
X_l.shape[1]

the semantics can still differ if columns were reordered.

The package does not store feature names after conversion to NumPy.

docs.title: Common mistake: too-small classification calibration set
docs.text:
A small:

y_l

can omit classes or create unstable internal K-fold composition.

The source does not automatically repair class coverage.

Inspect:

np.unique(
    y_l,
    return_counts=True,
)

before fitting.

docs.title: Common mistake: expecting split_ratio to modify explicit data
docs.text:
Once:

X_l
y_l

are present, the resolver does not use:

split_ratio
overlap.

Changing those parameters has no effect on your custom first-level split.

docs.title: Common mistake: combining X_l/y_l with as_predictions=True
docs.text:
Because as_predictions=True is checked first, your explicit calibration arrays are bypassed.

Choose one mode deliberately:

raw feature training + explicit aggregation features

or:

already-precomputed prediction space.

docs.title: Check mode
docs.text:
print(
    model.as_predictions_
)

Expected:

False

for raw-feature explicit X_l/y_l mode.

docs.title: Check stored arrays
docs.text:
print(
    model.X_k_.shape
)

print(
    model.X_l_.shape
)

docs.title: Check calibration target summary
docs.text:
Regression:

print(
    np.mean(
        model.y_l_
    )
)

Classification:

print(
    np.unique(
        model.y_l_,
        return_counts=True,
    )
)

docs.title: Check internal estimator count
docs.text:
print(
    len(
        model.estimators_
    )
)

In feature-based explicit aggregation mode, internal base estimators are still fitted.

docs.title: Check calibration prediction-space shape
docs.text:
GradientCOBRA or MixCOBRA:

P_l = model._load_predictions(
    model.X_l_
)

print(
    P_l.shape
)

CombinedClassifier:

print(
    model.pred_l_.shape
)

docs.title: Check CV uses calibration rows
docs.text:
for fold in model.cv_folds_:
    assert np.max(
        fold.eval_idx
    ) < len(
        model.X_l_
    )

for non-empty validation folds.

docs.title: Validation checklist
docs.text:
Before calling fit():

assert len(
    X_train
) == len(
    y_train
)

assert len(
    X_cal
) == len(
    y_cal
)

For ordinary feature mode:

assert (
    X_train.shape[1]
    ==
    X_cal.shape[1]
)

For numeric regression:

assert np.isfinite(
    X_train
).all()

assert np.isfinite(
    X_cal
).all()

assert np.isfinite(
    y_train
).all()

assert np.isfinite(
    y_cal
).all()

These checks are useful because the package's component-level validation is not uniform.

docs.title: Current source comparison
docs.text: Estimator Explicit X_l/y_l Base estimators fit on Aggregation representation built on GradientCOBRA Yes X/y predictions on X_l MixCOBRARegressor Yes X/y X_l + predictions on X_l CombinedClassifier Yes X/y hard predictions on X_l

docs.title: Calibration-derived fitted state
docs.text: Estimator Calibration-derived state GradientCOBRA X_l_, y_l_, Y_l_norm_, distance_matrix_, cv_folds_, global_mean_ MixCOBRARegressor X_l_, y_l_, normalized X/Y spaces, distance matrices, cv_folds_, global_mean_ CombinedClassifier X_l_, y_l_, pred_l_, distance_matrix_, cv_folds_, global_majority_class_

docs.title: Branch precedence quick reference
docs.text: Inputs Resolver mode as_predictions=True precomputed prediction mode X_l + y_l explicit aggregation mode pred_features only pred_features mode none of the above automatic split mode only one of X_l / y_l error

docs.title: Quick reference
docs.text: Goal Current source usage supply dedicated calibration features X_l=X_cal, y_l=y_cal bypass automatic overlap split provide both X_l and y_l keep internal base estimators use explicit X_l/y_l with as_predictions=False skip internal base estimators use as_predictions=True instead use external stratified first-level split prepare arrays externally, then pass X_l/y_l use external chronological first-level split prepare arrays externally, then pass X_l/y_l inspect resolved training rows X_k_, y_k_ inspect resolved calibration rows X_l_, y_l_ inspect internal calibration CV cv_folds_

docs.title: Mental model
docs.text:
Custom aggregation data lets you decide which observations train the model experts and which observations become the reference population for COBRA aggregation.

\[ \boxed{ (X_k,y_k) \rightarrow \text{fit experts} } \] \[ \boxed{ X_l \rightarrow \text{expert predictions} \rightarrow \text{COBRA geometry} \rightarrow \text{aggregation} } \]

with:

\[ \boxed{ y_l \rightarrow \text{CV objective + final reference targets} } \]

The explicit X_l/y_l path bypasses the automatic first-level split, but it does not bypass the COBRA distance, cross-validation, optimization, or final reference-set behavior.

docs.title: Extending KFC Procedure
docs.text:
kfc_procedure is designed around small abstract interfaces and registry-based factories.

That makes the package extensible in several places without changing the high-level KFC or COBRA orchestration code.

The current source exposes extension points for:

KFC layer
    Bregman divergences
    F-Step local models
    C-Step combiners

COBRA layer
    estimators
    distances
    kernel adapters
    kernels
    aggregators
    losses
    normalizers
    data splitters
    cross-validation strategies
    optimizers

Most of these components follow the same pattern:

1. implement the expected interface
2. register the class with the appropriate factory
3. refer to the implementation by its registered string name

docs.title: Extension architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    F["BaseFactory"]

    D["BregmanDivergenceFactory"]
    LM["LocalModelFactory"]
    C["CombinerFactory"]

    E["EstimatorFactory"]
    DS["DistanceFactory"]
    KA["KernelAdapterFactory"]
    K["KernelFactory"]
    A["AggregatorFactory"]
    L["LossFactory"]
    N["NormalizerFactory"]
    S["SplitterFactory"]
    CV["CVFactory"]
    O["OptimizerFactory"]

    F --> D
    F --> LM
    F --> C
    F --> E
    F --> DS
    F --> KA
    F --> K
    F --> A
    F --> L
    F --> N
    F --> S
    F --> CV
    F --> O

Each factory subclass receives its own independent registry.

docs.title: The common factory system
docs.text:
The central registry implementation is:

BaseFactory

from:

kfc_procedure/factory/base.py

Registration uses a decorator:

@SomeFactory.register(
    "name"
)
class MyComponent:
    ...

Creation uses:

component = SomeFactory.create(
    "name",
    **params,
)

docs.title: Independent registries
docs.text:
BaseFactory.__init_subclass__() performs:

cls._registry = {}

for every factory subclass.

Therefore:

DistanceFactory
KernelFactory
LossFactory
...

do not share one global name table.

The same symbolic name can exist in different factories without conflict.

For example, a distance and a loss can both use:

l1

in their own registries.

docs.title: Registration names are normalized
docs.text:
BaseFactory normalizes names by:

stripping surrounding whitespace
lowercasing

So:

"  My_Component  "

is stored as:

my_component

docs.title: Invalid names
docs.text:
Registration names must be strings and cannot become empty after stripping.

These are invalid:

@Factory.register("")

@Factory.register("   ")

and non-string names raise a TypeError.

docs.title: Multiple aliases
docs.text:
One class can be registered under several names:

@DistanceFactory.register(
    "my_distance",
    "my_dist",
    "md",
)
class MyDistance(
    BaseDistance
):
    ...

Every alias points to the same RegistryEntry.

docs.title: Duplicate names
docs.text:
Within one registration call:

@Factory.register(
    "demo",
    "DEMO",
)

the normalized names collide and the source raises:

ValueError

because both normalize to:

demo.

docs.title: Existing registry conflicts
docs.text:
If a normalized name is already registered, register() raises:

KeyError

before the decorator registers the new class.

The source does not silently overwrite an existing implementation.

docs.title: Categories
docs.text:
Factories can attach categories:

@CombinerFactory.register(
    "my_regression_combiner",
    categories={
        "regression",
    },
)
class MyRegressionCombiner(
    BaseCombiner
):
    ...

Categories are normalized in the same way as names.

docs.title: Category queries
docs.text:
Useful methods include:

Factory.available_categories()

Factory.available_by_category(
    "regression"
)

Factory.supports(
    "my_component",
    "regression",
)

The current KFC combiner and local-model layers use categories to distinguish:

regression
classification.

The optimizer factory also uses categories such as:

search
gradient.

docs.title: Metadata
docs.text:
register() accepts arbitrary keyword metadata:

@MyFactory.register(
    "example",
    version="1.0",
    experimental=True,
)
class Example:
    ...

The metadata are stored in the registration entry.

Inspect them with:

MyFactory.info(
    "example"
)

docs.title: Registry inspection
docs.text:
The common factory API provides:

Factory.available()

Factory.contains(
    "name"
)

Factory.info(
    "name"
)

Factory.find_by_class(
    MyClass
)

Factory.available_categories()

Factory.available_by_category(
    "category"
)

Factory.supports(
    "name",
    "category",
)

docs.title: Removing registrations
docs.text:
The source also provides:

Factory.unregister(
    "name"
)

and:

Factory.clear()

unregister() removes only one alias.

If one class is registered as:

foo
bar

then:

Factory.unregister(
    "foo"
)

leaves:

bar

registered.

docs.title: clear() caution
docs.text:
Factory.clear() removes every registration from that factory subclass.

This affects built-ins already imported into that registry.

It is primarily a low-level registry operation rather than a normal user-guide configuration step.

docs.title: Inspecting one registration
docs.text:
from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.distances import (
    DistanceFactory,
)

print(
    DistanceFactory.info(
        "euclidean"
    )
)

The returned dictionary contains:

name
class
module
categories
metadata.

docs.title: Extending Bregman divergences
docs.text:
KFC clustering divergences inherit:

BaseBregmanDivergence

and register with:

BregmanDivergenceFactory.

A concrete divergence is expected to provide:

in_domain()
phi()
grad_phi()

while the base class supplies the generic Bregman distance machinery.

docs.title: Required mathematical interface
docs.text:
For a convex generator:

\[ \phi(x), \]

the base class computes:

\[ D_\phi(x,y) = \phi(x) - \phi(y) - \langle \nabla\phi(y), x-y \rangle. \]

A custom divergence therefore implements:

domain validation
generator phi
gradient of phi.

docs.title: Minimal custom divergence
docs.text:
import numpy as np

from kfc_procedure.core.clustering.divergences.base import (
    BaseBregmanDivergence,
    BregmanDivergenceFactory,
)


@BregmanDivergenceFactory.register(
    "scaled_euclidean"
)
class ScaledEuclideanDivergence(
    BaseBregmanDivergence
):

    name = "scaled_euclidean"
    family = "custom"

    def __init__(
        self,
        scale=1.0,
        **kwargs,
    ):
        super().__init__(
            **kwargs,
        )

        self.scale = scale

    def in_domain(
        self,
        X,
    ):
        return True

    def phi(
        self,
        X,
    ):
        X = np.asarray(
            X,
            dtype=float,
        )

        return (
            self.scale
            *
            np.sum(
                X ** 2,
                axis=1,
            )
        )

    def grad_phi(
        self,
        X,
    ):
        X = np.asarray(
            X,
            dtype=float,
        )

        return (
            2.0
            *
            self.scale
            *
            X
        )

Then:

divergence = (
    BregmanDivergenceFactory
    .create(
        "scaled_euclidean",
        scale=2.0,
    )
)

docs.title: Base divergence functionality you inherit
docs.text:
BaseBregmanDivergence already implements methods such as:

distance()
pairwise()
centroid()
assign_clusters()

using the custom generator interface.

The distance() implementation also caches quantities associated with the reference matrix Y for repeated evaluations.

So a custom divergence normally should not need to reimplement the entire clustering distance engine.

docs.title: Domain validation
docs.text:
The base constructor accepts:

validate_domain=True

and concrete divergences define:

in_domain().

However, the generic current distance() implementation directly checks:

if not (
    self.in_domain(X)
    and self.in_domain(Y)
):
    raise ValueError(...)

rather than conditionally checking only when validate_domain is true.

So disabling validate_domain is not a universal way to bypass domain checks through all current base paths.

docs.title: Use custom divergence in KFC
docs.text:
model = KFCRegressor(
    divergences=[
        "scaled_euclidean",
    ],
    divergences_params={
        "scaled_euclidean": {
            "scale": 2.0,
        },
    },
    ...
)

The exact divergences_params lookup should match the string key used by K-Step.

docs.title: Divergence object path
docs.text:
K-Step also accepts a:

BaseBregmanDivergence

instance directly.

In that case, factory parameter lookup is bypassed and the object itself is used.

docs.title: Extending F-Step local models
docs.text:
Custom KFC local models inherit:

BaseLocalModel

and register with:

LocalModelFactory.

The required methods are:

fit(
    X,
    y,
)

and:

predict(
    X,
)

The base class also defines a default:

predict_proba()

that raises NotImplementedError.

docs.title: Custom regression local model
docs.text:
import numpy as np

from kfc_procedure.core.ml.base import (
    BaseLocalModel,
    LocalModelFactory,
)


@LocalModelFactory.register(
    "median_regressor",
    categories={
        "regression",
    },
)
class MedianRegressor(
    BaseLocalModel
):

    def fit(
        self,
        X,
        y,
    ):
        self.value_ = float(
            np.median(
                y
            )
        )

        return self

    def predict(
        self,
        X,
    ):
        return np.full(
            len(
                X
            ),
            self.value_,
            dtype=float,
        )

Then:

model = KFCRegressor(
    local_model="median_regressor",
    ...
)

can resolve it through the factory.

docs.title: Custom classification local model
docs.text:
@LocalModelFactory.register(
    "my_classifier",
    categories={
        "classification",
    },
)
class MyClassifier(
    BaseLocalModel
):

    def fit(
        self,
        X,
        y,
    ):
        ...
        return self

    def predict(
        self,
        X,
    ):
        ...

    def predict_proba(
        self,
        X,
    ):
        ...

The category is important because F-Step checks task support for string-based models.

docs.title: random_state constructor compatibility
docs.text:
For string local models, F-Step injects:

random_state

into the factory parameters when that key is not already present.

Built-in scikit-learn adapters filter unsupported constructor keywords.

A directly registered custom local model does not automatically receive that filtering layer.

Therefore a custom string model should either:

accept random_state explicitly

or:

accept **kwargs

if it will be used with the current F-Step construction path.

Current F-Step behavior

A registered custom class with:

def __init__(self):
    ...

can fail if F-Step calls it with:

random_state=...

and the class does not accept that keyword.

docs.title: Scikit-learn models are auto-registered
docs.text:
The package already provides:

register_all_sklearn_models()

which discovers scikit-learn classifiers and regressors using:

all_estimators()

and registers snake_case names in:

LocalModelFactory.

So you often do not need a custom wrapper just to use a normal scikit-learn estimator in F-Step.

docs.title: Custom scikit-learn-style behavior
docs.text:
If you do write a local model, inheriting from:

BaseLocalModel

also gives you a BaseEstimator ancestry through the source class hierarchy.

Following scikit-learn-style constructor conventions makes the object easier to inspect and compose.

docs.title: Extending C-Step combiners
docs.text:
A KFC combiner inherits:

BaseCombiner

and implements:

fit(
    X,
    y=None,
)

and:

combine(
    X,
)

The base class supplies:

predict(
    X,
)

as an alias for:

combine(
    X
).

docs.title: Regression combiner example
docs.text:
import numpy as np

from kfc_procedure.core.combiner.base import (
    BaseCombiner,
    CombinerFactory,
)


@CombinerFactory.register(
    "trimmed_mean",
    categories={
        "regression",
    },
)
class TrimmedMeanCombiner(
    BaseCombiner
):

    def __init__(
        self,
        trim=1,
        random_state=None,
    ):
        self.trim = trim
        self.random_state = random_state

    def fit(
        self,
        X,
        y=None,
    ):
        return self

    def combine(
        self,
        X,
    ):
        X = np.asarray(
            X,
            dtype=float,
        )

        X_sorted = np.sort(
            X,
            axis=1,
        )

        if self.trim == 0:
            kept = X_sorted
        else:
            kept = X_sorted[
                :,
                self.trim:
                -self.trim,
            ]

        return np.mean(
            kept,
            axis=1,
        )

The explicit:

random_state=None

parameter makes this example compatible with the current C-Step string construction behavior.

docs.title: Classification combiner example
docs.text:
from collections import Counter


@CombinerFactory.register(
    "last_tie_vote",
    categories={
        "classification",
    },
)
class LastTieVoteCombiner(
    BaseCombiner
):

    def __init__(
        self,
        random_state=None,
    ):
        self.random_state = random_state

    def fit(
        self,
        X,
        y=None,
    ):
        return self

    def combine(
        self,
        X,
    ):
        outputs = []

        for row in X:
            counts = Counter(
                row
            )

            max_count = max(
                counts.values()
            )

            tied = [
                value
                for value, count
                in counts.items()
                if count == max_count
            ]

            outputs.append(
                tied[
                    -1
                ]
            )

        return np.asarray(
            outputs,
            dtype=object,
        )

docs.title: Combiner category checks
docs.text:
C-Step checks:

CombinerFactory.supports(
    name,
    self.task,
)

for string-based combiners.

So a custom regression combiner should register category:

regression

and a classifier combiner should register:

classification.

docs.title: C-Step random_state caveat
docs.text:
Like F-Step, C-Step injects:

random_state

when constructing a string-based combiner.

Unlike SklearnLocalModel, CombinerFactory.create() forwards constructor kwargs directly.

Therefore custom string combiners should be designed to accept the injected keyword if they use the current C-Step pathway.

docs.title: Pre-built combiner objects
docs.text:
If you pass a combiner object instead of a string:

model = KFCRegressor(
    combiner=MyCombiner(...),
    ...
)

C-Step returns that object directly from _build_combiner().

No factory lookup or random_state injection occurs.

This can be useful when your custom constructor does not match the current string-factory path.

docs.title: Extending COBRA estimators
docs.text:
The COBRA core defines:

BaseEstimator

with required:

fit()
predict()

methods and a registry:

EstimatorFactory.

This is separate from KFC's:

LocalModelFactory.

docs.title: Minimal COBRA estimator
docs.text:
import numpy as np

from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.estimators.base import (
    BaseEstimator,
    EstimatorFactory,
)


@EstimatorFactory.register(
    "constant_regressor"
)
class ConstantRegressor(
    BaseEstimator
):

    def __init__(
        self,
        value=None,
    ):
        self.value = value

    def fit(
        self,
        x,
        y,
        **kwargs,
    ):
        self.value_ = (
            float(
                np.mean(
                    y
                )
            )
            if self.value is None
            else float(
                self.value
            )
        )

        return self

    def predict(
        self,
        x,
        **kwargs,
    ):
        return np.full(
            len(
                x
            ),
            self.value_,
        )

docs.title: COBRA estimator integration
docs.text:
The shared COBRA helper:

fit_estimators()

supports:

string names
(name, params) tuples
pre-built estimator objects.

So a registered estimator can be included in an estimator pool by name.

docs.title: Estimator categories
docs.text:
The current COBRA EstimatorFactory itself does not require task categories for the high-level helper in the same way KFC LocalModelFactory does.

If you add categories, they remain available through the generic factory query methods, but the current shared estimator helper does not use them for regression/classification validation.

docs.title: Extending distances
docs.text:
Custom COBRA distances inherit:

BaseDistance

and implement:

matrix(
    x,
    y,
)

The result should have shape:

(n_x, n_y).

docs.title: Custom squared L2 distance
docs.text:
import numpy as np

from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.distances import (
    BaseDistance,
    DistanceFactory,
)


@DistanceFactory.register(
    "squared_l2"
)
class SquaredL2Distance(
    BaseDistance
):

    def matrix(
        self,
        x,
        y,
    ):
        x = np.asarray(
            x,
            dtype=float,
        )

        y = np.asarray(
            y,
            dtype=float,
        )

        diff = (
            x[
                :,
                None,
                :
            ]
            -
            y[
                None,
                :,
                :
            ]
        )

        return np.sum(
            diff ** 2,
            axis=2,
        )

Use it with:

model = GradientCOBRA(
    distance="squared_l2",
)

docs.title: Distance parameters
docs.text:
BaseDistance stores arbitrary constructor kwargs through its own params/attribute system.

A custom distance can therefore expose configuration and receive it through:

distance_params.

Example:

distance="scaled_l2",
distance_params={
    "scale": 2.0,
}

docs.title: Extending kernel adapters
docs.text:
Kernel adapters sit between:

distance matrices
kernel functions.

They inherit:

BaseKernelAdapter

and must implement:

transform(
    *distances
)

The base class already provides:

params
set_params()
get_params()
parameter_vector().

docs.title: Custom adapter example
docs.text:
import numpy as np

from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.adapters import (
    BaseKernelAdapter,
    KernelAdapterFactory,
)


@KernelAdapterFactory.register(
    "power_scale"
)
class PowerScaleAdapter(
    BaseKernelAdapter
):

    def __init__(
        self,
        scale=1.0,
        power=1.0,
    ):
        super().__init__(
            scale=scale,
            power=power,
        )

    def transform(
        self,
        *distances,
    ):
        if len(
            distances
        ) != 1:
            raise ValueError(
                "power_scale expects one distance matrix"
            )

        D = np.asarray(
            distances[0],
            dtype=float,
        )

        return (
            self.scale
            *
            D ** self.power
        )

docs.title: Adapter parameter vector
docs.text:
The inherited:

parameter_vector()

returns:

np.array(
    list(
        self.params.values()
    ),
    dtype=float,
)

So parameter order follows insertion order in the adapter's internal parameter dictionary.

If an external optimizer depends on that vector order, construct parameters in a stable and intentional order.

docs.title: Adapter integration limitation
docs.text:
The current main:

GradientCOBRA
CombinedClassifier

construct:

OneParameterKernelAdapter

directly through the factory, while MixCOBRA chooses the one- or two-parameter built-in adapter based on:

one_parameter.

They do not currently expose:

adapter
adapter_params

as user-facing constructor arguments.

Therefore registering a custom adapter does not automatically make it selectable from those high-level estimators.

This is a lower-level extension point unless the estimator source is extended.

docs.title: Extending kernels
docs.text:
Custom kernels inherit:

BaseKernel

and implement:

__call__(
    D,
)

The base class also provides:

params
set_params()
get_params()
is_continuous()
is_discrete().

docs.title: Kernel metadata
docs.text:
Two important class attributes are:

requires_grad
mode

The current high-level regression COBRA estimators inspect:

requires_grad

when deciding whether gradient optimization can be used.

docs.title: Custom kernel example
docs.text:
import numpy as np

from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.kernels import (
    BaseKernel,
    KernelFactory,
)


@KernelFactory.register(
    "inverse_square"
)
class InverseSquareKernel(
    BaseKernel
):

    requires_grad = True
    mode = "continuous"

    def __call__(
        self,
        D,
    ):
        D = np.asarray(
            D,
            dtype=float,
        )

        return 1.0 / (
            1.0
            +
            D ** 2
        )

Then:

model = GradientCOBRA(
    kernel="inverse_square",
)

can resolve it.

docs.title: Kernel parameters
docs.text:
A custom kernel can call:

super().__init__(
    parameter=value
)

so the parameter appears in:

get_params()

and can be updated through:

set_params().

docs.title: requires_grad
docs.text:
Set:

requires_grad = True

only when the kernel should participate in the current gradient optimization path.

If set to:

False

GradientCOBRA and MixCOBRA can fall back from:

grad

to:

grid.

The package trusts this flag; it does not analyze differentiability automatically.

docs.title: Kernel mode
docs.text:
Current built-ins use:

continuous
compact
discrete.

The base helper:

is_continuous()

returns true only for exact mode:

continuous

and:

is_discrete()

returns true only for:

discrete.

There is no current:

is_compact()

helper.

docs.title: Extending aggregators
docs.text:
Custom aggregators inherit:

BaseAggregator

and implement:

aggregate(
    values,
    weights=None,
    **kwargs,
)

The base class provides a generic:

aggregate_matrix()

batch loop.

docs.title: Regression aggregator example
docs.text:
import numpy as np

from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.aggregators import (
    BaseAggregator,
    AggregatorFactory,
)


@AggregatorFactory.register(
    "median"
)
class MedianAggregator(
    BaseAggregator
):

    def aggregate(
        self,
        values,
        weights=None,
        **kwargs,
    ):
        return float(
            np.median(
                np.asarray(
                    values,
                    dtype=float,
                )
            )
        )

Then:

model = GradientCOBRA(
    aggregator="median",
)

can resolve it through the current high-level factory path.

docs.title: Classification probabilities
docs.text:
A classification aggregator can additionally implement:

aggregate_proba(
    values,
    weights=None,
    classes=None,
    **kwargs,
)

The base implementation raises:

NotImplementedError.

If a custom classifier aggregator should support:

CombinedClassifier.predict_proba()

implement this method explicitly.

docs.title: Batch optimization
docs.text:
If the aggregator can efficiently process all query rows together, override:

aggregate_matrix()

instead of using the base per-row loop.

WeightedVoteAggregator is an example of a current built-in that supplies a specialized vectorized batch path.

docs.title: Extending losses
docs.text:
A custom loss inherits:

BaseLoss

and implements:

__call__(
    y_true,
    y_pred,
) -> float

The optimizer assumes smaller returned values are better.

docs.title: RMSE example
docs.text:
import numpy as np

from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.losses import (
    BaseLoss,
    LossFactory,
)


@LossFactory.register(
    "rmse"
)
class RMSELoss(
    BaseLoss
):

    def __call__(
        self,
        y_true,
        y_pred,
    ):
        y_true = np.asarray(
            y_true
        )

        y_pred = np.asarray(
            y_pred
        )

        return float(
            np.sqrt(
                np.mean(
                    (
                        y_true
                        -
                        y_pred
                    ) ** 2
                )
            )
        )

Use:

model = GradientCOBRA(
    loss="rmse",
)

docs.title: Parameterized loss
docs.text:
Factories forward constructor parameters directly, so:

loss_params

can configure a custom loss.

@LossFactory.register(
    "scaled_mae"
)
class ScaledMAE(
    BaseLoss
):

    def __init__(
        self,
        scale=1.0,
    ):
        self.scale = scale

    def __call__(
        self,
        y_true,
        y_pred,
    ):
        return float(
            self.scale
            *
            np.mean(
                np.abs(
                    np.asarray(
                        y_true
                    )
                    -
                    np.asarray(
                        y_pred
                    )
                )
            )
        )

Then:

loss="scaled_mae",
loss_params={
    "scale": 2.0,
}

docs.title: Extending normalizers
docs.text:
Custom normalizers inherit:

BaseNormalizer

and implement:

fit()
transform()

The base class supplies:

fit_transform().

docs.title: Max-absolute example
docs.text:
import numpy as np

from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.normalizers import (
    BaseNormalizer,
    NormalizerFactory,
)


@NormalizerFactory.register(
    "maxabs"
)
class MaxAbsNormalizer(
    BaseNormalizer
):

    def fit(
        self,
        x,
        **kwargs,
    ):
        x = np.asarray(
            x,
            dtype=float,
        )

        self.scale_ = (
            np.max(
                np.abs(
                    x
                ),
                axis=0,
            )
            +
            1e-12
        )

        return self

    def transform(
        self,
        x,
        **kwargs,
    ):
        return (
            np.asarray(
                x,
                dtype=float,
            )
            /
            self.scale_
        )

docs.title: Normalizer integration limitation
docs.text:
The current main COBRA estimators do not resolve:

NormalizerFactory

inside their ordinary fitting workflows.

GradientCOBRA and MixCOBRA currently use scalar normalization through:

compute_normalization_constant()

and CombinedClassifier applies no normalizer layer.

So registering a custom normalizer makes it available at the lower level but does not automatically add it to the main estimator pipeline.

docs.title: Extending splitters
docs.text:
Custom train/calibration splitters inherit:

BaseDataSplitter

and return:

SplitIndices.

The abstract signature is:

split(
    x,
    y,
    *,
    groups=None,
)

docs.title: Fixed splitter example
docs.text:
import numpy as np

from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.splitters import (
    BaseDataSplitter,
    SplitterFactory,
)

from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.types import (
    SplitIndices,
)


@SplitterFactory.register(
    "first_70_percent"
)
class First70PercentSplitter(
    BaseDataSplitter
):

    def split(
        self,
        x,
        y,
        *,
        groups=None,
    ):
        n = len(
            x
        )

        cut = int(
            0.7
            *
            n
        )

        return SplitIndices(
            train_idx=np.arange(
                cut
            ),
            eval_idx=np.arange(
                cut,
                n,
            ),
        )

docs.title: Splitter high-level limitation
docs.text:
The shared:

resolve_training_context()

accepts:

splitter=

but the current public fit() signatures of:

GradientCOBRA
MixCOBRARegressor
CombinedClassifier

do not expose that argument.

Therefore custom splitter registration is a lower-level extension unless you:

call resolve_training_context() yourself
extend the estimator fit API
or prepare explicit X_l/y_l data externally.

docs.title: Extending cross-validation
docs.text:
Custom CV strategies inherit:

BaseCrossValidator

and implement:

split()
get_n_splits().

The split() method yields:

SplitIndices

objects.

docs.title: Fixed two-fold example
docs.text:
import numpy as np

from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.cv import (
    BaseCrossValidator,
    CVFactory,
)

from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.types import (
    SplitIndices,
)


@CVFactory.register(
    "fixed_two_fold"
)
class FixedTwoFold(
    BaseCrossValidator
):

    def split(
        self,
        x,
        y,
        *,
        groups=None,
    ):
        n = len(
            x
        )

        cut = n // 2

        a = np.arange(
            cut
        )

        b = np.arange(
            cut,
            n,
        )

        yield SplitIndices(
            train_idx=a,
            eval_idx=b,
            fold_id=0,
        )

        yield SplitIndices(
            train_idx=b,
            eval_idx=a,
            fold_id=1,
        )

    def get_n_splits(
        self,
    ):
        return 2

docs.title: CV high-level limitation
docs.text:
The current primary COBRA estimators construct:

kfold

internally.

Their constructors expose:

n_cv

but not:

cv
cv_params.

Therefore registering a custom CV implementation alone does not make it selectable from the current high-level estimator API.

An estimator source extension is required for direct selection.

docs.title: Extending optimizers
docs.text:
All optimizers inherit:

BaseOptimizer

and implement:

optimize(
    objective,
    init_param=None,
    **kwargs,
)

A custom optimizer intended for the high-level COBRA estimators should return at least:

x
score
history.

docs.title: Custom fixed optimizer
docs.text:
import numpy as np

from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.optimizers import (
    BaseOptimizer,
    OptimizerFactory,
)


@OptimizerFactory.register(
    "fixed_bandwidth",
    categories={
        "search",
    },
)
class FixedBandwidthOptimizer(
    BaseOptimizer
):

    def __init__(
        self,
        bandwidth=1.0,
        **kwargs,
    ):
        super().__init__(
            **kwargs,
        )

        self.bandwidth = bandwidth

    def optimize(
        self,
        objective,
        init_param=None,
        **kwargs,
    ):
        x = np.array([
            self.bandwidth
        ])

        score = float(
            objective(
                x
            )
        )

        return {
            "x": x,
            "score": score,
            "history": [
                {
                    "iter": 0,
                    "x": x.copy(),
                    "score": score,
                }
            ],
        }

docs.title: Optimizer categories matter
docs.text:
GradientCOBRA and MixCOBRA check categories.

For:

opt_method="grid"

they expect:

search.

For:

opt_method="grad"

they expect:

gradient.

So a custom optimizer must be registered with the appropriate category if it will be selected by those high-level estimators.

docs.title: Custom gradient update rule
docs.text:
For a new gradient algorithm, subclass:

BaseGradientOptimizer

and implement:

step(
    x,
    lr,
    grad,
    state,
).

The base class then supplies:

numerical gradients
learning-rate scheduling
stopping
history
best-point tracking.

docs.title: Sign-gradient example
docs.text:
@OptimizerFactory.register(
    "sign_gd",
    categories={
        "optimizer",
        "gradient",
    },
)
class SignGradientOptimizer(
    BaseGradientOptimizer
):

    def step(
        self,
        x,
        lr,
        grad,
        state,
    ):
        return (
            x
            -
            lr
            *
            np.sign(
                grad
            ),
            state,
        )

docs.title: Custom search optimizer
docs.text:
If the method works with an explicit candidate set, subclassing:

BaseSearchOptimizer

can reuse:

candidate evaluation
risk reduction
tie selection
history tracking.

Then implement the component-specific:

candidates()

method.

docs.title: Extending a high-level estimator
docs.text:
Some registries are not yet exposed by the main constructors.

In those cases, extending the estimator itself may be the right approach.

For example, a custom GradientCOBRA subclass could add:

splitter
splitter_params
cv
cv_params
adapter
adapter_params
normalizer
normalizer_params.

The current source does not provide those high-level constructor hooks directly.

docs.title: Example high-level subclass pattern
docs.text:
class MyGradientCOBRA(
    GradientCOBRA
):

    def __init__(
        self,
        *,
        cv="kfold",
        cv_params=None,
        **kwargs,
    ):
        super().__init__(
            **kwargs,
        )

        self.cv = cv
        self.cv_params = (
            {}
            if cv_params is None
            else dict(
                cv_params
            )
        )

    def _resolve_components(
        self,
    ):
        super()._resolve_components()

        self.cv_ = CVFactory.create(
            self.cv,
            **self.cv_params,
        )

This is an extension pattern inferred from the current component-resolution design.

The exact override point should be checked against the version of GradientCOBRA you are extending.

docs.title: Preserve scikit-learn constructor conventions
docs.text:
Many package classes follow a scikit-learn-like style.

For custom estimator-like objects:

store constructor parameters as attributes
avoid doing expensive fitting in __init__
return self from fit()
keep predict() deterministic given fitted state.

This is especially useful when objects are inspected or passed into wrappers.

docs.title: Factory constructor forwarding is direct
docs.text:
BaseFactory.create() does:

target_cls = cls.get_class(
    name
)

return target_cls(
    *args,
    **kwargs,
)

There is no generic signature filtering.

Therefore unsupported constructor arguments normally raise through the target class constructor.

docs.title: Exception: scikit-learn F-Step wrapper
docs.text:
SklearnLocalModel is a special case.

It inspects:

model_cls.__init__

and keeps only supported kwargs before creating the scikit-learn model.

This filtering behavior belongs to the adapter, not to BaseFactory.

Do not assume other factories silently discard unsupported parameters.

docs.title: Function registration caveat
docs.text:
BaseFactory.register() is typed/documented as registering classes.

The current register_all_sklearn_models() helper creates a closure:

def builder(
    model_cls=cls,
    **kwargs,
):
    return SklearnLocalModel(
        model_cls,
        **kwargs,
    )

and registers that callable through LocalModelFactory.

Because BaseFactory.create() simply calls the stored target, this works in practice.

However, info() assumes the registered target has attributes such as:

__name__
__module__.

A normal function does, so this dynamic builder remains compatible with that inspection.

docs.title: Import timing matters
docs.text:
Decorators execute when their modules are imported.

A custom registration is therefore active only after Python has imported the module containing the decorated class.

Example:

# my_extensions.py
@KernelFactory.register(
    "my_kernel"
)
class MyKernel(...):
    ...

Your application must import:

import my_extensions

before:

KernelFactory.create(
    "my_kernel"
)

docs.title: Built-in registration also depends on imports
docs.text:
The package __init__.py files import built-in implementation modules so their decorators populate the registries.

If you import an unusually narrow internal module directly, registry contents can depend on which implementation modules have already been imported.

When inspecting available components, use the normal public package imports where possible.

docs.title: Avoid registration at prediction time
docs.text:
Register custom components during application/module setup rather than inside a hot prediction loop.

Repeatedly executing the same decorator can produce a registry conflict because the normalized name is already present.

docs.title: Testing a custom component
docs.text:
A useful test sequence is:

1. register it
2. verify Factory.contains(name)
3. inspect Factory.info(name)
4. create it through Factory.create(name)
5. test its base interface directly
6. test integration with the high-level estimator
7. test fitted-state attributes
8. test serialization/deployment requirements separately.

docs.title: Factory smoke test
docs.text:
assert KernelFactory.contains(
    "inverse_square"
)

print(
    KernelFactory.info(
        "inverse_square"
    )
)

kernel = KernelFactory.create(
    "inverse_square"
)

docs.title: Interface smoke test
docs.text:
For a custom distance:

D = distance.matrix(
    X_a,
    X_b,
)

assert D.shape == (
    len(
        X_a
    ),
    len(
        X_b
    ),
)

For a custom kernel:

K = kernel(
    D
)

assert K.shape == D.shape

For a custom aggregator:

prediction = aggregator.aggregate(
    values,
    weights,
)

docs.title: Integration smoke test
docs.text:
Use a very small model configuration first:

model = GradientCOBRA(
    distance="squared_l2",
    kernel="inverse_square",
    max_iter=5,
    n_cv=2,
    n_jobs=1,
    random_state=42,
)

This makes extension failures easier to isolate before running a large optimization.

docs.title: Debug registry conflicts
docs.text:
print(
    MyFactory.available()
)

before registering a new name.

You can also test:

MyFactory.contains(
    "my_name"
)

The source does not provide an overwrite flag.

docs.title: Debug category mismatch
docs.text:
For a custom KFC combiner:

print(
    CombinerFactory.supports(
        "my_combiner",
        "regression",
    )
)

For a custom optimizer:

print(
    OptimizerFactory.supports(
        "my_optimizer",
        "gradient",
    )
)

docs.title: Debug constructor errors
docs.text:
Because most factories forward kwargs directly, inspect the actual custom constructor signature.

For example:

class MyKernel(
    BaseKernel
):

    def __init__(
        self,
        power=2.0,
    ):
        ...

then configure:

kernel_params={
    "power": 3.0,
}

rather than an unsupported key.

docs.title: Debug high-level non-selection
docs.text:
If:

Factory.create(
    "my_component"
)

works but the main estimator cannot select it, check whether that component type is actually exposed by the estimator API.

Current examples of lower-level registries not fully exposed include:

NormalizerFactory
SplitterFactory custom selection
CVFactory custom selection
KernelAdapterFactory custom selection.

Registration and high-level configurability are separate concepts.

docs.title: Extending package exports
docs.text:
A custom component defined in your application does not need to be added to the kfc_procedure package's __init__.py files for the factory to use it after import.

If you are contributing the component to the package itself, then updating the relevant __init__.py can make the class importable through the package's normal public namespace and can ensure its registration module is imported.

docs.title: Adding a built-in component to the project
docs.text:
A source-level contribution typically involves:

1. create the implementation module
2. inherit the appropriate base class
3. add the factory registration decorator
4. import the implementation from the package-level __init__.py if needed
5. add unit tests
6. add user/API documentation
7. verify existing registry names do not conflict.

docs.title: Suggested test areas
docs.text:
For new components, test at least:

constructor parameters
factory registration and aliases
factory category support
input shape handling
fit/predict or transform behavior
empty/invalid input behavior
deterministic behavior when relevant
integration with a small KFC/COBRA pipeline
error behavior for unsupported configuration.

docs.title: Current extension-point matrix
docs.text: Component Base class Factory Selectable by current high-level API? KFC divergence BaseBregmanDivergence BregmanDivergenceFactory Yes KFC local model BaseLocalModel LocalModelFactory Yes KFC combiner BaseCombiner CombinerFactory Yes COBRA estimator BaseEstimator EstimatorFactory Yes, via estimator pool helpers distance BaseDistance DistanceFactory Yes kernel adapter BaseKernelAdapter KernelAdapterFactory No direct public selector kernel BaseKernel KernelFactory Yes aggregator BaseAggregator AggregatorFactory Yes loss BaseLoss LossFactory Yes normalizer BaseNormalizer NormalizerFactory Not wired into main estimators splitter BaseDataSplitter SplitterFactory Resolver supports it; main fit APIs do not cross-validator BaseCrossValidator CVFactory Main estimators currently hard-code kfold optimizer BaseOptimizer OptimizerFactory Yes, subject to category/API behavior

docs.title: KFC
docs.text:
Directly configurable:

divergences
local_model
combiner

with corresponding parameter dictionaries.

docs.title: GradientCOBRA
docs.text:
Directly configurable component families include:

estimators
distance
kernel
aggregator
loss
optimizer.

Not currently exposed as general selectors:

normalizer
splitter
cross-validator
kernel adapter.

docs.title: MixCOBRA
docs.text:
Directly configurable:

estimators
distance
kernel
aggregator
loss
optimizer.

Adapter selection is controlled indirectly by:

one_parameter

rather than by a general adapter name.

docs.title: CombinedClassifier
docs.text:
Directly configurable:

estimators
distance
kernel
aggregator
loss
optimizer.

The current optimization path is primarily grid-oriented.

docs.title: Extension safety checklist
docs.text:
Before relying on a custom implementation, verify:

the module containing it has been imported
the registration name does not conflict
categories match high-level checks
constructor accepts all injected/forwarded parameters
matrix shapes match the expected interface
fit methods return self where expected
predict/transform methods use fitted state consistently
the component is actually selectable by the high-level estimator
random_state handling is explicit when stochastic
parallel execution can serialize the object if it enters Joblib loky workers.

docs.title: A complete custom COBRA component chain
docs.text:
Because components are independent, you can register several custom pieces:

model = GradientCOBRA(
    distance="squared_l2",
    kernel="inverse_square",
    aggregator="median",
    loss="rmse",
    optimizer="grid",
)

provided each name has already been registered with the correct factory.

The normal high-level component resolver will create those objects using their respective factories.

docs.title: A complete custom KFC chain
docs.text:
Likewise:

model = KFCRegressor(
    divergences=[
        "scaled_euclidean",
    ],
    divergences_params={
        "scaled_euclidean": {
            "scale": 2.0,
        },
    },
    local_model="median_regressor",
    combiner="trimmed_mean",
    combiner_params={
        "trim": 1,
    },
    random_state=42,
)

works conceptually when each custom registration satisfies the current K-Step, F-Step, and C-Step interfaces and constructor behavior.

docs.title: Extending versus passing objects directly
docs.text:
The source often supports both:

registered string
pre-built object.

Using a registered string gives you:

factory discovery
aliases
categories
parameter dictionaries.

Using a pre-built object can bypass:

factory constructor assumptions
automatic parameter injection.

The best path depends on the component and the current high-level integration.

docs.title: When direct objects are especially useful
docs.text:
A pre-built object can be useful when:

its constructor does not accept injected random_state
you need complex construction logic
you need to retain external references
you are prototyping before adding a formal registry entry.

Be aware that object reuse semantics differ by component.

For example, the current F-Step reuses a non-string local-model object across cluster fits rather than cloning it.

docs.title: Factory registration is process-local
docs.text:
The current registries are Python class-level dictionaries.

A custom registration exists in the Python process after its module has been imported.

The source does not provide persistent registry storage across separate process launches.

Your application or package must import the registration module again in each new process.

docs.title: Parallel worker considerations
docs.text:
COBRA base-estimator fitting uses Joblib's:

loky

backend when:

n_jobs != 1.

If a custom estimator object participates in that path, it needs to be usable by Joblib's worker process mechanism.

When debugging a custom estimator integration, setting:

n_jobs=1

can isolate factory/interface errors from process-serialization issues.

docs.title: Documentation conventions for extensions
docs.text:
When adding a new built-in component, document:

registry name and aliases
base interface
constructor parameters
mathematical formula or algorithm
expected shapes
task/category support
fitted attributes
high-level configuration example
known limitations
interaction with optimization and random_state.

This keeps extension documentation aligned with the rest of the user guide.

docs.title: Quick reference
docs.text: What you want to extend Register with KFC divergence BregmanDivergenceFactory KFC local model LocalModelFactory KFC combiner CombinerFactory COBRA estimator EstimatorFactory distance DistanceFactory kernel adapter KernelAdapterFactory kernel KernelFactory aggregator AggregatorFactory loss LossFactory normalizer NormalizerFactory splitter SplitterFactory CV strategy CVFactory optimizer OptimizerFactory

docs.title: Mental model
docs.text:
KFC Procedure is extensible through contracts and registries: implement the smallest required interface, register the implementation, then let the orchestration layer resolve it by name.

\[ \boxed{ \text{custom implementation} \rightarrow \text{factory registration} \rightarrow \text{string configuration} \rightarrow \text{existing KFC/COBRA pipeline} } \]

The main caveat is that not every registry is currently exposed as a high-level constructor option. For those components, the registry is already available at the lower layer, but the surrounding estimator must be extended before the new component can be selected through the public API.

docs.title: Parallel Execution
docs.text:
The current COBRA implementation supports parallel execution in two specific parts of the workflow:

  1. fitting and evaluating the base-estimator pool;
  2. computing a numerical gradient with the optional parallel central-difference method.

The primary user-facing parameter is:

n_jobs

on:

GradientCOBRA
MixCOBRARegressor
CombinedClassifier

For base-estimator work, the source delegates parallel execution to joblib.Parallel with the explicit backend:

loky

Parallel execution is not applied automatically to every part of COBRA. Distance computation, kernel transformation, cross-validation loops, aggregation, and grid candidate evaluation remain separate from this n_jobs pathway in the current source.

docs.title: Parallelism at a glance
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    X["Training data"]
    F["Fit base estimators"]
    P["Generate estimator predictions"]
    D["Distance matrices"]
    CV["Cross-validation"]
    O["Optimization"]

    X --> F --> P --> D --> CV --> O

    F -. "n_jobs / joblib loky" .-> F
    P -. "n_jobs / joblib loky" .-> P

    O2["Gradient method = parallel"]
    G["Parallel finite-difference coordinates"]

    O --> O2 --> G

The current source therefore has two distinct parallel mechanisms:

estimator-pool parallelism
    controlled by estimator `n_jobs`

gradient-coordinate parallelism
    selected with gradient_method="parallel"

They should not be treated as the same configuration.

docs.title: User-facing n_jobs
docs.text:
The three main COBRA estimators expose:

n_jobs

in their constructors.

Current defaults are:

Estimator Default n_jobs GradientCOBRA -1 MixCOBRARegressor 1 CombinedClassifier 1

This is an important source-level difference.

docs.title: GradientCOBRA default
docs.text:
The current constructor contains:

GradientCOBRA(
    ...
    n_jobs=-1,
    random_state=None,
)

and stores:

self.n_jobs = n_jobs

So GradientCOBRA requests parallel estimator-pool execution by default unless the value is changed.

docs.title: MixCOBRA default
docs.text:
The current constructor contains:

MixCOBRARegressor(
    ...
    n_jobs=1,
    one_parameter=False,
    random_state=None,
)

So MixCOBRA is sequential by default at the package's estimator-pool layer.

docs.title: CombinedClassifier default
docs.text:
The classifier constructor contains:

CombinedClassifier(
    ...
    n_jobs=1,
    ...
)

so it is also sequential by default for estimator fitting and prediction.

docs.title: Shared estimator-pool helpers
docs.text:
All three estimators use the same utility functions from:

kfc_procedure/cobra/utils/resolve.py

The functions are:

fit_estimators()
predict_estimators()

These functions implement the package's common estimator-pool parallelism.

docs.title: Parallel estimator fitting
docs.text:
The relevant signature is:

fit_estimators(
    X,
    y,
    estimators_params=None,
    estimators=None,
    n_jobs=1,
)

The function supports estimator specifications as:

string identifiers
(name, params) tuples
pre-built estimator objects

docs.title: Sequential branch
docs.text:
The source checks:

if n_jobs == 1:
    return [
        fit_one(est)
        for est
        in estimators
    ]

So:

n_jobs=1

does not invoke joblib.Parallel.

Each estimator is built and fitted one after another in the current process.

docs.title: Parallel branch
docs.text:
For every other n_jobs value, the source executes:

return Parallel(
    n_jobs=n_jobs,
    backend="loky",
)(
    delayed(
        fit_one
    )(
        est
    )
    for est
    in estimators
)

The backend is therefore explicitly:

loky

for base-estimator fitting.

docs.title: Parallel fitting unit of work
docs.text:
The parallelized task is:

fit_one(
    est_spec
)

For each estimator specification, the worker:

  1. builds or resolves the estimator;
  2. calls:
model.fit(
    X,
    y,
)
  1. returns the fitted estimator object.

So parallelism occurs across estimators, not across training rows or cross-validation folds.

docs.title: Conceptual execution
docs.text:
For an estimator pool:

estimator A
estimator B
estimator C
estimator D

with parallel execution, the package conceptually submits independent fit tasks:

fit(A, X, y)
fit(B, X, y)
fit(C, X, y)
fit(D, X, y)

to Joblib.

Each task receives the same:

X
y

training dataset.

docs.title: Default GradientCOBRA pool
docs.text:
The current default GradientCOBRA estimators are:

linear_regression
ridge_cv
lasso_cv
k_neighbors_regressor
random_forest_regressor
svr

With the default:

n_jobs=-1

their package-level fit tasks are sent through the parallel Joblib branch.

docs.title: Default MixCOBRA pool
docs.text:
MixCOBRA's current default pool is:

linear_regression
ridge
lasso
k_neighbors_regressor
random_forest_regressor
svr

but its default:

n_jobs=1

keeps those six package-level fit tasks sequential.

docs.title: Default CombinedClassifier pool
docs.text:
The current default classification pool is:

logistic_regression
decision_tree_classifier
svc
k_neighbors_classifier

and default:

n_jobs=1

keeps fitting sequential.

docs.title: Parallel prediction generation
docs.text:
The same n_jobs value is also used when creating a prediction-space matrix.

The shared helper is:

predict_estimators(
    X,
    estimators,
    n_jobs=1,
)

docs.title: Sequential prediction path
docs.text:
When:

n_jobs == 1

the source runs:

preds = [
    predict_one(est)
    for est
    in estimators
]

return np.column_stack(
    preds
)

where:

predict_one(
    est
)

is:

return est.predict(
    X
)

docs.title: Parallel prediction path
docs.text:
For other n_jobs values:

preds = Parallel(
    n_jobs=n_jobs,
    backend="loky",
)(
    delayed(
        predict_one
    )(
        est
    )
    for est
    in estimators
)

return np.column_stack(
    preds
)

So prediction generation also uses:

Joblib
loky backend
parallelism across fitted estimators.

docs.title: Prediction-space shape
docs.text:
If there are:

n_samples

rows and:

M estimators

the result is:

(n_samples, M)

because the returned prediction vectors are combined with:

np.column_stack(
    preds
)

docs.title: Estimator order is preserved
docs.text:
The source submits tasks using:

delayed(
    ...
)(
    est
)
for est in estimators

and then column-stacks the returned preds sequence.

The intended column layout therefore follows the estimator sequence supplied to the helper.

For example:

estimators=[
    "ridge",
    "lasso",
    "svr",
]

corresponds conceptually to prediction columns:

column 0 -> ridge
column 1 -> lasso
column 2 -> svr

Parallel execution does not introduce a package-level column-reordering step.

docs.title: n_jobs is used for both fit and predict
docs.text:
For GradientCOBRA:

def _fit_estimators(
    self,
    X_k,
    y_k,
):
    return fit_estimators(
        ...
        n_jobs=self.n_jobs,
    )

and:

def _load_predictions(
    self,
    X,
):
    return predict_estimators(
        ...
        n_jobs=self.n_jobs,
    )

The same pattern is used in MixCOBRA and CombinedClassifier.

Therefore one estimator-level setting controls both:

base-estimator fitting
base-estimator prediction generation.

docs.title: GradientCOBRA example
docs.text:
Use all Joblib workers according to the value forwarded by the package:

from kfc_procedure.cobra import (
    GradientCOBRA,
)

model = GradientCOBRA(
    n_jobs=-1,
    random_state=42,
)

model.fit(
    X_train,
    y_train,
)

Use sequential estimator execution:

model = GradientCOBRA(
    n_jobs=1,
)

docs.title: MixCOBRA example
docs.text:
Enable package-level parallelism explicitly:

from kfc_procedure.cobra import (
    MixCOBRARegressor,
)

model = MixCOBRARegressor(
    n_jobs=-1,
    random_state=42,
)

The same value is later used when MixCOBRA calls:

predict_estimators()

to construct prediction-space coordinates.

docs.title: CombinedClassifier example
docs.text:
from kfc_procedure.cobra import (
    CombinedClassifier,
)

classifier = CombinedClassifier(
    n_jobs=-1,
    random_state=42,
)

This parallelizes the package-level fit and prediction tasks across the classifier pool.

docs.title: What n_jobs does not parallelize
docs.text:
The current source does not pass estimator-level n_jobs into:

distance matrix calculation
kernel transformation
aggregator calls
K-fold loop construction
grid-search candidate loop
loss evaluation
normalization
data splitting

So setting:

n_jobs=-1

does not mean the entire COBRA training procedure is parallelized.

docs.title: Cross-validation remains a separate loop
docs.text:
The COBRA cross-validation objective iterates through:

cv_folds_

in normal Python loops.

For example, GradientCOBRA evaluates every stored fold while computing a candidate bandwidth error.

The current cross-validation classes do not expose a n_jobs parameter, and the main estimator n_jobs value is not passed into them.

docs.title: Grid search remains sequential at the search layer
docs.text:
GridSearchOptimizer creates all candidates and loops over them through the search optimizer's normal candidate-evaluation logic.

The current search optimizer does not use:

joblib.Parallel

and does not receive the COBRA estimator's:

n_jobs.

Therefore different bandwidth or alpha/beta candidates are not parallelized by the main estimator n_jobs setting.

docs.title: Distance matrices are not Joblib-parallelized by n_jobs
docs.text:
The built-in distance classes implement their own NumPy/SciPy/Numba numerical paths.

The COBRA estimator's:

n_jobs

is not forwarded to:

distance_.matrix(...)

in the current source.

docs.title: Aggregators are not Joblib-parallelized by n_jobs
docs.text:
The package's aggregator implementations operate on their supplied arrays directly.

For example:

WeightedMeanAggregator.aggregate_matrix(...)

and:

WeightedVoteAggregator.aggregate_matrix(...)

do not accept the estimator's n_jobs.

docs.title: Precomputed prediction mode
docs.text:
When:

as_predictions=True

the COBRA estimator skips internal base-estimator fitting.

For GradientCOBRA:

if not self.as_predictions_:
    self.estimators_ = self._fit_estimators(...)
else:
    prediction_space = self.X_l_

So package-level estimator-fitting parallelism does not run in this branch.

docs.title: GradientCOBRA prediction in precomputed mode
docs.text:
Because GradientCOBRA also treats query X directly as prediction space when as_predictions_ is true, it does not call:

predict_estimators()

for those predictions either.

Therefore n_jobs has little effect on the estimator-pool stage when using a fully precomputed GradientCOBRA workflow.

docs.title: CombinedClassifier precomputed mode
docs.text:
The classifier behaves similarly.

With:

as_predictions=True

it skips:

_fit_estimators()

and stores:

pred_l_ = X_l_

At prediction time it uses the supplied prediction-space matrix directly.

So the package-level n_jobs estimator pool is bypassed in this mode.

docs.title: MixCOBRA precomputed caveat
docs.text:
MixCOBRA also skips base-estimator fitting when:

as_predictions=True.

However, its current predict() method can still attempt to call:

_load_predictions(
    X
)

when pred_X is omitted.

That is the precomputed-mode asymmetry documented in:

Precomputed Predictions

and should not be interpreted as a useful parallel prediction path, because the required internal estimator pool was skipped during fit.

docs.title: Parallel gradient computation
docs.text:
The optimizer subsystem contains a second independent parallel mechanism:

parallel_central_difference_gradient()

in:

kfc_procedure/cobra/core/optimizers/_utils.py

This function parallelizes finite-difference gradient coordinates.

docs.title: Parallel gradient formula
docs.text:
For parameter coordinate \(i\), central difference computes:

\[ g_i = \frac{ f(x+\varepsilon e_i) - f(x-\varepsilon e_i) }{ 2\varepsilon}. \]

Each coordinate can be computed independently.

The source defines:

def compute_i(
    i,
):
    x = p.copy()

    x[i] += eps
    f_plus = objective(
        x
    )

    x[i] -= 2 * eps
    f_minus = objective(
        x
    )

    return (
        f_plus
        -
        f_minus
    ) / (
        2 * eps
    )

docs.title: Joblib use in parallel gradients
docs.text:
The helper returns:

np.array(
    Parallel(
        n_jobs=n_jobs
    )(
        delayed(
            compute_i
        )(
            i
        )
        for i
        in range(
            p.size
        )
    )
)

Unlike estimator fitting/prediction, this source call does not explicitly specify:

backend="loky"

It leaves backend choice to Joblib's normal behavior.

docs.title: Select parallel numerical gradients
docs.text:
The unified gradient dispatcher recognizes:

parallel

as one of:

central
forward
spsa
complex
parallel

So gradient-mode COBRA can request:

optimizer_params={
    "gradient_method": "parallel",
}

docs.title: Gradient example
docs.text:
model = GradientCOBRA(
    optimizer="adam",
    opt_method="grad",
    optimizer_params={
        "gradient_method": "parallel",
        "show_process": False,
    },
)

The optimizer then estimates each gradient coordinate through the parallel central-difference helper.

docs.title: Default worker count for parallel gradient method
docs.text:
The unified dispatcher accepts:

n_jobs=None

and contains:

if method == "parallel":
    return parallel_central_difference_gradient(
        objective,
        params,
        eps,
        n_jobs=(
            -1
            if n_jobs is None
            else n_jobs
        ),
    )

So an unspecified gradient worker count becomes:

-1

inside the dispatcher.

docs.title: High-level optimizer does not forward a gradient n_jobs
docs.text:
The current BaseGradientOptimizer.gradient() path calls compute_gradient() without providing an explicit:

n_jobs

argument.

Therefore the standard:

gradient_method="parallel"

path uses the dispatcher's:

n_jobs=-1

fallback.

docs.title: Important separation
docs.text:
This means:

model.n_jobs

does not control the parallel finite-difference worker count.

For example:

GradientCOBRA(
    n_jobs=1,
    optimizer="adam",
    opt_method="grad",
    optimizer_params={
        "gradient_method": "parallel",
    },
)

still reaches the gradient utility with its independent default worker setting.

Two independent controls

The current source has no shared worker-budget parameter connecting:

estimator-pool n_jobs

and:

parallel-gradient n_jobs.

docs.title: Gradient parallelism is across parameters
docs.text:
For one-dimensional GradientCOBRA:

x = [bandwidth]

there is only one finite-difference coordinate.

So the parallel gradient method has only one coordinate task to submit.

There is little coordinate-level parallel work available at dimension one.

docs.title: Two-dimensional MixCOBRA
docs.text:
In ordinary two-parameter MixCOBRA gradient mode:

x = [alpha, beta]

the parallel helper has two coordinate tasks:

d/d alpha
d/d beta

Each task performs two complete objective evaluations.

So the maximum coordinate-level task count is only two in that standard configuration.

docs.title: Objective evaluations are expensive
docs.text:
Every finite-difference objective call can itself run:

kernel transformation
cross-validation folds
aggregation
loss evaluation

Therefore parallel gradient execution parallelizes expensive complete objective evaluations across parameter coordinates.

It does not parallelize the individual CV folds within each objective call.

docs.title: Nested parallelism
docs.text:
The current source does not contain logic that coordinates or prevents nested parallel execution.

For example, a gradient objective may operate on a fitted model whose prediction-space construction previously used:

n_jobs=-1.

Likewise, individual scikit-learn estimators can have their own constructor parameters that control internal parallelism.

The package does not inspect or rewrite those estimator-specific settings.

docs.title: Source-level boundary
docs.text:
fit_estimators() forwards model constructor parameters through the estimator factory, while package-level:

n_jobs

controls only how many estimator tasks Joblib executes.

It does not automatically change an estimator's own:

n_jobs
threads
workers

constructor parameter.

docs.title: Estimator-specific parallelism
docs.text:
You can separately configure estimators that expose their own parallel parameter through:

estimators_params.

For example, if an estimator supports an n_jobs constructor parameter:

model = GradientCOBRA(
    n_jobs=2,
    estimators_params={
        "random_forest_regressor": {
            "n_jobs": 1,
        },
    },
)

The two values have different roles:

GradientCOBRA n_jobs=2
    package-level parallel estimator tasks

random_forest_regressor n_jobs=1
    estimator-internal setting forwarded to that model.

The exact effect of an estimator-specific parameter depends on that estimator's implementation.

docs.title: Factory parameter lookup
docs.text:
For string estimator specifications:

EstimatorFactory.create(
    est_spec,
    **estimators_params.get(
        est_spec,
        {}
    )
)

is used.

So the parameter dictionary key should match the estimator specification string used in the pool.

docs.title: Tuple estimator specifications
docs.text:
fit_estimators() also accepts:

(
    name,
    params,
)

and resolves:

EstimatorFactory.create(
    name,
    **(
        params
        or {}
    ),
)

This lets parameters travel with an individual estimator specification.

Example:

estimators=[
    (
        "random_forest_regressor",
        {
            "n_estimators": 300,
            "n_jobs": 1,
        },
    ),
    "ridge",
]

docs.title: Pre-built estimator objects
docs.text:
If an estimator specification is neither a tuple nor a string:

return est_spec

The same object is then fitted in the corresponding worker task.

Parallel execution still occurs at the fit_one(est_spec) task level when package-level:

n_jobs != 1.

docs.title: Process-based estimator execution
docs.text:
For fit and prediction helpers, the package explicitly requests:

backend="loky"

from Joblib.

This is the exact backend choice in the current source.

Operationally, custom/pre-built estimator objects therefore need to be usable through that Joblib execution path.

If a custom object cannot be serialized by the selected backend, execution may fail outside the package's own estimator logic.

This serialization consequence comes from the selected Joblib backend rather than from a custom kfc_procedure serializer.

docs.title: No package fallback from parallel to sequential
docs.text:
The current source does not wrap:

Parallel(...)

in a package-level try/except that retries sequentially.

So if the Joblib parallel branch fails, fit_estimators() or predict_estimators() does not automatically rerun with:

n_jobs=1.

docs.title: No package-level parallel error aggregation
docs.text:
Every parallel worker runs the ordinary estimator:

fit()

or:

predict()

call.
