The helper does not catch and convert errors into per-estimator result objects.

A worker failure therefore propagates through the Joblib call rather than being stored beside successful estimators.

docs.title: Reproducibility and parallel execution
docs.text:
The package-level Joblib helpers do not modify:

random_state

inside individual estimators.

Reproducibility therefore depends on how each estimator was configured by its factory parameters.

The high-level COBRA random_state is used by other components such as data splitting and CV, but the shared fit_estimators() helper does not inject that value itself.

docs.title: Important distinction
docs.text:
This code:

GradientCOBRA(
    random_state=42,
    n_jobs=-1,
)

does not mean that every default base estimator necessarily receives:

random_state=42.

The parallel helper simply builds each estimator from its normal factory specification and parameters.

docs.title: Compare with KFC F-Step
docs.text:
The top-level KFC FStep has its own local-model training loop.

The current source does not expose an F-Step:

n_jobs

parameter comparable to the COBRA estimator-pool utility.

Therefore the parallel behavior documented here applies specifically to the COBRA estimator-pool helpers and the gradient utility, not automatically to all KFC K-Step/F-Step work.

docs.title: Parallelism in GradientCOBRA.fit()
docs.text:
A normal feature-based fit can use package-level parallelism twice before optimization:

1. fit base estimators on X_k
2. generate their predictions on X_l.

The rest of fitting then proceeds from the generated prediction matrix.

docs.title: Parallelism in GradientCOBRA.predict()
docs.text:
In ordinary feature mode, prediction calls:

self._load_predictions(
    X
)

which uses:

predict_estimators(
    ...,
    n_jobs=self.n_jobs,
)

So every final prediction request can invoke Joblib parallel execution across the fitted estimator pool.

docs.title: Parallelism in CombinedClassifier.predict()
docs.text:
The classifier follows the same pattern in ordinary feature mode:

query X
    ↓
parallel hard prediction by base classifiers
    ↓
prediction-space matrix
    ↓
distance / kernel / weighted vote.

docs.title: Parallelism in MixCOBRA.predict()
docs.text:
Ordinary MixCOBRA uses:

pred_X = self._load_predictions(
    X
)

when pred_X is not supplied.

That prediction-space generation uses the estimator's configured:

n_jobs.

If you supply:

pred_X=

directly, that internal prediction helper is bypassed.

docs.title: pred_X can bypass prediction parallelism
docs.text:
For MixCOBRA:

model.predict(
    X,
    pred_X=P_test,
)

does not call:

predict_estimators()

because pred_X is already present.

So the package-level prediction n_jobs setting is not involved in generating that supplied matrix.

docs.title: Timing estimator fitting
docs.text:
A simple timing comparison:

from time import perf_counter

start = perf_counter()

model = GradientCOBRA(
    n_jobs=1,
)

model.fit(
    X_train,
    y_train,
)

elapsed = (
    perf_counter()
    -
    start
)

print(
    elapsed
)

Compare with:

start = perf_counter()

model = GradientCOBRA(
    n_jobs=-1,
)

model.fit(
    X_train,
    y_train,
)

elapsed_parallel = (
    perf_counter()
    -
    start
)

print(
    elapsed_parallel
)

This measures the whole fit, not only estimator-pool work, so differences also include fixed sequential stages.

docs.title: Timing prediction-space generation directly
docs.text:
After fitting an estimator pool:

from time import perf_counter

start = perf_counter()

P = predict_estimators(
    X_test,
    model.estimators_,
    n_jobs=1,
)

sequential_time = (
    perf_counter()
    -
    start
)

Then:

start = perf_counter()

P_parallel = predict_estimators(
    X_test,
    model.estimators_,
    n_jobs=-1,
)

parallel_time = (
    perf_counter()
    -
    start
)

Verify numerical agreement:

import numpy as np

print(
    np.allclose(
        P,
        P_parallel,
    )
)

for numeric regression predictions.

docs.title: Small estimator pools
docs.text:
The default pools contain only a small number of estimators:

GradientCOBRA
    6

MixCOBRA
    6

CombinedClassifier
    4

Therefore the number of package-level independent tasks is bounded by the estimator-pool size.

Parallel overhead can be significant when individual fit/predict tasks are very small.

The source itself does not benchmark or automatically decide whether parallel execution is worthwhile.

docs.title: Custom larger estimator pool
docs.text:
You can increase the number of independent package-level tasks by supplying a larger estimator list.

model = GradientCOBRA(
    estimators=[
        "linear_regression",
        "ridge",
        "lasso",
        "ridge_cv",
        "lasso_cv",
        "k_neighbors_regressor",
        "random_forest_regressor",
        "svr",
    ],
    n_jobs=-1,
)

Every list entry becomes one fit_one() task.

docs.title: Duplicate estimator specifications
docs.text:
The shared helper iterates the supplied list directly.

If the same estimator specification appears multiple times, the helper submits multiple tasks and the returned list can contain multiple independently built instances for string/tuple specifications.

The package does not deduplicate the estimator list before parallel fitting.

docs.title: Memory considerations
docs.text:
Every estimator task receives access to the same training arrays:

X
y.

The current source does not implement package-specific shared-memory controls or memory-mapping configuration around Joblib.

Likewise, every prediction task receives the same query matrix:

X.

Memory behavior is therefore delegated to Joblib and the underlying numerical libraries.

docs.title: Parallel gradient memory
docs.text:
The parallel finite-difference helper captures:

p
objective
eps

and runs one task per parameter coordinate.

Each task creates:

x = p.copy()

before evaluating the objective.

For the normal one- or two-parameter COBRA optimization cases, the parameter vector itself is tiny; most computational cost lies inside the objective.

docs.title: No parallel grid search
docs.text:
If your main cost is a very large two-parameter MixCOBRA grid, changing:

n_jobs

does not parallelize those:

alpha × beta

candidate evaluations in the current source.

For example, a:

300 × 300

grid remains an exhaustive search at the optimizer layer.

See:

Optimization

for the exact candidate-count behavior.

docs.title: No parallel CV-fold evaluation
docs.text:
Likewise, each objective loops through the stored CV folds sequentially.

The current source contains no:

Parallel(
    ...
)(
    delayed(
        evaluate_fold
    )
    ...
)

path for fold evaluation.

docs.title: Parallel gradient does not parallelize grid mode
docs.text:
The setting:

optimizer_params={
    "gradient_method": "parallel",
}

is relevant only when a gradient optimizer actually calls numerical gradient computation.

With:

opt_method="grid"

the gradient utility is not used.

docs.title: Kernel compatibility can disable gradient path
docs.text:
GradientCOBRA and MixCOBRA check:

kernel_.requires_grad

before using gradient optimization.

If a non-gradient kernel is configured, requested gradient mode falls back to grid mode.

In that case:

gradient_method="parallel"

does not create parallel finite-difference work because the gradient optimizer is not used.

docs.title: Example: package-level and gradient parallelism
docs.text:
model = GradientCOBRA(
    n_jobs=-1,
    optimizer="adam",
    opt_method="grad",
    optimizer_params={
        "gradient_method": "parallel",
        "show_process": False,
    },
)

This configuration enables:

package-level estimator-pool Joblib execution

and

parallel numerical gradient coordinate evaluation.

They are separate stages and separate Joblib calls.

docs.title: Avoid assuming one global worker budget
docs.text:
The current source does not contain a central scheduler that coordinates:

base-estimator parallelism
gradient parallelism
underlying estimator threads
NumPy / BLAS threads
SciPy internals
Numba parallel loops

So n_jobs should be understood narrowly as the value forwarded to the shared estimator-pool helper.

docs.title: Numba parallelism in Hamming distance
docs.text:
The current HammingDistance implementation uses a Numba function decorated with:

parallel=True

for its primary distance-matrix path.

That parallel behavior is independent of COBRA's estimator:

n_jobs

parameter.

So CombinedClassifier can involve another form of library-level parallelism inside Hamming distance without the high-level n_jobs value being passed to that component.

docs.title: Numerical-library parallelism
docs.text:
Several base estimators and NumPy/SciPy operations may themselves use threaded numerical libraries.

The kfc_procedure source does not set:

OMP_NUM_THREADS
MKL_NUM_THREADS
OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS

or similar environment variables.

Thread control at that level is outside the current package implementation.

docs.title: Inspect n_jobs
docs.text:
print(
    model.n_jobs
)

docs.title: Confirm estimator count
docs.text:
print(
    len(
        model.estimators_
    )
)

The number of independent fit/predict tasks equals the number of estimator entries.

docs.title: Inspect estimator order
docs.text:
for i, estimator in enumerate(
    model.estimators_
):
    print(
        i,
        estimator,
    )

This order corresponds to the prediction-space column order generated by:

predict_estimators().

docs.title: Debug sequential behavior
docs.text:
Set:

n_jobs=1

to force the explicit sequential branch in:

fit_estimators()
predict_estimators().

This can be useful when isolating whether a problem is specific to the Joblib parallel path.

docs.title: Debug custom estimators
docs.text:
If a custom estimator works with:

n_jobs=1

but fails with another n_jobs value, remember that the parallel path uses:

backend="loky".

The current package does not contain a fallback backend selection mechanism.

docs.title: Debug parallel gradient selection
docs.text:
Inspect:

print(
    model.optimizer_.gradient_method
)

Expected:

parallel

when configured and when a gradient optimizer is actually resolved.

docs.title: Debug effective optimization method
docs.text:
For GradientCOBRA:

print(
    model.optimization_outputs_[
        "method"
    ]
)

If a non-gradient kernel forced a fallback, this can show:

grid

even though:

opt_method="grad"

was configured.

docs.title: Parallel execution checklist
docs.text:
Before increasing concurrency:

1. identify whether the expensive stage is estimator fitting/prediction;
2. remember that CV and grid candidate loops are not covered by model.n_jobs;
3. check whether base estimators have their own parallel parameters;
4. check whether gradient_method="parallel" is independently active;
5. use n_jobs=1 when diagnosing process/backend issues;
6. keep prediction-column ordering identical across workflows.

docs.title: Current source summary
docs.text: Component Parallel? Control Backend / mechanism base-estimator fitting Yes estimator n_jobs Joblib loky base-estimator prediction Yes estimator n_jobs Joblib loky automatic data splitting No package Joblib path — ordinary code distance matrices not via estimator n_jobs component-specific NumPy/SciPy/Numba CV fold loop No — Python loop grid candidate loop No — search loop regression aggregation No Joblib path — NumPy/Python classification aggregation No Joblib path — NumPy/Python numerical gradient coordinates Yes gradient_method="parallel" Joblib Hamming calculation independent parallel path Numba internals parallel=True

docs.title: Default n_jobs quick reference
docs.text: Estimator Default GradientCOBRA -1 MixCOBRARegressor 1 CombinedClassifier 1

docs.title: What changes when n_jobs=1
docs.text:
The source explicitly chooses list comprehensions:

[
    fit_one(est)
    for est in estimators
]

and:

[
    predict_one(est)
    for est in estimators
]

instead of constructing a Joblib executor.

This is the clearest source-supported way to force sequential package-level estimator execution.

docs.title: What changes when n_jobs != 1
docs.text:
Both helpers switch to:

Parallel(
    n_jobs=n_jobs,
    backend="loky",
)

for estimator-pool tasks.

The source does not special-case:

0
negative values other than 1
values larger than estimator count.

Those values are forwarded to Joblib.

Their exact acceptance and worker semantics therefore follow Joblib rather than custom validation in kfc_procedure.

docs.title: No n_jobs validation
docs.text:
The current constructors simply assign:

self.n_jobs = n_jobs

and the helpers forward the value.

There is no package-level validation requiring:

integer >= 1
or -1.

Invalid values are handled by the underlying Joblib call if the parallel branch is reached.

docs.title: Mental model
docs.text:
The current COBRA n_jobs setting parallelizes the ensemble members, not the entire COBRA algorithm.

For ordinary feature-based fitting:

\[ \boxed{ \text{estimator specifications} \rightarrow \text{parallel fit} \rightarrow \text{parallel prediction columns} \rightarrow \text{sequential COBRA geometry/optimization} } \]

For optional gradient-coordinate parallelism:

\[ \boxed{ x \rightarrow \{f(x+\varepsilon e_i),f(x-\varepsilon e_i)\}_{i} \rightarrow \text{parallel coordinate gradients} \rightarrow \nabla f(x) } \]

These are independent execution paths in the current source and do not share a single package-wide concurrency controller.

docs.title: Precomputed Predictions
docs.text:
The COBRA subsystem can operate on a matrix that already contains model predictions instead of fitting and evaluating an internal estimator pool.

The main source-level switch is:

as_predictions=True

and it is supported directly by:

GradientCOBRA
MixCOBRARegressor
CombinedClassifier

through the shared:

resolve_training_context()

helper.

This mode is especially important for KFC integration because the KFC F-Step already produces a prediction matrix that can be passed directly into a COBRA combiner.

docs.title: What counts as a precomputed prediction matrix?
docs.text:
Suppose you already have predictions from \(M\) models for \(n\) observations.

For regression:

\[ P = \begin{bmatrix} f_1(x_1) & \cdots & f_M(x_1)\\ \vdots & & \vdots\\ f_1(x_n) & \cdots & f_M(x_n) \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times M}. \]

For classification, the current CombinedClassifier prediction space is based on hard class predictions, so a row can look like:

[0, 1, 1, 0]

rather than a probability vector.

The expected layout is:

rows
    samples

columns
    model predictions / prediction-space coordinates

docs.title: Why use precomputed predictions?
docs.text:
Precomputed mode is useful when prediction features were generated by another part of a pipeline.

Examples include:

KFC F-Step predictions
external ensemble predictions
out-of-fold predictions from another framework
predictions loaded from disk
predictions generated by models managed outside kfc_procedure

With as_predictions=True, COBRA skips its normal internal base-estimator training stage and treats the supplied matrix directly as its aggregation representation.

docs.title: Normal mode
docs.text:
raw X
    ↓
split into estimator-training and calibration subsets
    ↓
fit base estimators
    ↓
predict calibration data
    ↓
prediction space
    ↓
COBRA distance/kernel/aggregation

docs.title: Precomputed mode
docs.text:
prediction matrix P
    ↓
as_predictions=True
    ↓
use P directly as calibration prediction space
    ↓
COBRA distance/kernel/aggregation

docs.title: Shared training-context behavior
docs.text:
The central source logic is in:

resolve_training_context()

Its precomputed branch is:

if as_predictions:
    return TrainingContext(
        X_k=None,
        y_k=None,
        X_l=np.asarray(X),
        y_l=np.asarray(y),
        as_predictions=True,
    )

This branch runs before:

explicit X_l / y_l handling
pred_features handling
automatic data splitting

docs.title: Resulting TrainingContext
docs.text:
With:

model.fit(
    P,
    y,
    as_predictions=True,
)

the resolver returns:

X_k = None
y_k = None

X_l = P
y_l = y

as_predictions = True

So there is no separate base-estimator training subset.

docs.title: No automatic train/calibration split
docs.text:
Because the as_predictions branch returns immediately, parameters such as:

split_ratio
overlap

do not create an additional first-level COBRA split in this mode.

The entire supplied prediction matrix becomes the calibration-side data.

docs.title: Input validation
docs.text:
Before the branch logic, the shared resolver calls:

check_X_y(
    X,
    y,
)

So in precomputed mode:

P
y

must have a compatible number of rows.

For example:

P.shape[0]
==
len(y)

must hold.

docs.title: GradientCOBRA with precomputed predictions
docs.text:
GradientCOBRA.fit() accepts:

fit(
    X,
    y,
    X_l=None,
    y_l=None,
    split_ratio=0.5,
    overlap=0.0,
    as_predictions=False,
)

To supply a ready-made prediction matrix:

from kfc_procedure.cobra import (
    GradientCOBRA,
)

model = GradientCOBRA(
    random_state=42,
)

model.fit(
    P_train,
    y_train,
    as_predictions=True,
)

docs.title: GradientCOBRA fit behavior
docs.text:
After resolving the training context, the source stores:

self.X_k_ = ctx.X_k
self.y_k_ = ctx.y_k
self.X_l_ = ctx.X_l
self.y_l_ = ctx.y_l
self.as_predictions_ = ctx.as_predictions

Then:

if not self.as_predictions_:
    self.estimators_ = self._fit_estimators(
        self.X_k_,
        self.y_k_,
    )

    prediction_space = self._load_predictions(
        self.X_l_,
    )
else:
    prediction_space = self.X_l_

So with:

as_predictions=True

the supplied matrix is assigned directly to:

prediction_space

and:

estimators_

is not created by this branch.

docs.title: GradientCOBRA normalization still applies
docs.text:
Precomputed predictions do not bypass GradientCOBRA's scalar normalization.

The source computes:

self.normalize_constant_ = (
    compute_normalization_constant(
        y=y,
        norm_constant=self.norm_constant,
        scale_factor=30.0,
        M=prediction_space.shape[1],
    )
)

then:

self.Y_l_norm_ = (
    prediction_space
    *
    self.normalize_constant_
)

So the workflow is:

P_train
    ↓
scalar normalization
    ↓
Y_l_norm_
    ↓
distance matrix
    ↓
CV / optimization

docs.title: GradientCOBRA prediction is symmetrical
docs.text:
GradientCOBRA.predict() explicitly checks:

if self.as_predictions_:
    prediction_space = X
else:
    prediction_space = self._load_predictions(X)

Therefore, if fitting used:

as_predictions=True

prediction should also receive a prediction matrix:

y_pred = model.predict(
    P_test
)

The supplied P_test is interpreted directly as new prediction-space coordinates.

docs.title: Full GradientCOBRA example
docs.text:
from kfc_procedure.cobra import (
    GradientCOBRA,
)

cobra = GradientCOBRA(
    distance="euclidean",
    kernel="rbf",
    random_state=42,
)

cobra.fit(
    P_train,
    y_train,
    as_predictions=True,
)

y_pred = cobra.predict(
    P_test
)

docs.title: Required column consistency
docs.text:
The source does not store or validate semantic column names.

Therefore the caller is responsible for ensuring that:

P_train[:, 0]

and:

P_test[:, 0]

represent predictions from the same underlying model or prediction source.

The same requirement applies to every column.

docs.title: Inspect GradientCOBRA precomputed state
docs.text:
After fitting:

print(
    model.as_predictions_
)

should be:

True

and:

print(
    model.X_k_
)

print(
    model.y_k_
)

should show:

None
None

while:

print(
    model.X_l_.shape
)

print(
    model.Y_l_norm_.shape
)

should match the precomputed training-matrix row and column counts.

docs.title: No estimators_ in GradientCOBRA precomputed mode
docs.text:
Because the source skips:

self._fit_estimators(...)

when:

as_predictions_ == True

the fitted object does not rely on an internal estimator pool for prediction.

This is why:

predict(
    P_test
)

works directly.

docs.title: CombinedClassifier with precomputed predictions
docs.text:
CombinedClassifier.fit() supports the same switch:

classifier.fit(
    P_train,
    y_train,
    as_predictions=True,
)

docs.title: CombinedClassifier fit branch
docs.text:
The current source does:

if not self.as_predictions_:
    self.classes_ = np.unique(
        self.y_k_
    )

    self.estimators_ = self._fit_estimators(
        self.X_k_,
        self.y_k_,
    )

    self.pred_l_ = self._load_predictions(
        self.X_l_
    )
else:
    self.classes_ = np.unique(
        self.y_l_
    )

    self.pred_l_ = self.X_l_

So with precomputed mode:

P_train
    becomes pred_l_

classes_
    are derived from y_l_

internal estimators
    are not fitted

docs.title: CombinedClassifier prediction space
docs.text:
The calibration distance matrix is computed directly from:

self.pred_l_

using:

self.distance_.matrix(
    self.pred_l_,
    self.pred_l_,
)

The current default distance is:

hamming

which fits hard class-prediction vectors.

docs.title: CombinedClassifier prediction is symmetrical
docs.text:
At prediction time:

if self.as_predictions_:
    preds_space = X
else:
    preds_space = self._load_predictions(X)

Therefore:

classifier.predict(
    P_test
)

treats P_test directly as prediction-space data after a precomputed fit.

docs.title: CombinedClassifier probabilities
docs.text:
predict_proba() has the same source branch:

if self.as_predictions_:
    preds_space = X
else:
    preds_space = self._load_predictions(X)

So:

proba = classifier.predict_proba(
    P_test
)

also accepts precomputed prediction-space rows directly.

docs.title: Probability caveat
docs.text:
The current default:

WeightedVoteAggregator.aggregate_proba()

does not use the supplied kernel weights.

Therefore query-specific probabilities from the current default CombinedClassifier.predict_proba() are affected by that implementation limitation.

See:

Aggregators

for the exact behavior.

docs.title: Full CombinedClassifier example
docs.text:
from kfc_procedure.cobra import (
    CombinedClassifier,
)

classifier = CombinedClassifier(
    distance="hamming",
    kernel="rbf",
    random_state=42,
)

classifier.fit(
    P_train,
    y_train,
    as_predictions=True,
)

y_pred = classifier.predict(
    P_test
)

proba = classifier.predict_proba(
    P_test
)

docs.title: Hard predictions, not probabilities
docs.text:
When CombinedClassifier builds prediction space internally, it uses:

est.predict(X)

rather than:

est.predict_proba(X)

Therefore a precomputed matrix that mirrors the built-in semantics should normally contain hard class predictions.

Example:

P_train = np.array([
    [0, 0, 1, 0],
    [1, 1, 1, 1],
    [2, 1, 2, 2],
])

rather than concatenated probability vectors.

docs.title: MixCOBRA with precomputed predictions
docs.text:
MixCOBRARegressor.fit() also accepts:

as_predictions=True

and its fit branch initially behaves similarly.

if not self.as_predictions_:
    self.estimators_ = self._fit_estimators(
        self.X_k_,
        self.y_k_,
    )

    prediction_space = self._load_predictions(
        self.X_l_
    )
else:
    prediction_space = self.X_l_

So internal base-estimator fitting is skipped.

docs.title: MixCOBRA stores the same matrix in two roles
docs.text:
In precomputed mode, the shared resolver gives:

X_l_ = supplied P

and the fit branch sets:

prediction_space = supplied P.

MixCOBRA then computes:

self.X_l_norm_ = (
    self.X_l_
    *
    self.normalize_constant_x_
)

self.Y_l_norm_ = (
    prediction_space
    *
    self.normalize_constant_y_
)

Thus the same supplied prediction matrix participates as both:

input-space representation
prediction-space representation

under two different scalar normalizations.

docs.title: MixCOBRA one-parameter mode
docs.text:
If:

one_parameter=True

the source concatenates:

self.X_l_norm_
self.Y_l_norm_

into:

self.mix_features_

even though both originated from the same supplied matrix in as_predictions=True mode.

docs.title: MixCOBRA two-parameter mode
docs.text:
If:

one_parameter=False

the source computes:

distance_matrix_x_
distance_matrix_y_

from two differently scaled copies of the same supplied prediction matrix.

docs.title: Important MixCOBRA prediction limitation
docs.text:
The current MixCOBRARegressor.predict() does not mirror the as_predictions_ branch used by GradientCOBRA and CombinedClassifier.

Its code begins with:

if pred_X is None:
    pred_X = self._load_predictions(
        X
    )

There is no:

if self.as_predictions_:
    pred_X = X

branch.

docs.title: Consequence
docs.text:
When MixCOBRARegressor is fitted with:

as_predictions=True

the fit method skips creation of:

self.estimators_

but later:

predict(
    P_test
)

still tries to execute:

self._load_predictions(
    P_test
)

when pred_X is omitted.

That path expects internal estimators that were never fitted.

Current source limitation

MixCOBRARegressor(as_predictions=True) is not symmetrical between fit() and the default predict() path.

Unlike GradientCOBRA and CombinedClassifier, precomputed fit mode does not automatically make the predict(X) argument act as prediction space.

docs.title: Why pred_X= does not fully solve standalone precomputed MixCOBRA
docs.text:
MixCOBRARegressor.predict() accepts:

pred_X=None

and if pred_X is supplied it skips:

self._load_predictions(X)

However, it still separately computes:

X_norm = (
    X
    *
    self.normalize_constant_x_
)

Y_norm = (
    pred_X
    *
    self.normalize_constant_y_
)

So the method expects:

X
    an input-space matrix

pred_X
    a prediction-space matrix

This matches ordinary MixCOBRA's two-space design.

In as_predictions=True fit mode, however, the training code used the same supplied matrix for both roles.

docs.title: Source-aligned workaround
docs.text:
To reproduce the same source geometry during prediction, one can supply the same precomputed test matrix in both arguments:

y_pred = model.predict(
    P_test,
    pred_X=P_test,
)

This causes:

X_norm
    to come from P_test

Y_norm
    also to come from P_test

which mirrors the two differently scaled copies created during precomputed fitting.

Caution

This is a workaround inferred directly from the current implementation.

The source does not contain a dedicated high-level helper documenting this as the intended public precomputed-prediction API for MixCOBRA.

docs.title: MixCOBRA example with current source behavior
docs.text:
from kfc_procedure.cobra import (
    MixCOBRARegressor,
)

model = MixCOBRARegressor(
    one_parameter=False,
    random_state=42,
)

model.fit(
    P_train,
    y_train,
    as_predictions=True,
)

y_pred = model.predict(
    P_test,
    pred_X=P_test,
)

This avoids the internal-estimator lookup in predict().

docs.title: The separate pred_features argument
docs.text:
MixCOBRA also exposes:

pred_features=None

in:

fit()

Its docstring describes this as:

Pre-computed model predictions to use instead of internal estimator outputs.

However, the current resolver and fit implementation do not use that branch in the straightforward way the description suggests.

docs.title: Resolver behavior for pred_features
docs.text:
When:

pred_features is not None

and:

as_predictions=False

the resolver returns:

TrainingContext(
    X_k=np.asarray(X),
    y_k=np.asarray(y),
    X_l=pred_features,
    y_l=np.asarray(y),
    as_predictions=False,
)

So:

X_k
    original X

X_l
    pred_features

as_predictions
    False

docs.title: MixCOBRA fit after pred_features
docs.text:
Because:

as_predictions_ == False

the current MixCOBRA fit branch runs:

self.estimators_ = self._fit_estimators(
    self.X_k_,
    self.y_k_,
)

prediction_space = self._load_predictions(
    self.X_l_
)

But:

self.X_l_

now contains:

pred_features

rather than ordinary calibration feature rows.

Therefore the source attempts to feed those precomputed prediction rows into the newly fitted base estimators.

docs.title: Consequence
docs.text:
The current implementation does not directly assign:

prediction_space = pred_features

in the pred_features branch.

So pred_features is not presently a clean substitute for as_predictions=True.

Current source inconsistency

The MixCOBRA docstring describes pred_features as precomputed model predictions.

The actual current fit path passes those values back through internal base estimators.

This page documents the implementation rather than silently assuming the docstring's intended behavior.

docs.title: Prefer as_predictions=True when the whole matrix is already prediction space
docs.text:
For the current source:

GradientCOBRA
CombinedClassifier

have clean, symmetrical precomputed-prediction workflows through:

as_predictions=True

For MixCOBRA, the fit side supports that mode but the prediction side requires special care as described above.

docs.title: KFC integration
docs.text:
KFC's C-Step wrappers use precomputed mode automatically.

The F-Step already produces:

P_l

so the wrappers call their COBRA estimator with:

as_predictions=True

rather than fitting another base-estimator pool.

docs.title: GradientCOBRA KFC wrapper
docs.text:
The current wrapper is:

class GradientCOBRACombiner(
    BaseCombiner
):

    def __init__(
        self,
        **cobra_params,
    ):
        self.cobra = GradientCOBRA(
            **cobra_params
        )

    def fit(
        self,
        X,
        y,
    ):
        self.cobra.fit(
            X,
            y,
            as_predictions=True,
        )

        return self

    def combine(
        self,
        X,
    ):
        return self.cobra.predict(
            X
        )

This works naturally because GradientCOBRA.predict() honors as_predictions_.

docs.title: CombinedClassifier KFC wrapper
docs.text:
The classifier wrapper similarly uses:

self.cobra.fit(
    X,
    y,
    as_predictions=True,
)

and later:

self.cobra.predict(
    X
)

which is symmetrical in the current CombinedClassifier source.

docs.title: MixCOBRA KFC wrapper caveat
docs.text:
The current MixCOBRACombiner uses:

self.cobra.fit(
    X,
    y,
    as_predictions=True,
)

but its combine() method simply calls:

self.cobra.predict(
    X
)

without supplying:

pred_X=X.

Because MixCOBRARegressor.predict() does not branch on as_predictions_, this wrapper can encounter the same missing-internal-estimator problem.

Current KFC integration issue

The current MixCOBRA C-Step wrapper fits with as_predictions=True but predicts through the default MixCOBRARegressor.predict(X) path.

Those two code paths are not currently symmetrical.

docs.title: Precomputed regression predictions from external models
docs.text:
Suppose you train three external regressors and create:

P_train = np.column_stack([
    pred_a_train,
    pred_b_train,
    pred_c_train,
])

P_test = np.column_stack([
    pred_a_test,
    pred_b_test,
    pred_c_test,
])

Then GradientCOBRA can use them directly:

model = GradientCOBRA(
    random_state=42,
)

model.fit(
    P_train,
    y_train,
    as_predictions=True,
)

y_pred = model.predict(
    P_test
)

No estimator objects need to be passed into GradientCOBRA.

docs.title: Precomputed classification predictions from external models
docs.text:
P_train = np.column_stack([
    clf_a.predict(
        X_train
    ),
    clf_b.predict(
        X_train
    ),
    clf_c.predict(
        X_train
    ),
])

P_test = np.column_stack([
    clf_a.predict(
        X_test
    ),
    clf_b.predict(
        X_test
    ),
    clf_c.predict(
        X_test
    ),
])

Then:

classifier = CombinedClassifier(
    distance="hamming",
    random_state=42,
)

classifier.fit(
    P_train,
    y_train,
    as_predictions=True,
)

y_pred = classifier.predict(
    P_test
)

docs.title: Train/test column alignment
docs.text:
The package does not retain metadata such as:

model name per column
column semantic identifier
feature provenance

So you should preserve column order explicitly.

For example:

prediction_sources = [
    "ridge",
    "random_forest",
    "svr",
]

and construct both matrices in that order.

docs.title: Row alignment
docs.text:
Every training row must correspond to the same target row.

assert (
    P_train.shape[0]
    ==
    len(
        y_train
    )
)

Likewise, every row in:

P_test

must correspond to the output row you expect in:

y_pred.

docs.title: Prediction-space width
docs.text:
The training and prediction matrices should normally have the same number of columns:

assert (
    P_train.shape[1]
    ==
    P_test.shape[1]
)

Otherwise the configured distance operation is likely to fail because query and calibration vectors have incompatible coordinate dimensions.

docs.title: Numeric dtype
docs.text:
GradientCOBRA and MixCOBRA eventually perform numerical scaling and distance calculations, so their precomputed regression matrices should be numeric.

CombinedClassifier with Hamming distance can naturally work with discrete class prediction values, subject to the rest of the pipeline's dtype behavior.

docs.title: Missing values
docs.text:
The precomputed mode does not add a dedicated missing-value cleaning stage.

Downstream behavior depends on:

check_array
distance implementation
normalization
kernel
aggregator

For regression prediction matrices, verify finite values before fitting:

import numpy as np

print(
    np.isfinite(
        P_train
    ).all()
)

docs.title: Out-of-fold predictions
docs.text:
The source supports any matrix supplied through:

as_predictions=True

and does not inspect how those predictions were generated.

If the matrix was created externally, the responsibility for avoiding leakage or inappropriate reuse lies outside the COBRA implementation.

The package does not tag rows as:

in-sample
out-of-fold
held-out

or verify provenance.

docs.title: No internal estimator refitting in precomputed mode
docs.text:
A central benefit of as_predictions=True is that the COBRA estimator does not fit its configured estimator pool.

That means settings such as:

estimators
estimators_params
n_jobs used for estimator fitting

are not used for the skipped internal fit branch.

The downstream COBRA components are still resolved and optimized.

docs.title: Cross-validation still runs
docs.text:
Precomputed mode bypasses the first-level train/calibration split, but it does not bypass COBRA hyperparameter cross-validation.

For GradientCOBRA:

self.cv_folds_ = list(
    self.cv_.split(
        self.X_l_,
        self.Y_l_norm_,
    )
)

still executes.

CombinedClassifier and MixCOBRA likewise construct their internal CV folds.

docs.title: Optimization still runs
docs.text:
After distance matrices and folds are built, the normal optimization stage still selects parameters such as:

bandwidth
alpha
beta.

So:

as_predictions=True

means:

skip base-estimator construction

not:

skip COBRA training.

docs.title: Inspect whether precomputed mode was used
docs.text:
print(
    model.as_predictions_
)

Expected:

True

for a model fitted with:

as_predictions=True.

docs.title: Inspect calibration representation
docs.text:
GradientCOBRA:

print(
    model.X_l_
)

print(
    model.Y_l_norm_
)

CombinedClassifier:

print(
    classifier.pred_l_
)

MixCOBRA:

print(
    model.X_l_norm_
)

print(
    model.Y_l_norm_
)

docs.title: Verify GradientCOBRA did not fit estimators
docs.text:
A source-aligned check is:

print(
    hasattr(
        model,
        "estimators_",
    )
)

In a fresh model fitted only through:

as_predictions=True

the internal estimator-fit branch does not create that attribute.

docs.title: Verify CombinedClassifier did not fit estimators
docs.text:
Likewise:

print(
    hasattr(
        classifier,
        "estimators_",
    )
)

should normally be false for a fresh precomputed-mode fit.

docs.title: Reusing externally saved matrices
docs.text:
A simple workflow can save:

np.save(
    "P_train.npy",
    P_train,
)

np.save(
    "P_test.npy",
    P_test,
)

and later load:

P_train = np.load(
    "P_train.npy"
)

P_test = np.load(
    "P_test.npy"
)

before fitting a COBRA estimator.

The package itself does not define a custom persistence format specifically for prediction-space matrices.

docs.title: DataFrame input
docs.text:
check_X_y() and check_array() convert compatible tabular input into NumPy arrays.

Therefore a pandas DataFrame can be supplied, but column labels are not retained as semantic prediction-source metadata inside the fitted COBRA estimator.

If names matter, keep them separately.

docs.title: Precomputed probabilities are not the default classification representation
docs.text:
A matrix like:

[p(class=0), p(class=1), ...]

can be numeric input mathematically, but that is not the representation generated by the current CombinedClassifier base-estimator helper.

Its internal helper uses:

est.predict(X)

to build hard-label columns.

So a probability matrix would represent a custom prediction space rather than the current source's default semantics.

docs.title: GradientCOBRA
docs.text:
Still applies:

one scalar normalization constant

derived from:

y
prediction-space width M.

docs.title: MixCOBRA
docs.text:
Still applies:

normalize_constant_x_
normalize_constant_y_.

docs.title: CombinedClassifier
docs.text:
Applies no internal normalization before distance computation.

See:

Normalization

for the exact formulas.

docs.title: Precomputed predictions and distances
docs.text:
Once accepted, the matrix is just a coordinate representation.

The configured distance decides how rows are compared.

Examples:

GradientCOBRA
    default euclidean

CombinedClassifier
    default hamming

MixCOBRA
    default euclidean

See:

Distances

docs.title: Precomputed predictions and kernels
docs.text:
The prediction matrix itself does not determine neighbor weights directly.

The flow remains:

prediction matrix
    ↓
distance matrix
    ↓
adapter
    ↓
kernel
    ↓
aggregation weights.

So all normal kernel and optimization settings remain relevant in precomputed mode.

docs.title: KFC F-Step as precomputed prediction space
docs.text:
The KFC Procedure naturally creates a matrix:

P_l = model.fstep_.predict(
    X_l,
    clusters_l,
)

where each column is a divergence-specific prediction stream.

That matrix is already in the exact structural form expected by the COBRA precomputed mode:

rows
    observations

columns
    prediction sources.

This is why the COBRA C-Step wrappers call:

fit(
    P_l,
    y_l,
    as_predictions=True,
)

docs.title: Manual KFC-to-GradientCOBRA workflow
docs.text:
You can reproduce the idea explicitly.

clusters_train = (
    kfc_model
    .kstep_
    .predict(
        X_train
    )
)

P_train = (
    kfc_model
    .fstep_
    .predict(
        X_train,
        clusters_train,
    )
)

Then:

cobra = GradientCOBRA()

cobra.fit(
    P_train,
    y_train,
    as_predictions=True,
)

For test data:

clusters_test = (
    kfc_model
    .kstep_
    .predict(
        X_test
    )
)

P_test = (
    kfc_model
    .fstep_
    .predict(
        X_test,
        clusters_test,
    )
)

y_pred = cobra.predict(
    P_test
)

docs.title: Manual KFC-to-CombinedClassifier workflow
docs.text:
The same concept applies to classification:

classifier = CombinedClassifier(
    distance="hamming",
)

classifier.fit(
    P_train,
    y_train,
    as_predictions=True,
)

y_pred = classifier.predict(
    P_test
)

The F-Step rows become hard-label prediction-space coordinates.

docs.title: Precomputed mode is not the same as explicit calibration data
docs.text: These two interfaces have different meanings.

docs.title: Explicit calibration data
docs.text:
model.fit(
    X_k,
    y_k,
    X_l=X_l,
    y_l=y_l,
)

means:

fit internal base estimators on X_k/y_k
generate their predictions on X_l
use those predictions as calibration prediction space.

docs.title: Precomputed mode
docs.text:
model.fit(
    P,
    y,
    as_predictions=True,
)

means:

do not fit internal base estimators
treat P itself as calibration prediction space.

docs.title: Precomputed mode is not the same as pred_features
docs.text:
For current MixCOBRA source:

as_predictions=True

and:

pred_features=...

follow different code paths.

as_predictions=True directly assigns the supplied matrix to prediction space during fit.

pred_features currently becomes X_l while as_predictions remains false, after which internal estimators are still applied.

Do not treat these two arguments as equivalent in the current implementation.

docs.title: Mismatched sample count
docs.text:
ValueError

from the shared check_X_y() path can occur if:

P_train.shape[0]
!=
len(
    y_train
)

docs.title: Mismatched prediction width
docs.text:
If:

P_train.shape[1]
!=
P_test.shape[1]

distance computation can fail because query and calibration coordinates have different dimensions.

docs.title: Reordered prediction columns
docs.text:
This may not raise an error because shapes still match.

But it changes the geometry.

For example:

training:
    [ridge, random_forest, svr]

test:
    [svr, ridge, random_forest]

is semantically incorrect even though both matrices have three columns.

docs.title: Calling MixCOBRA predict(P_test) after precomputed fit
docs.text:
The current source can try to use missing internal estimators.

Use the source-aware workaround:

model.predict(
    P_test,
    pred_X=P_test,
)

if you intentionally use this current precomputed MixCOBRA mode.

docs.title: Validation checklist
docs.text:
Before fitting:

assert (
    P_train.ndim
    ==
    2
)

assert (
    len(
        P_train
    )
    ==
    len(
        y_train
    )
)

Before prediction:

assert (
    P_test.ndim
    ==
    2
)

assert (
    P_test.shape[1]
    ==
    P_train.shape[1]
)

For numeric regression spaces:

assert np.isfinite(
    P_train
).all()

assert np.isfinite(
    P_test
).all()

docs.title: Recommended metadata to keep externally
docs.text:
Because COBRA does not store prediction-column names, keep something like:

prediction_sources = [
    "ridge",
    "random_forest_regressor",
    "svr",
]

alongside saved matrices.

For reproducibility, also keep:

model versions
training split identifiers
column ordering
class encoding
data preprocessing version

outside the COBRA estimator.

docs.title: Current source comparison
docs.text: Estimator as_predictions=True fit predict(X) treats X as prediction space Notes GradientCOBRA Yes Yes clean symmetric path CombinedClassifier Yes Yes hard-label prediction space by default MixCOBRARegressor Yes No current predict path still derives pred_X unless supplied

docs.title: KFC wrapper comparison
docs.text: KFC combiner Fits wrapped model with as_predictions=True Current prediction compatibility GradientCOBRACombiner Yes compatible CobraClassifierCombiner Yes compatible MixCOBRACombiner Yes current wrapper affected by MixCOBRA predict asymmetry

docs.title: Quick reference
docs.text: Goal Current source path GradientCOBRA from external predictions fit(P, y, as_predictions=True) GradientCOBRA new prediction matrix predict(P_test) CombinedClassifier from hard predictions fit(P, y, as_predictions=True) CombinedClassifier new prediction matrix predict(P_test) CombinedClassifier probabilities predict_proba(P_test) MixCOBRA precomputed fit fit(P, y, as_predictions=True) MixCOBRA current-source prediction workaround predict(P_test, pred_X=P_test) Skip automatic data split use as_predictions=True Skip internal base estimators use as_predictions=True Keep COBRA CV/optimization happens automatically

docs.title: Mental model
docs.text:
Precomputed-prediction mode says: “the prediction space already exists; start the COBRA procedure from that matrix instead of fitting another ensemble to create it.”

For GradientCOBRA:

\[ \boxed{ P \rightarrow \text{normalize} \rightarrow \text{distance} \rightarrow \text{kernel} \rightarrow \text{weighted target aggregation} } \]

For CombinedClassifier:

\[ \boxed{ P_{\text{hard labels}} \rightarrow \text{distance} \rightarrow \text{kernel} \rightarrow \text{weighted class vote} } \]

The current MixCOBRA source also accepts the matrix during fitting, but its prediction API does not yet mirror that precomputed mode automatically.

docs.title: Reproducibility
docs.text:
Reproducibility in kfc_procedure depends on several independent sources of randomness.

The most important user-facing control is:

random_state

but a single seed does not automatically control every stochastic component in the package.

The current source uses several different random-number APIs:

sklearn.utils.check_random_state
np.random.RandomState
np.random.default_rng
sklearn.model_selection.train_test_split
global np.random

and different components receive the estimator seed in different ways.

This page documents the current source behavior so you can make experiments as repeatable as possible.

docs.title: Reproducibility map
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    R["random_state"]

    S["Top-level / COBRA split"]
    K["K-Step clustering"]
    C["COBRA CV folds"]
    F["F-Step local models"]
    CS["C-Step combiner"]
    E["COBRA base estimators"]
    O["Optimizer"]

    R --> S
    R --> K
    R --> C
    R --> F
    R --> CS

    E -. "not automatically seeded by shared COBRA helper" .- R
    O -. "SPSA uses global np.random" .- R

The estimator seed is propagated to several structural components, but not to all model-specific or optimizer-specific randomness.

docs.title: What random_state controls
docs.text:
At a high level, the current source uses random_state for:

KFC's top-level train/calibration split
K-Step Bregman clustering
COBRA automatic overlap/holdout splitting
COBRA K-fold cross-validation
some F-Step local-model construction
some C-Step combiner construction
some wrapped COBRA components

It does not provide one package-wide global RNG object shared by all of those components.

docs.title: Reproducibility in KFCProcedure
docs.text:
The top-level constructor stores:

self.random_state = random_state

and passes it into:

train/test splitting
K-Step
F-Step
C-Step.

docs.title: KFC data split
docs.text:
KFCProcedure.fit() performs:

X_k, X_l, y_k, y_l = train_test_split(
    X,
    y,
    test_size=0.5,
    random_state=self.random_state,
    stratify=(
        y
        if self.task == "classification"
        else None
    ),
)

So a fixed:

random_state

reproduces the same top-level KFC split for the same data order and compatible scikit-learn behavior.

docs.title: Classification stratification
docs.text:
For:

task="classification"

the top-level split uses:

stratify=y

whereas regression uses:

stratify=None.

Therefore the KFC classification split has a different sampling constraint from the standalone COBRA automatic splitter.

docs.title: K-Step reproducibility
docs.text:
KFC passes the same seed into:

KStep(
    random_state=self.random_state,
)

KStep then forwards that seed to each:

BregmanKMeans

instance it constructs.

docs.title: BregmanKMeans RNG
docs.text:
Inside:

BregmanKMeans.fit()

the current source creates:

rng = check_random_state(
    self.random_state
)

from scikit-learn.

This produces the RNG used by the internal clustering initialization and reinitialization logic.

docs.title: Multiple initializations
docs.text:
BregmanKMeans can run multiple initialization attempts through:

n_init

The current default is:

10

unless an explicit initial centroid matrix is provided.

The same seeded RNG object is reused across those attempts.

For a fixed seed and identical input ordering, this makes the sequence of initializations repeatable.

docs.title: Explicit clustering initialization
docs.text:
If:

init

is passed directly to:

BregmanKMeans.fit(
    X,
    init=...
)

the source sets:

n_init = 1

for that call.

That removes random centroid initialization from the clustering fit itself, although other parts of a surrounding pipeline can still be stochastic.

docs.title: K-Step fitted results to compare
docs.text:
For reproducibility checks, useful fitted attributes include:

model.kstep_.clusters_

and for each underlying Bregman model:

cluster_centers_
labels_
inertia_
n_iter_.

If these differ between otherwise identical runs, later local-model and combination stages can also differ.

docs.title: F-Step seed propagation
docs.text:
KFC creates:

FStep(
    ...,
    random_state=self.random_state,
)

When the configured local model is a string, FStep builds:

params = dict(
    self.local_model_params
)

if "random_state" not in params:
    params[
        "random_state"
    ] = self.random_state

then calls:

LocalModelFactory.create(
    name,
    **params,
)

docs.title: Explicit local-model seed wins
docs.text:
If you provide:

local_model_params={
    "random_state": 123,
}

FStep does not overwrite it with the KFC-level seed.

So:

local model random_state

takes precedence when explicitly present.

docs.title: SklearnLocalModel parameter filtering
docs.text:
String-based scikit-learn local models are typically wrapped by:

SklearnLocalModel

which inspects the estimator constructor signature and retains supported arguments.

Therefore the injected:

random_state

is passed through only when the target estimator accepts it.

For deterministic estimators without a random-state parameter, the key can be filtered out.

docs.title: F-Step custom object caveat
docs.text:
If:

local_model

is a pre-built non-string estimator object, FStep's _resolve() returns that object directly.

The source does not clone it and does not inject the KFC seed.

Therefore reproducibility of that custom object depends on how you configured the object itself.

docs.title: Same object is reused
docs.text:
The current F-Step source reuses the same non-string local-model object across cluster fits rather than cloning a fresh copy per cluster.

This is primarily a model-construction behavior, but it also matters for reproducibility because state is repeatedly overwritten on the same object.

docs.title: C-Step seed propagation
docs.text:
KFC also constructs:

CStep(
    ...,
    random_state=self.random_state,
)

For string-based combiners, CStep performs:

params = dict(
    self.combiner_params
)

if "random_state" not in params:
    params[
        "random_state"
    ] = self.random_state

and passes those parameters into:

CombinerFactory.create(...)

docs.title: C-Step constructor compatibility caveat
docs.text:
Not every built-in combiner constructor accepts:

random_state.

Because CStep injects it for every string-based combiner when absent, some string combiner paths can fail with an unexpected keyword argument.

This is a current source issue rather than a reproducibility guarantee.

Pre-instantiated combiner objects bypass that injection.

docs.title: Standalone COBRA reproducibility
docs.text:
The standalone estimators:

GradientCOBRA
MixCOBRARegressor
CombinedClassifier

also expose:

random_state

and use it mainly for:

automatic splitting
K-fold CV construction
some optimizer/component configuration.

docs.title: Automatic COBRA split
docs.text:
The shared:

resolve_training_context()

creates:

SplitterFactory.create(
    "split_overlap",
    split_ratio=split_ratio,
    overlap=overlap,
    random_state=random_state,
)

when no explicit aggregation dataset or precomputed prediction matrix is provided.

docs.title: OverlapSplitter RNG
docs.text:
The default automatic splitter uses:

rng = np.random.default_rng(
    self.random_state
)

and then:

rng.shuffle(
    shuffled
)

So the first-level standalone COBRA split is repeatable for a fixed seed and identical row order.

docs.title: Different RNG API from KFC clustering
docs.text:
This matters if you compare random sequences across components.

OverlapSplitter uses:

np.random.default_rng

while BregmanKMeans uses:

sklearn check_random_state

which is based on the older RandomState style.

Even with the same integer seed, these generators do not produce the same random sequence.

The seed is a reproducibility control within each component, not a promise that every component draws matching numbers.

docs.title: RandomHoldoutSplitter
docs.text:
The optional holdout splitter stores:

random_state

and passes it into:

train_test_split(
    indices,
    test_size=self.calibration_size,
    random_state=self.random_state,
    shuffle=True,
)

So its partition is reproducible for a fixed seed.

docs.title: COBRA K-fold reproducibility
docs.text:
The main standalone COBRA estimators build:

KFoldCV(
    n_splits=self.n_cv,
    shuffle=True,
    random_state=self.random_state,
)

through the factory.

docs.title: KFoldCV RNG
docs.text:
The current custom K-fold implementation uses:

rng = np.random.RandomState(
    self.random_state
)

and:

indices = rng.permutation(
    indices
)

when shuffling is enabled.

This is another RNG API distinct from the overlap splitter's default_rng.

docs.title: Fold assignment is deterministic after permutation
docs.text:
Once the index permutation is generated, the source distributes indices round-robin:

folds[
    i % self.n_splits
].append(
    idx
)

So the combination of:

input row order
n_splits
shuffle setting
random_state

determines the current fold assignment.

docs.title: Stored folds
docs.text:
The main estimators materialize CV folds in:

cv_folds_

You can compare them directly across runs.

Example:

for fold in model.cv_folds_:
    print(
        fold.fold_id,
        fold.train_idx,
        fold.eval_idx,
    )

docs.title: StratifiedKFoldCV uses another RNG API
docs.text:
The registered stratified cross-validator uses:

rng = np.random.default_rng(
    self.random_state
)

and shuffles each class-specific index array.

So its sequence differs from the custom ordinary KFoldCV even when both receive the same integer seed.

The main COBRA estimators currently hard-code ordinary kfold, so this matters mostly when using or extending the lower-level CV components directly.

docs.title: TimeSeriesCV is deterministic
docs.text:
The current time-series cross-validator does not shuffle data and has no random_state parameter.

For a fixed row order, n_splits, and test_size, it produces deterministic expanding windows.

docs.title: Explicit aggregation data improve split reproducibility
docs.text:
Supplying:

X_l=
y_l=

bypasses the automatic first-level COBRA splitter.

So if you preserve the exact external split arrays or row indices, the train/calibration boundary becomes independent of the estimator's random_state.

Other stochastic components, such as CV folds or base estimators, may still vary.

docs.title: Precomputed predictions remove estimator-pool randomness
docs.text:
With:

as_predictions=True

GradientCOBRA and CombinedClassifier skip internal base-estimator fitting.

This can remove a major source of stochastic variation when the prediction matrix itself is fixed.

However, internal cross-validation and optimizer behavior can still depend on other settings.

docs.title: COBRA base estimators are not globally reseeded
docs.text:
The shared helper:

fit_estimators()

builds estimators from their specification and parameters, but does not automatically inject the parent COBRA estimator's:

random_state

into every base estimator.

This is a crucial current source detail.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
This:

GradientCOBRA(
    random_state=42,
)

does not guarantee that every stochastic estimator in its default pool is constructed with:

random_state=42.

If a base estimator needs its own fixed seed, pass it through:

estimators_params.

docs.title: Configure estimator-specific seeds
docs.text:
Example:

model = GradientCOBRA(
    random_state=42,
    estimators_params={
        "random_forest_regressor": {
            "random_state": 42,
        },
    },
)

For several stochastic estimators:

model = GradientCOBRA(
    random_state=42,
    estimators_params={
        "random_forest_regressor": {
            "random_state": 42,
        },
        "some_other_estimator": {
            "random_state": 42,
        },
    },
)

Only parameters supported by each estimator constructor should be supplied.

docs.title: Tuple estimator specifications
docs.text:
The shared estimator helper also supports:

(
    name,
    params,
)

so a seed can travel with the individual specification:

estimators=[
    (
        "random_forest_regressor",
        {
            "random_state": 42,
        },
    ),
    "ridge",
]

docs.title: Pre-built estimator objects
docs.text:
If you pass an already-created estimator object, the COBRA helper uses that object directly.

Its reproducibility depends on its own configuration.

The parent COBRA random_state is not automatically written into the object.

docs.title: Parallel execution and reproducibility
docs.text:
The package can fit and predict base estimators in parallel using Joblib.

For current built-in helper logic:

n_jobs=1
    -> sequential list comprehension

n_jobs != 1
    -> Joblib Parallel with backend="loky".

Parallel execution does not automatically reseed base estimators.

So reproducibility still depends on the estimators' own deterministic behavior and seed configuration.

docs.title: Prediction column order
docs.text:
The shared prediction helper uses:

np.column_stack(
    preds
)

over predictions returned in estimator-list order.

To reproduce prediction-space geometry, preserve:

the estimator list
its ordering
its parameters.

A different column order changes distances even when the same models are present.

docs.title: Store estimator specifications
docs.text:
For repeatable experiments, keep an explicit ordered list:

estimators = [
    "linear_regression",
    "ridge",
    "random_forest_regressor",
    "svr",
]

and a matching parameter dictionary:

estimators_params = {
    "random_forest_regressor": {
        "random_state": 42,
    },
}

Do not rely on an unordered external configuration source to reconstruct the prediction-space columns.

docs.title: Optimization reproducibility
docs.text:
Grid search is deterministic when its candidate sequence and objective are deterministic.

The current grid optimizer enumerates:

itertools.product(
    *values
)

and evaluates candidates in that order.

docs.title: Grid-search ties
docs.text:
If multiple candidates have exactly the same minimum risk, the source selects the middle matching candidate index:

ids[
    len(ids) // 2
]

This tie rule is deterministic for a fixed candidate order.

docs.title: Preserve candidate ordering
docs.text:
Because parameter-vector meaning follows dictionary insertion order when the grid is built, preserve the construction order of custom multi-parameter grids.

For two-parameter MixCOBRA, the intended order is:

alpha
beta.

A different mapping order can change how candidate vectors are interpreted.

docs.title: Default generated grids
docs.text:
When custom candidate arrays are absent, the current source uses deterministic NumPy grids such as:

np.linspace(
    0.001,
    10.0,
    max_iter,
)

So the default grid itself contains no randomness.

docs.title: Gradient optimization
docs.text:
The deterministic status of gradient optimization depends on the configured gradient estimator.

Current methods are:

central
forward
spsa
complex
parallel

docs.title: Deterministic numerical gradient methods
docs.text:
For a deterministic objective, these source methods are normally deterministic:

central
forward
complex
parallel

The parallel variant changes execution strategy but computes the same coordinate-wise central-difference formula.

docs.title: SPSA is a reproducibility exception
docs.text:
The current SPSA helper uses:

delta = np.random.choice(
    [-1.0, 1.0],
    size=p.shape,
)

from NumPy's global random state.

It does not accept:

random_state

and is not seeded from:

GradientCOBRA.random_state

or:

MixCOBRARegressor.random_state.

Current source limitation

A fixed estimator random_state does not make gradient_method="spsa" reproducible by itself.

docs.title: Reproducing SPSA manually
docs.text:
If you choose to use the current SPSA implementation and need repeatable global NumPy draws, the source itself does not provide a dedicated estimator argument for that seed.

The observable implementation uses the global:

np.random

state.

A more robust package-level solution would require a source change to pass a dedicated RNG or seed into the SPSA helper.

This documentation does not assume such a change exists today.

docs.title: Gradient initialization
docs.text:
The high-level GradientCOBRA path supplies:

init_param=np.array([
    1.0
])

and two-parameter MixCOBRA supplies:

np.array([
    1.0,
    1.0,
])

so those starting points are deterministic.

docs.title: Learning-rate schedules
docs.text:
The current learning-rate schedules are deterministic mathematical functions of iteration count and the initial gradient norm.

Therefore they do not introduce randomness themselves.

docs.title: Randomness from the objective still matters
docs.text:
Even a deterministic optimizer becomes non-reproducible if the objective changes from call to call.

For COBRA, that can happen if stochastic components are refitted between objective evaluations.

The current optimization path normally works with already-fitted estimators, stored calibration geometry, and stored CV folds, so it does not refit the base estimator pool on every optimization step.

That design helps keep the objective stable within one fitted run.

docs.title: Random state in GradientCOBRA
docs.text:
A single:

GradientCOBRA(
    random_state=42,
)

currently influences at least:

automatic first-level splitter
KFoldCV construction
optimizer parameter dictionaries where forwarded.

It does not automatically seed every base estimator or SPSA.

docs.title: Random state in MixCOBRA
docs.text:
Similarly:

MixCOBRARegressor(
    random_state=42,
)

is passed into:

automatic split
KFoldCV
optimizer creation

but base-estimator and SPSA reproducibility remain separate concerns.

docs.title: Random state in CombinedClassifier
docs.text:
CombinedClassifier.random_state is used for:

automatic split
KFoldCV
optimizer configuration.

Its base classifier pool must still be considered separately if any configured classifier is stochastic.

docs.title: Reproducibility with custom split data
docs.text:
If you create a split externally, save the indices.

Example:

np.save(
    "train_idx.npy",
    train_idx,
)

np.save(
    "cal_idx.npy",
    cal_idx,
)

Then reconstruct:

X_train = X[
    train_idx
]

y_train = y[
    train_idx
]

X_cal = X[
    cal_idx
]

y_cal = y[
    cal_idx
]

and fit with:

model.fit(
    X_train,
    y_train,
    X_l=X_cal,
    y_l=y_cal,
)

This is more robust than relying only on a remembered random seed if external data ordering might later change.

docs.title: Data order is part of reproducibility
docs.text:
A fixed seed does not compensate for changing input row order.

Several random splitters begin with:

indices = np.arange(
    n
)

and then shuffle those indices.

If the rows associated with those indices change, the same shuffled index sequence selects different observations.

Preserve both:

seed
input ordering.

docs.title: Feature order is part of reproducibility
docs.text:
Distance-based COBRA behavior depends on coordinate order and meaning.

For precomputed predictions, preserve model-column order.

For raw input features, preserve feature order and preprocessing.

The package often converts tabular data to NumPy arrays, so external DataFrame column names are not a persistent source of alignment inside the fitted model.

docs.title: Precomputed prediction matrices
docs.text:
For reproducible precomputed workflows, save:

P_train
P_test
target vectors
prediction-source ordering
upstream model metadata.

Example:

np.save(
    "P_train.npy",
    P_train,
)

np.save(
    "P_test.npy",
    P_test,
)

and separately record:

prediction_sources = [
    "ridge",
    "random_forest",
    "svr",
]

docs.title: Prediction-space width affects normalization
docs.text:
GradientCOBRA and MixCOBRA scale prediction space using a denominator that contains:

M = number of prediction columns.

So adding, removing, or reordering estimator columns can change more than just the raw geometry.

It can also change the normalization constant.

Preserve the exact estimator/prediction-space definition across runs.

docs.title: Preserve normalization configuration
docs.text:
GradientCOBRA reproducibility depends on:

norm_constant
prediction-space width
the main y array.

MixCOBRA depends on:

norm_constant_x
norm_constant_y
prediction-space width
main X/y arrays.

Record those values explicitly if they differ from defaults.

docs.title: Explicit calibration arrays and normalization
docs.text:
The current source computes some normalization constants from the main X or y fit arguments even when explicit X_l/y_l calibration data are supplied.

So reproducibility requires preserving both:

training-side data
calibration-side data.

Changing only the training target scale can change the normalized calibration prediction geometry.

docs.title: Loss configuration
docs.text:
The optimizer's selected parameter can change when:

loss
loss_params

change.

For example:

MSE
MAE
Huber
Quantile

produce different CV objectives.

Record the exact configured loss and parameters.

docs.title: Kernel configuration
docs.text:
Preserve:

kernel
kernel_params

because the same distances can produce different weights.

Also preserve the adapter-related settings:

bandwidth candidates
alpha candidates
beta candidates
opt_method
optimizer.

docs.title: Distance configuration
docs.text:
Preserve:

distance
distance_params

including parameters such as:

p

for Minkowski distance.

Different geometry changes CV scores and selected optimization parameters even with identical random seeds.

docs.title: Cross-validation configuration
docs.text:
At minimum, preserve:

n_cv
random_state.

For lower-level custom CV use, also preserve:

CV class
shuffle behavior
test_size
other constructor parameters.

docs.title: Number of folds and data size
docs.text:
Changing:

n_cv

changes fold membership and therefore the objective.

Even with the same seed, a different fold count gives a different optimization problem.

docs.title: Software versions matter
docs.text:
The project source relies on:

NumPy
SciPy
scikit-learn
Joblib
Numba
pandas

in different components.

The source does not pin runtime versions inside fitted model objects.

For repeatable experiments across machines or time, preserve the environment outside the estimator.

Examples include:

requirements file
lock file
conda environment
container image
package version metadata.

docs.title: Floating-point reproducibility
docs.text:
The source performs many floating-point operations:

distance matrices
kernel transforms
means
dot products
optimizer finite differences.

The package does not promise bit-for-bit identical floating-point results across all hardware, BLAS libraries, thread counts, or dependency versions.

Use tolerance-based comparisons when validating numeric results:

np.allclose(
    a,
    b,
    rtol=...,
    atol=...,
)

rather than expecting byte-identical arrays in every environment.

docs.title: Parallel execution can affect practical reproducibility
docs.text:
The package parallelizes base-estimator tasks through Joblib when:

n_jobs != 1.

The returned prediction-space order follows estimator-list order, but underlying estimators or numerical libraries can have their own concurrency behavior.

For the most controlled debugging setup, use:

n_jobs=1

and explicitly seed stochastic estimators.

docs.title: Hamming distance uses Numba parallelism
docs.text:
The current Hamming implementation uses a Numba function with:

parallel=True

for its primary path.

That execution mode is independent of the estimator's:

n_jobs.

For ordinary integer/discrete mismatch counts, the computation is structurally simple, but this is another example of package-wide computation not controlled by one central concurrency setting.

docs.title: Reproducibility checklist for KFCProcedure
docs.text:
A source-aligned configuration might look like:

model = KFCRegressor(
    divergences=[
        "euclidean",
    ],
    local_model="random_forest_regressor",
    local_model_params={
        "random_state": 42,
    },
    combiner=prebuilt_combiner,
    random_state=42,
)

Important pieces to preserve:

input row order
random_state
divergence order
local model name
local model parameters
combiner configuration
n_clusters
max_iter
tol.

docs.title: Reproducibility checklist for GradientCOBRA
docs.text:
model = GradientCOBRA(
    estimators=[
        "linear_regression",
        "random_forest_regressor",
        "svr",
    ],
    estimators_params={
        "random_forest_regressor": {
            "random_state": 42,
        },
    },
    distance="euclidean",
    kernel="rbf",
    loss="mse",
    optimizer="grid",
    opt_method="grid",
    n_cv=5,
    n_jobs=1,
    random_state=42,
)

This controls the package-level split/CV seed and explicitly seeds the stochastic base estimator in this example.

docs.title: Reproducibility checklist for MixCOBRA
docs.text:
Preserve:

estimator list and order
estimator-specific seeds
random_state
distance
kernel
normalization settings
one_parameter
alpha/beta candidate arrays
optimizer and opt_method
n_cv
n_jobs.

For gradient optimization, also preserve:

gradient_method
eps
learning_rate
max_iter
tol
speed.

docs.title: Reproducibility checklist for CombinedClassifier
docs.text:
Preserve:

classifier pool and order
classifier-specific seeds
random_state
distance
kernel
aggregator
loss
bandwidth candidate list
n_cv
n_jobs
class encoding.

Class encoding matters especially because the current default loss is:

mse

on hard class labels.

docs.title: Class encoding is part of reproducibility
docs.text:
For the current CombinedClassifier default objective, class labels are used numerically by MSE.

Changing encoding from:

0, 1, 2

to:

0, 10, 20

changes the CV loss geometry even if class membership is otherwise identical.

Preserve the exact target representation.

docs.title: Inspect seeds after construction
docs.text:
KFC:

print(
    model.random_state
)

Standalone COBRA:

print(
    model.random_state
)

Fitted components can also be inspected individually where the source stores their seed.

docs.title: Compare KFC splits indirectly
docs.text:
KFCProcedure.fit() does not retain:

X_k
X_l
y_k
y_l

as top-level fitted attributes.

They are local variables inside fit().

Therefore the current source does not provide direct post-fit access to the exact top-level split arrays.

For strict experiment auditing, preserve external data and reproduce the same train_test_split() call yourself if you need explicit split indices.

docs.title: Compare COBRA splits directly
docs.text:
Standalone COBRA estimators do retain:

X_k_
y_k_
X_l_
y_l_.

So you can compare resolved datasets between runs:

np.array_equal(
    model_a.X_l_,
    model_b.X_l_,
)

docs.title: Compare prediction spaces
docs.text:
GradientCOBRA:

np.allclose(
    model_a.Y_l_norm_,
    model_b.Y_l_norm_,
)

CombinedClassifier:

np.array_equal(
    model_a.pred_l_,
    model_b.pred_l_,
)

MixCOBRA:

np.allclose(
    model_a.X_l_norm_,
    model_b.X_l_norm_,
)

np.allclose(
    model_a.Y_l_norm_,
    model_b.Y_l_norm_,
)

docs.title: Compare CV folds
docs.text:
for a, b in zip(
    model_a.cv_folds_,
    model_b.cv_folds_,
):
    assert np.array_equal(
        a.train_idx,
        b.train_idx,
    )

    assert np.array_equal(
        a.eval_idx,
        b.eval_idx,
    )

This isolates split/fold reproducibility from later optimization.

docs.title: Compare optimization results
docs.text:
GradientCOBRA:

print(
    model_a.bandwidth_,
    model_b.bandwidth_,
)

MixCOBRA:

print(
    model_a.optimization_outputs_[
        "params"
    ]
)

print(
    model_b.optimization_outputs_[
        "params"
    ]
)

Also compare:

optimization_outputs_[
    "history"
]

when debugging differences.

docs.title: Compare final predictions
docs.text:
For numeric regression:

np.allclose(
    model_a.predict(
        X_test
    ),
    model_b.predict(
        X_test
    ),
)

For hard classification:

np.array_equal(
    model_a.predict(
        X_test
    ),
    model_b.predict(
        X_test
    ),
)

docs.title: Debugging a reproducibility difference
docs.text:
A useful source-aligned sequence is:

1. compare input row and column order
2. compare first-level split or explicit calibration data
3. compare fitted base estimators / local models
4. compare prediction-space matrices
5. compare normalization constants
6. compare distance matrices
7. compare CV folds
8. compare optimizer history
9. compare selected parameters
10. compare final predictions.

This locates the first stage at which two runs diverge.

docs.title: Stage 1 — input identity
docs.text:
Check:

np.array_equal(
    X_a,
    X_b,
)

np.array_equal(
    y_a,
    y_b,
)

or use tolerance-based comparison for floating-point input pipelines.

docs.title: Stage 2 — resolved split
docs.text:
Standalone COBRA:

np.array_equal(
    model_a.X_k_,
    model_b.X_k_,
)

np.array_equal(
    model_a.X_l_,
    model_b.X_l_,
)

docs.title: Stage 3 — prediction space
docs.text:
GradientCOBRA:

np.allclose(
    model_a.Y_l_norm_,
    model_b.Y_l_norm_,
)

If this fails while the split matches, investigate base-estimator randomness or column configuration.

docs.title: Stage 4 — normalization constants
docs.text:
print(
    model_a.normalize_constant_,
    model_b.normalize_constant_,
)

or for MixCOBRA:

print(
    model_a.normalize_constant_x_,
    model_b.normalize_constant_x_,
)

print(
    model_a.normalize_constant_y_,
    model_b.normalize_constant_y_,
)

docs.title: Stage 5 — distance geometry
docs.text:
GradientCOBRA:

np.allclose(
    model_a.distance_matrix_,
    model_b.distance_matrix_,
)

MixCOBRA can compare its separate X/Y distance matrices.

docs.title: Stage 6 — CV folds
docs.text:
Inspect:

cv_folds_

as shown above.

If these differ with identical calibration data, investigate:

random_state
n_cv
CV implementation/version.

docs.title: Stage 7 — optimization history
docs.text:
For grid search, identical objective geometry should normally give identical candidate history.

For gradient mode, compare:

gradient_method
eps
learning_rate
tol
speed.

If using SPSA, remember the global NumPy RNG exception.

docs.title: random_state=None
docs.text:
When the user leaves:

random_state=None

different components follow the behavior of their underlying RNG APIs.

In practical terms, this does not provide the same reproducibility guarantee as a fixed integer seed.

For repeatable experiments, use an explicit integer wherever the source exposes one.

docs.title: Same integer does not imply one shared random stream
docs.text:
The package passes the same integer seed into several independently initialized random-number generators.

That means each component starts its own deterministic sequence.

It does not mean:

one global RNG is advanced from K-Step through CV and optimization.

This is often desirable because changing one component does not necessarily consume random numbers from another component's stream.

docs.text: Component Current RNG mechanism Uses estimator seed? KFC top-level split sklearn train_test_split Yes BregmanKMeans check_random_state Yes OverlapSplitter np.random.default_rng Yes RandomHoldoutSplitter sklearn train_test_split Yes KFoldCV np.random.RandomState Yes StratifiedKFoldCV np.random.default_rng Yes TimeSeriesCV none not needed Grid search deterministic enumeration not needed central/forward/complex gradient deterministic if objective is not needed parallel central gradient deterministic formula if objective is not needed SPSA gradient global np.random.choice No COBRA base estimators estimator-specific not automatically F-Step string local models injected when supported Yes C-Step string combiners injected, constructor-dependent Yes
