docs.title: Minimal reproducibility recipe
docs.text:
A compact source-aligned recipe is:

1. set an explicit model random_state;
2. explicitly seed stochastic base/local estimators;
3. use n_jobs=1 while debugging;
4. preserve exact row and feature/prediction-column order;
5. save explicit train/calibration indices when important;
6. preserve estimator/kernel/distance/loss/optimizer configuration;
7. avoid SPSA when model-level seed reproducibility is required, or account for
   its separate global NumPy RNG behavior;
8. record package and dependency versions;
9. compare intermediate fitted state when runs differ.

docs.title: Mental model
docs.text:
random_state makes several important package components repeatable, but reproducibility is a pipeline property rather than a single-seed switch.

For KFC:

\[ \boxed{ \text{seed} \rightarrow \text{data split} \rightarrow \text{clustering} \rightarrow \text{local models} \rightarrow \text{combiner} } \]

For standalone COBRA:

\[ \boxed{ \text{seed} \rightarrow \text{split} \rightarrow \text{CV folds} } \]

while:

\[ \boxed{ \text{base-estimator RNGs} } \]

and:

\[ \boxed{ \text{SPSA global RNG} } \]

remain separate concerns in the current source.

docs.title: Bregman Divergences
docs.text:
KFC uses Bregman divergences to construct several candidate clusterings of the same feature matrix.

Instead of assuming that every dataset should be partitioned with ordinary Euclidean geometry, the K-Step can fit one BregmanKMeans model for each selected divergence:

\[ \boxed{ X \rightarrow \left\{ D_{\text{Euclidean}}, D_{\text{GKL}}, D_{\text{Logistic}}, D_{\text{Itakura--Saito}} \right\} \rightarrow \text{candidate clusterings} } \]

The built-in divergence implementations live in:

kfc_procedure/core/clustering/divergences/

and are registered through:

BregmanDivergenceFactory

docs.title: What is a Bregman divergence?
docs.text:
The package defines a Bregman divergence from a convex differentiable generator \(\phi\) as

\[ D_\phi(x,y) = \phi(x) - \phi(y) - \left\langle \nabla\phi(y), x-y \right\rangle. \]

A Bregman divergence is a dissimilarity measure, but it is not generally a metric.

In particular, it does not have to satisfy

\[ D_\phi(x,y)=D_\phi(y,x), \]

and it does not have to satisfy the triangle inequality.

That asymmetry is important when interpreting Bregman clustering.

docs.title: Built-in divergences
docs.text:
Importing:

from kfc_procedure.core.clustering.divergences import (
    SquaredEuclidean,
    GKLDivergence,
    LogisticLoss,
    ItakuraSaito,
)

loads and registers all four built-in divergences.

Registry name Class Family Domain euclidean SquaredEuclidean Gaussian \(\mathbb{R}^d\) gkl GKLDivergence Poisson \((0,\infty)^d\) logistic LogisticLoss Bernoulli / Binomial \((0,1)^d\) is ItakuraSaito Exponential / Gamma \((0,\infty)^d\)

These are the names used by the K-Step:

divergences=[
    "euclidean",
    "gkl",
    "logistic",
    "is",
]

docs.title: Squared Euclidean
docs.text:
Use:

divergences=["euclidean"]

The implementation class is:

SquaredEuclidean

with:

name = "Euclidean"
family = "Gaussian"

docs.title: Generator
docs.text:
The source implements

\[ \phi(x) = \|x\|_2^2 = \sum_j x_j^2. \]

Its gradient is

\[ \nabla\phi(x) = 2x. \]

The resulting divergence is

\[ D(x,y) = \|x-y\|_2^2. \]

docs.title: Domain
docs.text:
Squared Euclidean divergence accepts the full real feature space:

\[ x\in\mathbb{R}^d. \]

The implementation's domain check simply returns:

True

so there is no positivity or interval restriction.

This makes it the safest built-in divergence for arbitrary real-valued features.

docs.title: Optimized distance computation
docs.text:
SquaredEuclidean overrides the generic Bregman formula and uses

\[ \|x-y\|_2^2 = \|x\|_2^2 - 2x^\top y + \|y\|_2^2. \]

The implementation computes the pairwise distance matrix using a matrix multiplication:

xy = X @ Y.T

rather than explicitly constructing an (n_samples, n_centroids, n_features) tensor.

This reduces peak memory usage for the Euclidean case.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
from kfc_procedure.core.clustering.divergences import (
    SquaredEuclidean,
)

div = SquaredEuclidean()

D = div.distance(
    X,
    centroids,
)

The result has shape:

(n_samples, n_centroids)

docs.title: Generalized Kullback–Leibler
docs.text:
Use:

divergences=["gkl"]

The class is:

GKLDivergence

with:

name = "GKL"
family = "Poisson"

The module also describes it as the generalized KL divergence or I-divergence.

docs.title: Divergence
docs.text:
The implemented pairwise divergence is

\[ D(x,y) = \sum_j \left[ x_j \log\left( \frac{x_j}{y_j} \right) - (x_j-y_j) \right]. \]

The class implementation uses the generator

\[ \phi(x) = \sum_j x_j\log x_j \]

with gradient

\[ \nabla\phi(x) = \log x + 1. \]

The module-level documentation also writes the generator with an additional linear \(-x_j\) term. That affine difference does not change the resulting Bregman divergence; the concrete phi() method in the current source returns \(\sum x_j\log x_j\).

docs.title: Domain
docs.text:
The implementation requires:

\[ x_j>0 \]

for every value.

The domain check is:

np.all(X > 0)

Therefore zero and negative feature values are rejected by BregmanKMeans.fit().

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
from kfc_procedure.core.clustering.divergences import (
    GKLDivergence,
)

div = GKLDivergence()

D = div.distance(
    X_positive,
    centroids_positive,
)

docs.title: Typical KFC configuration
docs.text:
model = KFCRegressor(
    divergences=["gkl"],
    local_model="ridge",
    combiner="gradientcobra",
    random_state=42,
)

The source associates GKL with the Poisson exponential family.

docs.title: Logistic divergence
docs.text:
Use:

divergences=["logistic"]

The implementation class is:

LogisticLoss

with:

name = "Logit"
family = "Bernoulli / Binomial"

docs.title: Generator
docs.text:
The implementation uses

\[ \phi(x) = \sum_j \left[ x_j\log x_j + (1-x_j)\log(1-x_j) \right]. \]

Its gradient is

\[ \nabla\phi(x) = \log x - \log(1-x). \]

docs.title: Divergence
docs.text:
The logistic Bregman divergence is

\[ D(x,y) = \sum_j \left[ x_j \log\left( \frac{x_j}{y_j} \right) + (1-x_j) \log\left( \frac{1-x_j}{1-y_j} \right) \right]. \]

The module describes this as the logistic or binary cross-entropy Bregman divergence.

docs.title: Domain
docs.text:
Every value must satisfy

\[ 0<x_j<1. \]

The exact domain check is:

np.all(
    (0 < X)
    & (X < 1)
)

Values equal to 0 or 1 are therefore outside the declared domain.

docs.title: Numerical handling of reference points
docs.text:
Inside distance(), the current source clips the reference matrix Y to

[1e-12, 1 - 1e-12]

before evaluating logarithms.

However, BregmanKMeans.fit() validates the training matrix against the strict \((0,1)\) domain before clustering.

Therefore the public clustering workflow should still be treated as requiring

\[ 0<X<1. \]

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
from kfc_procedure.core.clustering.divergences import (
    LogisticLoss,
)

div = LogisticLoss()

D = div.distance(
    X_unit_interval,
    centroids_unit_interval,
)

docs.title: Itakura–Saito
docs.text:
Use:

divergences=["is"]

The implementation class is:

ItakuraSaito

with:

name = "Ita"
family = "Exponential / Gamma"

The module describes the divergence as scale invariant and associates it with signal-processing and spectral-analysis settings.

docs.title: Generator
docs.text:
The generator is

\[ \phi(x) = -\sum_j\log x_j. \]

Its gradient is

\[ \nabla\phi(x) = -\frac{1}{x}. \]

docs.title: Divergence
docs.text:
The implementation computes

\[ D(x,y) = \sum_j \left[ \frac{x_j}{y_j} - \log\left( \frac{x_j}{y_j} \right) - 1 \right]. \]

docs.title: Domain
docs.text:
Every value must satisfy

\[ x_j>0. \]

The source uses:

np.all(X > 0)

for domain validation.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
from kfc_procedure.core.clustering.divergences import (
    ItakuraSaito,
)

div = ItakuraSaito()

D = div.distance(
    X_positive,
    centroids_positive,
)

docs.title: Domain requirements at a glance
docs.text:
Divergence Negative values Zero One Values \(>1\) Euclidean ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ GKL ✗ ✗ ✓ ✓ Logistic ✗ ✗ ✗ ✗ Itakura–Saito ✗ ✗ ✓ ✓

The strictest built-in domain is Logistic:

\[ 0<x<1. \]

Therefore if all four built-in divergences are selected together, the common valid domain is

\[ 0<x<1. \]

docs.title: Preparing data for all four divergences
docs.text:
For documentation examples, one simple preprocessing strategy is:

from sklearn.preprocessing import MinMaxScaler

eps = 1e-6

scaler = MinMaxScaler(
    feature_range=(
        eps,
        1.0 - eps,
    )
)

X_train_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(
    X_train
)

X_test_scaled = scaler.transform(
    X_test
)

Then:

model = KFCRegressor(
    divergences=[
        "euclidean",
        "gkl",
        "logistic",
        "is",
    ],
    local_model="ridge",
    combiner="gradientcobra",
    random_state=42,
)

model.fit(
    X_train_scaled,
    y_train,
)

Important

This is a preprocessing example, not an automatic transformation performed by kfc-procedure.

The package itself expects the supplied data to already satisfy each divergence's domain.

docs.title: Domain validation in BregmanKMeans
docs.text:
Before fitting, BregmanKMeans calls:

validate_divergence_domain(
    self.divergence,
    X,
)

The validator performs two checks.

First:

np.isfinite(X).all()

must be true.

If not, it raises:

[<divergence name>] Input contains NaN or Inf.

Second:

div.in_domain(X)

must be true.

Otherwise it raises:

[<divergence name>] Input outside valid domain.

docs.title: The base divergence API
docs.text:
All built-in divergences inherit from:

BaseBregmanDivergence

A divergence must implement:

in_domain(X)
phi(X)
grad_phi(X)

The base class provides:

distance(X, Y)
pairwise(X, Y)

for the generic Bregman formula unless a subclass overrides it.

docs.title: Constructor
docs.text:
The base constructor is:

BaseBregmanDivergence(
    validate_domain=True,
    **kwargs,
)

It stores:

self.validate_domain

and any extra keyword arguments as object attributes.

Current implementation detail

Although validate_domain is stored by the base class, the generic distance() implementation directly checks in_domain(X) and in_domain(Y).

The current distance code does not branch on self.validate_domain.

Likewise, BregmanKMeans.fit() always calls its separate domain validator.

Therefore setting:

validate_domain=False

does not currently disable all domain checks in the clustering workflow.

docs.title: Pairwise distance output
docs.text:
For:

X.shape == (n_samples, n_features)
Y.shape == (n_reference, n_features)

calling:

D = divergence.distance(
    X,
    Y,
)

returns:

(n_samples, n_reference)

with:

\[ D_{ij} = D_\phi(X_i,Y_j). \]

This is exactly the matrix used by BregmanKMeans when assigning samples to centroids.

docs.title: Numerical clipping
docs.text:
Every built-in distance() accepts:

clip=True

by default.

After computing the divergence matrix, the implementation applies:

np.maximum(
    D,
    0.0,
    out=D,
)

This prevents tiny floating-point errors from producing negative divergence values.

You can disable this in direct divergence calls:

D = div.distance(
    X,
    Y,
    clip=False,
)

KFC's clustering path uses the default clipped behavior.

docs.title: Caching in the base implementation
docs.text:
The generic BaseBregmanDivergence.distance() caches quantities that depend only on the reference matrix Y.

It stores:

_cache_key
_phi_Y
_grad_Y
_dot_Y

When the same reference array is reused, these values can avoid repeated generator and gradient calculations.

This is useful in iterative centroid-based algorithms where many samples are repeatedly compared with a fixed centroid matrix.

The built-in divergence classes currently override distance() with their own specialized formulas, so the base-class cache applies directly to custom divergences that use the inherited implementation.

docs.title: Divergences in Bregman K-means
docs.text:
BregmanKMeans replaces Euclidean distance in Lloyd's assignment step with the selected divergence.

For each iteration:

\[ c_i = \operatorname*{arg\,min}_k D_\phi(X_i,\mu_k). \]

Then cluster centroids are recomputed.

flowchart LR
    X["Samples X"]
    C["Current centroids"]
    D["Bregman distance matrix"]
    A["Nearest-centroid assignment"]
    M["Arithmetic mean update"]

    X --> D
    C --> D
    D --> A --> M --> C

docs.title: Centroid update in the current source
docs.text:
The current implementation updates every cluster centroid using the arithmetic mean:

\[ \mu_k = \frac{1}{|C_k|} \sum_{i\in C_k}X_i. \]

This update is used for all built-in divergence choices.

The source describes this as the Euclidean mean surrogate in the BregmanKMeans class documentation.

docs.title: Distortion
docs.text:
For fitted centroids, the clustering distortion is:

\[ \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \min_k D_\phi(X_i,\mu_k). \]

The selected run stores it as:

model.inertia_

Despite the inertia_ name, the value is an average minimum Bregman divergence in the current implementation, not necessarily Euclidean sum-of-squares.

docs.title: Multiple initializations
docs.text:
BregmanKMeans uses:

n_init=10

by default.

For every initialization:

  1. sample initial centroids from the training observations;
  2. run Lloyd iterations;
  3. compute final average distortion.

The run with the smallest final distortion is retained.

The K-Step currently does not expose n_init, so it uses this default.

docs.title: Initialization
docs.text:
When no explicit centroid matrix is provided, BregmanKMeans samples n_clusters training observations without replacement:

idx = rng.choice(
    X.shape[0],
    self.n_clusters,
    replace=False,
)

Although a source comment describes this as “k-means++ style,” the implemented behavior is random sample selection rather than probability-weighted k-means++ seeding.

docs.title: Empty clusters
docs.text:
If an iteration produces an empty cluster, the current implementation reinitializes its centroid using a random training sample:

centroids[k] = X[
    rng.randint(n)
]

This allows fitting to continue instead of dividing by zero.

docs.title: Factory usage
docs.text:
The registry is:

BregmanDivergenceFactory

You can create a built-in divergence by name:

from kfc_procedure.core.clustering.divergences import (
    BregmanDivergenceFactory,
)

div = BregmanDivergenceFactory.create(
    "euclidean"
)

Likewise:

gkl = BregmanDivergenceFactory.create(
    "gkl"
)

docs.title: Inspect registered divergences
docs.text:
The factory inherits the package's registry behavior.

Depending on which helper you want to use, you can inspect the available entries through the factory API.

The four built-ins registered when the divergence package is imported are:

euclidean
gkl
is
logistic

docs.title: Using divergence objects directly
docs.text:
The K-Step accepts an instance of BaseBregmanDivergence as well as a string identifier.

Example:

from kfc_procedure.core.clustering.divergences import (
    SquaredEuclidean,
)

div = SquaredEuclidean()

model = KFCRegressor(
    divergences=[
        div,
    ],
    local_model="ridge",
    combiner="gradientcobra",
)

When an object is supplied, K-Step uses the object directly rather than creating another instance through the factory.

docs.title: String names vs object names
docs.text:
The registry identifiers are:

euclidean
gkl
logistic
is

but the built-in class-level human-readable names are:

SquaredEuclidean -> Euclidean
GKLDivergence    -> GKL
LogisticLoss     -> Logit
ItakuraSaito     -> Ita

This distinction matters when inspecting K-Step dictionary keys.

With strings, keys follow the configured registry name.

With direct objects, K-Step derives its key from the object's name attribute and lowercases it.

Therefore object-based keys can be:

euclidean
gkl
logit
ita

rather than:

euclidean
gkl
logistic
is

docs.title: divergences_params
docs.text:
For string-based divergences, K-Step can pass constructor parameters through:

divergences_params

For example:

model = KFCRegressor(
    divergences=[
        "euclidean",
        "gkl",
    ],
    divergences_params={
        "euclidean": {
            "validate_domain": True,
        },
        "gkl": {
            "validate_domain": True,
        },
    },
    local_model="ridge",
    combiner="gradientcobra",
)

The base divergence constructor also accepts arbitrary **kwargs and stores them as attributes.

The built-in divergences do not currently define additional specialized constructor parameters.

docs.title: Custom divergence
docs.text:
A custom divergence should subclass:

BaseBregmanDivergence

and implement:

in_domain()
phi()
grad_phi()

For example:

import numpy as np

from kfc_procedure.core.clustering.divergences import (
    BaseBregmanDivergence,
)


class MyDivergence(
    BaseBregmanDivergence
):

    name = "MyDivergence"
    family = "Custom"

    def in_domain(
        self,
        X,
    ):
        X = np.asarray(X)

        return np.isfinite(
            X
        ).all()

    def phi(
        self,
        X,
    ):
        X = np.asarray(
            X,
            dtype=float,
        )

        # one value per observation
        ...

    def grad_phi(
        self,
        X,
    ):
        X = np.asarray(
            X,
            dtype=float,
        )

        # same feature dimension as X
        ...

If distance() is not overridden, the base class evaluates the standard Bregman expression.

docs.title: Register a custom divergence
docs.text:
To use a custom divergence by string name:

from kfc_procedure.core.clustering.divergences import (
    BregmanDivergenceFactory,
)


@BregmanDivergenceFactory.register(
    "my_divergence"
)
class MyDivergence(
    BaseBregmanDivergence
):
    ...

Then:

model = KFCRegressor(
    divergences=[
        "my_divergence",
    ],
    local_model="ridge",
    combiner="gradientcobra",
)

docs.title: Choosing a divergence
docs.text:
A practical source-aligned summary is:

  • Euclidean

    No domain restriction.

    Uses squared Euclidean separation.

    Registry: euclidean

  • GKL

    Requires strictly positive features.

    Associated with the Poisson family.

    Registry: gkl

  • Logistic

    Requires all values strictly between 0 and 1.

    Associated with Bernoulli / Binomial.

    Registry: logistic

  • Itakura–Saito

    Requires strictly positive features.

    Associated with Exponential / Gamma.

    Registry: is

docs.title: Several divergences vs one divergence
docs.text:
With one divergence:

divergences=[
    "euclidean",
]

KFC constructs one partition and one corresponding F-Step prediction column.

With four divergences:

divergences=[
    "euclidean",
    "gkl",
    "logistic",
    "is",
]

KFC constructs four independent clustering views.

The F-Step then generates four prediction columns, which the C-Step can aggregate.

The package does not select one “best” divergence during K-Step.

docs.title: Divergence choice and the C-Step
docs.text:
The K-Step only controls the candidate partitions.

Its output affects the C-Step indirectly:

divergence
    ↓
cluster assignment
    ↓
local model selected by F-Step
    ↓
divergence-specific prediction
    ↓
C-Step aggregation

So changing the divergence changes which local model handles each observation, which can change the final prediction even when the local estimator type and C-Step combiner remain fixed.

docs.title: NaN or infinity
docs.text:
Check:

import numpy as np

print(
    np.isfinite(
        X_train
    ).all()
)

Expected:

True

docs.title: GKL or Itakura–Saito
docs.text:
Check:

print(
    (
        X_train > 0
    ).all()
)

docs.title: Logistic
docs.text:
Check:

print(
    (
        (X_train > 0)
        &
        (X_train < 1)
    ).all()
)

docs.title: Inspect the actual divergence object
docs.text:
After fitting:

km = model.kstep_.models_[
    "euclidean"
]

print(
    km.divergence
)

print(
    km.divergence.name
)

print(
    km.divergence.family
)

docs.title: Quick reference
docs.text: Property Euclidean GKL Logistic Itakura–Saito Registry euclidean gkl logistic is Class name SquaredEuclidean GKLDivergence LogisticLoss ItakuraSaito Human name Euclidean GKL Logit Ita Family Gaussian Poisson Bernoulli / Binomial Exponential / Gamma Domain all real \(x>0\) \(0<x<1\) \(x>0\) Specialized distance() Yes Yes Yes Yes

docs.title: Mental model
docs.text:
A divergence defines what “closest cluster” means. KFC keeps several plausible definitions of closeness instead of committing to only one.

\[ \boxed{ \text{same observations} \rightarrow \text{different Bregman geometries} \rightarrow \text{different partitions} \rightarrow \text{different local predictions} } \]

docs.title: Aggregators
docs.text:
Aggregators are the final numerical step in the COBRA pipeline.

After a distance matrix has been transformed by a kernel, each query has one weight for each calibration observation. The aggregator combines those weights with the calibration targets or class labels.

\[ \boxed{ \text{distance} \rightarrow \text{kernel weights} \rightarrow \text{aggregator} \rightarrow \text{prediction} } \]

The current source provides two built-in aggregators:

weighted_mean
weighted_vote

implemented by:

WeightedMeanAggregator
WeightedVoteAggregator

under:

kfc_procedure/cobra/core/aggregators/
├── base.py
├── weighted_mean.py
└── weighted_vote.py

They are registered through:

AggregatorFactory

docs.title: Where aggregators sit in the pipeline
docs.text:
For one query, COBRA first computes a kernel-weight row:

\[ w = (w_1,\ldots,w_m), \]

where the \(m\) entries correspond to the calibration observations.

The aggregator then receives:

values
    calibration targets or labels

weights
    kernel similarities to those calibration observations

and returns one prediction.

flowchart LR
    Q["Query"]
    D["Distance to calibration data"]
    K["Kernel"]
    W["Weight vector"]
    V["Calibration values"]
    A["Aggregator"]
    Y["Prediction"]

    Q --> D --> K --> W
    W --> A
    V --> A
    A --> Y

docs.title: Built-in aggregators
docs.text:
Registry name Alias Class Task used by default weighted_mean wm WeightedMeanAggregator regression weighted_vote wv WeightedVoteAggregator classification

The factory itself does not attach explicit regression/classification categories to these registrations.

The task distinction comes from which estimator selects which aggregator by default.

docs.title: Default aggregator by estimator
docs.text:
The current high-level defaults are:

Estimator Default aggregator GradientCOBRA weighted_mean MixCOBRARegressor weighted_mean CombinedClassifier weighted_vote

So the normal mapping is:

regression
    -> weighted_mean

classification
    -> weighted_vote

docs.title: BaseAggregator
docs.text:
Every aggregator inherits:

BaseAggregator

The abstract interface centers on:

aggregate(
    values,
    weights=None,
    **kwargs,
)

The base class also provides:

aggregate_matrix(...)

for batch aggregation and defines:

aggregate_proba(...)

as an optional classification extension.

docs.title: aggregate()
docs.text:
The required method is:

aggregate(
    values: np.ndarray,
    weights: np.ndarray | None = None,
    **kwargs,
)

It aggregates one query.

Conceptually:

values  = calibration values
weights = one query's kernel-weight vector

and returns one scalar or class prediction.

docs.title: aggregate_matrix()
docs.text:
The base implementation supports batch prediction.

Its signature is:

aggregate_matrix(
    values,
    weights,
    fallback=None,
    **kwargs,
)

with:

values
    shared calibration values

weights
    matrix of shape
    (n_queries, n_calibration_samples)

The method applies:

aggregate(
    values,
    weights[i],
    fallback=fallback,
)

independently for each query row.

docs.title: Base batch validation
docs.text:
The current base implementation requires:

weights.ndim == 2

otherwise it raises:

ValueError:
weights must be 2D (n_queries, n_models), got ...

The terminology in the base docstring says n_models, but in the actual COBRA usage the second dimension corresponds to calibration observations.

docs.title: Base batch output dtype
docs.text:
The base class creates:

out = np.empty(
    W.shape[0],
    dtype=object,
)

fills it query by query, and finally returns:

np.asarray(out)

So the generic batch path supports either numeric or object-valued aggregate outputs.

WeightedVoteAggregator overrides this method with its own vectorized implementation.

docs.title: aggregate_proba()
docs.text:
The base class defines:

aggregate_proba(
    values,
    weights=None,
    classes=None,
    **kwargs,
)

but the default implementation raises:

NotImplementedError

Classification aggregators may override this method.

Both current built-ins define an aggregate_proba() implementation, although the regression weighted-mean version is only meaningful when the supplied values are already probability vectors.

docs.title: AggregatorFactory
docs.text:
Create a registered aggregator with:

from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.aggregators import (
    AggregatorFactory,
)

aggregator = AggregatorFactory.create(
    "weighted_mean"
)

or:

aggregator = AggregatorFactory.create(
    "weighted_vote"
)

docs.title: Aliases
docs.text:
The current registrations are:

@AggregatorFactory.register(
    "weighted_mean",
    "wm",
)

and:

@AggregatorFactory.register(
    "weighted_vote",
    "wv",
)

So these pairs are equivalent:

weighted_mean == wm
weighted_vote == wv

docs.title: Inspect available aggregators
docs.text:
print(
    AggregatorFactory.available()
)

The current registry should include:

weighted_mean
weighted_vote
wm
wv

after the aggregator package has been imported.

docs.title: Weighted mean aggregation
docs.text:
WeightedMeanAggregator is the default regression aggregator.

It is registered as:

weighted_mean
wm

The source formula is:

\[ \widehat y = \frac{ \sum_i w_i v_i }{ \sum_i w_i }. \]

Here:

  • \(v_i\) is a calibration target;
  • \(w_i\) is its kernel weight for the query.

docs.title: Single-query implementation
docs.text:
The implementation begins with:

V = np.asarray(
    values,
    dtype=float,
).reshape(-1)

So the target values are flattened into a one-dimensional numeric vector.

docs.title: Empty values
docs.text:
If:

V.size == 0

the source raises:

ValueError:
values cannot be empty

docs.title: No weights: arithmetic mean
docs.text:
If:

weights is None

the aggregator returns:

float(
    np.mean(V)
)

So without a weight vector:

\[ \widehat y = \frac1m \sum_i v_i. \]

docs.title: Default fallback
docs.text:
If:

fallback is None

the source computes:

fallback = float(
    np.mean(V)
)

Therefore the default fallback for a single weighted-mean call is the unweighted mean of the supplied values.

docs.title: Weight sanitization
docs.text:
Weights are converted with:

W = np.asarray(
    weights,
    dtype=float,
).reshape(-1)

then sanitized using:

np.nan_to_num(
    W,
    nan=0.0,
    posinf=0.0,
    neginf=0.0,
)

So:

NaN
+Inf
-Inf

weights are replaced with:

0

before aggregation.

docs.title: Important consequence
docs.text:
Non-finite weights do not directly propagate into the regression prediction.

They simply contribute zero weight.

This sanitization occurs inside:

WeightedMeanAggregator.aggregate()

docs.title: Zero denominator
docs.text:
The source computes:

denom = np.sum(W)

and checks:

np.isclose(
    denom,
    0.0,
)

If the total weight is effectively zero, the method returns:

fallback

instead of dividing by zero.

docs.title: Weighted result
docs.text:
Otherwise:

return float(
    np.dot(
        W,
        V,
    )
    / denom
)

which is exactly:

\[ \frac{w^\top v}{\sum_iw_i}. \]

docs.title: Direct weighted-mean example
docs.text:
import numpy as np

from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.aggregators import (
    WeightedMeanAggregator,
)


values = np.array([
    10.0,
    20.0,
    30.0,
])

weights = np.array([
    0.8,
    0.1,
    0.1,
])


aggregator = WeightedMeanAggregator()

prediction = aggregator.aggregate(
    values,
    weights,
)

print(
    prediction
)

The first calibration target contributes most strongly because it has the largest kernel weight.

docs.title: Regression fallback example
docs.text:
values = np.array([
    10.0,
    20.0,
    30.0,
])

weights = np.zeros(3)

prediction = aggregator.aggregate(
    values,
    weights,
    fallback=15.0,
)

Because:

np.sum(weights) == 0

the result is:

15.0

docs.title: Default fallback example
docs.text:
If no fallback is supplied:

prediction = aggregator.aggregate(
    values,
    weights,
)

the source uses:

np.mean(values)

which in this example is:

20.0

docs.title: GradientCOBRA regression aggregation
docs.text:
GradientCOBRA resolves its aggregator with:

AggregatorFactory.create(
    self.aggregator,
    **(
        self.aggregator_params
        or {}
    ),
)

Its default is:

weighted_mean

docs.title: GradientCOBRA cross-validation
docs.text:
During bandwidth evaluation:

preds = self.aggregator_.aggregate_matrix(
    values=y_train,
    weights=K_val_train,
    fallback=0.0,
)

So inside cross-validation the explicit fallback is:

0.0

rather than the local mean.

docs.title: GradientCOBRA final prediction
docs.text:
At prediction time:

preds = self.aggregator_.aggregate_matrix(
    values=self.y_l_,
    weights=K,
    fallback=self.global_mean_,
)

Therefore the final prediction fallback is:

global_mean_

when a query has effectively zero total kernel weight.

This distinction matters:

cross-validation fallback -> 0.0
final prediction fallback -> global calibration mean

docs.title: MixCOBRA regression aggregation
docs.text:
MixCOBRARegressor also defaults to:

weighted_mean

and uses the same batch aggregator.

During cross-validation:

fallback=0.0

is passed.

During final prediction:

fallback=self.global_mean_

is passed.

So its regression fallback pattern matches the current GradientCOBRA implementation.

docs.title: Weighted-mean batch aggregation
docs.text:
WeightedMeanAggregator does not override:

aggregate_matrix()

so it uses the base-class loop.

For:

weights.shape == (
    n_queries,
    n_calibration,
)

the base code performs one:

aggregate(...)

call per query.

Conceptually:

\[ \hat y_q = \frac{ \sum_i W_{qi}v_i }{ \sum_i W_{qi} } \]

for every query \(q\).

docs.title: Weighted-mean probability aggregation
docs.text:
WeightedMeanAggregator also defines:

aggregate_proba()

The source explicitly notes that this is only meaningful when:

values already represent probabilities

docs.title: Probability input shape
docs.text:
Here values is not treated as a one-dimensional target vector.

The code uses:

V = np.asarray(
    values,
    dtype=float,
)

without flattening.

A natural expected shape is:

(n_items, n_classes)

docs.title: No weights
docs.text:
If:

weights is None

the method returns:

np.mean(
    V,
    axis=0,
)

which averages the supplied probability vectors class by class.

docs.title: With weights
docs.text:
Weights are converted and sanitized:

W = np.asarray(
    weights,
    dtype=float,
)

W = np.nan_to_num(
    W,
    nan=0.0,
    posinf=0.0,
    neginf=0.0,
)

Then they are normalized with:

W = W / (
    np.sum(W)
    + 1e-12
)

and the result is:

np.sum(
    W[:, None]
    * V,
    axis=0,
)

docs.title: Probability normalization caveat
docs.text:
Because the source divides by:

np.sum(W) + 1e-12

rather than explicitly falling back when the sum is zero, an all-zero weight vector produces a zero probability vector rather than a fallback distribution.

The method does not apply a final probability renormalization after summing.

docs.title: Weighted vote aggregation
docs.text:
WeightedVoteAggregator is the default classifier aggregator.

It is registered as:

weighted_vote
wv

The single-query rule is:

\[ \widehat c = \operatorname*{arg\,max}_c \sum_i w_i \mathbf{1}(v_i=c). \]

Here:

  • \(v_i\) is a calibration class label;
  • \(w_i\) is the corresponding query-to-calibration kernel weight.

docs.title: Unweighted vote
docs.text:
If:

weights is None

the source computes:

classes, counts = np.unique(
    V,
    return_counts=True,
)

and returns:

classes[
    np.argmax(counts)
]

So this path is an ordinary majority vote over the supplied values.

docs.title: Tie behavior without weights
docs.text:
np.unique() returns classes in sorted order for sortable data.

np.argmax(counts) selects the first maximum.

Therefore in an equal-count tie, the current unweighted path tends to select the first class in the np.unique() ordering.

The package does not implement a separate explicit tie-policy parameter.

docs.title: Weighted vote input validation
docs.text:
The values are flattened:

V = np.asarray(
    values
).reshape(-1)

If:

V.size == 0

the method raises:

ValueError:
values cannot be empty

docs.title: Weight length validation
docs.text:
Weights are converted with:

W = np.asarray(
    weights,
    dtype=float,
).reshape(-1)

Then the source requires:

W.size == V.size

otherwise it raises:

ValueError:
weights and values must match length

docs.title: Non-finite weighted-vote weights
docs.text:
The implementation computes:

mask = np.isfinite(W)

then:

V, W = V[mask], W[mask]

So calibration observations with:

NaN
+Inf
-Inf

weights are removed entirely from the voting calculation.

This differs from WeightedMeanAggregator, which converts those weights to zero.

docs.title: Weighted class scores
docs.text:
After filtering, the source obtains:

classes = np.unique(V)

and constructs a one-hot matrix:

one_hot = (
    V[:, None]
    ==
    classes[None, :]
).astype(float)

If there are:

M calibration values
C observed classes

the one-hot matrix has shape:

(M, C)

docs.title: Score calculation
docs.text:
The class scores are:

scores = W @ one_hot

which gives one total weight per class:

\[ s_c = \sum_i w_i \mathbf{1}(v_i=c). \]

The final class is:

classes[
    np.argmax(scores)
]

docs.title: Direct weighted-vote example
docs.text:
import numpy as np

from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.aggregators import (
    WeightedVoteAggregator,
)


values = np.array([
    0,
    1,
    1,
    0,
])

weights = np.array([
    0.1,
    0.4,
    0.3,
    0.2,
])


aggregator = WeightedVoteAggregator()

prediction = aggregator.aggregate(
    values,
    weights,
)

print(
    prediction
)

Class 1 receives:

0.4 + 0.3 = 0.7

while class 0 receives:

0.1 + 0.2 = 0.3

so the result is:

1

docs.title: Negative weights
docs.text:
The source does not constrain weighted-vote weights to be non-negative.

If the supplied kernel or custom weighting stage produces negative finite values, those values participate directly in:

W @ one_hot

and can reduce a class score.

The built-in similarity kernels normally return non-negative outputs, but the aggregator itself does not enforce that assumption.

docs.title: Empty data after finite-weight filtering
docs.text:
There is an important edge case in the current source.

The method checks:

V.size == 0

before removing non-finite weights.

If every weight is non-finite, then:

V, W = V[mask], W[mask]

can produce empty arrays afterward.

The source does not perform a second empty check at that point.

Subsequent operations such as:

np.argmax(scores)

can therefore fail.

This is a current implementation edge case rather than a documented fallback behavior.

docs.title: Weighted-vote batch aggregation
docs.text:
Unlike WeightedMeanAggregator, WeightedVoteAggregator overrides:

aggregate_matrix()

with a vectorized implementation.

Its inputs are:

values
    shape (n_calibration,)

weights
    shape (n_queries, n_calibration)

docs.title: Batch implementation
docs.text:
The source computes the class one-hot matrix once:

classes = np.unique(V)

one_hot = (
    V[:, None]
    ==
    classes[None, :]
).astype(float)

Then all query scores are computed with:

scores = W @ one_hot

giving:

(n_queries, n_classes)

Finally:

classes[
    np.argmax(
        scores,
        axis=1,
    )
]

returns one class per query.

docs.title: Batch validation
docs.text:
The override checks only:

W.ndim == 2

and raises:

ValueError:
weights must be 2D, got ...

if not.

It does not explicitly check:

W.shape[1] == len(values)

before matrix multiplication.

A mismatch will therefore fail through NumPy's matrix multiplication rules.

docs.title: Batch path does not filter non-finite weights
docs.text:
The single-query:

aggregate()

filters non-finite weights.

But the vectorized:

aggregate_matrix()

does not apply:

np.isfinite()

or:

np.nan_to_num()

before:

W @ one_hot

This means single and batch weighted-vote behavior differs for non-finite weights.

Current source inconsistency

WeightedVoteAggregator.aggregate() removes non-finite weights.

WeightedVoteAggregator.aggregate_matrix() uses the weight matrix directly.

Non-finite values can therefore propagate differently depending on which method is called.

docs.title: CombinedClassifier uses single weighted vote
docs.text:
The current CombinedClassifier does not use the vectorized aggregate_matrix() path for ordinary hard-label prediction.

Instead, it iterates over query rows and calls:

self.aggregator_.aggregate(
    self.y_l_,
    w,
)

for each query.

Therefore the single-query finite-weight filtering logic applies to the main CombinedClassifier hard-prediction path.

docs.title: CombinedClassifier zero-weight fallback
docs.text:
Before calling the aggregator, the classifier checks:

if np.sum(w) <= 0:
    outputs.append(
        self.global_majority_class_
    )

Otherwise it calls:

self.aggregator_.aggregate(
    self.y_l_,
    w,
)

So an all-zero or non-positive-sum kernel row is handled by CombinedClassifier itself rather than by WeightedVoteAggregator.

docs.title: CombinedClassifier cross-validation fallback
docs.text:
During cross-validation, the source similarly performs:

if np.sum(w) <= 0:
    pred = self.global_majority_class_
else:
    pred = self.aggregator_.aggregate(
        y_train,
        w,
    )

Thus its fallback class is the global majority class computed by the fitted classifier.

docs.title: Probability aggregation in WeightedVoteAggregator
docs.text:
The current:

aggregate_proba()

implementation deserves special attention.

The method receives:

values
weights
classes

but the source does not actually use:

weights

when constructing the probabilities.

docs.title: Current implementation
docs.text:
The method computes:

V = np.asarray(
    values
).reshape(-1)

Then:

if classes is None:
    classes = np.unique(V)

and:

one_hot = (
    V[:, None]
    ==
    classes[None, :]
).astype(float)

Next:

probs = one_hot.mean(
    axis=0
)

and finally:

return probs / (
    np.sum(probs)
    + 1e-12
)

docs.title: Consequence of ignoring weights
docs.text:
For values:

[0, 0, 1]

the returned class frequencies are approximately:

class 0 -> 2/3
class 1 -> 1/3

regardless of whether the kernel weights are:

[0.99, 0.01, 0.00]

or:

[0.00, 0.01, 0.99]

because the current method does not use the supplied weight vector.

Current source behavior

WeightedVoteAggregator.aggregate_proba() currently returns normalized unweighted class frequencies.

It does not compute weighted class probabilities from the provided kernel weights.

docs.title: Effect on CombinedClassifier.predict_proba()
docs.text:
CombinedClassifier.predict_proba() computes the query kernel row:

w = K[i]

and then calls:

self.aggregator_.aggregate_proba(
    values=self.y_l_,
    weights=w,
    classes=classes,
)

However, with the current default:

weighted_vote

the weights=w argument is ignored by aggregate_proba().

Therefore non-fallback CombinedClassifier.predict_proba() rows are based on the class distribution of:

y_l_

rather than query-specific kernel weighting.

docs.title: Zero-weight probability fallback
docs.text:
Before calling aggregate_proba(), CombinedClassifier checks:

if np.sum(w) <= 0:

and sets probability 1.0 on:

global_majority_class_

for that query.

So the current probability behavior is:

zero/non-positive kernel sum
    -> one-hot global-majority fallback

positive kernel sum
    -> unweighted calibration class frequencies

with the default weighted-vote aggregator.

docs.title: aggregate_proba_batch()
docs.text:
WeightedVoteAggregator also defines:

aggregate_proba_batch()

This method does use the weight matrix.

It computes:

scores = W @ one_hot

then:

scores / (
    np.sum(
        scores,
        axis=1,
        keepdims=True,
    )
    + 1e-12
)

So batch probability aggregation is weighted.

docs.title: Current API mismatch
docs.text:
The base BaseAggregator class does not define:

aggregate_proba_batch()

as part of its abstract or shared interface.

CombinedClassifier also does not call it in its standard probability path.

Therefore the current weighted probability behavior implemented in aggregate_proba_batch() is not used by the normal CombinedClassifier predict_proba() loop.

docs.title: Probability batch zero-score behavior
docs.text:
If one query has all zero weighted class scores:

scores[row] == 0

then division by:

sum(scores) + 1e-12

returns an all-zero probability row.

There is no majority-class fallback inside:

aggregate_proba_batch()

itself.

docs.title: Aggregator configuration
docs.text:
The high-level COBRA estimators accept:

aggregator

and:

aggregator_params

For example:

from kfc_procedure.cobra import GradientCOBRA

model = GradientCOBRA(
    aggregator="weighted_mean",
)

or:

from kfc_procedure.cobra import CombinedClassifier

classifier = CombinedClassifier(
    aggregator="weighted_vote",
)

docs.title: Current built-in aggregator parameters
docs.text:
The two concrete built-ins do not define custom __init__() methods.

So the current source exposes no specialized constructor parameters for:

weighted_mean
weighted_vote

Although the high-level estimators accept:

aggregator_params

passing arbitrary parameters to either built-in can fail through the factory constructor call because the classes do not define corresponding constructor arguments.

docs.title: Inspect the fitted aggregator
docs.text:
After fitting a COBRA estimator:

print(
    model.aggregator_
)

For regression, the default type is:

WeightedMeanAggregator

For classification:

WeightedVoteAggregator

docs.title: Direct factory example
docs.text:
from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.aggregators import (
    AggregatorFactory,
)

mean_aggregator = AggregatorFactory.create(
    "wm"
)

vote_aggregator = AggregatorFactory.create(
    "wv"
)

docs.title: Aggregation values are calibration targets, not base-model predictions
docs.text:
A subtle but important distinction:

The aggregator in GradientCOBRA or CombinedClassifier usually does not aggregate the original base-estimator prediction columns directly.

Instead:

  1. prediction-space representations determine distances;
  2. distances produce kernel weights over calibration observations;
  3. the aggregator combines the calibration targets or labels.

For regression:

values=self.y_l_

For classification:

values=self.y_l_

The difference is the type of values and the aggregation rule.

docs.title: Regression example
docs.text:
Suppose one query has kernel weights:

[0.8, 0.1, 0.1]

over calibration targets:

[10, 20, 30]

Then weighted mean returns:

\[ \frac{ 0.8(10)+0.1(20)+0.1(30) }{ 0.8+0.1+0.1 } = 13. \]

docs.title: Classification example
docs.text:
Suppose one query has weights:

[0.1, 0.4, 0.3, 0.2]

over labels:

[0, 1, 1, 0]

Then class scores are:

\[ s_0 = 0.1+0.2 = 0.3 \]

and:

\[ s_1 = 0.4+0.3 = 0.7. \]

The weighted-vote output is class:

1

docs.title: Weight normalization
docs.text:
The two built-ins treat weight normalization differently.

WeightedMeanAggregator.aggregate() does not explicitly normalize W first.

Instead it computes:

dot(W, V) / sum(W)

which is algebraically equivalent to using normalized weights when the sum is nonzero.

WeightedVoteAggregator.aggregate() does not normalize weights at all because multiplying all class weights by the same positive constant leaves:

argmax

unchanged.

docs.title: Kernel weights need not sum to one
docs.text:
The kernel layer can return arbitrary non-negative similarity values.

For example:

[0.92, 0.36, 0.08]

The aggregators handle those raw values directly.

No separate normalization step is required before:

weighted_mean
weighted_vote

for hard prediction.

docs.title: Compact kernels and aggregator fallback
docs.text:
Compact kernels such as:

epanechnikov
biweight
triweight
triangular
cobra

can produce all-zero query rows.

This makes fallback behavior particularly important.

For regression:

GradientCOBRA / MixCOBRA
    -> global_mean_ during final prediction

For classification:

CombinedClassifier
    -> global_majority_class_

The fallback behavior belongs partly to the estimator and partly to the aggregator.

docs.title: Naive kernel interaction
docs.text:
The source's:

naive

kernel returns the adapted distance unchanged.

That means larger distances become larger "weights."

The aggregators do not know whether their input came from a proper similarity kernel.

They simply consume the numeric weights they are given.

So with a naive kernel, weighted mean and weighted vote will give more influence to larger distance values unless some earlier transformation changes them.

This follows directly from the current component separation.

docs.title: Custom aggregator
docs.text:
A custom aggregator should subclass:

BaseAggregator

and implement:

aggregate()

The base batch implementation can then be inherited if query-by-query looping is acceptable.

Example:

import numpy as np

from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.aggregators import (
    BaseAggregator,
    AggregatorFactory,
)


@AggregatorFactory.register(
    "median"
)
class MedianAggregator(
    BaseAggregator
):

    def aggregate(
        self,
        values,
        weights=None,
        **kwargs,
    ):
        values = np.asarray(
            values,
            dtype=float,
        )

        return float(
            np.median(
                values
            )
        )

Then:

model = GradientCOBRA(
    aggregator="median",
)

can resolve it through the normal factory.

docs.title: Custom weighted regression aggregator
docs.text:
For example:

@AggregatorFactory.register(
    "positive_weighted_mean"
)
class PositiveWeightedMean(
    BaseAggregator
):

    def aggregate(
        self,
        values,
        weights=None,
        fallback=None,
        **kwargs,
    ):
        V = np.asarray(
            values,
            dtype=float,
        ).reshape(-1)

        if weights is None:
            return float(
                np.mean(V)
            )

        W = np.maximum(
            np.asarray(
                weights,
                dtype=float,
            ).reshape(-1),
            0.0,
        )

        denom = np.sum(W)

        if np.isclose(
            denom,
            0.0,
        ):
            return (
                float(np.mean(V))
                if fallback is None
                else fallback
            )

        return float(
            W @ V
            / denom
        )

docs.title: Custom classification aggregator
docs.text:
A custom classifier aggregator can implement both:

aggregate()

and:

aggregate_proba()

Example interface:

class MyVoteAggregator(
    BaseAggregator
):

    def aggregate(
        self,
        values,
        weights=None,
        **kwargs,
    ):
        ...

    def aggregate_proba(
        self,
        values,
        weights=None,
        classes=None,
        **kwargs,
    ):
        ...

This is the appropriate extension point if query-specific weighted probabilities are required.

docs.title: Implementing weighted probabilities correctly
docs.text:
A custom probability aggregator can compute:

\[ p(c) = \frac{ \sum_i w_i \mathbf{1}(v_i=c) }{ \sum_iw_i }. \]

For example:

def aggregate_proba(
    self,
    values,
    weights=None,
    classes=None,
    **kwargs,
):
    V = np.asarray(
        values
    ).reshape(-1)

    if classes is None:
        classes = np.unique(V)

    classes = np.asarray(
        classes
    )

    if weights is None:
        W = np.ones(
            len(V),
            dtype=float,
        )
    else:
        W = np.asarray(
            weights,
            dtype=float,
        ).reshape(-1)

    scores = np.array([
        np.sum(
            W[
                V == c
            ]
        )
        for c in classes
    ])

    total = np.sum(scores)

    if np.isclose(
        total,
        0.0,
    ):
        return np.zeros(
            len(classes),
            dtype=float,
        )

    return scores / total

This is an extension example; it is not what the current built-in aggregate_proba() implementation does.

docs.title: Custom batch optimization
docs.text:
If a custom aggregator can be vectorized efficiently, override:

aggregate_matrix()

instead of inheriting the base Python loop.

WeightedVoteAggregator demonstrates this pattern.

Likewise, a classification aggregator may define a custom batch probability method, although the current base interface does not standardize one.

docs.text:
values:
    (n_calibration,)

weights:
    (n_calibration,)

returns:

scalar

docs.title: Batch regression queries
docs.text:
values:
    (n_calibration,)

weights:
    (n_queries, n_calibration)

returns:

(n_queries,)

docs.text:
values:
    (n_calibration,)

weights:
    (n_calibration,)

one class label

docs.title: Classification probabilities
docs.text:
values:
    calibration class labels

weights:
    one query's calibration weights

classes:

returns:

(n_classes,)

for the current WeightedVoteAggregator.aggregate_proba() API.

docs.text:
print(
    model.y_l_

docs.title: Inspect kernel weights

print(

A near-zero total can trigger a fallback in weighted mean.

docs.title: Reproduce one prediction

prediction = model.aggregator_.aggregate(

docs.title: Inspect calibration labels

docs.text:
values = model.y_l_
weights = K[0]

classes = np.unique(
    values

scores = {
    c: weights[
        values == c
    ].sum()
    for c in classes
}

print(
    scores

Compare the largest score with:

docs.title: Debugging probabilities
docs.text:
For the current built-in weighted-vote probability method:

proba = model.aggregator_.aggregate_proba(
    values=model.y_l_,
    weights=K[0],
    classes=model.classes_,
)

Then compare with unweighted calibration class frequencies:

freq = np.array([
    np.mean(
        model.y_l_ == c
    )
    for c in model.classes_
])

print(
    proba
)

print(
    freq

With the current implementation, these should match apart from the final tiny 1e-12 normalization adjustment.

docs.text:
WeightedMeanAggregator.aggregate() flattens both arrays but does not explicitly check:

len(values)
==

If they differ, the later:

np.dot(

operation raises through NumPy.

filters non-finite weights.

So:

currently has little practical use with the two built-in aggregator classes.

It remains useful as an extension mechanism for custom registered aggregators.
