docs.title: Mental model
docs.text:
The kernel decides how strongly each calibration observation should influence the query; the aggregator decides how those weighted calibration values become the final prediction.

For regression:

\[ \boxed{ (w_i,y_i) \rightarrow \frac{\sum_iw_iy_i}{\sum_iw_i} } \]

For classification:

\[ \boxed{ (w_i,c_i) \rightarrow \operatorname*{arg\,max}_c \sum_i w_i \mathbf{1}(c_i=c) } \]

The current source implements these two hard-prediction rules directly, while its classification probability path has a separate implementation caveat: WeightedVoteAggregator.aggregate_proba() currently ignores the supplied weights.

docs.title: Cross-validation
docs.text:
Cross-validation in the COBRA subsystem is used primarily to evaluate aggregation hyperparameters such as:

bandwidth
alpha
beta

on the aggregation/calibration dataset.

It is separate from the earlier train/calibration split described in Data Splitting.

The current source provides three registered cross-validation strategies:

kfold
stratified_kfold
time_series
tscv

implemented under:

kfc_procedure/cobra/core/cv/
├── base.py
├── kfold.py
├── stratified_kfold.py
└── time_series.py

and resolved through:

CVFactory

docs.title: Where cross-validation sits
docs.text:
COBRA training has two different partitioning levels.

First, the data can be separated into:

X_k, y_k
    base-estimator training data

X_l, y_l
    aggregation/calibration data

Then cross-validation operates inside the calibration side while tuning COBRA hyperparameters.

flowchart TD
    D["Training data"]
    S["Train / calibration split"]

    K["X_k, y_k"]
    L["X_l, y_l"]

    E["Fit base estimators"]
    P["Build calibration prediction space"]

    CV["Cross-validation folds on calibration data"]
    O["Optimize bandwidth / alpha / beta"]

    D --> S
    S --> K
    S --> L

    K --> E
    E --> P
    L --> P

    P --> CV
    L --> CV
    CV --> O

So:

data splitting

and:

cross-validation

are different operations in the current architecture.

docs.title: Why COBRA cross-validation is used
docs.text:
The source-level objective is not to refit the original base estimators for every fold.

Instead, COBRA first constructs the calibration representation and its pairwise distance matrix.

For a candidate hyperparameter setting, it:

  1. adapts the stored distance matrix;
  2. applies the kernel;
  3. extracts validation-to-training kernel blocks;
  4. aggregates the calibration targets;
  5. evaluates a loss;
  6. averages the fold losses.

Conceptually:

\[ \boxed{ \text{candidate parameter} \rightarrow \text{kernel matrix} \rightarrow \text{fold predictions} \rightarrow \text{fold loss} \rightarrow \text{mean CV loss} } \]

docs.title: BaseCrossValidator
docs.text:
All built-in cross-validation classes inherit:

BaseCrossValidator

The abstract interface defines:

split(
    x,
    y,
    *,
    groups=None,
)

and:

get_n_splits()

The split() method yields:

SplitIndices

objects.

docs.title: SplitIndices
docs.text:
Each fold is represented by:

SplitIndices(
    train_idx=...,
    eval_idx=...,
    fold_id=...,
)

The fields are:

train_idx
    indices used as the fold's aggregation-training subset

eval_idx
    indices used as the fold's validation subset

fold_id
    integer fold identifier

For the built-in cross-validation classes:

fold_id

starts at:

0

and increases sequentially.

docs.title: CVFactory
docs.text:
Cross-validation implementations are registered with:

CVFactory

which inherits the package's common:

BaseFactory

Create a CV strategy with:

from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.cv import (
    CVFactory,
)

cv = CVFactory.create(
    "kfold",
    n_splits=5,
    random_state=42,
)

docs.title: Inspect available strategies
docs.text:
print(
    CVFactory.available()
)

The current source registers:

kfold
stratified_kfold
time_series
tscv

where:

time_series
tscv

are aliases for the same class.

docs.title: KFoldCV
docs.text:
The default cross-validator used by the current main COBRA estimators is:

KFoldCV

registered as:

kfold

Its constructor is:

KFoldCV(
    n_splits=5,
    shuffle=True,
    random_state=None,
)

docs.title: K-fold behavior
docs.text:
The implementation:

  1. creates all sample indices;
  2. optionally shuffles them;
  3. distributes them round-robin across n_splits lists;
  4. uses each list once as validation data;
  5. concatenates the other lists as training data.

The source does not delegate to scikit-learn's KFold.

It implements its own fold assignment.

docs.title: K-fold index construction
docs.text:
First:

n = len(x)

indices = np.arange(n)

Then:

rng = np.random.RandomState(
    self.random_state
)

If:

self.shuffle

is true:

indices = rng.permutation(
    indices
)

docs.title: Round-robin fold assignment
docs.text:
The source constructs:

folds = [
    []
    for _
    in range(
        self.n_splits
    )
]

and then:

for i, idx in enumerate(
    indices
):
    folds[
        i % self.n_splits
    ].append(
        idx
    )

So observations are distributed cyclically across folds.

This differs in implementation detail from simply cutting a shuffled index array into contiguous chunks.

docs.title: Example K-fold assignment
docs.text:
Suppose:

indices = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]
n_splits = 3
shuffle = False

The current algorithm produces:

fold 0 = [0, 3, 6]
fold 1 = [1, 4, 7]
fold 2 = [2, 5]

because assignment is based on:

i % n_splits

docs.title: K-fold train and validation indices
docs.text:
For each fold:

val_idx = folds[i]

and:

train_idx = np.concatenate([
    folds[j]
    for j
    in range(
        self.n_splits
    )
    if j != i
])

Then the training indices are sorted:

train_idx = np.sort(
    train_idx
)

The validation indices are not explicitly sorted after shuffling.

docs.title: Consequence of sorting only training indices
docs.text:
With:

shuffle=True

the validation array retains the order produced by the shuffled round-robin assignment.

The training array is sorted back into ascending original-index order.

This does not change which observations belong to each set, but it is an exact behavior of the current implementation.

docs.title: K-fold reproducibility
docs.text:
KFoldCV uses:

np.random.RandomState(
    random_state
)

rather than:

np.random.default_rng(...)

With the same input order, n_splits, and seed, the fold assignment is reproducible.

docs.title: Disable K-fold shuffling
docs.text:
cv = KFoldCV(
    n_splits=5,
    shuffle=False,
)

Then the original row order is distributed round-robin among folds.

This does not produce contiguous validation blocks.

For temporal data, use TimeSeriesCV rather than assuming KFoldCV(shuffle=False) creates chronological windows.

docs.title: get_n_splits()
docs.text:
KFoldCV defines:

get_n_splits(
    x=None,
    y=None,
)

and returns:

self.n_splits

The optional x and y parameters are ignored.

docs.title: K-fold direct example
docs.text:
from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.cv import (
    KFoldCV,
)

cv = KFoldCV(
    n_splits=5,
    shuffle=True,
    random_state=42,
)

for fold in cv.split(
    X,
    y,
):
    print(
        fold.fold_id,
        fold.train_idx,
        fold.eval_idx,
    )

docs.title: StratifiedKFoldCV
docs.text:
The source also provides:

StratifiedKFoldCV

registered as:

stratified_kfold

Its purpose is to distribute each class across folds.

The constructor is:

StratifiedKFoldCV(
    n_splits=5,
    random_state=None,
)

There is no separate:

shuffle=

parameter.

The class always shuffles class-specific indices internally.

docs.title: Stratified construction
docs.text:
The implementation converts:

x
y

with:

np.asarray(...)

then creates:

rng = np.random.default_rng(
    self.random_state
)

Next it builds a dictionary:

class_map = {}

mapping each observed label to the list of row indices belonging to that class.

docs.title: Per-class split
docs.text:
For each class:

idxs = np.array(
    idxs
)

rng.shuffle(
    idxs
)

parts = np.array_split(
    idxs,
    self.n_splits,
)

Then part i for every class is appended to fold i.

So every fold receives approximately:

\[ \frac{n_c}{K} \]

observations from class \(c\), subject to integer division.

docs.title: Stratified example
docs.text:
Suppose:

class 0 has 6 observations
class 1 has 3 observations
n_splits = 3

Then each fold receives approximately:

2 class-0 observations
1 class-1 observation

after the within-class shuffling.

This is the source mechanism behind its class-distribution preservation.

docs.title: Stratified train and validation indices
docs.text:
After building all folds:

val_idx = folds[i]

and:

train_idx = np.concatenate([
    folds[j]
    for j
    in range(
        self.n_splits
    )
    if j != i
])

Unlike KFoldCV, the current stratified implementation does not sort the training indices before yielding them.

docs.title: Stratified reproducibility
docs.text:
StratifiedKFoldCV uses:

np.random.default_rng(
    self.random_state
)

which differs from the RandomState API used by KFoldCV.

A fixed seed makes the source implementation reproducible, but the exact permutation sequence should not be assumed to match KFoldCV or scikit-learn splitters using a different RNG API.

docs.title: TimeSeriesCV
docs.text:
Temporal cross-validation is implemented by:

TimeSeriesCV

registered under:

time_series
tscv

Its constructor is:

TimeSeriesCV(
    n_splits=5,
    test_size=None,
)

It does not shuffle data and does not accept random_state.

docs.title: Time-series design
docs.text:
The source uses expanding training windows.

For each split:

training:
    starts at index 0
    grows forward

validation:
    follows immediately after training

Conceptually:

fold 0
train: [------]
valid:       [--]

fold 1
train: [----------]
valid:           [--]

fold 2
train: [--------------]
valid:               [--]

docs.title: Time-series step size
docs.text:
The implementation computes:

step = (
    self.test_size
    or (
        n
        // (
            self.n_splits
            + 1
        )
    )
)

So if:

test_size

is provided and truthy, it becomes the step size.

Otherwise:

\[ \text{step} = \left\lfloor \frac{n} {n_{\text{splits}}+1} \right\rfloor. \]

docs.title: Time-series fold boundaries
docs.text:
For fold:

i

the source computes:

train_end = step * (
    i + 1
)

val_end = step * (
    i + 2
)

Training indices are:

np.arange(
    train_end
)

and validation indices are:

np.arange(
    train_end,
    min(
        val_end,
        n,
    )
)

docs.title: Time-series example
docs.text:
For:

n = 60
n_splits = 5
test_size = None

the default step is:

\[ 60 // 6 = 10. \]

The folds are:

fold 0:
    train 0:10
    valid 10:20

fold 1:
    train 0:20
    valid 20:30

fold 2:
    train 0:30
    valid 30:40

fold 3:
    train 0:40
    valid 40:50

fold 4:
    train 0:50
    valid 50:60

docs.title: Explicit time-series test_size
docs.text:
For:

TimeSeriesCV(
    n_splits=3,
    test_size=5,
)

the source uses:

step = 5

for both the growth increment and validation-window width.

For example:

fold 0:
    train 0:5
    valid 5:10

fold 1:
    train 0:10
    valid 10:15

fold 2:
    train 0:15
    valid 15:20

subject to clipping at n.

docs.title: Current validation limitations
docs.text:
The built-in CV classes do not perform comprehensive constructor validation.

For example, the source does not explicitly reject:

n_splits <= 0
n_splits > n_samples
test_size <= 0
test_size too large

when the objects are created.

This can produce empty folds or lower-level NumPy errors later.

docs.title: KFold with too many folds
docs.text:
If:

n_splits > n_samples

some round-robin folds remain empty.

Those empty validation folds are still yielded.

The source contains no explicit minimum fold-size validation.

docs.title: KFold with one split
docs.text:
With:

n_splits=1

the training-set construction attempts to concatenate all folds except the single validation fold.

That produces an empty list for:

np.concatenate(...)

which can raise a NumPy error.

The current source does not intercept this case with a custom message.

docs.title: Stratified folds with rare classes
docs.text:
If a class has fewer samples than:

n_splits

then:

np.array_split(...)

creates empty class-specific parts for some folds.

A fold may therefore lack that class.

The source does not reject this situation.

So "stratified" should be understood as distributing available class examples as evenly as the implementation can, not guaranteeing every class appears in every fold.

docs.title: Time-series empty windows
docs.text:
If:

n

is too small relative to:

n_splits

then:

n // (n_splits + 1)

can become:

0.

That creates empty train and validation arrays.

Likewise, a large explicit test_size can cause later validation windows to be empty once:

train_end >= n.

The current class does not validate these conditions.

docs.title: COBRA defaults to K-fold
docs.text:
Although three CV strategies are registered, the current main COBRA estimators hard-code:

CVFactory.create(
    "kfold",
    n_splits=self.n_cv,
    shuffle=True,
    random_state=self.random_state,
)

inside component resolution.

This is true for:

GradientCOBRA
MixCOBRARegressor
CombinedClassifier

docs.title: Important API consequence
docs.text:
The public constructors expose:

n_cv

but do not expose:

cv
cv_params
cross_validator

as constructor arguments.

Therefore, in the current high-level APIs, you can change the number of folds but not select:

stratified_kfold
time_series

through ordinary estimator configuration.

Current API boundary

StratifiedKFoldCV and TimeSeriesCV are registered and can be used directly through CVFactory, but the current primary COBRA estimators construct kfold internally.

Using a different CV strategy in those estimators requires extending or modifying the source.

docs.title: n_cv
docs.text:
The public parameter controlling fold count is:

n_cv

with current default:

5

for:

GradientCOBRA
MixCOBRARegressor
CombinedClassifier

During component resolution it becomes:

KFoldCV(
    n_splits=n_cv,
    shuffle=True,
    random_state=random_state,
)

docs.title: Fitted CV object
docs.text:
After component resolution, the cross-validator is stored as:

model.cv_

For the current main estimators:

type(
    model.cv_
).__name__

should be:

KFoldCV

unless source code has been changed.

docs.title: Stored folds
docs.text:
The concrete folds used during optimization are materialized as a list:

model.cv_folds_

For GradientCOBRA:

self.cv_folds_ = list(
    self.cv_.split(
        self.X_l_,
        self.Y_l_norm_,
    )
)

For MixCOBRA:

self.cv_folds_ = list(
    self.cv_.split(
        self.X_l_,
        self.y_l_,
    )
)

For CombinedClassifier:

self.cv_folds_ = list(
    self.cv_.split(
        self.X_l_,
        self.y_l_,
    )
)

docs.title: GradientCOBRA's unusual y argument
docs.text:
GradientCOBRA calls:

self.cv_.split(
    self.X_l_,
    self.Y_l_norm_,
)

rather than:

self.y_l_

as the second argument.

With the current default:

KFoldCV

this makes no difference because KFoldCV.split() ignores y.

Current source detail

If GradientCOBRA were changed to use a cross-validator whose fold construction depends on y, this call would matter because the supplied second argument is the normalized prediction-space matrix rather than the regression target vector.

The current high-level source avoids that issue by always resolving kfold.

docs.title: CombinedClassifier does not use stratified CV by default
docs.text:
Although:

StratifiedKFoldCV

is available in the registry, CombinedClassifier currently creates:

"kfold"

rather than:

"stratified_kfold"

for its bandwidth optimization.

Therefore classification CV inside CombinedClassifier does not explicitly preserve class proportions.

This is separate from the package's top-level KFC split, which has its own classification stratification logic.

docs.title: How GradientCOBRA uses folds
docs.text:
GradientCOBRA first stores a square calibration distance matrix:

self.distance_matrix_

For a candidate bandwidth:

bandwidth

it sets:

self.adapter_.set_params(
    bandwidth=bandwidth
)

then computes:

D = self.adapter_.transform(
    self.distance_matrix_
)

K = self.kernel_(D)

docs.title: Fold-specific kernel block
docs.text:
For each stored fold:

train_idx = fold.train_idx
val_idx = fold.eval_idx

the validation-to-training kernel block is:

K_val_train = K[
    np.ix_(
        val_idx,
        train_idx,
    )
]

If:

n_val = len(val_idx)
n_train = len(train_idx)

then:

K_val_train.shape
==
(n_val, n_train)

docs.title: Fold prediction in GradientCOBRA
docs.text:
The fold training targets are:

y_train = self.y_l_[
    train_idx
]

and validation targets:

y_val = self.y_l_[
    val_idx
]

Predictions are produced by:

self.aggregator_.aggregate_matrix(
    values=y_train,
    weights=K_val_train,
    fallback=0.0,
)

Then the fold error is:

self.loss_(
    y_val,
    preds,
)

docs.title: Mean GradientCOBRA CV error
docs.text:
Errors are appended:

errors.append(
    error
)

and the objective returns:

float(
    np.mean(
        errors
    )
)

So optimization minimizes the mean loss across folds.

docs.title: GradientCOBRA CV fallback
docs.text:
Inside cross-validation, GradientCOBRA explicitly passes:

fallback=0.0

to the regression aggregator.

This differs from final prediction, where the source uses:

fallback=self.global_mean_

for the fitted model.

Therefore candidate bandwidths are evaluated under a zero-weight fallback of:

0.0

during CV.

docs.title: MixCOBRA cross-validation
docs.text:
MixCOBRA uses the same basic fold structure but has two objective forms.

With:

one_parameter=True

it evaluates one:

bandwidth

parameter.

With:

one_parameter=False

it evaluates:

alpha
beta

jointly.

docs.title: MixCOBRA one-parameter CV
docs.text:
The objective:

kappa_cross_validation_error_1d()

sets:

self.adapter_.set_params(
    bandwidth=bandwidth
)

then transforms:

self.distance_matrix_mix_

and applies the kernel.

The same fold extraction pattern is used:

K_val_train = K[
    np.ix_(
        val_idx,
        train_idx,
    )
]

docs.title: MixCOBRA two-parameter CV
docs.text:
The objective:

kappa_cross_validation_error_2d()

receives:

alpha, beta

and updates:

self.adapter_.set_params(
    alpha=alpha,
    beta=beta,
)

The two stored distance matrices are fused by:

self.adapter_.transform(
    self.distance_matrix_x_,
    self.distance_matrix_y_,
)

before kernel application.

Each fold is then evaluated with the same target aggregation process.

docs.title: MixCOBRA CV fallback
docs.text:
Like GradientCOBRA, MixCOBRA uses:

fallback=0.0

inside its regression cross-validation objectives.

The fold losses are averaged with:

np.mean(errors)

docs.title: CombinedClassifier cross-validation
docs.text:
CombinedClassifier also starts from a square calibration distance matrix.

For a candidate:

bandwidth

it computes a kernel matrix and extracts:

K_vt = K[
    np.ix_(
        val_idx,
        train_idx,
    )
]

docs.title: Fold-level classification prediction
docs.text:
For each validation row:

w = K_vt[i]

the source checks:

if np.sum(w) <= 0:
    pred = self.global_majority_class_
else:
    pred = self.aggregator_.aggregate(
        y_train,
        w,
    )

Predictions are collected into an array and compared with:

y_true = self.y_l_[
    val_idx
]

using:

self.loss_

docs.title: CombinedClassifier fallback during CV
docs.text:
If a validation query receives a non-positive kernel-weight sum, the fallback is:

self.global_majority_class_

This differs from the regression CV fallback of:

0.0

docs.title: CombinedClassifier loss default
docs.text:
The current constructor default is:

loss="mse"

even though the estimator is a classifier.

Therefore, unless changed, the CV objective applies the registered MSE loss to the numeric class predictions and targets.

This is a current source default, not a generic classification recommendation.

For supported alternatives, see:

Loss Functions

docs.title: CV and optimization
docs.text:
Cross-validation itself does not choose the final hyperparameter.

It defines the objective function consumed by the optimizer.

For example:

candidate bandwidth
    ↓
mean cross-validation loss
    ↓
optimizer compares candidates
    ↓
selected bandwidth_

The optimizer layer is documented separately in:

Optimization

docs.title: Grid search and folds
docs.text:
With the default grid optimization, every candidate bandwidth is evaluated by calling the CV objective.

For GradientCOBRA and CombinedClassifier, the default candidate list is:

np.linspace(
    0.001,
    10.0,
    max_iter,
)

when no custom bandwidth list is supplied.

So with:

max_iter = 300
n_cv = 5

the CV objective conceptually performs:

300 parameter evaluations
×
5 fold losses

although the expensive pairwise distance matrix is precomputed once before those evaluations.

docs.title: Why the distance matrix is precomputed
docs.text:
The source does not recompute prediction-space distances for every fold and every candidate parameter.

Instead:

self.distance_matrix_

or the MixCOBRA distance matrices are created once.

Each candidate parameter only changes the adapter transformation and kernel weights.

This makes CV operate on:

stored geometry

rather than repeatedly reconstructing the full distance computation.

docs.title: Inspect the fitted folds
docs.text:
After fitting:

print(
    len(
        model.cv_folds_
    )
)

Normally:

5

with the default:

n_cv=5

docs.title: Inspect fold sizes
docs.text:
for fold in model.cv_folds_:
    print(
        "fold:",
        fold.fold_id,
        "train:",
        len(
            fold.train_idx
        ),
        "validation:",
        len(
            fold.eval_idx
        ),
    )

docs.title: Inspect exact indices
docs.text:
fold = model.cv_folds_[0]

print(
    fold.train_idx
)

print(
    fold.eval_idx
)

These indices refer to rows of the calibration arrays:

X_l_
y_l_

not to the original unsplit full dataset.

docs.title: Map fold indices to calibration targets
docs.text:
fold = model.cv_folds_[0]

y_train_fold = model.y_l_[
    fold.train_idx
]

y_val_fold = model.y_l_[
    fold.eval_idx
]

This reproduces the target subsets used by the CV objective.

docs.title: Reproduce the default K-fold object
docs.text:
For a fitted model configured with:

n_cv=5
random_state=42

the equivalent current CV constructor is:

from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.cv import (
    KFoldCV,
)

cv = KFoldCV(
    n_splits=5,
    shuffle=True,
    random_state=42,
)

Then:

folds = list(
    cv.split(
        model.X_l_,
        model.y_l_,
    )
)

matches the same K-fold logic for MixCOBRA and CombinedClassifier.

For GradientCOBRA, its source call supplies:

model.Y_l_norm_

as the second argument, but KFoldCV ignores that value.

docs.title: Using stratified CV directly
docs.text:
Although current high-level COBRA estimators do not expose it as a constructor choice, the CV class itself can be used directly.

from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.cv import (
    StratifiedKFoldCV,
)

cv = StratifiedKFoldCV(
    n_splits=5,
    random_state=42,
)

for fold in cv.split(
    X,
    y,
):
    ...

This can be useful when extending the estimator source or testing fold construction independently.

docs.title: Inspect class balance
docs.text:
import numpy as np

for fold in cv.split(
    X,
    y,
):
    labels, counts = np.unique(
        y[
            fold.eval_idx
        ],
        return_counts=True,
    )

    print(
        fold.fold_id,
        dict(
            zip(
                labels,
                counts,
            )
        ),
    )

This shows the approximate class distribution achieved by the source implementation.

docs.title: Using time-series CV directly
docs.text:
from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.cv import (
    TimeSeriesCV,
)

cv = TimeSeriesCV(
    n_splits=5,
)

for fold in cv.split(
    X,
    y,
):
    print(
        fold.train_idx,
        fold.eval_idx,
    )

The input order is treated as chronological order.

The class itself does not inspect timestamps or sort rows by a time column.

docs.title: Important time-order requirement
docs.text:
If temporal rows are not already ordered correctly before calling:

TimeSeriesCV.split()

the source does not reorder them.

Chronology is assumed to be encoded by row order.

docs.title: Custom cross-validator
docs.text:
A custom CV strategy can subclass:

BaseCrossValidator

and register with:

CVFactory

For example:

import numpy as np

from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.cv import (
    BaseCrossValidator,
    CVFactory,
)

from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.types import (
    SplitIndices,
)


@CVFactory.register(
    "two_fold_fixed"
)
class TwoFoldFixed(
    BaseCrossValidator
):

    def split(
        self,
        x,
        y,
        *,
        groups=None,
    ):
        n = len(x)
        cut = n // 2

        first = np.arange(
            cut
        )

        second = np.arange(
            cut,
            n,
        )

        yield SplitIndices(
            train_idx=first,
            eval_idx=second,
            fold_id=0,
        )

        yield SplitIndices(
            train_idx=second,
            eval_idx=first,
            fold_id=1,
        )

    def get_n_splits(
        self,
    ):
        return 2

docs.title: Current custom-CV integration limitation
docs.text:
Registering a custom strategy makes it available through:

CVFactory.create(...)

but the current:

GradientCOBRA
MixCOBRARegressor
CombinedClassifier

constructors still hard-code:

kfold

inside their component resolution.

Therefore registration alone does not make a custom CV strategy selectable via a high-level estimator argument.

The estimator source would need a configurable:

cv
cv_params

path to expose that extension fully.

docs.title: Groups parameter
docs.text:
BaseCrossValidator.split() includes:

groups=None

in its abstract interface.

However:

KFoldCV
StratifiedKFoldCV
TimeSeriesCV

do not implement group-based splitting logic.

Their concrete split() signatures also do not all preserve the abstract keyword-only groups parameter.

So group-aware cross-validation is not implemented by the current built-ins.

docs.title: Data splitting vs cross-validation
docs.text:
A useful comparison:

Layer Purpose Current default data splitter create X_k/y_k and X_l/y_l OverlapSplitter cross-validator create optimization folds within calibration data KFoldCV optimizer choose bandwidth / alpha / beta from CV objective grid

These layers should not be treated as interchangeable.

docs.title: KFC C-Step and CV
docs.text:
When KFC wraps:

GradientCOBRA
MixCOBRA
CombinedClassifier

it passes the F-Step matrix with:

as_predictions=True

This bypasses COBRA's first-level train/calibration split.

However, the wrapped estimator still resolves its internal:

KFoldCV

and builds:

cv_folds_

over the supplied KFC C-Step training matrix.

So:

as_predictions=True

bypasses data splitting but does not bypass COBRA hyperparameter cross-validation.

docs.title: KFC example: GradientCOBRA
docs.text:
KFC's C-Step wrapper runs conceptually:

cobra.fit(
    P_l,
    y_l,
    as_predictions=True,
)

Inside GradientCOBRA:

P_l
    becomes calibration prediction space

KFoldCV
    splits rows of P_l into CV folds

bandwidth optimizer
    minimizes mean fold loss

So the C-Step aggregation data is itself cross-validated for bandwidth selection.

docs.title: Classification KFC example
docs.text:
For:

combined_classifier

the KFC F-Step class-prediction matrix becomes:

pred_l_

inside CombinedClassifier.

Then ordinary K-fold CV is used to optimize the classifier's bandwidth.

The current wrapper does not switch to StratifiedKFoldCV.

docs.title: Reproducibility
docs.text:
For the main COBRA estimators, the same:

random_state

is passed to:

KFoldCV(
    shuffle=True,
    random_state=...
)

Therefore changing the estimator's random_state can change:

calibration K-fold membership

in addition to any other random components of the model.

docs.title: Cross-validation does not refit base estimators
docs.text:
The current CV objective works from:

distance matrices
kernel matrices
calibration targets

It does not call:

fit_estimators()

inside every fold.

That means the fold "training" indices refer to the aggregation stage, not to freshly refitted base learners.

This is important when interpreting the CV design.

docs.title: No out-of-fold base-prediction construction inside CV
docs.text:
Base estimators are fitted before COBRA hyperparameter cross-validation.

The source does not use each cv_folds_ split to regenerate base-estimator predictions out of fold.

Instead, the already-constructed calibration prediction-space geometry is partitioned for aggregation evaluation.

docs.title: Inspect the CV object
docs.text:
print(
    model.cv_
)

docs.title: Inspect the number of configured folds
docs.text:
print(
    model.cv_.get_n_splits()
)

docs.title: Inspect materialized folds
docs.text:
for fold in model.cv_folds_:
    print(
        fold.fold_id,
        fold.train_idx.shape,
        fold.eval_idx.shape,
    )

docs.title: Check validation coverage
docs.text:
For K-fold:

import numpy as np

all_validation = np.concatenate([
    fold.eval_idx
    for fold
    in model.cv_folds_
])

print(
    np.sort(
        all_validation
    )
)

With a normal valid K-fold configuration, every calibration row should occur once in the concatenated validation indices.

docs.title: Check for empty folds
docs.text:
for fold in model.cv_folds_:
    if len(
        fold.eval_idx
    ) == 0:
        print(
            "empty validation fold:",
            fold.fold_id,
        )

This is especially useful if:

n_cv

is large relative to the calibration sample count.

docs.title: Check fold loss manually
docs.text:
For GradientCOBRA, one candidate bandwidth can be evaluated directly:

score = model.kappa_cross_validation_error([
    model.bandwidth_
])

print(
    score
)

This reuses:

model.cv_folds_

and the already-fitted component state.

docs.text: CV Registry Default folds Shuffle RNG Main behavior KFoldCV kfold 5 Yes RandomState shuffled round-robin folds StratifiedKFoldCV stratified_kfold 5 internally default_rng split each class with array_split TimeSeriesCV time_series, tscv 5 No none expanding chronological windows
