docs.title: Mental model
docs.text:
COBRA cross-validation does not rebuild the entire learning pipeline for every fold. It reuses the calibration geometry and asks which aggregation hyperparameters predict held-out calibration rows best.

\[ \boxed{ \text{calibration distance matrix} \rightarrow \text{candidate kernel parameters} \rightarrow \text{K-fold aggregation predictions} \rightarrow \text{mean loss} } \]

The current high-level estimators all use the package's custom shuffled KFoldCV, while stratified and temporal strategies exist as registered components that are not yet exposed through the main estimator constructors.

docs.title: Data Splitting
docs.text:
COBRA-style estimators separate base-estimator fitting data from aggregation/calibration data.

The current source represents these two roles as:

X_k, y_k
    estimator-training data

X_l, y_l
    aggregation / calibration data

This separation is handled primarily by:

resolve_training_context()

in:

kfc_procedure/cobra/utils/resolve.py

and by the splitter implementations under:

kfc_procedure/cobra/core/splitters/
├── base.py
├── holdout.py
└── overlap.py

The main splitters are:

RandomHoldoutSplitter
OverlapSplitter

docs.title: Why COBRA uses two datasets
docs.text:
In the normal feature-based workflow, base estimators are first fitted on:

\[ (X_k,y_k). \]

Those fitted estimators then generate predictions on:

\[ X_l. \]

The resulting prediction representation is paired with:

\[ y_l \]

and used by the aggregation procedure.

Conceptually:

flowchart LR
    X["Full training data"]
    S["Data split"]

    XK["X_k, y_k"]
    XL["X_l, y_l"]

    E["Fit base estimators"]
    P["Predictions on X_l"]
    A["COBRA aggregation / optimization"]

    X --> S
    S --> XK
    S --> XL

    XK --> E
    E --> P
    XL --> P
    P --> A
    XL --> A

This distinction is used by:

GradientCOBRA
MixCOBRARegressor
CombinedClassifier

when they are fitted from ordinary feature matrices.

docs.title: TrainingContext
docs.text:
The resolved datasets are stored in:

TrainingContext

defined in:

kfc_procedure/cobra/core/types.py

Its fields are:

@dataclass(slots=True)
class TrainingContext:
    X_k: np.ndarray | None
    y_k: np.ndarray | None

    X_l: np.ndarray
    y_l: np.ndarray

    as_predictions: bool

docs.title: Meaning of the fields
docs.text:
Field Purpose X_k data used to fit base estimators y_k targets for base-estimator fitting X_l aggregation/calibration input y_l aggregation/calibration targets as_predictions whether the supplied matrix is already prediction space

When:

as_predictions=True

the training side is intentionally absent:

X_k = None
y_k = None

because no base estimators need to be fitted.

docs.title: Split indices
docs.text:
Concrete splitters return:

SplitIndices

with:

train_idx
eval_idx
fold_id

The dataclass is:

@dataclass(slots=True)
class SplitIndices:
    train_idx: np.ndarray
    eval_idx: np.ndarray
    fold_id: int | None = None

For ordinary train/calibration splitting:

fold_id

remains None.

docs.title: The splitter interface
docs.text:
All splitters inherit:

BaseDataSplitter

and are expected to implement:

split(
    x,
    y,
    *,
    groups=None,
)

returning a:

SplitIndices

object.

The base abstraction describes splitters as index generators rather than data transformers.

They operate on sample indices and do not modify the feature matrix or target vector directly.

docs.title: Splitter registry
docs.text:
Splitters are registered through:

SplitterFactory

The current built-in names are:

holdout
random_holdout
split_overlap

where:

holdout
random_holdout

are aliases for:

RandomHoldoutSplitter

and:

split_overlap

creates:

OverlapSplitter

docs.title: Inspect available splitters
docs.text:
from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.splitters import (
    SplitterFactory,
)

print(
    SplitterFactory.available()
)

The current registry should contain:

holdout
random_holdout
split_overlap

after the splitter package has been imported.

docs.title: Default COBRA split
docs.text:
The shared resolver uses:

OverlapSplitter

by default.

If no explicit splitter is passed to:

resolve_training_context()

the source creates:

SplitterFactory.create(
    "split_overlap",
    split_ratio=split_ratio,
    overlap=overlap,
    random_state=random_state,
)

Therefore the default automatic COBRA split is not RandomHoldoutSplitter.

It is:

OverlapSplitter

with:

split_ratio=0.5
overlap=0.0
shuffle=True

unless different values are supplied.

docs.title: OverlapSplitter
docs.text:
OverlapSplitter is registered as:

split_overlap

Its constructor is:

OverlapSplitter(
    split_ratio=0.5,
    overlap=0.0,
    shuffle=True,
    random_state=None,
)

It can create disjoint or overlapping training/calibration index sets.

docs.title: Parameter validation
docs.text:
The constructor requires:

\[ 0 < \text{split_ratio} < 1. \]

Otherwise:

ValueError:
split_ratio must be in (0,1)

It also requires:

\[ 0 \leq \text{overlap} < 1. \]

Otherwise:

ValueError:
overlap must be in [0,1)

Finally:

\[ \text{overlap} < \text{split_ratio}. \]

If not, the implementation first prints:

Invalid parameters: split_ratio=..., overlap=...

and then raises:

ValueError:
overlap must be smaller than split_ratio

docs.title: Overlap split geometry
docs.text:
For:

\[ n \]

observations, the implementation computes:

\[ k_1 = \operatorname{int} \left[ n \left( r-\frac{o}{2} \right) \right] \]

and:

\[ k_2 = \operatorname{int} \left[ n \left( r+\frac{o}{2} \right) \right], \]

where:

r = split_ratio
o = overlap

Then:

train_idx = indices[:k2]
eval_idx = indices[k1:]

So the region:

indices[k1:k2]

belongs to both subsets.

docs.title: Visual model
docs.text:
0                                                n
|------------------------------------------------|

                split_ratio = r

              k1          k2
               |-----------|
               |  overlap  |
               |-----------|

train:
|---------------------------|

evaluation:
               |------------------------------|

The training subset ends at:

k2

while the evaluation subset begins at:

k1

docs.title: No-overlap case
docs.text:
With:

split_ratio=0.5
overlap=0.0

the boundaries are:

\[ k_1 = k_2 = \operatorname{int}(0.5n). \]

Therefore:

train_idx = indices[:k]
eval_idx  = indices[k:]

and the partitions are disjoint.

This is the default behavior used by the COBRA estimators.

docs.title: Example: 50/50 split
docs.text:
For:

n = 100
split_ratio = 0.5
overlap = 0.0

the implementation gives approximately:

train size = 50
evaluation size = 50
shared = 0

subject to integer truncation when the sample count does not divide exactly.

docs.title: Example: overlap
docs.text:
For:

n = 100
split_ratio = 0.5
overlap = 0.2

the boundaries are:

\[ k_1 = 100(0.5-0.1) = 40 \]

and:

\[ k_2 = 100(0.5+0.1) = 60. \]

So:

train_idx = first 60 shuffled indices
eval_idx  = shuffled indices from position 40 onward

giving:

train size = 60
evaluation size = 60
shared samples = 20

docs.title: Approximate subset sizes
docs.text:
Ignoring integer truncation:

\[ n_{\text{train}} \approx n \left( r+\frac{o}{2} \right), \]

and:

\[ n_{\text{eval}} \approx n \left( 1-r+\frac{o}{2} \right). \]

The shared region is approximately:

\[ n_{\text{shared}} \approx no. \]

Because the implementation uses Python int(), exact counts can differ by one or more samples from these continuous expressions for small datasets.

docs.title: split_ratio is not simply the final train fraction when overlap is used
docs.text:
With:

overlap > 0

the final training set extends beyond:

n * split_ratio

by approximately:

\[ \frac{no}{2}. \]

Likewise, the evaluation set begins before the split-ratio boundary by the same amount.

So:

split_ratio=0.5
overlap=0.2

does not create a 50-sample training subset and a 50-sample evaluation subset with 20 shared samples.

The implementation creates approximately:

60 training samples
60 evaluation samples
20 shared samples

for n=100.

docs.title: Shuffling
docs.text:
OverlapSplitter defaults to:

shuffle=True

Before computing subsets, it creates:

indices = np.arange(n)

and passes them through:

_shuffle_indices()

docs.title: Random generator
docs.text:
When shuffling is enabled, the implementation uses:

rng = np.random.default_rng(
    self.random_state
)

rng.shuffle(
    shuffled
)

Therefore:

random_state

controls the permutation produced by the overlap splitter.

docs.title: Disable shuffling
docs.text:
You can create:

splitter = OverlapSplitter(
    split_ratio=0.5,
    overlap=0.0,
    shuffle=False,
)

Then:

train_idx

contains the first portion of the original row order and:

eval_idx

contains the remaining portion.

Warning

The high-level COBRA fit() methods do not currently expose a shuffle argument for the default splitter.

Their automatic split path constructs the default overlap splitter with its own default:

shuffle=True

docs.title: Target values are not used by OverlapSplitter
docs.text:
The splitter's split() method receives:

x
y

but the implementation uses only:

np.asarray(x).shape[0]

to obtain the sample count.

It does not use:

target values
class labels
target distribution

when generating the partition.

Therefore the automatic overlap split is not stratified.

docs.title: No group-aware splitting in the concrete implementation
docs.text:
BaseDataSplitter.split() includes an optional abstract:

groups

parameter.

However, the current concrete:

RandomHoldoutSplitter
OverlapSplitter

implementations do not expose a groups argument in their own method signatures.

So the current built-ins do not implement group-aware partitioning.

docs.title: RandomHoldoutSplitter
docs.text:
The second built-in strategy is:

RandomHoldoutSplitter

registered as:

holdout
random_holdout

Its constructor is:

RandomHoldoutSplitter(
    calibration_size=0.5,
    random_state=None,
)

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
It creates:

indices = np.arange(
    n_samples
)

and calls:

train_test_split(
    indices,
    test_size=self.calibration_size,
    random_state=self.random_state,
    shuffle=True,
)

The result is returned as:

SplitIndices(
    train_idx=...,
    eval_idx=...,
)

docs.title: Holdout partitions are disjoint
docs.text:
Unlike OverlapSplitter with:

overlap > 0

the random holdout strategy produces disjoint subsets.

No observation is placed in both:

train_idx
eval_idx

by train_test_split.

docs.title: Holdout calibration size
docs.text:
The intended constructor domain is:

\[ 0 < \text{calibration_size} < 1. \]

The source stores:

self.calibration_size = float(
    calibration_size
)

without an explicit manual interval check in __init__().

Validation of unsupported values is therefore left to:

sklearn.model_selection.train_test_split

when split() is called.

docs.title: Holdout is also not stratified
docs.text:
Although split() receives y, it does not pass:

stratify=y

to train_test_split().

The actual call uses:

train_test_split(
    indices,
    test_size=self.calibration_size,
    random_state=self.random_state,
    shuffle=True,
)

Therefore classification label balance is not explicitly preserved by the current holdout implementation.

docs.title: Overlap splitter
docs.text:
from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.splitters import (
    OverlapSplitter,
)

splitter = OverlapSplitter(
    split_ratio=0.5,
    overlap=0.1,
    random_state=42,
)

indices = splitter.split(
    X,
    y,
)

print(
    indices.train_idx
)

print(
    indices.eval_idx
)

docs.title: Holdout splitter
docs.text:
from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.splitters import (
    RandomHoldoutSplitter,
)

splitter = RandomHoldoutSplitter(
    calibration_size=0.4,
    random_state=42,
)

indices = splitter.split(
    X,
    y,
)

docs.title: Factory usage
docs.text:
Create an overlap splitter:

from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.splitters import (
    SplitterFactory,
)

splitter = SplitterFactory.create(
    "split_overlap",
    split_ratio=0.5,
    overlap=0.1,
    random_state=42,
)

Create a holdout splitter:

splitter = SplitterFactory.create(
    "holdout",
    calibration_size=0.4,
    random_state=42,
)

The alias:

random_holdout

creates the same class.

docs.title: resolve_training_context()
docs.text:
Most COBRA estimators use the shared:

resolve_training_context()

function.

Its relevant signature is:

resolve_training_context(
    X,
    y,
    *,
    X_l=None,
    y_l=None,
    pred_features=None,
    as_predictions=False,
    splitter=None,
    split_ratio=0.5,
    overlap=0.0,
    random_state=None,
)

The function supports several distinct data-resolution modes.

docs.title: Mode 1 — precomputed prediction data
docs.text:
The first branch is:

if as_predictions:
    return TrainingContext(
        X_k=None,
        y_k=None,
        X_l=np.asarray(X),
        y_l=np.asarray(y),
        as_predictions=True,
    )

So when:

as_predictions=True

no split is performed.

The entire supplied matrix becomes:

X_l

and the entire target vector becomes:

y_l.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
ctx = resolve_training_context(
    P_train,
    y_train,
    as_predictions=True,
)

produces conceptually:

X_k = None
y_k = None

X_l = P_train
y_l = y_train

as_predictions = True

The splitter arguments are bypassed in this mode.

docs.title: Mode 2 — explicit calibration data
docs.text:
If both:

X_l
y_l

are supplied, the resolver does not create a split.

Instead:

X
y

become:

X_k
y_k

and the explicitly supplied data become:

X_l
y_l.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
ctx = resolve_training_context(
    X_train,
    y_train,
    X_l=X_cal,
    y_l=y_cal,
)

produces:

X_k = X_train
y_k = y_train

X_l = X_cal
y_l = y_cal

docs.title: Both explicit arrays are required
docs.text:
Providing only:

X_l

or only:

y_l

raises:

ValueError:
Both 'X_l' and 'y_l' must be provided together.

This check occurs before automatic splitting.

docs.title: Mode 3 — pred_features
docs.text:
The resolver also contains a special:

pred_features

branch.

If present, it checks:

pred_features.shape[0]
==
X.shape[0]

and returns:

TrainingContext(
    X_k=np.asarray(X),
    y_k=np.asarray(y),
    X_l=pred_features,
    y_l=np.asarray(y),
    as_predictions=False,
)

No automatic train/calibration split occurs in this branch.

docs.title: Important current MixCOBRA caveat
docs.text:
MixCOBRARegressor.fit() passes its:

pred_features

argument into this resolver.

However, after resolution, the current MixCOBRA code still treats:

X_l_

as an input to the fitted base estimators in the normal as_predictions=False path.

Therefore the source does not currently use this resolver branch as a direct, clean precomputed-prediction path.

See:

Prediction Space

for the source-level behavior.

docs.title: Mode 4 — automatic splitting
docs.text:
If none of the earlier modes applies, the resolver performs an automatic split.

If:

splitter is None

it creates:

OverlapSplitter

through:

SplitterFactory.create(
    "split_overlap",
    split_ratio=split_ratio,
    overlap=overlap,
    random_state=random_state,
)

Then:

split_indices = splitter.split(
    X,
    y,
)

and the arrays are sliced by those indices.

docs.title: Returned arrays
docs.text:
The final context is:

TrainingContext(
    X_k=np.asarray(X)[train_idx],
    y_k=np.asarray(y)[train_idx],
    X_l=np.asarray(X)[eval_idx],
    y_l=np.asarray(y)[eval_idx],
    as_predictions=False,
)

So all overlap behavior is reflected literally in the data arrays.

If a sample index occurs in both index sets, that observation occurs in both X_k and X_l.

docs.title: Input validation
docs.text:
At the beginning of:

resolve_training_context()

the source calls:

X, y = check_X_y(
    X,
    y,
)

from scikit-learn.

Explicit:

X_l
y_l

data are also validated with:

check_X_y(
    X_l,
    y_l,
)

before they are placed in the TrainingContext.

docs.title: GradientCOBRA splitting
docs.text:
The current GradientCOBRA.fit() signature contains:

fit(
    X,
    y,
    X_l=None,
    y_l=None,
    split_ratio=0.5,
    overlap=0.0,
    as_predictions=False,
)

It calls:

resolve_training_context(
    X,
    y,
    X_l=X_l,
    y_l=y_l,
    as_predictions=as_predictions,
    split_ratio=split_ratio,
    overlap=overlap,
    random_state=self.random_state,
)

So GradientCOBRA exposes:

explicit calibration data
split_ratio
overlap
as_predictions

through its public fit() method.

docs.title: CombinedClassifier splitting
docs.text:
The current classifier signature is:

fit(
    X,
    y,
    X_l=None,
    y_l=None,
    split_ratio=0.5,
    overlap=False,
    as_predictions=False,
)

It passes these values to the same resolver.

The default:

overlap=False

is accepted by OverlapSplitter because Python False behaves numerically as zero.

So the default classifier split is effectively:

overlap=0.0

docs.title: MixCOBRA splitting
docs.text:
The current MixCOBRARegressor.fit() signature contains:

fit(
    X,
    y,
    X_l=None,
    y_l=None,
    split_ratio=0.5,
    overlap=0.0,
    pred_features=None,
    as_predictions=False,
)

It therefore exposes:

explicit calibration data
automatic split ratio
overlap
pred_features
as_predictions

to the shared resolver.

docs.title: The high-level COBRA estimators do not expose splitter=
docs.text:
Although:

resolve_training_context()

accepts a custom:

splitter

object, the current public fit() signatures of:

GradientCOBRA
CombinedClassifier
MixCOBRARegressor

do not include a:

splitter=

argument.

Therefore normal estimator usage cannot currently select:

holdout

instead of:

split_overlap

through a public fit parameter.

Current API boundary

The splitter factory is implemented and usable directly, but the main estimator fit() methods currently route automatic splitting through the default overlap splitter.

Using another splitter inside those workflows requires source extension or manually preparing X_k/y_k and X_l/y_l.

docs.title: Using holdout behavior with an estimator
docs.text:
Because public COBRA fit() methods accept explicit calibration data, you can manually split first.

from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.splitters import (
    RandomHoldoutSplitter,
)

splitter = RandomHoldoutSplitter(
    calibration_size=0.4,
    random_state=42,
)

indices = splitter.split(
    X,
    y,
)

X_k = X[
    indices.train_idx
]

y_k = y[
    indices.train_idx
]

X_l = X[
    indices.eval_idx
]

y_l = y[
    indices.eval_idx
]

Then:

model.fit(
    X_k,
    y_k,
    X_l=X_l,
    y_l=y_l,
)

This uses the holdout split you constructed rather than the estimator's automatic overlap-split path.

docs.title: Reproducibility
docs.text:
The default overlap splitter uses:

np.random.default_rng(
    random_state
)

while RandomHoldoutSplitter delegates its seed to scikit-learn's:

train_test_split()

So both splitters support reproducible partitions when a fixed random_state is supplied.

docs.title: COBRA estimator seed
docs.text:
The high-level estimators pass:

self.random_state

into resolve_training_context().

Therefore:

GradientCOBRA(
    random_state=42
)

with automatic splitting uses the seed:

42

for the default overlap permutation.

The same applies to the other COBRA estimators that pass their random_state into the resolver.

docs.title: Reproduce an automatic split
docs.text:
To reproduce the default automatic split outside a COBRA estimator:

from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.splitters import (
    OverlapSplitter,
)

splitter = OverlapSplitter(
    split_ratio=0.5,
    overlap=0.0,
    random_state=42,
)

indices = splitter.split(
    X,
    y,
)

For the same sample ordering and seed, this follows the same splitter logic used by the resolver.

docs.title: Inspect train/evaluation overlap
docs.text:
train = set(
    indices.train_idx.tolist()
)

evaluation = set(
    indices.eval_idx.tolist()
)

shared = train.intersection(
    evaluation
)

print(
    len(shared)
)

With:

overlap=0.0

expected:

0

With nonzero overlap, the value should be approximately:

n_samples * overlap

subject to integer truncation.

docs.title: Inspect split sizes
docs.text:
print(
    "train:",
    len(
        indices.train_idx
    )
)

print(
    "evaluation:",
    len(
        indices.eval_idx
    )
)

And:

print(
    "total unique:",
    len(
        set(indices.train_idx)
        |
        set(indices.eval_idx)
    )
)

For OverlapSplitter, the two subset sizes can sum to more than the total dataset size because shared observations are counted twice.

docs.title: Example split table
docs.text:
For:

n = 10
split_ratio = 0.5
overlap = 0.2
shuffle = False

the implementation computes:

\[ k_1 = \operatorname{int}(10\times0.4) = 4 \]

and:

\[ k_2 = \operatorname{int}(10\times0.6) = 6. \]

Therefore:

train_idx = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

eval_idx  = [4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9]

and:

shared = [4, 5]

This directly illustrates the source algorithm.

docs.title: Automatic splitting is not cross-validation
docs.text:
The train/calibration splitter is distinct from the cross-validation machinery used later for COBRA hyperparameter optimization.

The initial split determines:

base-estimator fitting data
aggregation/calibration data

Then the COBRA estimator can create CV folds within the calibration side for bandwidth or parameter optimization.

So these are two different data-partitioning levels:

level 1:
    X_k / X_l split

level 2:
    CV folds over aggregation data

See:

Cross-validation

for the second level.

docs.title: Relationship to KFC Procedure splitting
docs.text:
The top-level KFC Procedure has its own internal split logic.

KFCProcedure.fit() uses scikit-learn:

train_test_split(
    X,
    y,
    test_size=0.5,
    random_state=self.random_state,
    stratify=(
        y
        if self.task == "classification"
        else None
    ),
)

This is separate from the COBRA splitter framework described on this page.

Therefore:

KFC top-level split

and:

standalone COBRA automatic split

should not be assumed to use identical logic.

Notably:

  • KFC classification uses stratify=y;
  • the current COBRA OverlapSplitter does not stratify.

docs.title: KFC C-Step and as_predictions=True
docs.text:
When COBRA estimators are wrapped inside the KFC C-Step, the wrappers fit them with:

as_predictions=True

on the already-created F-Step matrix.

In that mode:

resolve_training_context()

returns immediately and performs no additional COBRA train/calibration split.

For example:

GradientCOBRACombiner.fit(
    P_l,
    y_l,
)

internally calls:

GradientCOBRA.fit(
    P_l,
    y_l,
    as_predictions=True,
)

so:

P_l

is treated directly as the aggregation prediction space.

docs.title: Avoiding an additional split
docs.text:
If you already prepared separate estimator-training and aggregation datasets, use:

X_l=
y_l=

instead of letting the COBRA estimator split the combined data again.

For example:

model.fit(
    X_k,
    y_k,
    X_l=X_l,
    y_l=y_l,
)

This bypasses the automatic OverlapSplitter.

docs.title: 70/30 disjoint
docs.text:
model.fit(
    X,
    y,
    split_ratio=0.7,
    overlap=0.0,
)

Approximately:

70% estimator training
30% aggregation/calibration

subject to integer truncation.

docs.title: 50/50 disjoint
docs.text:
model.fit(
    X,
    y,
    split_ratio=0.5,
    overlap=0.0,
)

Approximately:

50% training
50% calibration

docs.title: 50/50 center with 20% overlap
docs.text:
model.fit(
    X,
    y,
    split_ratio=0.5,
    overlap=0.2,
)

Approximately:

60% in training
60% in calibration
20% shared

This follows the source's symmetric overlap around the split-ratio boundary.

docs.title: What overlap changes statistically
docs.text:
From the source alone, overlap changes only which sample indices are included in each subset.

The implementation does not attach special weights or labels to shared observations.

A shared observation simply occurs in both:

X_k/y_k

and:

X_l/y_l.

Any statistical consequence follows from that reuse; the splitter itself adds no correction.

docs.title: What the splitters do not do
docs.text:
The current built-in splitter implementations do not perform:

feature scaling
target transformation
stratification
group-aware splitting
time-series ordering constraints
cross-validation
class balancing
sample weighting

Their job is limited to constructing train/evaluation sample indices.

docs.title: Custom splitter
docs.text:
The extension interface is:

BaseDataSplitter

A custom splitter should return:

SplitIndices

Example:

import numpy as np

from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.splitters import (
    BaseDataSplitter,
    SplitterFactory,
)

from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.types import (
    SplitIndices,
)


@SplitterFactory.register(
    "first_half"
)
class FirstHalfSplitter(
    BaseDataSplitter
):

    def split(
        self,
        x,
        y,
        *,
        groups=None,
    ):
        n = len(x)
        cut = n // 2

        return SplitIndices(
            train_idx=np.arange(
                cut
            ),
            eval_idx=np.arange(
                cut,
                n,
            ),
        )

Then:

splitter = SplitterFactory.create(
    "first_half"
)

can resolve it directly.

docs.title: Using a custom splitter with resolve_training_context
docs.text:
The resolver itself supports:

splitter=

For example:

ctx = resolve_training_context(
    X,
    y,
    splitter=splitter,
)

However, as noted earlier, the current high-level COBRA fit() methods do not expose this parameter directly.

docs.title: Check the automatic split parameters
docs.text:
print(
    model.random_state
)

and record the values passed to:

split_ratio
overlap

during fit().

docs.title: Reproduce indices
docs.text:
splitter = OverlapSplitter(
    split_ratio=0.5,
    overlap=0.0,
    random_state=model.random_state,
)

indices = splitter.split(
    X,
    y,
)

docs.title: Check overlap
docs.text:
shared = np.intersect1d(
    indices.train_idx,
    indices.eval_idx,
)

print(
    len(shared)
)

docs.title: Check all samples are covered
docs.text:
For OverlapSplitter:

covered = np.union1d(
    indices.train_idx,
    indices.eval_idx,
)

print(
    len(covered)
)

Because of the construction:

train = prefix
eval  = suffix

all shuffled indices are covered.

docs.title: Check class proportions manually
docs.text:
Because the built-in COBRA splitters are not stratified:

import numpy as np

print(
    np.unique(
        y[
            indices.train_idx
        ],
        return_counts=True,
    )
)

print(
    np.unique(
        y[
            indices.eval_idx
        ],
        return_counts=True,
    )
)

This is useful for classification diagnostics.

docs.title: Current source caveats
docs.text: Area Current behavior default automatic splitter split_overlap default split_ratio 0.5 default overlap 0.0 / False overlap shuffling True overlap RNG np.random.default_rng holdout backend sklearn train_test_split stratification not implemented by built-in COBRA splitters group-aware split not implemented by concrete built-ins public estimator splitter= argument not exposed explicit X_l, y_l supported as_predictions=True bypasses splitting pred_features branch present; current MixCOBRA integration has caveat KFC top-level split separate implementation

docs.title: Quick reference
docs.text: Mode X_k/y_k X_l/y_l Automatic splitter used? as_predictions=True None supplied X/y No explicit X_l/y_l supplied X/y supplied calibration data No pred_features supplied X/y pred_features/y No automatic splitter training rows splitter evaluation rows Yes

docs.title: Mental model
docs.text:
COBRA splitting decides which observations train the base estimators and which observations define the aggregation problem.

\[ \boxed{ (X,y) \rightarrow \begin{cases} (X_k,y_k) & \text{fit estimators}\\ (X_l,y_l) & \text{fit aggregation} \end{cases} } \]

The current automatic path uses OverlapSplitter, which can either create disjoint subsets or deliberately reuse a controlled region in both roles.

docs.title: Distances
docs.text:
Distance functions are a core part of the COBRA components in kfc_procedure.

They define how two observations are compared once those observations have been represented in the relevant COBRA space.

The current source provides five built-in distance implementations:

euclidean
manhattan
minkowski
cosine
hamming

The implementation lives under:

kfc_procedure/cobra/core/distances/
├── base.py
├── euclidean.py
├── manhattan.py
├── minkowski.py
├── cosine.py
└── hamming.py

These distances are used by:

GradientCOBRA
MixCOBRARegressor
CombinedClassifier

through the shared:

DistanceFactory

docs.title: Distance in the COBRA pipeline
docs.text:
The general flow is:

flowchart LR
    P["Prediction/input representation"]
    D["Pairwise distance matrix"]
    A["Kernel adapter"]
    K["Kernel weights"]
    G["Aggregator"]
    Y["Final prediction"]

    P --> D --> A --> K --> G --> Y

The distance step converts two matrices:

x
y

into a pairwise matrix:

\[ D \in \mathbb{R}^{n_x\times n_y}. \]

Each entry is:

\[ D_{ij} = d(x_i,y_j). \]

docs.title: Built-in distances
docs.text: Registry name Alias Class Main idea euclidean l2 EuclideanDistance L2 distance manhattan l1 ManhattanDistance L1 distance minkowski lp MinkowskiDistance generalized Lp distance cosine — CosineDistance angular dissimilarity hamming — HammingDistance fraction of mismatched coordinates

docs.title: The distance interface
docs.text:
Every distance implementation inherits:

BaseDistance

The abstract interface is:

class BaseDistance(ABC):

    def __init__(
        self,
        **kwargs,
    ):
        ...

    def set_params(
        self,
        **params,
    ):
        ...

    def get_params(
        self,
        deep=True,
    ):
        ...

    @abstractmethod
    def matrix(
        self,
        x,
        y,
    ):
        ...

The only required computational method is:

matrix(x, y)

docs.title: Expected matrix shapes
docs.text:
If:

x.shape == (
    n_x,
    n_features,
)

and:

y.shape == (
    n_y,
    n_features,
)

then:

distance.matrix(
    x,
    y,
).shape

is expected to be:

(n_x, n_y)

docs.title: BaseDistance parameters
docs.text:
The base constructor stores every keyword argument in:

self.params

and also creates same-named attributes.

Conceptually:

distance = SomeDistance(
    alpha=2.0,
)

results in:

distance.params == {
    "alpha": 2.0,
}

and:

distance.alpha == 2.0

docs.title: get_params()
docs.text:
distance.get_params()

returns a copy of:

self.params

The signature includes:

deep=True

for scikit-learn-style compatibility, but the current implementation does not use deep.

docs.title: set_params()
docs.text:
distance.set_params(
    alpha=3.0,
)

updates both:

distance.alpha

and:

distance.params["alpha"]

and returns:

self

for chaining.

docs.title: DistanceFactory
docs.text:
Distances are registered with:

DistanceFactory

which subclasses the package's:

BaseFactory

You can create a distance by name:

from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.distances import (
    DistanceFactory,
)

distance = DistanceFactory.create(
    "euclidean"
)

docs.title: Aliases
docs.text:
The current registrations are:

@DistanceFactory.register(
    "euclidean",
    "l2",
)

@DistanceFactory.register(
    "manhattan",
    "l1",
)

@DistanceFactory.register(
    "minkowski",
    "lp",
)

while:

cosine
hamming

have one registered name each.

docs.title: Registry normalization
docs.text:
Because DistanceFactory inherits BaseFactory, registry names are:

stripped
lowercased

before lookup.

So:

DistanceFactory.create(
    "EUCLIDEAN"
)

resolves the same normalized key as:

euclidean

docs.title: Euclidean distance
docs.text:
The implementation class is:

EuclideanDistance

registered as:

euclidean
l2

The source defines:

\[ d(x,y) = \sqrt{ \|x-y\|_2^2 }. \]

Equivalent form:

\[ d(x,y) = \sqrt{ \sum_k (x_k-y_k)^2 }. \]

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
The source uses the identity:

\[ \|x-y\|^2 = \|x\|^2 + \|y\|^2 - 2x^\top y. \]

The code is:

x2 = np.sum(
    x ** 2,
    axis=1,
    keepdims=True,
)

y2 = np.sum(
    y ** 2,
    axis=1,
    keepdims=True,
).T

xy = x @ y.T

dist = np.sqrt(
    np.maximum(
        x2 + y2 - 2 * xy,
        0.0,
    )
)

docs.title: Numerical clipping
docs.text:
Before the square root, the source applies:

np.maximum(
    ...,
    0.0,
)

This prevents tiny floating-point errors from producing negative squared distances.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
import numpy as np

from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.distances import (
    EuclideanDistance,
)

x = np.array([
    [0.0, 0.0],
    [1.0, 1.0],
])

y = np.array([
    [1.0, 0.0],
])

distance = EuclideanDistance()

D = distance.matrix(
    x,
    y,
)

print(
    D
)

The result has shape:

(2, 1)

docs.title: Manhattan distance
docs.text:
The implementation class is:

ManhattanDistance

registered as:

manhattan
l1

The source defines:

\[ d(x,y) = \sum_k |x_k-y_k|. \]

docs.title: Implementation backend
docs.text:
The current source delegates to:

scipy.spatial.distance_matrix

with:

p=1

The implementation is:

return distance_matrix(
    x,
    y,
    p=1,
)

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.distances import (
    ManhattanDistance,
)

distance = ManhattanDistance()

D = distance.matrix(
    x,
    y,
)

docs.title: Minkowski distance
docs.text:
The implementation class is:

MinkowskiDistance

registered as:

minkowski
lp

It generalizes L1 and L2 distances:

\[ d_p(x,y) = \left( \sum_k |x_k-y_k|^p \right)^{1/p}. \]

docs.title: Constructor
docs.text:
MinkowskiDistance(
    p=3,
    **kwargs,
)

The default is:

p = 3

This is a source-specific default.

docs.title: Special cases
docs.text:
The source documentation identifies:

\[ p=1 \]

as Manhattan distance and:

\[ p=2 \]

as Euclidean distance.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
The current implementation constructs pairwise coordinate differences through broadcasting:

x[:, None, :]
-
y[None, :, :]

then computes:

np.sum(
    np.abs(...) ** p,
    axis=2,
) ** (1 / p)

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.distances import (
    MinkowskiDistance,
)

distance = MinkowskiDistance(
    p=4,
)

D = distance.matrix(
    x,
    y,
)

docs.title: distance_params
docs.text:
Because MinkowskiDistance exposes:

p

through its constructor, COBRA estimators can configure it using:

distance_params

For example:

model = GradientCOBRA(
    distance="minkowski",
    distance_params={
        "p": 4,
    },
)

The source passes:

**distance_params

directly into:

DistanceFactory.create(...)

docs.title: Cosine distance
docs.text:
The implementation class is:

CosineDistance

registered as:

cosine

The source defines cosine similarity as:

\[ s(x,y) = \frac{ x^\top y }{ \|x\| \|y\| } \]

and cosine distance as:

\[ d(x,y) = 1-s(x,y). \]

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
The code computes row norms:

x_norm = np.linalg.norm(
    x,
    axis=1,
    keepdims=True,
)

y_norm = np.linalg.norm(
    y,
    axis=1,
    keepdims=True,
).T

then:

sim = (
    x @ y.T
) / (
    x_norm * y_norm
    + 1e-12
)

and returns:

1.0 - sim

docs.title: Zero-vector protection
docs.text:
The denominator contains:

1e-12

to avoid division by zero.

This means the implementation does not raise simply because one of the vectors has norm zero.

docs.title: Range noted by the source
docs.text:
The module notes that cosine distance is theoretically in:

\[ [0,2]. \]

It also notes that values are typically in:

\[ [0,1] \]

for non-negative data.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.distances import (
    CosineDistance,
)

distance = CosineDistance()

D = distance.matrix(
    x,
    y,
)

docs.title: Hamming distance
docs.text:
The implementation class is:

HammingDistance

registered as:

hamming

The source defines normalized Hamming distance as:

\[ d(x,y) = \frac{1}{d} \sum_{k=1}^{d} \mathbf{1} [x_k\neq y_k]. \]

So the output measures the fraction of coordinates that differ.

docs.title: Output range
docs.text:
Because the distance is normalized by the number of features:

\[ 0 \leq d(x,y) \leq 1. \]

docs.title: Intended data type
docs.text:
The source explicitly describes Hamming distance as intended for:

discrete
binary
categorical
symbolic

representations.

It also states that continuous features should be discretized before use.

docs.title: Numba implementation
docs.text:
The primary Hamming path uses:

@nb.jit(
    nopython=True,
    parallel=True,
    fastmath=True,
)

for:

hamming_matrix_numba()

The function loops over all sample pairs and all feature coordinates.

For every pair:

if x[i, k] != y[j, k]:
    diff_count += 1.0

then:

distances[i, j] = (
    diff_count
    / n_features
)

docs.title: NumPy fallback
docs.text:
The public matrix() method wraps the Numba path in:

try:
    ...
except Exception:
    ...

If the Numba path fails, it uses:

np.mean(
    x[:, None, :]
    !=
    y[None, :, :],
    axis=2,
)

This produces the same normalized mismatch fraction.

docs.title: Hamming and CombinedClassifier
docs.text:
The default distance for:

CombinedClassifier

is:

hamming

This aligns with the current prediction-space representation used by CombinedClassifier, which consists of hard class predictions such as:

[0, 1, 1, 0]

For two prediction vectors:

[0, 1, 1, 0]
[0, 0, 1, 0]

one of four coordinates differs, so:

\[ d_{\text{Hamming}} = \frac14. \]

docs.title: Distance defaults by estimator
docs.text:
The current source defaults are:

Estimator Default distance GradientCOBRA euclidean MixCOBRARegressor euclidean CombinedClassifier hamming

These defaults reflect the representations used by the corresponding estimators.

docs.title: Distance configuration
docs.text:
Each high-level COBRA estimator accepts:

distance

and:

distance_params

For example:

model = GradientCOBRA(
    distance="cosine",
)

or:

model = GradientCOBRA(
    distance="minkowski",
    distance_params={
        "p": 4,
    },
)

docs.title: How distance objects are resolved
docs.text:
The shared resolver contains:

return DistanceFactory.create(
    distance,
    **(
        distance_params
        or {}
    ),
)

The high-level estimators use equivalent factory construction.

Therefore:

distance

selects the registered implementation and:

distance_params

are forwarded to its constructor.

docs.title: Inspect the fitted distance object
docs.text:
After fitting a COBRA estimator:

print(
    model.distance_
)

To inspect parameters:

print(
    model.distance_.get_params()
)

For Minkowski:

print(
    model.distance_.p
)

docs.title: Prediction-space distance
docs.text:
For GradientCOBRA, the distance is computed on normalized prediction vectors.

During fitting:

self.distance_matrix_ = self.distance_.matrix(
    self.Y_l_norm_,
    self.Y_l_norm_,
)

At prediction time:

distance_matrix = self.distance_.matrix(
    Y_norm,
    self.Y_l_norm_,
)

So the distance object itself is independent of COBRA's normalization step.

It receives whatever representation the estimator passes into it.

docs.title: CombinedClassifier distance
docs.text:
CombinedClassifier stores its calibration prediction representation as:

pred_l_

and computes:

self.distance_matrix_ = self.distance_.matrix(
    self.pred_l_,
    self.pred_l_,
)

New prediction patterns are compared with:

self.distance_.matrix(
    preds_space,
    self.pred_l_,
)

No separate prediction normalization is applied by the current CombinedClassifier before this distance calculation.

docs.title: MixCOBRA distances
docs.text:
MixCOBRA can maintain two separate distance matrices.

In two-parameter mode:

self.distance_matrix_x_

is computed on:

X_l_norm_

and:

self.distance_matrix_y_

is computed on:

Y_l_norm_

The same configured distance implementation is used for both spaces.

docs.title: Two-space combination
docs.text:
The distance matrices are later combined by the two-parameter adapter as:

\[ D_{\text{mix}} = \alpha D_X + \beta D_Y. \]

The distance class itself does not know about:

alpha
beta

Those parameters belong to the adapter layer.

docs.title: One-parameter MixCOBRA
docs.text:
With:

one_parameter=True

the source first concatenates:

X_l_norm_
Y_l_norm_

into:

mix_features_

Then the configured distance is computed once on the combined representation.

So:

distance

still controls geometry, while the one-parameter adapter later scales the result.

docs.title: Distance vs kernel
docs.text:
Distance and kernel are separate concepts.

The distance computes:

\[ D = d(x,y). \]

The adapter may rescale it, for example:

\[ D' = hD. \]

Then the kernel turns that value into a similarity weight:

\[ K(D'). \]

So choosing:

distance="euclidean"

does not by itself define the final aggregation weight.

docs.title: Example with RBF kernel
docs.text:
Suppose Euclidean distance produces:

\[ D=2. \]

If the adapter applies:

\[ h=0.5, \]

then:

\[ D'=1. \]

The RBF kernel then receives:

1

rather than the original:

2.

This separation is why distance configuration and bandwidth optimization are handled independently in the source.

docs.title: Euclidean vs Minkowski p=2
docs.text:
The source provides both:

euclidean

and:

minkowski with p=2

These represent the same L2 distance mathematically.

However, the implementation paths differ.

EuclideanDistance uses the dot-product identity:

||x||² + ||y||² - 2<x,y>

while MinkowskiDistance uses explicit pairwise broadcasting.

Therefore they are not implemented identically even when:

p=2

docs.title: Manhattan vs Minkowski p=1
docs.text:
Similarly:

manhattan

and:

minkowski with p=1

represent the same L1 formula mathematically.

But:

ManhattanDistance

delegates to SciPy's:

distance_matrix(..., p=1)

while:

MinkowskiDistance

uses NumPy broadcasting.

docs.title: Memory behavior
docs.text:
The implementations differ in how they form pairwise distances.

EuclideanDistance avoids a full:

(n_x, n_y, n_features)

difference tensor.

ManhattanDistance delegates to SciPy.

MinkowskiDistance explicitly creates the broadcasted expression:

x[:, None, :]
-
y[None, :, :]

which conceptually has three dimensions.

HammingDistance uses a Numba loop first, avoiding the broadcasted tensor in its primary path, with a broadcasted NumPy fallback.

The source does not contain an automatic memory-based distance selector.

docs.title: Shape compatibility
docs.text:
The current distance implementations assume compatible feature dimensions.

For example:

x.shape[1]

and:

y.shape[1]

must represent the same coordinate dimension.

The classes do not define a common explicit manual check for mismatched feature counts.

Incompatible shapes therefore fail through the underlying NumPy/SciPy operations.

docs.title: Input validation scope
docs.text:
The built-in distance classes mainly perform:

np.asarray(...)

before calculation.

They do not define a shared validation layer for:

NaN
infinity
empty arrays
dtype compatibility
feature-count agreement

Those conditions are therefore handled implicitly by the mathematical operations or by later stages.

docs.title: Custom distance
docs.text:
A custom metric can subclass:

BaseDistance

and implement:

matrix()

For example:

import numpy as np

from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.distances import (
    BaseDistance,
    DistanceFactory,
)


@DistanceFactory.register(
    "squared_l2"
)
class SquaredL2Distance(
    BaseDistance
):

    def matrix(
        self,
        x,
        y,
    ):
        x = np.asarray(x)
        y = np.asarray(y)

        diff = (
            x[:, None, :]
            -
            y[None, :, :]
        )

        return np.sum(
            diff ** 2,
            axis=2,
        )

Then:

distance = DistanceFactory.create(
    "squared_l2"
)

can resolve it.

docs.title: Custom distance with parameters
docs.text:
Because BaseDistance already supports arbitrary keyword parameters, a custom distance can expose them through the constructor.

@DistanceFactory.register(
    "scaled_l1"
)
class ScaledL1Distance(
    BaseDistance
):

    def __init__(
        self,
        scale=1.0,
    ):
        super().__init__(
            scale=scale,
        )

    def matrix(
        self,
        x,
        y,
    ):
        x = np.asarray(x)
        y = np.asarray(y)

        return self.scale * np.sum(
            np.abs(
                x[:, None, :]
                -
                y[None, :, :]
            ),
            axis=2,
        )

Then:

model = GradientCOBRA(
    distance="scaled_l1",
    distance_params={
        "scale": 2.0,
    },
)

works through the normal factory path.

docs.title: Registering aliases
docs.text:
The factory supports multiple names:

@DistanceFactory.register(
    "scaled_l1",
    "my_l1",
)
class ScaledL1Distance(
    BaseDistance
):
    ...

Both names resolve to the same class.

docs.title: Duplicate registration
docs.text:
Because DistanceFactory inherits BaseFactory, duplicate normalized names are rejected.

For example, registering both:

MyMetric
mymetric

in the same call is considered a duplicate after normalization.

Existing registry conflicts raise:

KeyError

docs.title: Inspect available distances
docs.text:
from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.distances import (
    DistanceFactory,
)

print(
    DistanceFactory.available()
)

The current built-ins include aliases, so the list should include names such as:

cosine
euclidean
hamming
l1
l2
lp
manhattan
minkowski

subject to normal module loading.

docs.title: Inspect one registration
docs.text:
print(
    DistanceFactory.info(
        "euclidean"
    )
)

This uses the common factory metadata interface inherited from BaseFactory.

docs.title: Direct comparison example
docs.text:
import numpy as np

from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.distances import (
    DistanceFactory,
)

x = np.array([
    [1.0, 0.0],
    [1.0, 1.0],
])

y = np.array([
    [0.0, 1.0],
])

for name in [
    "euclidean",
    "manhattan",
    "minkowski",
    "cosine",
]:
    distance = DistanceFactory.create(
        name
    )

    print(
        name,
        distance.matrix(
            x,
            y,
        ),
    )

This compares the source implementations on the same coordinate representation.

docs.title: Hamming example
docs.text:
x = np.array([
    [0, 1, 1, 0],
    [1, 1, 0, 0],
])

y = np.array([
    [0, 0, 1, 0],
])

distance = DistanceFactory.create(
    "hamming"
)

D = distance.matrix(
    x,
    y,
)

print(
    D
)

For the first row, one of four coordinates differs:

\[ d=\frac14. \]

docs.title: Choosing a distance
docs.text:
The source exposes different geometries rather than enforcing one globally.

A source-aligned summary is:

  • Euclidean

    Standard L2 geometry.

    Registry:

    euclidean
l2

  • Manhattan

    Coordinate-wise absolute differences.

    Registry:

    manhattan
l1

  • Minkowski

    Generalized Lp distance with configurable:

    p

  • Cosine

    Compares vector direction through angular dissimilarity.

  • Hamming

    Counts normalized coordinate mismatches.

    Used by default in CombinedClassifier.

docs.title: Check the configured name
docs.text:
print(
    model.distance
)

docs.title: Check parameters
docs.text:
print(
    model.distance_params
)

docs.title: Check the resolved object
docs.text:
After fitting:

print(
    model.distance_
)

docs.title: Check effective parameters
docs.text:
print(
    model.distance_.get_params()
)

docs.title: Check matrix shape
docs.text:
D = model.distance_.matrix(
    A,
    B,
)

print(
    D.shape
)

Expected:

(A.shape[0], B.shape[0])

docs.title: Check symmetry carefully
docs.text:
A metric such as Euclidean satisfies:

\[ d(x,y)=d(y,x). \]

But the returned matrices:

distance.matrix(
    A,
    B,
)

and:

distance.matrix(
    B,
    A,
)

have transposed shapes.

To compare them:

np.allclose(
    distance.matrix(
        A,
        B,
    ),
    distance.matrix(
        B,
        A,
    ).T,
)

docs.title: Current implementation summary
docs.text: Distance Formula Constructor parameter Implementation Euclidean \(\sqrt{\sum (x-y)^2}\) none vectorized dot-product identity Manhattan (\sum x-y ) Minkowski ((\sum x-y ^p)^{1/p}) Cosine \(1-\frac{x^\top y}{\|x\|\|y\|}\) none vectorized norms/dot products Hamming mean coordinate mismatch none Numba, NumPy fallback

docs.title: Quick reference
docs.text: Registry Alias Typical current use euclidean l2 default GradientCOBRA / MixCOBRA manhattan l1 alternative L1 geometry minkowski lp configurable Lp geometry cosine — angular comparison hamming — default CombinedClassifier prediction-space comparison

docs.title: Mental model
docs.text:
The distance layer decides what “nearby” means before the kernel turns that geometry into aggregation weights.

\[ \boxed{ \text{representation} \rightarrow d(x,y) \rightarrow \text{distance matrix} \rightarrow \text{kernel} \rightarrow \text{aggregation} } \]

Distance selection changes the geometry of the COBRA neighborhood, while the kernel and optimizer determine how that geometry is converted into prediction weights.

docs.title: Gradient Optimization
docs.text:
Gradient optimization is the continuous-parameter optimization path used by the COBRA subsystem.

The current source provides three registered gradient optimizers:

gd
momentum
adam

implemented under:

kfc_procedure/cobra/core/optimizers/gradient/
├── base.py
├── gd.py
├── momentum.py
└── adam.py

Numerical-gradient utilities live in:

kfc_procedure/cobra/core/optimizers/_utils.py

The gradient family is used by:

GradientCOBRA
MixCOBRARegressor

when:

opt_method="grad"

and the selected kernel advertises:

requires_grad = True

docs.title: What gradient optimization tunes
docs.text:
The gradient subsystem minimizes a scalar objective:

\[ \min_x f(x). \]

In COBRA, \(x\) usually represents aggregation parameters rather than the coefficients of the original base estimators.

Examples include:

GradientCOBRA
    x = [bandwidth]

MixCOBRA one-parameter mode
    x = [bandwidth-like parameter]

MixCOBRA two-parameter mode
    x = [alpha, beta]

The objective itself is the cross-validation loss produced by the fitted COBRA aggregation pipeline.

docs.title: Position in the pipeline
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    X["Parameter vector"]
    A["Adapter"]
    K["Kernel"]
    G["Aggregator"]
    L["Cross-validation loss"]
    N["Numerical gradient"]
    O["Gradient optimizer"]

    X --> A --> K --> G --> L
    L --> N
    N --> O
    O --> X

The optimizer does not directly train:

base estimators
distance models
kernel models

Instead, it repeatedly evaluates how changing the adapter parameters affects the cross-validation objective.

docs.title: Registered gradient optimizers
docs.text:
Registry name Class Update strategy gd GradientDescentOptimizer plain gradient descent momentum MomentumOptimizer gradient descent with velocity adam AdamOptimizer adaptive first/second moments

All three are registered with categories:

optimizer
gradient

through:

OptimizerFactory

docs.title: BaseGradientOptimizer
docs.text:
All gradient implementations inherit:

BaseGradientOptimizer

which provides:

gradient calculation
learning-rate schedules
parameter initialization
main optimization loop
early stopping
history tracking

Subclasses only need to implement:

step(
    x,
    lr,
    grad,
    state,
)

docs.title: Constructor
docs.text:
The current base constructor is:

BaseGradientOptimizer(
    learning_rate=0.01,
    max_iter=300,
    tol=1e-7,
    speed="constant",
    gradient_method="central",
    eps=1e-7,
    n_tries=5,
    init_range=(1e-4, 3.0),
    show_process=True,
    **kwargs,
)

docs.title: Core parameters
docs.text: Parameter Current default Purpose learning_rate 0.01 initial learning-rate scale max_iter 300 maximum optimizer iterations tol 1e-7 gradient-norm stopping threshold speed "constant" learning-rate schedule gradient_method "central" numerical-gradient method eps 1e-7 finite-difference step n_tries 5 initialization candidates init_range (1e-4, 3.0) initialization interval show_process True progress display

docs.title: Gradient computation
docs.text:
The base optimizer calls:

compute_gradient(
    objective=objective,
    params=params,
    gradient=grad_fn,
    method=self.gradient_method,
    eps=self.eps,
)

If:

grad_fn

is supplied, it overrides numerical differentiation.

Otherwise, the requested numerical-gradient method is used.

docs.title: Supported numerical-gradient methods
docs.text:
The current dispatcher supports:

central
forward
spsa
complex
parallel

through:

GRADIENT_METHODS

docs.title: Central difference
docs.text:
The default method is:

central

For parameter coordinate \(i\):

\[ g_i = \frac{ f(x+\varepsilon e_i) - f(x-\varepsilon e_i) }{ 2\varepsilon }. \]

The source temporarily perturbs one coordinate at a time.

Implementation concept:

p[i] = original + eps
f_plus = objective(p)

p[i] = original - eps
f_minus = objective(p)

grad[i] = (
    f_plus
    -
    f_minus
) / (
    2 * eps
)

docs.title: Central-difference cost
docs.text:
For a parameter vector of dimension:

\[ d, \]

one gradient calculation requires approximately:

\[ 2d \]

objective evaluations.

Since a COBRA objective itself runs cross-validation, numerical gradients can be computationally expensive even for low-dimensional parameter vectors.

docs.title: Forward difference
docs.text:
The source also supports:

forward

with:

\[ g_i = \frac{ f(x+\varepsilon e_i) - f(x) }{ \varepsilon }. \]

The implementation evaluates:

f0 = objective(p)

once, then one positive perturbation per dimension.

Approximate cost:

\[ d+1 \]

objective calls per gradient evaluation.

docs.title: SPSA
docs.text:
The method:

spsa

uses Simultaneous Perturbation Stochastic Approximation.

The source samples:

delta = np.random.choice(
    [-1.0, 1.0],
    size=p.shape,
)

then computes:

\[ g \approx \frac{ f(x+\varepsilon\Delta) - f(x-\varepsilon\Delta) }{ 2\varepsilon\Delta }. \]

docs.title: SPSA cost
docs.text:
Only two objective evaluations are required regardless of parameter dimension:

f(x + eps * delta)
f(x - eps * delta)

This can make SPSA attractive for higher-dimensional black-box objectives.

docs.title: SPSA reproducibility caveat
docs.text:
The current helper uses:

np.random.choice(...)

from NumPy's global random state.

It does not accept:

random_state

and does not use the COBRA estimator's seed.

Current source behavior

Selecting:

gradient_method="spsa"

introduces stochastic perturbations whose sequence is not controlled by the normal estimator random_state parameter.

docs.title: Complex-step gradient
docs.text:
The method:

complex

uses:

\[ g_i = \frac{ \operatorname{Im} f(x+i\varepsilon e_i) }{ \varepsilon }. \]

The source default inside the standalone function is:

eps=1e-20

docs.title: Important dispatcher detail
docs.text:
BaseGradientOptimizer passes:

self.eps

into:

compute_gradient()

and its default is:

1e-7.

Therefore when complex-step differentiation is selected through the optimizer, the effective epsilon is normally:

1e-7

unless you explicitly configure another value.

The standalone helper's own:

1e-20

default is bypassed because compute_gradient() supplies the optimizer epsilon.

docs.title: Complex compatibility
docs.text:
The objective must support complex-valued parameter perturbations.

The source does not test that compatibility before running.

If downstream code discards imaginary components or rejects complex arrays, the method may not produce a meaningful gradient.

docs.title: Parallel central difference
docs.text:
The method:

parallel

uses the same central-difference formula as the default method but evaluates coordinates with:

joblib.Parallel

and:

delayed(...)

docs.title: Worker count
docs.text:
compute_gradient() has:

n_jobs=None

and, for parallel mode, maps that to:

n_jobs=-1

unless a value is explicitly provided.

However, BaseGradientOptimizer.gradient() currently calls compute_gradient() without passing an n_jobs argument.

Therefore the standard optimizer path uses:

all available workers

for the parallel gradient helper.

docs.title: Unknown gradient methods
docs.text:
If the method name is not one of:

central
forward
spsa
complex
parallel

the dispatcher raises:

ValueError:
Unknown method '...'. Available: [...]

docs.title: Analytical gradients
docs.text:
The optimization API supports:

grad_fn=

in:

BaseGradientOptimizer.optimize()

When present:

compute_gradient()

returns:

np.asarray(
    gradient(params),
    dtype=float,
)

and skips numerical differentiation.

docs.title: High-level COBRA usage
docs.text:
The current GradientCOBRA and MixCOBRA optimization paths call the optimizer without supplying a custom:

grad_fn

so they use numerical gradients.

Analytical gradients are available as a lower-level optimizer feature rather than a high-level estimator feature in the current source.

docs.title: Initialization
docs.text:
When:

init_param is None

the base optimizer runs:

_initialize(
    objective,
    dim=1,
)

docs.title: Initialization grid
docs.text:
The source builds:

grid = np.linspace(
    low,
    high,
    n_tries,
)

from:

init_range

then constructs:

candidates = np.array([
    np.full(
        dim,
        g,
    )
    for g in grid
])

and chooses the candidate with the lowest objective score.

docs.title: Initialization limitation
docs.text:
Inside:

optimize()

the source always calls:

_initialize(
    objective,
    dim=1,
)

when init_param is absent.

So the automatic initialization path is effectively one-dimensional from this entry point.

For multi-parameter optimization, a caller should provide an explicit init_param.

The high-level MixCOBRA source does exactly that.

docs.title: COBRA initial parameters
docs.text:
GradientCOBRA uses:

init_param=np.array([
    1.0
])

for gradient mode.

MixCOBRA one-parameter mode uses:

np.array([
    1.0
])

and two-parameter mode uses:

np.array([
    1.0,
    1.0,
])

Therefore the internal automatic initialization search is normally bypassed in the main COBRA integrations.

docs.title: Initial gradient scaling
docs.text:
After choosing x, the optimizer computes:

grad = self.gradient(
    objective,
    x,
    grad_fn,
)

Then:

r0 = self.learning_rate / (
    np.linalg.norm(
        grad
    )
    +
    1e-12
)

This is an important implementation detail.

The value configured as:

learning_rate

is divided by the initial gradient norm before the learning-rate schedule is applied.

docs.title: Effective first step scale
docs.text:
For constant schedule:

\[ r_0 = \frac{ \eta }{ \|\nabla f(x_0)\|+10^{-12} }. \]

So the first step size is normalized by the initial gradient magnitude.

The optimizer does not directly use:

learning_rate

as the first raw multiplier.

docs.title: Learning-rate schedules
docs.text:
The source supports:

constant
linear
log
sqrt_root
quad
exp

through:

_rate(
    t,
    r0,
)

docs.title: Current formulas
docs.text:
The source dictionary is:

{
    "constant": lambda x, y: y,
    "linear": lambda x, y: x * y,
    "log": lambda x, y: np.log(1 + x) * y,
    "sqrt_root": lambda x, y: np.sqrt(1 + x) * y,
    "quad": lambda x, y: (1 + x**2) * y,
    "exp": lambda x, y: np.exp(x) * y,
}

where:

x = iteration index t
y = r0

docs.title: Important schedule behavior
docs.text:
Several names may sound like decay schedules, but the current formulas do not decay.

For example:

linear
    lr_t = t * r0

log
    lr_t = log(1+t) * r0

sqrt_root
    lr_t = sqrt(1+t) * r0

quad
    lr_t = (1+t²) * r0

exp
    lr_t = exp(t) * r0

These increase with iteration.

docs.title: linear starts at zero
docs.text:
At:

t = 0

the linear schedule returns:

\[ 0\times r_0 = 0. \]

So the first update under:

speed="linear"

does not move the parameters.

docs.title: Exponential growth
docs.text:
With:

speed="exp"

the learning rate becomes:

\[ e^t r_0. \]

This can grow extremely quickly.

The current source does not cap or clip the scheduled learning rate.

Current implementation

The non-constant schedules are increasing functions as implemented.

Do not assume names such as linear, log, or sqrt_root mean learning rate decay.

docs.title: Unknown schedule names
docs.text:
The source uses:

schedules.get(
    self.speed,
    schedules["constant"],
)

Therefore an unknown:

speed

does not raise an error.

It silently uses:

constant

behavior.

docs.title: Main optimization loop
docs.text:
After initialization, the optimizer stores:

best_x = x.copy()

best_score = objective(
    x
)

Then it runs up to:

max_iter

iterations.

For iteration t:

1. compute scheduled learning rate
2. call subclass step()
3. repair NaN parameter vectors
4. compute new gradient
5. evaluate new objective
6. update best solution
7. check gradient-norm stopping
8. optionally shrink r0 after gradient sign changes
9. record history

docs.title: NaN parameter repair
docs.text:
After the subclass update:

x_new, state = self.step(
    x,
    lr_t,
    grad,
    state,
)

the source checks:

if np.any(
    np.isnan(
        x_new
    )
):
    x_new = x * 0.95

So if any coordinate becomes NaN, the entire new parameter vector is replaced by:

\[ 0.95x. \]

docs.title: Infinite values are not repaired
docs.text:
The check is specifically:

np.isnan(
    x_new
)

The source does not separately repair:

+Inf
-Inf

parameter values.

docs.title: Best-solution tracking
docs.text:
After evaluating:

score = objective(
    x_new
)

the source updates:

if score < best_score:
    best_score = score
    best_x = x_new.copy()

The optimizer returns the best point encountered, not necessarily the final iteration point.

docs.title: Early stopping
docs.text:
The gradient is recomputed at:

x_new

and stopping occurs when:

\[ \|\nabla f(x_{\text{new}})\| < \text{tol}. \]

The exact check is:

if np.linalg.norm(
    grad_new
) < self.tol:
    x = x_new
    break

docs.title: History omission on early stopping
docs.text:
This stopping check happens before the history entry is appended.

Therefore the final converged step is not added to:

history

when optimization terminates through this gradient-norm condition.

The score can still update:

best_score
best_x

before the break.

docs.title: Gradient-sign adjustment
docs.text:
After at least four previous iterations:

if (
    t > 3
    and np.any(
        np.sign(
            grad_new
        )
        !=
        np.sign(
            prev_grad
        )
    )
):
    r0 *= 0.99

So if any gradient coordinate changes sign, the base learning-rate scale is reduced by:

1%

docs.title: Sign comparison detail
docs.text:
The comparison is between:

grad_new

and:

prev_grad

not directly between grad_new and the current grad.

At the end of each completed iteration:

prev_grad = grad_new.copy()
grad = grad_new.copy()

so after normal completed iterations those values become identical for the next loop.

This means the effective comparison is against the prior stored gradient.

docs.title: Optimization history
docs.text:
A completed iteration appends:

{
    "iter": t + 1,
    "x": x.copy(),
    "score": score,
    "grad": grad,
    "grad_norm": float(
        np.linalg.norm(
            grad
        )
    ),
    "lr": lr_t,
}

docs.title: History fields
docs.text: Field Meaning iter one-based iteration number x parameter vector after update score objective value at that vector grad gradient at that vector grad_norm Euclidean gradient norm lr scheduled step multiplier used for the update

docs.title: History is not total objective-call history
docs.text:
A finite-difference gradient can call the objective multiple times per iteration.

Those internal calls are not recorded as history entries.

The following are also evaluated outside normal history rows:

initial gradient
initial best-score calculation
terminating early-stop step
initialization candidate search, when used

So:

len(
    result["history"]
)

is the number of recorded optimizer iterations, not the total number of objective evaluations.

docs.title: Progress display
docs.text:
When:

show_process=True

the optimizer wraps the iteration range in:

tqdm(
    range(
        max_iter
    ),
    desc="GD",
    leave=True,
)

This description remains:

GD

even for:

MomentumOptimizer
AdamOptimizer

because the progress loop is implemented in the shared base class.

docs.title: Progress text
docs.text:
After a completed iteration, the description is changed to:

iter=N | score=... | grad_norm=...

docs.title: Gradient Descent
docs.text:
The simplest registered optimizer is:

GradientDescentOptimizer

under:

gd

Its update rule is:

\[ x_{t+1} = x_t - \eta_tg_t. \]

The implementation is exactly:

x_new = (
    x
    -
    lr
    *
    grad
)

The state dictionary is unchanged.

docs.title: Direct use
docs.text:
import numpy as np

from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.optimizers import (
    GradientDescentOptimizer,
)


def objective(
    params,
):
    x = params[0]

    return (
        x - 2.0
    ) ** 2


optimizer = GradientDescentOptimizer(
    learning_rate=0.1,
    max_iter=100,
    show_process=False,
)

result = optimizer.optimize(
    objective,
    init_param=np.array([
        1.0
    ]),
)

print(
    result["x"]
)

print(
    result["score"]
)

docs.title: Momentum
docs.text:
MomentumOptimizer is registered as:

momentum

and adds:

momentum=0.9

to the base optimizer parameters.

docs.title: Momentum state
docs.text:
On the first step:

state["v"] = np.zeros_like(
    x
)

The state stores one velocity vector:

v

docs.title: Momentum update
docs.text:
The source computes:

\[ v_t = \mu v_{t-1} - \eta_tg_t \]

then:

\[ x_{t+1} = x_t+v_t. \]

Implementation:

v = (
    self.momentum
    *
    v
    -
    lr
    *
    grad
)

state["v"] = v

x_new = x + v

docs.title: Configure momentum
docs.text:
optimizer = MomentumOptimizer(
    momentum=0.95,
    learning_rate=0.05,
    max_iter=200,
    show_process=False,
)

The current constructor does not validate that:

0 <= momentum < 1

or any other interval.

The supplied value is used directly.

docs.title: Adam
docs.text:
AdamOptimizer is registered as:

adam

and adds:

beta1=0.9
beta2=0.999

to the base configuration.

docs.title: Adam state
docs.text:
On first use, the source creates:

state["m"] = np.zeros_like(
    x
)

state["v"] = np.zeros_like(
    x
)

state["t"] = 0

The state therefore tracks:

m
    first moment

v
    second moment

t
    optimizer timestep

docs.title: Adam moment updates
docs.text:
The source computes:

\[ m_t = \beta_1m_{t-1} + (1-\beta_1)g_t \]

and:

\[ v_t = \beta_2v_{t-1} + (1-\beta_2)g_t^2. \]

docs.title: Bias correction
docs.text:
The implementation applies:

\[ \hat m_t = \frac{ m_t }{ 1-\beta_1^t } \]

and:

\[ \hat v_t = \frac{ v_t }{ 1-\beta_2^t }. \]

docs.title: Adam update
docs.text:
The source uses:

\[ x_{t+1} = x_t - \eta_t \frac{ \hat m_t }{ \sqrt{\hat v_t} + 10^{-8} }. \]

The stabilizer:

1e-8

is hard-coded inside:

AdamOptimizer.step()

docs.title: No configurable Adam epsilon
docs.text:
The class docstring mentions an epsilon numerical stability constant, but the constructor is:

AdamOptimizer(
    beta1=0.9,
    beta2=0.999,
    **kwargs,
)

There is no explicit:

epsilon=

parameter.

The update always uses:

1e-8

in the current source.

Documentation/source mismatch

The class documentation mentions an Adam epsilon parameter, but the current constructor does not expose one.

docs.title: Configure Adam
docs.text:
optimizer = AdamOptimizer(
    beta1=0.9,
    beta2=0.999,
    learning_rate=0.05,
    max_iter=200,
    gradient_method="central",
    show_process=False,
)

The current source does not explicitly validate the ranges of:

beta1
beta2.

docs.title: OptimizerFactory usage
docs.text:
Create gradient descent:

from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.optimizers import (
    OptimizerFactory,
)

optimizer = OptimizerFactory.create(
    "gd",
    learning_rate=0.05,
)

Momentum:

optimizer = OptimizerFactory.create(
    "momentum",
    momentum=0.9,
)

Adam:

optimizer = OptimizerFactory.create(
    "adam",
    beta1=0.9,
    beta2=0.999,
)

docs.title: Inspect gradient optimizers
docs.text:
print(
    OptimizerFactory.available_by_category(
        "gradient"
    )
)

The current registry should include:

adam
gd
momentum

docs.title: Kernel compatibility
docs.text:
GradientCOBRA and MixCOBRA do not blindly use gradient optimization.

Before choosing the optimizer family, they check:

kernel_.requires_grad

docs.title: Gradient-compatible built-in kernels
docs.text:
The current continuous kernels advertise:

requires_grad = True

including:

rbf / radial / gaussian
exponential
reverse_cosh
cauchy

docs.title: Non-gradient kernels
docs.text:
The current compact/discrete kernels advertise:

requires_grad = False

including:

epanechnikov
biweight
triweight
triangular
naive
cobra

docs.title: Automatic fallback to grid search
docs.text:
If:

opt_method="grad"

but:

kernel_.requires_grad == False

both GradientCOBRA and MixCOBRA change the local effective method to:

grid

before optimizer resolution.

So:

GradientCOBRA(
    kernel="cobra",
    opt_method="grad",
    optimizer="adam",
)

does not continue with Adam under the normal source path.

It falls back to grid-family optimization.

docs.title: Category validation
docs.text:
For GradientCOBRA and MixCOBRA, effective:

grad

mode requires:

OptimizerFactory.supports(
    optimizer,
    category="gradient",
)

So:

optimizer="grid"
opt_method="grad"

is rejected when the effective method remains gradient-based.

Likewise, grid mode requires the:

search

category.

docs.title: GradientCOBRA configuration
docs.text:
The relevant constructor parameters include:

optimizer="grid"
optimizer_params=None
opt_method="grid"
learning_rate=0.1
max_iter=300

To enable gradient optimization:

from kfc_procedure.cobra import (
    GradientCOBRA,
)

model = GradientCOBRA(
    optimizer="adam",
    opt_method="grad",
    learning_rate=0.05,
    max_iter=200,
)

docs.title: GradientCOBRA optimizer parameters
docs.text:
The source copies:

optimizer_params

then, in gradient mode, updates:

{
    "learning_rate": self.learning_rate,
    "max_iter": self.max_iter,
}

before creating the optimizer.

Therefore top-level:

learning_rate
max_iter

take precedence over same-named values previously placed in optimizer_params.

docs.title: Additional GradientCOBRA optimizer settings
docs.text:
Use optimizer_params for options such as:

optimizer_params={
    "tol": 1e-6,
    "gradient_method": "forward",
    "eps": 1e-6,
    "speed": "constant",
    "show_process": False,
    "beta1": 0.9,
    "beta2": 0.999,
}

Parameters irrelevant to a given subclass may be absorbed by **kwargs depending on the constructor path.

docs.title: GradientCOBRA starting point
docs.text:
The current gradient path calls the optimizer with:

init_param=np.array([
    1.0
])

so bandwidth optimization starts from:

\[ h_0=1. \]

docs.title: GradientCOBRA result
docs.text:
After optimization:

self.bandwidth_ = float(
    np.atleast_1d(
        result["x"]
    )[0]
)

and the source stores:

self.optimization_outputs_ = {
    "method": method,
    "optimizer": optimizer,
    "bandwidth": self.bandwidth_,
    "score": result["score"],
    "history": history_df,
    "evaluations": len(
        result["history"]
    ),
}

docs.title: GradientCOBRA records effective method
docs.text:
The stored:

optimization_outputs_[
    "method"
]

uses the local effective method.

Therefore if the kernel forces a fallback from:

grad

to:

grid,

GradientCOBRA reports:

grid.

docs.title: MixCOBRA configuration
docs.text:
Relevant constructor parameters include:

optimizer="grid"
optimizer_params=None
opt_method="grid"
learning_rate=0.01
max_iter=300
one_parameter=False

Gradient mode example:

from kfc_procedure.cobra import (
    MixCOBRARegressor,
)

model = MixCOBRARegressor(
    optimizer="adam",
    opt_method="grad",
    learning_rate=0.01,
)

docs.title: MixCOBRA one-parameter start
docs.text:
With:

one_parameter=True

the gradient optimizer starts from:

np.array([
    1.0
])

docs.title: MixCOBRA two-parameter start
docs.text:
With:

one_parameter=False

the optimizer starts from:

np.array([
    1.0,
    1.0,
])

representing:

\[ (\alpha,\beta) = (1,1). \]

docs.title: MixCOBRA result
docs.text:
The optimization output stores:

{
    "method": self.opt_method,
    "score": result["score"],
    "history": history_df,
    "evaluations": len(
        result["history"]
    ),
    "params": result["x"],
}

docs.title: MixCOBRA reporting caveat
docs.text:
The current source stores:

self.opt_method

rather than the local effective method after kernel fallback.

Therefore a model configured with:

opt_method="grad"

can still report:

grad

even if a non-gradient kernel caused the actual path to use grid optimization.

This differs from GradientCOBRA.

docs.title: No positivity constraints
docs.text:
The base gradient optimizer performs ordinary unconstrained vector updates.

There is no generic source-level projection such as:

x_new = np.maximum(
    x_new,
    0.0,
)

or clipping to a configured interval.

Therefore parameters such as:

bandwidth
alpha
beta

can become negative during gradient optimization.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
For the one-parameter adapter:

\[ D' = hD. \]

A negative:

\[ h \]

turns non-negative distances into negative adapted values.

With the default RBF kernel:

\[ K=e^{-D'}, \]

this can produce weights larger than one:

\[ e^{-hD} > 1 \]

when:

\[ h<0. \]

The current optimizer does not prevent this.

Current gradient path is unconstrained

Grid search uses an explicitly positive default candidate range 0.001 to 10.0.

Gradient optimization is not restricted to that interval.

docs.title: No general parameter clipping
docs.text:
The same applies to MixCOBRA:

\[ D_{\text{mix}} = \alpha D_X + \beta D_Y. \]

Gradient mode can produce:

negative alpha
negative beta

because no projection step is implemented.

The source leaves those parameter semantics to the objective and optimizer trajectory.

docs.title: Objective smoothness
docs.text:
The gradient path uses finite differences over the full cross-validation objective.

That objective contains several components:

adapter
kernel
aggregator
loss
fold averaging

Whether the numerical gradient behaves smoothly depends on the entire composed pipeline.

docs.title: Hard operations and gradient compatibility
docs.text:
The high-level source uses:

kernel_.requires_grad

as its explicit compatibility gate.

However, this flag describes the kernel only.

Other parts of the objective can still contain non-smooth behavior, for example:

classification argmax
zero-weight fallbacks
piecewise losses

The current optimizer does not perform symbolic differentiability analysis of the whole objective.

docs.title: Gradient methods are black-box approximations
docs.text:
The finite-difference helpers only need:

objective(
    params
) -> scalar

They do not require access to analytical derivatives of:

kernel
aggregator
loss

This makes the gradient subsystem effectively a black-box numerical optimizer.

docs.title: Central difference with COBRA CV
docs.text:
For one GradientCOBRA bandwidth:

\[ h, \]

central difference approximates:

\[ J'(h) \approx \frac{ J(h+\varepsilon) - J(h-\varepsilon) }{ 2\varepsilon }, \]

where each:

\[ J(\cdot) \]

is itself a full mean cross-validation loss.

docs.title: Two-parameter central difference
docs.text:
For MixCOBRA:

\[ x = (\alpha,\beta), \]

central difference requires approximately four full objective evaluations per gradient:

\[ J(\alpha+\varepsilon,\beta), \] \[ J(\alpha-\varepsilon,\beta), \] \[ J(\alpha,\beta+\varepsilon), \] \[ J(\alpha,\beta-\varepsilon). \]

The optimizer then separately evaluates the objective at the new parameter vector.

docs.title: eps sensitivity
docs.text:
The default finite-difference step is:

1e-7.

If the objective changes very little at that scale, numerical cancellation can make the estimated gradient noisy.

If the objective has abrupt changes, a tiny epsilon can sample two points on different sides of a discontinuity.

The current source exposes:

eps

through optimizer_params, so it can be tuned manually.

docs.title: Example with forward differences
docs.text:
model = GradientCOBRA(
    optimizer="gd",
    opt_method="grad",
    learning_rate=0.05,
    optimizer_params={
        "gradient_method": "forward",
        "eps": 1e-5,
        "show_process": False,
    },
)

docs.title: Example with SPSA
docs.text:
model = MixCOBRARegressor(
    optimizer="adam",
    opt_method="grad",
    optimizer_params={
        "gradient_method": "spsa",
        "eps": 1e-4,
        "show_process": False,
    },
)

Remember that the current SPSA helper is not seeded from:

model.random_state.

docs.title: Example with parallel central differences
docs.text:
model = MixCOBRARegressor(
    optimizer="adam",
    opt_method="grad",
    optimizer_params={
        "gradient_method": "parallel",
        "show_process": False,
    },
)

The standard BaseGradientOptimizer.gradient() call does not expose a custom n_jobs, so the parallel helper uses its fallback worker count:

-1.

docs.title: Custom analytical gradient
docs.text:
At lower optimizer level:

def objective(
    x,
):
    return (
        x[0] - 3.0
    ) ** 2


def gradient(
    x,
):
    return np.array([
        2.0
        *
        (
            x[0] - 3.0
        )
    ])

Then:

optimizer = GradientDescentOptimizer(
    learning_rate=0.1,
    show_process=False,
)

result = optimizer.optimize(
    objective,
    init_param=np.array([
        1.0
    ]),
    grad_fn=gradient,
)

The numerical-gradient dispatcher is bypassed.

docs.title: Learning-rate schedule example
docs.text:
optimizer = GradientDescentOptimizer(
    learning_rate=0.1,
    speed="constant",
    show_process=False,
)

For experimentation, the current source also accepts:

linear
log
sqrt_root
quad
exp

but remember that these formulas increase rather than decay.

docs.text:
For GradientCOBRA:

history = (
    model
    .optimization_outputs_[
        "history"
    ]

print(
    history.head()

Gradient history is converted to a pandas DataFrame.

Typical columns include:

score
grad
grad_norm
lr

for one-dimensional optimization.

docs.title: MixCOBRA history
docs.text:
For two parameters, the history conversion names coordinates:

alpha
beta

while retaining:

score
grad
grad_norm
lr

docs.title: evaluations is not objective-call count
docs.text:
The high-level estimators set:

"evaluations": len(
    result["history"]
)

This is the number of recorded optimizer iterations.

It is not the number of cross-validation objective evaluations.

With central differences, actual objective calls can be many times larger.

docs.title: Reconstruct a gradient manually
docs.text:
For a fitted GradientCOBRA model, the numerical helper can be used directly.

Conceptually:

from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.optimizers._utils import (
    central_difference_gradient,
)

x = np.array([
    model.bandwidth_
])

grad = central_difference_gradient(
    model.kappa_cross_validation_error,
    x,
    eps=1e-7,
)

This evaluates the fitted model's CV objective around the chosen bandwidth.

docs.text:
GradientCOBRA:
