docs.title: Debugging convergence
docs.text:
Inspect:

history[
    [
        "iter",
        "score",
        "grad_norm",
        "lr",
    ]
]

Useful patterns include:

grad_norm decreasing
score decreasing
learning rate remaining stable

but the source itself does not classify convergence quality.

docs.title: Debugging missing final iteration
docs.text:
If the returned best score seems better than the final row in history, remember that a gradient-norm early-stop step is evaluated before the history append.

The terminating point can therefore be returned as:

best_x
best_score

without appearing as the last DataFrame row.

docs.title: Custom gradient optimizer
docs.text:
To implement a new update rule, subclass:

BaseGradientOptimizer

and implement:

step()

Example:

import numpy as np

from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.optimizers import (
    OptimizerFactory,
)

from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.optimizers.gradient import (
    BaseGradientOptimizer,
)


@OptimizerFactory.register(
    "sign_gd",
    categories={
        "optimizer",
        "gradient",
    },
)
class SignGradientOptimizer(
    BaseGradientOptimizer
):

    def step(
        self,
        x,
        lr,
        grad,
        state,
    ):
        x_new = (
            x
            -
            lr
            *
            np.sign(
                grad
            )
        )

        return (
            x_new,
            state,
        )

This automatically inherits:

gradient estimation
learning-rate schedules
early stopping
history
initialization
progress display

from the base class.

docs.title: Custom optimizer result contract
docs.text:
The inherited optimize() method returns:

{
    "x": best_x,
    "score": best_score,
    "history": history,
}

which matches the result contract expected by GradientCOBRA and MixCOBRA.

docs.title: Mental model
docs.text:
Gradient optimization treats the complete COBRA cross-validation pipeline as a black-box scalar function and numerically follows parameter directions that reduce that loss.

For GradientCOBRA:

\[ \boxed{ h \rightarrow J(h) \rightarrow \frac{dJ}{dh} \rightarrow h_{\text{new}} } \]

For two-parameter MixCOBRA:

\[ \boxed{ (\alpha,\beta) \rightarrow J(\alpha,\beta) \rightarrow \nabla J \rightarrow (\alpha,\beta)_{\text{new}} } \]

The current implementation provides GD, Momentum, and Adam update rules over the same shared numerical-gradient and stopping machinery.

docs.title: Kernels
docs.text:
Kernels convert adapted COBRA distance matrices into similarity or weight matrices.

They sit after the distance and adapter layers:

\[ \boxed{ \text{representation} \rightarrow \text{distance} \rightarrow \text{adapter} \rightarrow \text{kernel} \rightarrow \text{aggregation} } \]

The current source implements ten kernel classes under:

kfc_procedure/cobra/core/kernels/
├── base.py
├── radial.py

All kernels are registered through:

KernelFactory

docs.title: Kernel layer vs bandwidth layer
docs.text:
A key design choice in the current source is that the kernel usually does not own the COBRA bandwidth.

Instead, a kernel adapter transforms the raw distance matrix first.

For the one-parameter adapter:

\[ D' = hD, \]

where:

h = bandwidth

Then the kernel receives:

\[ D'. \]

For example, the default RBF kernel computes:

\[ K(D') = e^{-D'}. \]

So the effective default one-parameter COBRA weight is:

\[ K_h(D) = e^{-hD}. \]

This is important when interpreting the package's bandwidth parameter.

docs.title: COBRA kernel pipeline
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A["Representation"]
    D["Distance matrix D"]
    T["Kernel adapter"]
    DP["Adapted distance D'"]
    K["Kernel K(D')"]
    W["Similarity / weight matrix"]
    G["Aggregator"]

    A --> D --> T --> DP --> K --> W --> G

The distance determines the geometry.

The adapter inserts tunable parameters such as:

bandwidth
alpha
beta

The kernel maps the adapted distances to weights.

docs.title: Built-in kernels
docs.text:
The current source registers:

Registry name Aliases Class Formula / behavior Mode radial gaussian, rbf RadialKernel \(e^{-D}\) continuous exponential — ExponentialKernel \(e^{-D^p}\) continuous reverse_cosh — ReverseCoshKernel \(\cosh(D)^{-p}\) continuous cauchy — CauchyKernel \(1/(1+D)\) continuous epanechnikov — EpanechnikovKernel \(1-D\) for \(D<1\), else 0 compact biweight — BiweightKernel \((1-D)^2\) for \(D<1\), else 0 compact triweight — TriweightKernel \((1-D)^3\) for \(D<1\), else 0 compact triangular — TriangularKernel (1- D naive — NaiveKernel identity \(K(D)=D\) discrete cobra — COBRAKernel 1 if \(D<t\), else 0 discrete

docs.title: BaseKernel
docs.text:
Every built-in kernel inherits from:

BaseKernel

The base interface provides:

__call__(D)
set_params(**params)
get_params(deep=True)
is_continuous()
is_discrete()

A custom kernel must implement:

__call__(D)

which returns the transformed matrix.

docs.title: Base metadata
docs.text:
BaseKernel defines two class-level attributes:

requires_grad = True
mode = "continuous"

Concrete kernels override these values where needed.

The source uses:

requires_grad

to decide whether gradient-style optimization is allowed.

The source uses:

mode

to describe the kernel behavior.

docs.title: Kernel modes
docs.text:
The source documents three modes:

continuous
compact
discrete

The helper:

is_continuous()

returns:

self.mode == "continuous"

and:

is_discrete()

returns:

self.mode == "discrete"

Compact kernels are a third category

A kernel with:

mode = "compact"

returns False from both:

is_continuous()
is_discrete()

because the current helper methods test only exact string equality.

docs.title: Kernel parameters
docs.text:
BaseKernel.__init__() stores keyword parameters in:

self.params

and also sets same-named attributes.

For example:

kernel = ExponentialKernel(
    exponent=2.0,
)

stores:

kernel.params == {
    "exponent": 2.0,
}

and:

kernel.exponent == 2.0

docs.title: get_params()
docs.text:
kernel.get_params()

returns a copy of the internal parameter dictionary.

The deep argument exists for scikit-learn-style compatibility but is not otherwise used by the current implementation.

docs.title: set_params()
docs.text:
kernel.set_params(
    exponent=3.0,
)

updates both:

kernel.exponent

and:

kernel.params["exponent"]

and returns the same object.

docs.title: KernelFactory
docs.text:
Create a registered kernel with:

from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.kernels import (
    KernelFactory,
)

kernel = KernelFactory.create(
    "rbf"
)

Because KernelFactory inherits the package's BaseFactory, names are normalized before lookup.

docs.title: RBF aliases
docs.text:
The radial kernel is registered as:

@KernelFactory.register(
    "radial",
    "gaussian",
    "rbf",
)

Therefore all three names create:

RadialKernel

The high-level COBRA estimators use:

rbf

as their default kernel name.

docs.title: Radial / RBF kernel
docs.text:
The class is:

RadialKernel

with registry names:

radial
gaussian
rbf

Its formula is:

\[ K(D) = e^{-D}. \]

The implementation is exactly:

return np.exp(
    -D
)

docs.title: No gamma parameter in RadialKernel
docs.text:
The current RadialKernel constructor is inherited from BaseKernel.

Its implementation does not define or use:

gamma
sigma
bandwidth

inside the kernel formula.

Bandwidth scaling is handled by the adapter layer.

So for the one-parameter adapter:

\[ D' = hD \]

followed by:

\[ K(D') = e^{-D'} \]

gives:

\[ K_h(D) = e^{-hD}. \]

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
import numpy as np

from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.kernels import (
    RadialKernel,
)

D = np.array([
    [0.0, 0.5],
    [1.0, 2.0],
])

kernel = RadialKernel()

K = kernel(D)

print(
    K
)

docs.title: Exponential kernel
docs.text:
The class is:

ExponentialKernel

registered as:

exponential

Its formula is:

\[ K(D) = \exp\left( -D^{p} \right), \]

where:

p = exponent

docs.title: Constructor
docs.text:
ExponentialKernel(
    exponent=1.0,
)

The default:

exponent=1.0

makes the formula identical to the radial kernel:

\[ e^{-D}. \]

So with its default constructor:

exponential

and:

rbf

produce the same mathematical mapping.

docs.title: Change curvature
docs.text:
kernel = ExponentialKernel(
    exponent=2.0,
)

then:

\[ K(D) = e^{-D^2}. \]

Configure through a COBRA estimator with:

kernel="exponential",
kernel_params={
    "exponent": 2.0,
}

docs.title: Reverse-cosh kernel
docs.text:
The class is:

ReverseCoshKernel

registered as:

reverse_cosh

Its formula is:

\[ K(D) = \frac{1} {\cosh(D)^p}, \]

where:

p = exponent

docs.title: Constructor
docs.text:
ReverseCoshKernel(
    exponent=1.0,
)

The source describes this as a smooth kernel that strongly suppresses large distances.

docs.title: Example configuration
docs.text:
model = GradientCOBRA(
    kernel="reverse_cosh",
    kernel_params={
        "exponent": 2.0,
    },
)

docs.title: Cauchy kernel
docs.text:
The class is:

CauchyKernel

registered as:

cauchy

Its formula is:

\[ K(D) = \frac{1}{1+D}. \]

The source describes it as a heavy-tailed kernel with robust similarity decay.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
return 1.0 / (
    1.0 + D
)

It has no specialized constructor parameters in the current source.

docs.title: Compact-support kernels
docs.text:
Four built-ins have:

mode = "compact"

and:

requires_grad = False

They produce exactly zero weight outside their support.

The current compact kernels are:

epanechnikov
biweight
triweight
triangular

All use a cutoff at:

\[ D=1. \]

docs.title: Epanechnikov kernel
docs.text:
The class is:

EpanechnikovKernel

registered as:

epanechnikov

The current source formula is:

\[ K(D) = \begin{cases} 1-D, & D<1,\\ 0, & D\geq1. \end{cases} \]

The implementation is:

np.where(
    D < 1.0,
    1.0 - D,
    0.0,
)

docs.title: Important naming detail
docs.text:
The implementation called EpanechnikovKernel is exactly the linear compact mapping shown above.

This page preserves the package's source formula rather than substituting a different textbook normalization or polynomial form.

docs.title: Biweight kernel
docs.text:
The class is:

BiweightKernel

registered as:

biweight

Its source formula is:

\[ K(D) = \begin{cases} (1-D)^2, & D<1,\\ 0, & D\geq1. \end{cases} \]

Implementation:

np.where(
    D < 1.0,
    (1.0 - D) ** 2,
    0.0,
)

docs.title: Triweight kernel
docs.text:
The class is:

TriweightKernel

registered as:

triweight

Its source formula is:

\[ K(D) = \begin{cases} (1-D)^3, & D<1,\\ 0, & D\geq1. \end{cases} \]

Implementation:

np.where(
    D < 1.0,
    (1.0 - D) ** 3,
    0.0,
)

docs.title: Triangular kernel
docs.text:
The class is:

TriangularKernel

registered as:

triangular

The implementation is:

np.where(
    D < 1.0,
    1.0 - np.abs(D),
    0.0,
)

So the source formula is:

\[ K(D) = \begin{cases} 1-|D|, & D<1,\\ 0, & D\geq1. \end{cases} \]

For ordinary non-negative distance matrices this reduces to:

\[ 1-D \]

inside the support.

docs.title: Source boundary condition
docs.text:
The condition used in the current implementation is:

D < 1.0

not:

abs(D) < 1.0

The absolute value is applied only inside:

1.0 - abs(D)

This distinction normally does not matter for valid non-negative distances, but it is the exact current source behavior.

docs.title: COBRA threshold kernel
docs.text:
The class is:

COBRAKernel

registered as:

cobra

It implements hard neighborhood selection.

Its formula is:

\[ K(D) = \begin{cases} 1, & D<t,\\ 0, & D\geq t. \end{cases} \]

docs.title: Constructor
docs.text:
COBRAKernel(
    threshold=0.5,
)

The default cutoff is:

0.5

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
return (
    D < self.threshold
).astype(float)

So the output is a floating-point binary matrix.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.kernels import (
    COBRAKernel,
)

kernel = COBRAKernel(
    threshold=0.7,
)

K = kernel(D)

docs.title: Naive kernel
docs.text:
The class is:

NaiveKernel

registered as:

naive

It performs no similarity transformation:

\[ K(D) = D. \]

The implementation simply returns:

D

docs.title: Important interpretation
docs.text:
Unlike most other kernels, larger distances remain larger output values.

So if the output is later used as aggregation weights, the naive kernel does not convert "near" into "large similarity."

The source describes it mainly as useful for:

debugging
baseline comparison

docs.title: Source metadata
docs.text:
Despite being an identity mapping, the current class sets:

mode = "discrete"
requires_grad = False

This page preserves that metadata exactly as implemented.

docs.title: requires_grad
docs.text:
The current continuous kernels set or inherit:

requires_grad = True

These are:

radial / rbf
exponential
reverse_cosh
cauchy

The compact and discrete kernels set:

requires_grad = False

These are:

epanechnikov
biweight
triweight
triangular
naive
cobra

docs.title: Why requires_grad matters
docs.text:
GradientCOBRA checks:

if (
    method == "grad"
    and not self.kernel_.requires_grad
):
    method = "grid"

MixCOBRARegressor uses the same logic.

Therefore if:

opt_method="grad"

is requested with a non-gradient kernel, the current source silently changes the local optimization method to:

grid

rather than continuing with gradient optimization.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Conceptually:

model = GradientCOBRA(
    kernel="cobra",
    opt_method="grad",
)

resolves a kernel with:

requires_grad == False

and the optimization method is switched internally to grid mode.

docs.title: Default kernels
docs.text:
The current defaults are:

Estimator Default kernel GradientCOBRA rbf MixCOBRARegressor rbf CombinedClassifier rbf

Because:

rbf

is an alias for:

RadialKernel

all three default to:

\[ K(D) = e^{-D} \]

after adapter transformation.

docs.title: Kernel parameters in COBRA estimators
docs.text:
The high-level estimators accept:

kernel

and:

kernel_params

For example:

model = GradientCOBRA(
    kernel="exponential",
    kernel_params={
        "exponent": 2.0,
    },
)

The source resolves this with:

KernelFactory.create(
    self.kernel,
    **(
        self.kernel_params
        or {}
    ),
)

docs.title: Inspect the resolved kernel
docs.text:
After component resolution or fitting:

print(
    model.kernel_
)

Inspect its parameters:

print(
    model.kernel_.get_params()
)

Inspect optimization metadata:

print(
    model.kernel_.requires_grad
)

print(
    model.kernel_.mode
)

docs.title: Adapter scaling in GradientCOBRA
docs.text:
GradientCOBRA creates:

OneParameterKernelAdapter(
    bandwidth=1.0,
)

through the factory.

During cross-validation:

self.adapter_.set_params(
    bandwidth=bandwidth
)

D = self.adapter_.transform(
    self.distance_matrix_
)

K = self.kernel_(D)

Therefore candidate bandwidths act before the kernel.

docs.title: Effective RBF formula in GradientCOBRA
docs.text:
The adapter computes:

\[ D' = hD. \]

The radial kernel computes:

\[ K(D') = e^{-D'}. \]

Therefore:

\[ K_h(D) = e^{-hD}. \]

Bandwidth direction

In this source, increasing:

bandwidth

multiplies the distance by a larger number before applying exp(-D).

So larger bandwidth values produce faster decay and narrower effective neighborhoods.

This is the opposite parameter direction from conventions written as:

\[ K(D/h), \]

where increasing \(h\) broadens the neighborhood.

docs.title: Effective compact-kernel support with bandwidth
docs.text:
The same adapter logic changes the support radius of compact kernels.

For example, Epanechnikov is positive when:

\[ D' < 1. \]

Since:

\[ D'=hD, \]

the nonzero condition is:

\[ hD<1, \]

or:

\[ D < \frac{1}{h}. \]

Thus larger bandwidth values shrink the raw-distance support.

docs.title: Effective COBRA threshold with bandwidth
docs.text:
With:

kernel="cobra"

the source applies:

\[ K(D') = 1 \quad\text{if}\quad D'<t. \]

With:

\[ D'=hD, \]

this becomes:

\[ D < \frac{t}{h}. \]

Therefore both:

threshold
bandwidth

influence the effective hard neighborhood radius.

docs.title: MixCOBRA two-parameter kernel input
docs.text:
In two-parameter MixCOBRA, the adapter combines two distance matrices:

\[ D' = \alpha D_X + \beta D_Y. \]

Then the selected kernel receives this fused distance:

\[ K( \alpha D_X+\beta D_Y ). \]

With the default RBF kernel:

\[ K = \exp[ -(\alpha D_X+\beta D_Y) ]. \]

docs.title: MixCOBRA one-parameter kernel input
docs.text:
With:

one_parameter=True

MixCOBRA first computes a distance on a concatenated representation and then uses:

\[ D' = hD. \]

The selected kernel is applied to that scaled distance exactly as in GradientCOBRA.

docs.title: CombinedClassifier kernel flow
docs.text:
CombinedClassifier also creates:

OneParameterKernelAdapter(
    bandwidth=1.0,
)

and during optimization:

self.adapter_.set_params(
    bandwidth=bandwidth
)

D = self.adapter_.transform(
    self.distance_matrix_
)

K = self.kernel_(D)

So the same bandwidth-before-kernel interpretation applies.

docs.title: Kernel matrix shape
docs.text:
The kernel does not change matrix shape.

If:

D.shape == (
    n_query,
    n_reference,
)

then:

K = kernel(D)

normally has:

K.shape == (
    n_query,
    n_reference,
)

The values are transformed element-wise by all current built-in kernels.

docs.title: Pairwise training kernel
docs.text:
During calibration and hyperparameter optimization, COBRA estimators often start with a square distance matrix:

(n_l, n_l)

The kernel transforms it to a square similarity/weight matrix of the same shape.

Cross-validation then extracts blocks such as:

K_val_train = K[
    np.ix_(
        val_idx,
        train_idx,
    )
]

for aggregation.

docs.title: Query-to-calibration kernel
docs.text:
At prediction time, a query-to-calibration distance matrix:

(n_query, n_l)

is transformed into a kernel matrix of the same shape.

Each row then provides the calibration-sample weights used by the aggregator.

docs.title: Zero-weight rows
docs.text:
Compact and threshold kernels can easily produce rows containing only zeros.

For example, if every adapted distance is outside the compact support:

D' >= 1

then:

epanechnikov
biweight
triweight
triangular

produce zero for every calibration point.

Likewise, cobra produces all zeros when no distance is below its threshold.

The downstream aggregator/fitted estimator determines the fallback behavior.

docs.title: Regression fallback
docs.text:
For GradientCOBRA final prediction, the source passes:

fallback=self.global_mean_

to the weighted-mean aggregator.

Thus if kernel weights have effectively zero total mass, regression can fall back to the global calibration target mean.

Cross-validation code may use a different explicit fallback such as:

fallback=0.0

inside its objective.

docs.title: Classification fallback
docs.text:
CombinedClassifier explicitly checks:

if np.sum(w) <= 0:
    pred = self.global_majority_class_

during cross-validation prediction.

The final prediction path similarly has class-fallback logic in the wrapped classifier.

This matters most for compact or hard-threshold kernels.

docs.title: Continuous vs compact behavior
docs.text:
A practical source-level distinction is:

continuous kernels:
    normally assign a nonzero decaying value over broad distance ranges

compact kernels:
    assign exactly zero at D >= 1 after adaptation

discrete kernels:
    hard / special mappings in current source

The package does not enforce a universal probabilistic normalization on kernel outputs.

They become raw weights for the configured aggregator.

docs.title: Kernel outputs are not normalized probabilities
docs.text:
For example, the RBF kernel may return:

[0.95, 0.45, 0.02]

for one query row.

These values are not normalized to sum to one by the kernel itself.

A weighted aggregator can normalize them internally when computing a weighted mean or vote.

docs.title: Direct kernel comparison
docs.text:
import numpy as np

from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.kernels import (
    KernelFactory,
)


D = np.array([
    [0.0, 0.25, 0.75, 1.25],
])


for name in [
    "rbf",
    "cauchy",
    "epanechnikov",
    "biweight",
    "triweight",
    "triangular",
    "cobra",
    "naive",
]:
    kernel = KernelFactory.create(
        name
    )

    print(
        name,
        kernel(D),
    )

This uses the same adapted-distance values for every source implementation.

docs.title: Direct RBF with adapter
docs.text:
from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.adapters import (
    OneParameterKernelAdapter,
)

from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.kernels import (
    RadialKernel,
)


adapter = OneParameterKernelAdapter(
    bandwidth=2.0,
)

kernel = RadialKernel()

D_adapted = adapter.transform(
    D
)

K = kernel(
    D_adapted
)

This computes:

\[ K = e^{-2D}. \]

docs.title: Exponential vs RBF
docs.text:
With:

ExponentialKernel(
    exponent=1.0,
)

the mapping is:

\[ e^{-D}, \]

which is the same as:

RadialKernel()

The difference appears when:

exponent != 1.

For example:

exponent=2

produces:

\[ e^{-D^2}. \]

docs.title: Compact-kernel comparison
docs.text:
For:

\[ 0\leq D<1, \]

the current source gives:

\[ K_{\text{Epan}}(D) = 1-D, \] \[ K_{\text{Bi}}(D) = (1-D)^2, \] \[ K_{\text{Triweight}}(D) = (1-D)^3. \]

As the power increases, values inside the support decay more strongly away from zero.

At:

\[ D\geq1, \]

all three are exactly zero.

For non-negative distances, the current triangular implementation also reduces to:

\[ 1-D \]

inside the support, making it numerically equivalent to the current Epanechnikov implementation on ordinary non-negative distance input.

Current source equivalence

Because valid distance matrices are normally non-negative:

epanechnikov
triangular

currently produce the same values for ordinary COBRA distance inputs.

Their code differs only through abs(D) inside the triangular branch.

docs.text:
List registered names:

from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.kernels import (

print(

cauchy
cobra

docs.text:
print(
    KernelFactory.info(
        "rbf"

Because:

rbf
gaussian

docs.title: Custom kernel
docs.text:
A custom kernel should subclass:

BaseKernel

and implement:

__call__(D)

Example:

import numpy as np

from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.kernels import (
    BaseKernel,
    KernelFactory,
)


@KernelFactory.register(
    "inverse_square"
)
class InverseSquareKernel(
    BaseKernel
):

    requires_grad = True
    mode = "continuous"

    def __call__(
        self,
        D,
    ):
        D = np.asarray(D)

        return 1.0 / (
            1.0 + D ** 2
        )

Then:

model = GradientCOBRA(
    kernel="inverse_square",
)

can resolve it through the normal factory path.

docs.title: Custom kernel with parameters
docs.text:
@KernelFactory.register(
    "scaled_cauchy"
)
class ScaledCauchyKernel(
    BaseKernel
):

    requires_grad = True
    mode = "continuous"

    def __init__(
        self,
        power=1.0,
    ):
        super().__init__(
            power=power,
        )

    def __call__(
        self,
        D,
    ):
        return 1.0 / (
            1.0 + D
        ) ** self.power

Configure with:

kernel="scaled_cauchy",
kernel_params={
    "power": 2.0,
}

docs.title: Choosing requires_grad for a custom kernel
docs.text:
The optimizer compatibility check trusts the kernel's:

requires_grad

attribute.

Set:

requires_grad = True

only when the kernel is intended to participate in the package's gradient-style optimization path.

Set:

requires_grad = False

for non-smooth, compact-threshold, or otherwise unsupported cases.

The current source does not derive this capability automatically from the kernel formula.

docs.title: Custom kernel mode
docs.text:
Use one of the source's descriptive mode strings:

continuous
compact
discrete

For example:

mode = "compact"

for a bounded-support mapping.

Remember that the current convenience helpers only explicitly recognize:

continuous
discrete

and have no separate:

is_compact()

method.

docs.text:

print(
    model.adapter_.get_params()

This is essential when interpreting the effective similarity rule.

docs.title: Debugging unexpected zero weights
docs.text:
If using a compact kernel:

D = model.adapter_.transform(
    distance_matrix
)

K = model.kernel_(
    D
)

print(
    np.min(D),
    np.max(D),
)

print(
    np.sum(
        K > 0,
        axis=1,
    )
)

Rows with zero positive entries have no neighbors inside the current support.

docs.title: Debugging RBF decay
docs.text:
For the default RBF path:

h = model.adapter_.bandwidth

and:

D_adapted = h * distance_matrix

Then:

K = np.exp(
    -D_adapted
)

Inspecting both matrices can reveal whether the optimized bandwidth makes the kernel too concentrated or too broad.

docs.text: Kernel requires_grad Mode Parameters radial / gaussian / rbf Yes continuous none exponential Yes continuous exponent=1.0 reverse_cosh Yes continuous exponent=1.0 cauchy Yes continuous none epanechnikov No compact none biweight No compact none triweight No compact none triangular No compact none naive No discrete none cobra No discrete threshold=0.5

docs.title: Quick reference
docs.text: Goal Source option default smooth decay rbf alternate smooth power decay exponential heavy-tailed decay cauchy hyperbolic decay reverse_cosh compact linear support epanechnikov / triangular stronger compact decay biweight, triweight hard neighborhood cobra identity/debug mapping naive

docs.title: Mental model
docs.text:
The distance says how far two prediction representations are apart; the adapter decides how strongly that distance is scaled; the kernel turns the adapted distance into the weight used for consensus.

\[ \boxed{ D \rightarrow D' \rightarrow K(D') \rightarrow \text{aggregation weight} } \]

For the default KFC/COBRA RBF path:

\[ \boxed{ D \rightarrow hD \rightarrow e^{-hD} } \]

so the optimized bandwidth belongs to the adapter rather than to the RadialKernel implementation itself.

docs.title: Loss Functions
docs.text:
Loss functions connect COBRA predictions to the optimization objective.

During cross-validation, a COBRA estimator:

  1. builds predictions for the validation rows;
  2. compares those predictions with the validation targets;
  3. evaluates a registered loss;
  4. averages the fold losses;
  5. asks the optimizer to minimize that value.

The current source provides six built-in losses:

mse
mae
huber
log_loss
hinge
quantile

with aliases for several of them.

The implementations live under:

kfc_procedure/cobra/core/losses/
├── base.py
├── mse.py
├── mae.py
├── huber.py
├── log_loss.py
├── hinge.py
└── quantile.py

and are registered through:

LossFactory

docs.title: Losses in the COBRA pipeline
docs.text:
The loss layer appears after fold-level aggregation:

flowchart LR
    P["Candidate parameters"]
    K["Kernel weights"]
    A["Aggregator"]
    YH["Fold predictions"]
    Y["Validation targets"]
    L["Loss"]
    O["Optimizer"]

    P --> K --> A --> YH
    YH --> L
    Y --> L
    L --> O

For one cross-validation fold, the objective has the form:

\[ \mathcal{L} \left( y_{\text{validation}}, \widehat y_{\text{validation}} \right). \]

The optimizer minimizes the average of these fold losses.

docs.title: Built-in losses
docs.text: Registry name Aliases Class Primary source formula mse l2, squared_error MSELoss mean squared error mae l1 MAELoss mean absolute error huber — HuberLoss quadratic/linear robust loss log_loss cross_entropy LogLoss binary cross-entropy hinge — HingeLoss mean hinge loss quantile — QuantileLoss pinball / quantile loss

docs.title: BaseLoss
docs.text:
Every built-in loss inherits:

BaseLoss

The abstract interface is intentionally small:

class BaseLoss(ABC):

    @abstractmethod
    def __call__(
        self,
        y_true,
        y_pred,
    ) -> float:
        ...

A loss object is therefore callable:

value = loss(
    y_true,
    y_pred,
)

and must return one scalar float.

docs.title: LossFactory
docs.text:
Losses are created through:

LossFactory

which inherits the package's common:

BaseFactory

Example:

from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.losses import (
    LossFactory,
)

loss = LossFactory.create(
    "mse"
)

Then:

score = loss(
    y_true,
    y_pred,
)

docs.title: Inspect registered losses
docs.text:
print(
    LossFactory.available()
)

The current source registers names including:

cross_entropy
hinge
huber
l1
l2
log_loss
mae
mse
quantile
squared_error

subject to normal module loading.

docs.title: Mean squared error
docs.text:
MSELoss is registered as:

mse
l2
squared_error

The source formula is:

\[ \mathcal{L}_{\text{MSE}} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left( y_i-\widehat y_i \right)^2. \]

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
The implementation is:

y_true = np.asarray(
    y_true
)

y_pred = np.asarray(
    y_pred
)

return float(
    np.mean(
        (
            y_true
            -
            y_pred
        ) ** 2
    )
)

No additional weighting, clipping, or regularization is applied.

docs.title: Direct example
docs.text:
import numpy as np

from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.losses import (
    MSELoss,
)

y_true = np.array([
    1.0,
    2.0,
    3.0,
])

y_pred = np.array([
    1.2,
    1.8,
    2.5,
])

loss = MSELoss()

value = loss(
    y_true,
    y_pred,
)

print(
    value
)

docs.title: MSE behavior
docs.text:
Squaring the residual means larger absolute errors contribute disproportionately more to the objective.

For residual:

\[ e_i = y_i-\widehat y_i, \]

the contribution is:

\[ e_i^2. \]

The source module describes MSE as the most common regression loss and notes that it strongly penalizes large errors.

docs.title: Mean absolute error
docs.text:
MAELoss is registered as:

mae
l1

The source formula is:

\[ \mathcal{L}_{\text{MAE}} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left| y_i-\widehat y_i \right|. \]

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
y_true = np.asarray(
    y_true
)

y_pred = np.asarray(
    y_pred
)

return float(
    np.mean(
        np.abs(
            y_true
            -
            y_pred
        )
    )
)

docs.title: Direct example
docs.text:
from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.losses import (
    MAELoss,
)

loss = MAELoss()

value = loss(
    y_true,
    y_pred,
)

The source describes MAE as more robust to outliers than MSE because it uses absolute rather than squared error.

docs.title: Huber loss
docs.text:
HuberLoss combines quadratic behavior for small residuals with linear behavior for large residuals.

It is registered as:

huber

docs.title: Constructor
docs.text:
HuberLoss(
    delta=1.0,
)

The parameter:

delta

controls the transition point.

The current source does not validate that delta is positive.

docs.title: Huber formula
docs.text:
Let:

\[ e = y-\widehat y. \]

The implementation computes:

\[ q(e) = \frac12e^2 \]

and:

\[ \ell(e) = \delta \left( |e| - \frac12\delta \right). \]

Then:

\[ L_\delta(e) = \begin{cases} \frac12e^2, & |e|\leq\delta, \\[6pt] \delta \left( |e|-\frac12\delta \right), & |e|>\delta. \end{cases} \]

The final loss is the mean across samples.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
error = (
    y_true
    -
    y_pred
)

abs_error = np.abs(
    error
)

quadratic = (
    0.5
    *
    error ** 2
)

linear = (
    self.delta
    *
    (
        abs_error
        -
        0.5
        *
        self.delta
    )
)

return float(
    np.mean(
        np.where(
            abs_error
            <=
            self.delta,
            quadratic,
            linear,
        )
    )
)

docs.title: Configure Huber loss
docs.text:
High-level COBRA estimators pass:

loss_params

to LossFactory.create().

Example:

model = GradientCOBRA(
    loss="huber",
    loss_params={
        "delta": 1.5,
    },
)

This creates:

HuberLoss(
    delta=1.5,
)

docs.title: Quantile loss
docs.text:
QuantileLoss is registered as:

quantile

and is intended for quantile regression.

Its constructor is:

QuantileLoss(
    tau=0.5,
)

docs.title: Source formula
docs.text:
Let:

\[ e = y-\widehat y. \]

The source computes:

\[ \max \left( \tau e, (\tau-1)e \right). \]

The returned loss is the mean of those values.

Equivalent piecewise form:

\[ L_\tau(e) = \begin{cases} \tau e, & e\geq0, \\[4pt] (\tau-1)e, & e<0. \end{cases} \]

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
error = (
    y_true
    -
    y_pred
)

return float(
    np.mean(
        np.maximum(
            self.tau
            *
            error,
            (
                self.tau
                -
                1
            )
            *
            error,
        )
    )
)

docs.title: tau
docs.text:
The source documentation states:

\[ \tau\in(0,1). \]

However, the constructor currently performs no explicit interval validation.

So values outside:

(0, 1)

are not rejected when the loss object is constructed.

Source contract vs enforcement

The module documents tau as a quantile level in (0, 1), but the current implementation simply stores the supplied value.

docs.title: Median-like quantile loss
docs.text:
With:

tau=0.5

the formula gives symmetric linear penalties on positive and negative residuals.

The resulting value is proportional to absolute error:

\[ L_{0.5}(e) = 0.5|e|. \]

So the default quantile loss is not numerically identical to MAELoss; it is half its value for the same residuals.

docs.title: Binary log loss
docs.text:
LogLoss is registered as:

log_loss
cross_entropy

The source formula is:

\[ \mathcal{L} = -\frac1n \sum_i \left[ y_i\log p_i + (1-y_i) \log(1-p_i) \right]. \]

This is a binary cross-entropy formula.

docs.title: Prediction clipping
docs.text:
Before evaluating logs, the source clips predictions:

y_pred = np.clip(
    np.asarray(
        y_pred
    ),
    1e-12,
    1
    -
    1e-12,
)

This protects against:

log(0)

at exactly 0 or 1.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
return float(
    -np.mean(
        y_true
        *
        np.log(
            y_pred
        )
        +
        (
            1
            -
            y_true
        )
        *
        np.log(
            1
            -
            y_pred
        )
    )
)

docs.title: Expected log-loss inputs
docs.text:
The source module describes this loss as being used for probabilistic classification.

The formula expects values conceptually like:

y_true:
    binary 0/1 labels

y_pred:
    probabilities for the positive class

The implementation does not itself verify:

binary targets
probability semantics
matching one-dimensional shape

beyond NumPy's normal broadcasting behavior.

docs.title: Multiclass limitation
docs.text:
The current LogLoss implementation is not a general multiclass cross-entropy implementation.

It does not:

one-hot encode labels
index class probabilities
sum over class dimensions
accept class labels as a `classes` argument

It directly evaluates the binary formula above.

Therefore it should not be interpreted as a source-supported multiclass cross-entropy implementation.

docs.title: Hinge loss
docs.text:
HingeLoss is registered as:

hinge

The module explicitly states:

Assumes:
    y_true in {-1, +1}

Its formula is:

\[ \mathcal{L}_{\text{hinge}} = \frac1n \sum_i \max \left( 0, 1-y_i\widehat y_i \right). \]

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
y_true = np.asarray(
    y_true
)

y_pred = np.asarray(
    y_pred
)

return float(
    np.mean(
        np.maximum(
            0.0,
            1.0
            -
            y_true
            *
            y_pred,
        )
    )
)

docs.title: Expected hinge inputs
docs.text:
The source describes the loss as common in SVM-style classification and expects:

y_true in {-1, +1}

The implementation does not convert labels from:

0/1

to:

-1/+1

and does not convert hard class labels into decision margins.

It uses whatever arrays are passed directly into:

y_true * y_pred

docs.title: Important classifier integration detail
docs.text:
CombinedClassifier produces hard class predictions during its cross-validation objective.

It does not produce probability vectors or decision-function margins for the loss layer.

Therefore classification losses such as:

log_loss
hinge

are not automatically supplied the conventional inputs implied by their source modules.

This is important when configuring the current classifier.

docs.title: Default loss in COBRA estimators
docs.text:
The current constructors use:

loss="mse"

by default in all three main estimators:

GradientCOBRA
MixCOBRARegressor
CombinedClassifier

That includes the classification estimator:

CombinedClassifier

docs.title: Regression defaults
docs.text:
For:

GradientCOBRA()

and:

MixCOBRARegressor()

the default objective is therefore ordinary mean squared error.

This matches their numeric regression outputs.

docs.title: CombinedClassifier default
docs.text:
The current CombinedClassifier constructor also specifies:

loss="mse"

Its cross-validation loop produces hard predicted class labels and evaluates:

self.loss_(
    y_true,
    preds,
)

So with the default, class labels are numerically compared using squared error.

Current source behavior

CombinedClassifier does not default to classification error, log loss, or hinge loss.

Its current default is the same registered MSELoss used by the regression estimators.

docs.title: Consequence for encoded class labels
docs.text:
Because MSE is applied directly to class labels, the numeric encoding matters.

For example:

true class = 0
predicted class = 1

contributes:

\[ (0-1)^2 = 1. \]

But:

true class = 0
predicted class = 2

contributes:

\[ (0-2)^2 = 4. \]

So with class labels:

0, 1, 2

the default classifier objective treats the numeric distance between class codes as meaningful.

That is a direct consequence of the current source default.

docs.title: String labels with MSE
docs.text:
If classification targets are strings such as:

"cat"
"dog"

then the default:

MSELoss

cannot perform:

y_true - y_pred

on those string arrays.

So the default CombinedClassifier loss path assumes numerically subtractable labels.

The loss layer itself does not encode categorical labels before evaluation.

docs.title: Loss resolution
docs.text:
The high-level estimators all resolve the configured loss through:

LossFactory.create(
    self.loss,
    **(
        self.loss_params
        or {}
    ),
)

and store the result in:

self.loss_

docs.title: Inspect the fitted loss
docs.text:
After component resolution or fitting:

print(
    model.loss_
)

For the default:

MSELoss

docs.title: Configure MAE
docs.text:
model = GradientCOBRA(
    loss="mae",
)

Alias:

model = GradientCOBRA(
    loss="l1",
)

Both resolve to:

MAELoss

docs.title: Configure MSE
docs.text:
These names all resolve to MSELoss:

loss="mse"

loss="l2"

loss="squared_error"

docs.title: Configure Huber
docs.text:
model = MixCOBRARegressor(
    loss="huber",
    loss_params={
        "delta": 1.0,
    },
)

docs.title: Configure quantile loss
docs.text:
model = GradientCOBRA(
    loss="quantile",
    loss_params={
        "tau": 0.9,
    },
)

The current source simply forwards:

tau=0.9

to the constructor.

docs.title: How GradientCOBRA uses the loss
docs.text:
For every stored cross-validation fold, GradientCOBRA creates fold predictions:

preds = self.aggregator_.aggregate_matrix(
    values=y_train,
    weights=K_val_train,
    fallback=0.0,
)

Then:

error = self.loss_(
    y_val,
    preds,
)

The fold errors are collected and returned as:

float(
    np.mean(
        errors
    )
)

docs.title: GradientCOBRA objective
docs.text:
For bandwidth \(h\), the cross-validation objective is conceptually:

\[ J(h) = \frac{1}{K} \sum_{k=1}^{K} \mathcal{L} \left( y_k^{\text{val}}, \widehat y_k(h) \right). \]

The configured loss determines the definition of:

\[ \mathcal{L}. \]

The optimizer then searches for a parameter value minimizing:

\[ J(h). \]

docs.title: How MixCOBRA uses the loss
docs.text:
MixCOBRA follows the same pattern.

For one-parameter mode:

bandwidth
    -> adapted mixed-space distance
    -> kernel
    -> fold predictions
    -> loss

For two-parameter mode:

alpha, beta
    -> alpha * D_X + beta * D_Y
    -> kernel
    -> fold predictions
    -> loss

In both cases the fold objective calls:

self.loss_(
    y_val,
    preds,
)

docs.title: How CombinedClassifier uses the loss
docs.text:
For each validation row, CombinedClassifier first obtains a hard class prediction.

Then:

preds = np.asarray(
    preds
)

y_true = self.y_l_[
    val_idx
]

error = self.loss_(
    y_true,
    preds,
)

Thus the loss receives:

hard predicted classes

rather than probability vectors.

docs.title: log_loss with CombinedClassifier
docs.text:
Although:

log_loss

is registered and can be requested through the factory, the current CombinedClassifier CV path does not call:

predict_proba()

inside its objective.

Therefore LogLoss receives hard predicted labels if selected there.

For binary numeric classes 0/1, clipping transforms hard predictions into:

1e-12
1 - 1e-12

before the logarithms.

That is valid numerically but is not the same input as calibrated probability predictions.

docs.title: hinge with CombinedClassifier
docs.text:
Likewise, HingeLoss expects:

y_true in {-1, +1}

and conventional hinge use expects margin-like predictions.

The current classifier CV objective instead passes hard predicted labels.

No label conversion or margin calculation is performed by the loss class or the classifier objective.

docs.title: Loss functions do not know the task
docs.text:
LossFactory registrations do not carry regression or classification categories in the current source.

The factory itself therefore does not prevent configurations such as:

GradientCOBRA(
    loss="hinge",
)

or:

CombinedClassifier(
    loss="quantile",
)

The package resolves the requested registered class and lets the arrays and formula determine the resulting behavior.

docs.title: Loss validation scope
docs.text:
The built-in losses are intentionally lightweight.

They do not share a common validation layer for:

shape equality
finite values
target dtype
task compatibility
sample weighting
multiclass semantics

Most implementations simply call:

np.asarray(...)

and apply the formula.

docs.title: Broadcasting
docs.text:
Because the losses use NumPy expressions directly, differently shaped arrays can sometimes broadcast rather than immediately raise an error.

For example:

y_true.shape == (
    n,
    1,
)

and:

y_pred.shape == (
    n,
)

can produce an (n, n) broadcasted result in some formulas.

The current source does not call a shared:

check_consistent_length()

or shape-equality validator inside the loss classes.

Warning

Ensure y_true and y_pred have the intended matching shape before evaluating a built-in loss.

docs.title: Empty arrays
docs.text:
The current loss classes do not explicitly reject empty arrays.

Calling:

np.mean(...)

on an empty result can return:

nan

with a NumPy runtime warning.

No custom ValueError is implemented for empty input.

docs.title: Non-finite values
docs.text:
The losses do not generally sanitize:

NaN
+Inf
-Inf

in the inputs.

LogLoss clips numeric prediction values but does not replace NaN.

So non-finite values can propagate to the returned loss.

docs.title: No sample weights
docs.text:
The built-in BaseLoss interface accepts only:

y_true
y_pred

There is no:

sample_weight

argument.

Therefore the current built-in cross-validation objectives compute ordinary unweighted means over samples within each fold.

docs.title: Mean of fold losses
docs.text:
The estimators compute:

np.mean(
    errors
)

where each item is already a mean loss for one fold.

Therefore the final CV objective is a mean of fold means.

It is not explicitly weighted by fold size.

With the current K-fold implementation, fold sizes are usually close, but can differ by one sample when the calibration sample count is not divisible by n_cv.

docs.title: Direct loss comparison
docs.text:
import numpy as np

from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.losses import (
    LossFactory,
)


y_true = np.array([
    1.0,
    2.0,
    3.0,
])

y_pred = np.array([
    1.2,
    1.8,
    2.5,
])


for name in [
    "mse",
    "mae",
    "huber",
    "quantile",
]:
    loss = LossFactory.create(
        name
    )

    print(
        name,
        loss(
            y_true,
            y_pred,
        ),
    )

docs.title: Inspect aliases
docs.text:
mse = LossFactory.create(
    "mse"
)

l2 = LossFactory.create(
    "l2"
)

squared = LossFactory.create(
    "squared_error"
)

print(
    type(mse).__name__,
    type(l2).__name__,
    type(squared).__name__,
)

All three should resolve to:

MSELoss

docs.title: Binary log-loss example
docs.text:
import numpy as np

from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.losses import (
    LogLoss,
)

y_true = np.array([
    0,
    1,
    1,
    0,
])

p = np.array([
    0.1,
    0.8,
    0.7,
    0.2,
])

loss = LogLoss()

print(
    loss(
        y_true,
        p,
    )
)

This matches the binary formula implemented in the source.

docs.title: Hinge example
docs.text:
from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.losses import (
    HingeLoss,
)

y_true = np.array([
    -1,
    1,
    1,
    -1,
])

margin = np.array([
    -1.2,
    0.8,
    1.4,
    -0.6,
])

loss = HingeLoss()

print(
    loss(
        y_true,
        margin,
    )
)

The loss class itself does not create those margin values; they must already be supplied by the caller.

docs.title: Quantile example
docs.text:
from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.losses import (
    QuantileLoss,
)

loss = QuantileLoss(
    tau=0.9,
)

value = loss(
    y_true,
    y_pred,
)

This evaluates the exact pinball formula used by the current source.

docs.title: Custom loss
docs.text:
A custom loss only needs to subclass:

BaseLoss

and implement:

__call__()

For example:

import numpy as np

from kfc_procedure.cobra.core.losses import (
    BaseLoss,
    LossFactory,
)


@LossFactory.register(
    "root_mse"
)
class RootMSELoss(
    BaseLoss
):

    def __call__(
        self,
        y_true,
        y_pred,
    ):
        y_true = np.asarray(
            y_true
        )

        y_pred = np.asarray(
            y_pred
        )

        return float(
            np.sqrt(
                np.mean(
                    (
                        y_true
                        -
                        y_pred
                    ) ** 2
                )
            )
        )

Then:

model = GradientCOBRA(
    loss="root_mse",
)

can resolve it through the ordinary factory path.

docs.title: Custom loss with parameters
docs.text:
@LossFactory.register(
    "scaled_mae"
)
class ScaledMAELoss(
    BaseLoss
):

    def __init__(
        self,
        scale=1.0,
    ):
        self.scale = scale

    def __call__(
        self,
        y_true,
        y_pred,
    ):
        return float(
            self.scale
            *
            np.mean(
                np.abs(
                    np.asarray(
                        y_true
                    )
                    -
                    np.asarray(
                        y_pred
                    )
                )
            )
        )

Use:

model = GradientCOBRA(
    loss="scaled_mae",
    loss_params={
        "scale": 2.0,
    },
)

docs.title: Loss values and optimizer direction
docs.text:
The current optimizers are supplied objective functions that represent losses, and their search logic minimizes those objectives.

Therefore a custom loss should follow the same convention:

smaller value
    = better candidate

If a metric is naturally "higher is better," convert it into a minimization objective before registering it as a loss.

docs.title: Loss vs aggregator
docs.text:
The aggregator creates predictions.

The loss scores them.

For regression:

kernel weights
    ↓
WeightedMeanAggregator
    ↓
numeric predictions
    ↓
MSE / MAE / Huber / Quantile

For classification:

kernel weights
    ↓
WeightedVoteAggregator
    ↓
hard class labels
    ↓
configured loss

The loss does not influence how aggregation itself is computed.

It influences which hyperparameters the optimizer prefers.

docs.title: Loss vs final prediction
docs.text:
After the optimal bandwidth or other adapter parameter has been chosen, the loss is not called for every ordinary prediction.

The final prediction path uses:

distance
adapter
kernel
aggregator

The loss is primarily part of the training-time optimization objective.

docs.title: Loss vs cross-validation
docs.text:
The loss is applied separately inside every stored fold.

For a candidate parameter vector \(\theta\):

\[ J(\theta) = \frac{1}{K} \sum_{k=1}^{K} L_k(\theta). \]

Changing the loss changes:

candidate ranking
selected bandwidth
selected alpha/beta

without changing the distance or kernel implementation itself.

docs.title: Inspect configured name
docs.text:
print(
    model.loss
)

docs.title: Inspect constructor parameters
docs.text:
print(
    model.loss_params
)

docs.title: Inspect resolved object
docs.text:
print(
    model.loss_
)

docs.title: Evaluate manually
docs.text:
score = model.loss_(
    y_true,
    y_pred,
)

print(
    score
)

docs.title: Debugging shape issues
docs.text:
import numpy as np

print(
    np.asarray(
        y_true
    ).shape
)

print(
    np.asarray(
        y_pred
    ).shape
)

For the current scalar-per-sample losses, the safest shape is typically:

(n_samples,)

unless intentionally using a matrix-valued probability representation with a custom loss.

docs.title: Debugging classification MSE
docs.text:
With CombinedClassifier:

print(
    model.loss
)

print(
    np.unique(
        model.y_l_
    )
)

If the default is still:

mse

remember that the numeric class codes directly affect the cross-validation objective.

docs.title: Debugging log loss
docs.text:
Before calling the built-in LogLoss manually:

print(
    np.min(
        y_pred
    ),
    np.max(
        y_pred
    ),
)

The loss clips predictions internally to:

[1e-12, 1 - 1e-12]

but does not transform hard class labels into calibrated probabilities.

docs.title: Debugging quantile configuration
docs.text:
print(
    model.loss_.tau
)

The source will report whatever value was passed, including values outside the documented (0, 1) range.

docs.title: Current implementation summary
