docs.title: Quick reference
docs.text: Task Combiner Registry Regression arithmetic mean mean Regression OLS weighting weighted_mean Regression meta-regression stacking_regressor Regression GradientCOBRA gradientcobra Regression MixCOBRA mixcobra Classification hard vote majority_vote Classification meta-classification stacking_classifier Classification CombinedClassifier combined_classifier

docs.title: Mental model
docs.text:
Consensus is the stage that turns several divergence-specific answers into one final answer.

\[ \boxed{ \begin{bmatrix} p_1(x) & p_2(x) & \cdots & p_M(x) \end{bmatrix} \rightarrow \text{consensus strategy} \rightarrow \widehat y(x) } \]

The strategy can be a fixed rule, a learned meta-model, or a COBRA-style prediction-space aggregation method.

docs.title: Regression Combiners
docs.text:
Regression combiners are the C-Step strategies that turn the F-Step prediction matrix into one final numeric prediction.

The C-Step receives:

\[ P \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times M}, \]

where each row is one sample and each column is the prediction produced by one divergence-specific F-Step model family.

Conceptually:

F-Step predictions
        │
        ▼
┌──────────────────────────────┐
│ euclidean  gkl  logistic ... │
├──────────────────────────────┤
│   12.4    12.8    12.1      │
│   20.7    21.0    20.4      │
│    8.3     8.1     8.5      │
└──────────────────────────────┘
        │
        ▼
 regression combiner
        │
        ▼
 final prediction

The current source registers five regression combiners:

Registry name Implementation mean MeanCombiner weighted_mean WeightedMeanCombiner stacking_regressor StackingRegressorCombiner gradientcobra GradientCOBRACombiner mixcobra MixCOBRACombiner

docs.title: Choosing a regression combiner
docs.text:
The five strategies fall into three broad groups.

  • Fixed averaging

    mean

    Uses the same weight for every prediction column.

  • Learned meta-models

    weighted_mean

    stacking_regressor

    Learn how F-Step prediction columns map to the target.

  • COBRA-style aggregation

    gradientcobra

    mixcobra

    Use the F-Step prediction matrix as precomputed prediction-space input.

docs.title: mean
docs.text:
MeanCombiner is the simplest regression consensus strategy.

It is registered as:

mean

and computes the arithmetic mean across prediction columns.

For one sample:

\[ \widehat y = \frac{1}{M} \sum_{m=1}^{M}p_m. \]

The implementation is:

return np.mean(
    X,
    axis=1,
)

docs.title: Fit behavior
docs.text:
MeanCombiner is stateless.

Its fit() method simply returns:

self

and does not use the target vector.

def fit(
    self,
    X,
    y=None,
):
    return self

docs.title: Input validation
docs.text:
combine() converts the input with:

np.asarray(X)

and requires a two-dimensional matrix.

If:

X.ndim != 2

it raises:

ValueError: Expected 2D array, got ...

docs.title: Direct example
docs.text:
import numpy as np

from kfc_procedure.core.combiner.regression import (
    MeanCombiner,
)

P = np.array([
    [10.0, 12.0, 11.0],
    [20.0, 19.0, 22.0],
])

combiner = MeanCombiner()

combiner.fit(P)

prediction = combiner.predict(P)

print(prediction)

Conceptually:

[11.0, 20.333...]

docs.title: KFC example
docs.text:
from kfc_procedure import KFCRegressor
from kfc_procedure.core.combiner.regression import (
    MeanCombiner,
)

model = KFCRegressor(
    divergences=["euclidean"],
    local_model="ridge",
    combiner=MeanCombiner(),
    random_state=42,
)

Using an instance is important in the current source because of the C-Step random_state forwarding issue described later on this page.

docs.title: weighted_mean
docs.text:
WeightedMeanCombiner is registered as:

weighted_mean

Despite the name, the current implementation is not a constrained weighted average.

It fits:

LinearRegression

on the F-Step prediction matrix.

The model is:

\[ y \approx Pw. \]

With an intercept enabled:

\[ y \approx Pw+b. \]

docs.title: Constructor
docs.text:
WeightedMeanCombiner(
    fit_intercept=False,
)

The only constructor parameter is:

fit_intercept

with default:

False

Internally:

self.model = LinearRegression(
    fit_intercept=fit_intercept
)

docs.title: Fit behavior
docs.text:
The input is converted using:

np.asarray(X)

and must be two-dimensional.

Then:

self.model.fit(
    X,
    y,
)

is called.

docs.title: Prediction
docs.text:
combine() delegates directly to:

self.model.predict(X)

docs.title: Important interpretation
docs.text:
The learned coefficients are not constrained.

The implementation does not enforce:

\[ w_m \geq 0 \]

and does not enforce:

\[ \sum_m w_m=1. \]

So the learned model can use:

negative coefficients
coefficients greater than one
coefficients whose sum is not one

This is ordinary least-squares combination.

docs.title: Direct example
docs.text:
from kfc_procedure.core.combiner.regression import (
    WeightedMeanCombiner,
)

combiner = WeightedMeanCombiner(
    fit_intercept=False,
)

combiner.fit(
    P_train,
    y_train,
)

y_pred = combiner.predict(
    P_test
)

docs.title: Inspect learned coefficients
docs.text:
print(
    combiner.model.coef_
)

and:

print(
    combiner.model.intercept_
)

If F-Step columns are ordered as:

euclidean
gkl
logistic
is

then the coefficient vector follows the same matrix-column order.

docs.title: KFC example
docs.text:
from kfc_procedure import KFCRegressor
from kfc_procedure.core.combiner.regression import (
    WeightedMeanCombiner,
)

model = KFCRegressor(
    divergences=["euclidean"],
    local_model="ridge",
    combiner=WeightedMeanCombiner(
        fit_intercept=False,
    ),
    random_state=42,
)

docs.title: stacking_regressor
docs.text:
StackingRegressorCombiner is registered as:

stacking_regressor

It learns a second-level regression model from the F-Step prediction matrix.

Conceptually:

\[ P \rightarrow g_{\text{meta}} \rightarrow \widehat y. \]

docs.title: Default meta-model
docs.text:
If no model is supplied, the constructor uses:

LinearRegression()

The constructor is:

StackingRegressorCombiner(
    meta_model=None,
)

with:

self.meta_model = (
    meta_model
    or LinearRegression()
)

docs.title: Fit behavior
docs.text:
Before fitting, the configured meta-model is cloned:

self.meta_model_ = clone(
    self.meta_model
)

Then:

self.meta_model_.fit(
    X,
    y,
)

is called.

The fitted clone is stored as:

meta_model_

docs.title: Why clone?
docs.text:
The source deliberately keeps:

meta_model

as the configuration object and:

meta_model_

as the fitted object.

This follows standard scikit-learn fitted-state conventions.

docs.title: Fitted-state check
docs.text:
The implementation also stores:

self._is_fitted = True

after training.

Calling combine() before fitting raises:

RuntimeError:
StackingRegressorCombiner is not fitted.

docs.title: Direct example
docs.text:
from kfc_procedure.core.combiner.regression import (
    StackingRegressorCombiner,
)

combiner = StackingRegressorCombiner()

combiner.fit(
    P_train,
    y_train,
)

y_pred = combiner.predict(
    P_test
)

docs.title: Custom meta-regressor
docs.text:
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor

combiner = StackingRegressorCombiner(
    meta_model=RandomForestRegressor(
        n_estimators=200,
        random_state=42,
    )
)

The fitted version is then available as:

combiner.meta_model_

docs.title: KFC example
docs.text:
from kfc_procedure import KFCRegressor
from kfc_procedure.core.combiner.regression import (
    StackingRegressorCombiner,
)

model = KFCRegressor(
    divergences=["euclidean"],

docs.title: gradientcobra
docs.text:
GradientCOBRACombiner is registered as:

gradientcobra

It wraps the package's:

GradientCOBRA

estimator.

The constructor is:

GradientCOBRACombiner(
    **cobra_params
)

and internally creates:

self.cobra = GradientCOBRA(
    **cobra_params
)

docs.title: KFC integration
docs.text:
The important implementation detail is the fit call:

self.cobra.fit(
    X,
    y,
    as_predictions=True,
)

Here X is the F-Step prediction matrix.

Therefore GradientCOBRA does not fit a new set of base estimators when used as a C-Step wrapper.

It receives the divergence-level F-Step predictions directly as its prediction-space representation.

docs.title: Prediction
docs.text:
The wrapper delegates to:

self.cobra.predict(X)

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
from kfc_procedure import KFCRegressor

model = KFCRegressor(
    divergences=["euclidean"],
    local_model="ridge",
    combiner="gradientcobra",
    combiner_params={
        "distance": "euclidean",
        "kernel": "rbf",
        "n_cv": 5,
    },
    random_state=42,
)

Because the wrapper accepts:

**cobra_params

the random_state keyword injected by C-Step is accepted and forwarded to GradientCOBRA.

docs.title: Inspect the fitted wrapper
docs.text:
After fitting:

strategy = model.cstep_.strategy_

The wrapped estimator is:

strategy.cobra

For example:

print(
    strategy.cobra
)

Fitted GradientCOBRA attributes depend on the selected configuration.

For the algorithm and bandwidth optimization behavior, see:

GradientCOBRA

docs.title: mixcobra
docs.text:
MixCOBRACombiner is registered as:

mixcobra

It wraps:

MixCOBRARegressor

The constructor is:

MixCOBRACombiner(
    **cobra_params
)

and creates:

self.cobra = MixCOBRARegressor(
    **cobra_params
)

docs.title: KFC integration
docs.text:
The wrapper fits MixCOBRA using:

self.cobra.fit(
    X,
    y,
    as_predictions=True,
)

Again, X is the F-Step prediction matrix.

This is a specific KFC integration path.

docs.title: Important distinction from standalone MixCOBRA
docs.text:
Standalone MixCOBRA is organized around input-space and prediction-space information.

Inside the KFC C-Step wrapper, the F-Step prediction matrix is supplied as precomputed predictions using:

as_predictions=True

So this wrapper should be understood as KFC feeding its divergence-level prediction representation into MixCOBRA's precomputed-prediction mode.

For the standalone algorithm, see:

MixCOBRA

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
from kfc_procedure import KFCRegressor

model = KFCRegressor(
    divergences=["euclidean"],
    local_model="ridge",
    combiner="mixcobra",
    combiner_params={
        "distance": "euclidean",
        "kernel": "rbf",
        "n_cv": 5,
    },
    random_state=42,
)

docs.title: Inspect the fitted wrapper
docs.text:
strategy = model.cstep_.strategy_

cobra = strategy.cobra

print(
    cobra
)

The wrapper itself adds no additional learned state beyond the underlying MixCOBRARegressor.

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text: Combiner Uses target during fit() Learned object Main operation mean No none arithmetic mean weighted_mean Yes LinearRegression linear coefficients stacking_regressor Yes cloned meta-regressor second-level regression gradientcobra Yes GradientCOBRA prediction-space kernel aggregation mixcobra Yes MixCOBRARegressor MixCOBRA precomputed-prediction aggregation

docs.title: Current C-Step random_state issue
docs.text:
The current C-Step builds string-based combiners with:

params = dict(
    self.combiner_params
)

if "random_state" not in params:
    params["random_state"] = self.random_state

and then:

CombinerFactory.create(
    name,
    **params
)

This means every string-based combiner receives a random_state keyword.

docs.title: Affected regression combiners
docs.text:
These constructors do not accept random_state:

MeanCombiner()

WeightedMeanCombiner(
    fit_intercept=False
)

StackingRegressorCombiner(
    meta_model=None
)

Therefore the current string-based C-Step path can attempt calls equivalent to:

MeanCombiner(
    random_state=42
)

or even:

MeanCombiner(
    random_state=None
)

and raise:

TypeError:
... got an unexpected keyword argument 'random_state'

docs.title: COBRA wrappers are not affected
docs.text:
These constructors accept arbitrary keyword arguments:

GradientCOBRACombiner(
    **cobra_params
)

MixCOBRACombiner(
    **cobra_params
)

So:

gradientcobra
mixcobra

remain compatible with the current C-Step parameter forwarding design.

docs.title: Workaround for simple combiners
docs.text: Pass a pre-instantiated combiner object instead of a string.

from kfc_procedure.core.combiner.regression import (
    MeanCombiner,

model = KFCRegressor(
    divergences=["euclidean"],
    local_model="ridge",
    combiner=MeanCombiner(),
    random_state=42,

docs.title: Weighted mean
docs.text:
from kfc_procedure.core.combiner.regression import (
    WeightedMeanCombiner,

model = KFCRegressor(
    divergences=["euclidean"],

docs.title: Stacking
docs.text:
from kfc_procedure.core.combiner.regression import (
    StackingRegressorCombiner,
)

model = KFCRegressor(
    divergences=["euclidean"],
    local_model="ridge",
    combiner=StackingRegressorCombiner(),
    random_state=42,
)

For a non-string object, C-Step returns it directly:

if not isinstance(
    self.combiner,
    str,
):
    return self.combiner

so the automatic constructor keyword injection is bypassed.

docs.title: Direct combiner use
docs.text:
The regression combiners can also be used outside the full KFC pipeline.

Suppose:

P_train

already contains model predictions.

Then:

combiner.fit(
    P_train,
    y_train,
)

followed by:

combiner.predict(
    P_test
)

uses the same combiner API as C-Step.

docs.title: Example prediction matrix
docs.text:
import numpy as np

P_train = np.array([
    [10.1, 10.4, 10.0],
    [12.0, 12.2, 11.8],
    [18.5, 18.0, 18.8],
    [25.1, 24.7, 25.4],
])

y_train = np.array([
    10.2,
    12.1,
    18.4,
    25.0,
])

Then any regression combiner can consume:

P_train.shape == (4, 3)

where the three columns represent three prediction sources.

docs.title: Inspect the C-Step prediction matrix
docs.text:
For a fitted KFC regressor:

clusters = model.kstep_.predict(
    X_test
)

P_test = model.fstep_.predict(
    X_test,
    clusters,
)

print(
    P_test.shape
)

print(
    P_test[:5]
)

The column names can be recovered with:

divergence_names = list(
    model.fstep_.models_.keys()
)

docs.title: Interpret weighted coefficients
docs.text:
If:

divergence_names = [
    "euclidean",
    "gkl",
    "logistic",
]

and:

weights = np.array([
    0.5,
    -0.2,
    0.9,
])

then the learned model corresponds to:

\[ \widehat y = 0.5p_{\text{euclidean}} - 0.2p_{\text{gkl}} + 0.9p_{\text{logistic}} \]

when fit_intercept=False.

This illustrates why weighted_mean should not be interpreted as a convex average.

docs.title: Inspect stacking state
docs.text:
For a fitted stacking strategy:

strategy = model.cstep_.strategy_

print(
    strategy.meta_model_
)

If the default LinearRegression is used:

print(
    strategy.meta_model_.coef_
)

You can compare these coefficients with the F-Step column order.

docs.title: Inspect COBRA state
docs.text:
For either COBRA regression wrapper:

strategy = model.cstep_.strategy_

cobra = strategy.cobra

The exact fitted attributes belong to the underlying COBRA estimator.

For example, depending on the implementation and mode:

print(
    cobra.optimization_outputs_
)

may expose optimization information after fitting.

Refer to the dedicated concept pages for algorithm-specific details rather than assuming both COBRA classes expose identical fitted state.

docs.title: Input shape requirements
docs.text:
mean, weighted_mean, and stacking_regressor explicitly validate their training or combination input as a two-dimensional array.

Expected shape:

(n_samples, n_prediction_columns)

For KFC:

(n_samples, n_divergences)

A one-dimensional input such as:

(n_samples,)

is not accepted by these strategies.

docs.title: One divergence
docs.text:
A KFC model can use a single divergence:

divergences=[
    "euclidean"
]

Then the C-Step matrix has shape:

(n_samples, 1)

With mean, the one input column is returned unchanged numerically.

With learned combiners, the strategy can still fit a transformation from that single column to the target.

docs.title: Several divergences
docs.text:
With:

divergences=[
    "euclidean",
    "gkl",
    "logistic",
    "is",
]

the C-Step receives:

(n_samples, 4)

This allows the combiner to aggregate or learn relationships across the four divergence-specific predictions.

docs.title: Learned combiners train on the KFC aggregation subset
docs.text:
KFCProcedure.fit() internally separates the data into:

D_k
D_l

The K-Step and F-Step are fitted using:

D_k

Then D_l is passed through the fitted K/F stages to create:

P_l

and the C-Step is fitted with:

cstep.fit(
    P_l,
    y_l,
)

Therefore learned regression combiners are trained on prediction vectors generated for the aggregation subset.

docs.title: Which combiner is simplest?
docs.text:
The source itself does not rank the combiners.

Their behavior differs as follows:

mean
    fixed arithmetic rule

weighted_mean
    fitted linear rule

stacking_regressor
    fitted customizable regression rule

gradientcobra
    fitted GradientCOBRA rule

mixcobra
    fitted MixCOBRA rule

Use the strategy that matches the aggregation behavior you want to evaluate.

docs.title: Custom regression combiner
docs.text:
You can implement a custom strategy by subclassing:

BaseCombiner

and registering it under:

regression

Example:

import numpy as np

from kfc_procedure.core.combiner.base import (
    BaseCombiner,
)

from kfc_procedure.core.combiner import (
    CombinerFactory,
)


@CombinerFactory.register(
    "median",
    categories={"regression"},
)
class MedianCombiner(
    BaseCombiner
):

    def __init__(
        self,
        random_state=None,
    ):
        self.random_state = random_state

    def fit(
        self,
        X,
        y=None,
    ):
        return self

    def combine(
        self,
        X,
    ):
        X = np.asarray(X)

        return np.median(
            X,
            axis=1,
        )

The random_state parameter is included because the current C-Step injects it for every string-based combiner.

Current string-path compatibility mean MeanCombiner() Yes affected by random_state injection weighted_mean WeightedMeanCombiner(fit_intercept=False) No affected stacking_regressor StackingRegressorCombiner(meta_model=None) No affected gradientcobra GradientCOBRACombiner(**cobra_params) No compatible mixcobra MixCOBRACombiner(**cobra_params) No compatible

docs.title: Mental model
docs.text:
Regression consensus answers one question: given several divergence-specific numeric predictions, how should they become one final number?

\[ \boxed{ \begin{bmatrix} p_1(x) & p_2(x) & \cdots & p_M(x) \end{bmatrix} \rightarrow g \rightarrow \widehat y(x) } \]

The current source provides a fixed arithmetic rule, two learned meta-model approaches, and two COBRA wrappers.

docs.title: Stacking
docs.text:
Stacking is a learned C-Step strategy that uses the F-Step prediction matrix as input to a second-level predictive model.

The package provides two task-specific stacking combiners:

stacking_regressor
stacking_classifier

They are implemented by:

StackingRegressorCombiner
StackingClassifierCombiner

Both follow the same structure:

\[ \boxed{ \text{F-Step prediction matrix} \rightarrow \text{meta-model} \rightarrow \text{final prediction} } \]

docs.title: Core idea
docs.text:
Suppose the F-Step produces predictions from \(M\) divergence-specific local model families.

For \(n\) observations, the C-Step receives:

\[ P = \begin{bmatrix} p_{1,1} & \cdots & p_{1,M}\\ \vdots & & \vdots\\ p_{n,1} & \cdots & p_{n,M} \end{bmatrix}. \]

Stacking treats the columns of \(P\) as features for a new predictive model.

For regression:

\[ \widehat y = g_{\text{reg}}(P). \]

For classification:

\[ \widehat c = g_{\text{clf}}(P). \]

The source calls these second-level models:

meta_model
meta_model_

where:

meta_model
    configured estimator

meta_model_
    fitted clone

docs.title: Where stacking appears in KFC
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    K["K-Step"]
    F["F-Step"]
    P["Prediction matrix"]
    M["Meta-model"]
    Y["Final prediction"]

    K --> F --> P --> M --> Y

The stacking combiner does not use the original KFC feature matrix directly.

It receives only the F-Step prediction matrix and the target values supplied to the C-Step.

docs.title: Regression stacking
docs.text:
The regression implementation is:

StackingRegressorCombiner

and is registered as:

stacking_regressor

The class documentation describes it as:

Stacking combiner using a regression meta-model.

Its purpose is to learn a mapping from base predictions to target values.

docs.title: Constructor
docs.text:
StackingRegressorCombiner(
    meta_model=None,
)

If no meta-model is supplied, the current source uses:

LinearRegression()

through:

self.meta_model = (
    meta_model
    or LinearRegression()
)

It also initializes:

self._is_fitted = False

docs.title: Regression fit flow
docs.text:
The fit() method first converts the prediction matrix:

X = np.asarray(X)

Then it requires two-dimensional input:

if X.ndim != 2:
    raise ValueError(
        f"Expected 2D array, got {X.shape}"
    )

Next it clones the configured meta-model:

self.meta_model_ = clone(
    self.meta_model
)

and fits the clone:

self.meta_model_.fit(
    X,
    y,
)

Finally:

self._is_fitted = True

and the method returns:

self

docs.title: Why the meta-model is cloned
docs.text:
The source does not fit:

self.meta_model

directly.

Instead:

meta_model

remains the configured template while:

meta_model_

becomes the fitted estimator.

This is useful when inspecting configuration versus learned state.

docs.title: Regression prediction
docs.text:
The combine() method first checks:

self._is_fitted

If stacking has not been fitted, it raises:

RuntimeError:
StackingRegressorCombiner is not fitted.

Otherwise prediction is:

return self.meta_model_.predict(
    np.asarray(X)
)

Because BaseCombiner.predict() delegates to combine(), both:

combiner.combine(P)

and:

combiner.predict(P)

use the fitted meta-regressor.

docs.title: Direct regression example
docs.text:
from kfc_procedure.core.combiner.regression import (
    StackingRegressorCombiner,
)

combiner = StackingRegressorCombiner()

combiner.fit(
    P_train,
    y_train,
)

y_pred = combiner.predict(
    P_test
)

With the default constructor, the fitted model is a cloned:

LinearRegression

instance.

docs.title: Inspect the fitted regression meta-model
docs.text:
print(
    combiner.meta_model_
)

For the default linear regression model:

print(
    combiner.meta_model_.coef_
)

print(
    combiner.meta_model_.intercept_
)

The coefficients correspond to the prediction-matrix columns.

docs.title: Classification stacking
docs.text:
The classification implementation is:

StackingClassifierCombiner

and is registered as:

stacking_classifier

The source describes it as a stacking-based classification combiner that learns a mapping from base predictions to final class labels.

docs.title: Constructor
docs.text:
StackingClassifierCombiner(
    meta_model=None,
)

The default meta-classifier is:

LogisticRegression(
    max_iter=1000,
)

through:

self.meta_model = (
    meta_model
    or LogisticRegression(
        max_iter=1000
    )
)

The source also initializes:

self._is_fitted = False

docs.title: Classification fit flow
docs.text:
Like regression, fitting begins with:

X = np.asarray(X)

and validates:

X.ndim == 2

Then:

self.meta_model_ = clone(
    self.meta_model
)

followed by:

self.meta_model_.fit(
    X,
    y,
)

Finally:

self._is_fitted = True

docs.title: Classification prediction
docs.text:
Before prediction:

if not self._is_fitted:
    raise RuntimeError(
        "StackingClassifierCombiner is not fitted."
    )

Then:

return self.meta_model_.predict(
    np.asarray(X)
)

docs.title: Direct classification example
docs.text:
from kfc_procedure.core.combiner.classification import (
    StackingClassifierCombiner,
)

combiner = StackingClassifierCombiner()

combiner.fit(
    P_train,
    y_train,
)

y_pred = combiner.predict(
    P_test
)

docs.title: Inspect the fitted classifier
docs.text:
print(
    combiner.meta_model_
)

For the default logistic regression classifier:

print(
    combiner.meta_model_.classes_
)

print(
    combiner.meta_model_.coef_
)

print(
    combiner.meta_model_.intercept_
)

docs.title: Prediction matrix shape
docs.text:
Both stacking classes expect:

(n_samples, n_models)

In KFC, this means:

(n_samples, n_divergences)

For example, if KFC uses:

divergences=[
    "euclidean",
    "gkl",
    "logistic",
    "is",
]

the stacking meta-model receives four features per sample.

docs.title: Regression matrix example
docs.text:
euclidean      gkl      logistic      is
sample 1        12.4        12.8       12.1       12.5
sample 2        20.7        21.0       20.4       20.8
sample 3         8.3         8.1        8.5        8.2

docs.title: Classification matrix example
docs.text:
euclidean      gkl      logistic      is
sample 1          0           0           1          0
sample 2          1           1           1          1
sample 3          2           1           2          2

The current stacking classes do not transform or encode the prediction matrix themselves.

They pass it directly to the configured meta-model.

docs.title: Important classification detail
docs.text:
For classification, divergence-level class predictions are passed directly as features.

For example:

[0, 0, 1, 0]

is presented to the default logistic-regression meta-classifier as a numeric feature vector.

The stacking implementation does not one-hot encode those divergence-specific class predictions.

Note

This means the numeric representation of class labels becomes part of the meta-classifier input when using the current stacking implementation.

docs.title: Default regression meta-model
docs.text:
The default regression stacking configuration is equivalent to:

StackingRegressorCombiner(
    meta_model=LinearRegression()
)

This learns a linear mapping:

\[ \widehat y = \beta_0 + \sum_{m=1}^{M} \beta_m p_m. \]

Unlike WeightedMeanCombiner, the default LinearRegression() used by StackingRegressorCombiner uses scikit-learn's normal default fit_intercept=True.

docs.title: Difference from weighted_mean
docs.text:
Both default regression stacking and weighted_mean use LinearRegression, but their source defaults differ.

WeightedMeanCombiner creates:

LinearRegression(
    fit_intercept=False
)

by default.

StackingRegressorCombiner creates:

LinearRegression()

which uses the estimator's default intercept behavior.

So even before custom meta-models are introduced, the two classes are not identical in their default configuration.

docs.title: Default classification meta-model
docs.text:
The classification combiner uses:

LogisticRegression(
    max_iter=1000
)

when no custom model is supplied.

The stacking source does not add any further default parameters.

docs.title: Custom regression meta-model
docs.text:
Pass any compatible cloneable regressor through:

meta_model

For example:

from sklearn.ensemble import (
    RandomForestRegressor,
)

from kfc_procedure.core.combiner.regression import (
    StackingRegressorCombiner,
)

combiner = StackingRegressorCombiner(
    meta_model=RandomForestRegressor(
        n_estimators=200,
        random_state=42,
    )
)

Then:

combiner.fit(
    P_train,
    y_train,
)

clones and fits the configured random forest.

docs.title: Custom classification meta-model
docs.text:
Likewise:

from sklearn.ensemble import (
    RandomForestClassifier,
)

from kfc_procedure.core.combiner.classification import (
    StackingClassifierCombiner,
)

combiner = StackingClassifierCombiner(
    meta_model=RandomForestClassifier(
        n_estimators=200,
        random_state=42,
    )
)

The source clones the supplied estimator before training it.

docs.title: Clone compatibility
docs.text:
Both stacking implementations use:

sklearn.base.clone

Therefore a custom meta-model must be compatible with scikit-learn cloning.

In practice, it should behave like a scikit-learn estimator and expose its constructor configuration through the normal estimator parameter interface.

If clone() cannot reconstruct the supplied object from its parameters, stacking fitting will fail before the meta-model's own fit() call.

docs.title: KFC regression usage
docs.text:
Conceptually, the intended string configuration is:

from kfc_procedure import KFCRegressor

model = KFCRegressor(
    divergences=[
        "euclidean",
        "gkl",
    ],
    local_model="ridge",
    combiner="stacking_regressor",
)

However, the current C-Step implementation injects random_state into every string-based combiner constructor.

StackingRegressorCombiner.__init__() currently accepts only:

meta_model=None

and does not accept:

random_state

Therefore the string path is affected by the current constructor mismatch.

docs.title: Current KFC regression workaround
docs.text:
Pass an instance:

from kfc_procedure import KFCRegressor
from kfc_procedure.core.combiner.regression import (
    StackingRegressorCombiner,
)

model = KFCRegressor(
    divergences=[
        "euclidean",
        "gkl",
    ],
    local_model="ridge",
    combiner=StackingRegressorCombiner(),
    random_state=42,
)

Because the combiner is already an object, C-Step returns it directly rather than reconstructing it through CombinerFactory.

docs.title: KFC classification usage
docs.text:
The intended string name is:

stacking_classifier

but the same current C-Step issue applies because:

StackingClassifierCombiner.__init__(
    meta_model=None
)

does not accept random_state.

Use an instance with the current source version:

from kfc_procedure import KFCClassifier
from kfc_procedure.core.combiner.classification import (
    StackingClassifierCombiner,
)

model = KFCClassifier(
    divergences=[
        "euclidean",
        "gkl",
    ],
    local_model="logistic_regression",
    combiner=StackingClassifierCombiner(),
    random_state=42,
)

docs.title: Custom meta-model in KFC
docs.text:
Regression:

from sklearn.ensemble import (
    RandomForestRegressor,
)

stacker = StackingRegressorCombiner(
    meta_model=RandomForestRegressor(
        n_estimators=200,
        random_state=42,
    )
)

model = KFCRegressor(
    divergences=["euclidean"],
    local_model="ridge",
    combiner=stacker,
    random_state=42,
)

Classification:

from sklearn.ensemble import (
    RandomForestClassifier,
)

stacker = StackingClassifierCombiner(
    meta_model=RandomForestClassifier(
        n_estimators=200,
        random_state=42,
    )
)

model = KFCClassifier(
    divergences=["euclidean"],
    local_model="logistic_regression",
    combiner=stacker,
    random_state=42,
)

docs.title: How KFC trains stacking
docs.text:
KFC internally separates the supplied training data into two subsets.

Conceptually:

D_k
    │
    ├── K-Step
    └── F-Step
          │
          ▼
     fitted local models

D_l
    │
    └── pass through fitted K-Step and F-Step
          │
          ▼
         P_l
          │
          ▼
      stacking fit

The stacking combiner therefore fits on:

P_l

and:

y_l

rather than on the same rows used to fit the cluster-local F-Step estimators.

docs.title: Reconstruct stacking input
docs.text:
After fitting a KFC model, create the same kind of prediction representation for new data:

clusters = model.kstep_.predict(
    X_test
)

P_test = model.fstep_.predict(
    X_test,
    clusters,
)

Then the fitted C-Step does:

y_pred = model.cstep_.predict(
    P_test
)

docs.title: Inspect the F-Step column order
docs.text:
The stacking meta-model sees columns in the order returned by F-Step.

Inspect them with:

divergence_names = list(
    model.fstep_.models_.keys()
)

print(
    divergence_names
)

This is especially useful for interpreting:

meta_model_.coef_

in linear stacking models.

docs.title: Interpret regression stacking coefficients
docs.text:
Suppose:

divergence_names = [
    "euclidean",
    "gkl",
    "logistic",
]

and the fitted default linear meta-model has:

coef_ = [
    0.4,
    -0.1,
    0.8,
]

Then the learned stacking rule has the form:

\[ \widehat y = \beta_0 + 0.4p_{\text{euclidean}} - 0.1p_{\text{gkl}} + 0.8p_{\text{logistic}}. \]

The coefficients are not constrained by the stacking class.

Their behavior is determined by the selected meta-model.

docs.title: Inspect classification stacking coefficients
docs.text:
For the default logistic-regression meta-model:

strategy = model.cstep_.strategy_

meta = strategy.meta_model_

print(
    meta.classes_
)

print(
    meta.coef_
)

print(
    meta.intercept_
)

Interpretation follows scikit-learn's LogisticRegression representation.

The stacking combiner itself adds no additional coefficient transformation.

docs.title: No stacking predict_proba()
docs.text:
The classification stacking implementation does not expose:

predict_proba()

even though its default:

LogisticRegression

supports probabilities.

The combiner only defines:

fit()
combine()

and inherits:

predict()

from BaseCombiner.

Therefore:

CStep.predict_proba()

does not find a predict_proba method on StackingClassifierCombiner.

docs.title: Direct access to meta-model probabilities
docs.text:
If you already have a fitted StackingClassifierCombiner, you can technically access the fitted underlying meta-model directly:

strategy = model.cstep_.strategy_

proba = strategy.meta_model_.predict_proba(
    P_test
)

when the configured meta-classifier supports that method.

This is direct use of the underlying estimator, not a probability API exposed by StackingClassifierCombiner itself.

docs.title: Fit-before-predict requirement
docs.text:
Both stacking classes use their own flag:

_is_fitted

rather than scikit-learn's check_is_fitted() inside combine().

Immediately after construction:

combiner._is_fitted == False

After successful fitting:

combiner._is_fitted == True

Calling:

combiner.predict(P)

too early raises the task-specific RuntimeError.

docs.title: Input validation scope
docs.text:
During fit(), both classes explicitly check only:

X is two-dimensional

The stacking classes themselves do not add explicit checks for:

X and y length agreement
finite values
target type
minimum sample count

Those conditions are left to the selected meta-model or NumPy/scikit-learn operations.

During combine(), the source converts with:

np.asarray(X)

but does not explicitly repeat the ndim == 2 check before calling the fitted meta-model.

docs.title: One divergence
docs.text:
If KFC uses one divergence:

divergences=[
    "euclidean"
]

then the stacking matrix has shape:

(n_samples, 1)

A meta-model can still be trained on this single prediction feature.

For default regression stacking, that means fitting a linear relationship from one F-Step prediction column to the target.

For default classification stacking, it means fitting logistic regression on one numeric prediction feature.

docs.title: Several divergences
docs.text:
With several divergences, stacking can learn interactions only to the extent that the chosen meta-model supports them.

The default regression meta-model is linear:

LinearRegression

The default classification meta-model is also linear in its input features:

LogisticRegression

If nonlinear meta-level relationships are needed, supply a different clone-compatible meta-model.

docs.title: Stacking is supervised
docs.text:
Unlike:

mean
majority_vote

stacking requires target values during fit().

Regression:

combiner.fit(
    P_train,
    y_train,
)

Classification:

combiner.fit(
    P_train,
    y_train,
)

The target values determine the fitted meta_model_.

docs.title: Stacking vs weighted mean
docs.text:
The current regression implementations differ in structure.

Property weighted_mean stacking_regressor Default learner LinearRegression(fit_intercept=False) LinearRegression() Custom learner No constructor hook meta_model= Fitted estimator attribute model meta_model_ Clone configured estimator No Yes Explicit fitted flag No Yes

Both operate on the same kind of prediction matrix, but stacking_regressor is the customizable meta-regression abstraction.

docs.title: Stacking vs majority vote
docs.text:
For classification:

majority_vote
    no training
    counts row labels

stacking_classifier
    supervised training
    learns mapping from prediction rows to labels

Stacking can learn that different divergence columns carry different information, subject to the selected meta-model.

docs.title: Stacking vs CombinedClassifier
docs.text:
Both are learned classification C-Step strategies, but the implementations are different.

stacking_classifier:

prediction matrix
    ↓
meta-classifier
    ↓
class label

combined_classifier:

prediction matrix
    ↓
CombinedClassifier
    ↓
prediction-space distance/kernel consensus
    ↓
class label

For the second approach, see:

CombinedClassifier

docs.text:

stacker.fit(

prediction = stacker.predict(

print(

docs.title: Check the current string-path error
docs.text:
If KFC raises:

unexpected keyword argument 'random_state'

while using:

stacking_regressor

or:

stacking_classifier

pass a pre-instantiated stacking combiner instead.

docs.title: Current source limitations
docs.text: Area Current behavior regression default meta-model LinearRegression() classification default meta-model LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000) custom meta-model supported meta-model cloning supported fit input validation only explicit 2D X check regression probability output not applicable classification combiner predict_proba() not implemented classification F-Step labels passed directly as meta-features one-hot encoding of F-Step labels not implemented string KFC integration affected by C-Step random_state injection combiner instance integration supported nonlinear stacking possible through custom meta-model

docs.title: Quick reference
docs.text: Feature Regression Classification Registry name stacking_regressor stacking_classifier Class StackingRegressorCombiner StackingClassifierCombiner Default model LinearRegression() LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000) Fitted model meta_model_ meta_model_ Clones meta-model Yes Yes Requires target in fit() Yes Yes predict_proba() on combiner — No Current string path affected by random_state injection Yes Yes

docs.title: Mental model
docs.text:
Stacking treats the F-Step predictions as a new feature space and learns a second-level model on top of them.

\[ \boxed{ P = \begin{bmatrix} p_1 & p_2 & \cdots & p_M \end{bmatrix} \rightarrow \text{meta-model} \rightarrow \widehat y } \]

The regression and classification implementations differ mainly in their default meta-models; their fitting structure is otherwise closely parallel.

docs.title: Weighted Mean
docs.text:
WeightedMeanCombiner is a supervised regression combiner used by the KFC C-Step.

It learns a linear relationship between the F-Step prediction matrix and the true regression target.

The implementation is registered under:

weighted_mean

and lives in:

kfc_procedure/core/combiner/regression/weighted_mean.py

The source describes it as:

Weighted mean combiner (regression).

Learns optimal linear weights using Ordinary Least Squares (OLS).

docs.title: Core idea
docs.text:
Assume the F-Step produces a prediction matrix

\[ X \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times K}, \]

where:

  • \(n\) is the number of observations;
  • \(K\) is the number of prediction columns.

In KFC, those columns correspond to divergence-specific prediction families.

The source models the target as

\[ y \approx Xw, \]

where:

\[ w \in \mathbb{R}^{K} \]

contains the learned coefficients.

Conceptually:

F-Step predictions
        │
        ▼
┌──────────────────────────────┐
│ euclidean   gkl   logistic   │
├──────────────────────────────┤
│   12.4      12.8     12.1    │
│   20.7      21.0     20.4    │
│    8.3       8.1      8.5    │
└──────────────────────────────┘
        │
        ▼
LinearRegression
        │
        ▼
learned coefficients
        │
        ▼
final regression prediction

docs.title: Constructor
docs.text:
The current implementation is:

WeightedMeanCombiner(
    fit_intercept=False,
)

The constructor creates:

self.model = LinearRegression(
    fit_intercept=fit_intercept
)

So the only combiner-specific constructor parameter is:

fit_intercept

with default:

False

docs.title: Default model
docs.text:
With the default:

fit_intercept=False

the learned rule is approximately:

\[ \widehat y = \sum_{k=1}^{K}w_kX_k. \]

If:

fit_intercept=True

then the model becomes:

\[ \widehat y = b + \sum_{k=1}^{K}w_kX_k. \]

docs.title: Important: this is not a constrained weighted average
docs.text:
The name weighted_mean can suggest a convex weighted average, but the current source does not impose such constraints.

The learned coefficients are produced by ordinary:

LinearRegression

and are not constrained to satisfy:

\[ w_k \ge 0 \]

or:

\[ \sum_{k=1}^{K}w_k = 1. \]

Therefore coefficients may be:

negative
greater than one
or sum to a value other than one

A more precise description of the current implementation is:

OLS linear combiner over F-Step prediction columns

rather than a mathematically constrained weighted mean.

docs.title: Fit behavior
docs.text:
The implementation is:

def fit(
    self,
    X,
    y,
):
    X = np.asarray(X)

    if X.ndim != 2:
        raise ValueError(
            f"Expected 2D array, got {X.shape}"
        )

    self.model.fit(
        X,
        y,
    )

    return self

There are three important behaviors here:

  1. input is converted with np.asarray();
  2. X must be two-dimensional;
  3. the internal LinearRegression is fitted directly on X and y.

docs.title: Required input shape
docs.text:
The expected shape is:

(n_samples, n_prediction_columns)

In KFC:

(n_samples, n_divergences)

For example, with four divergences:

X.shape == (
    n_samples,
    4,
)

docs.title: Invalid one-dimensional input
docs.text:
This is invalid:

X.shape == (
    n_samples,
)

because the source explicitly checks:

X.ndim != 2

and raises:

ValueError:
Expected 2D array, got ...

Even if you have only one prediction source, the matrix should still have shape:

(n_samples, 1)

rather than:

(n_samples,)

docs.title: Prediction behavior
docs.text:
WeightedMeanCombiner.combine() is:

def combine(
    self,
    X,
):
    X = np.asarray(X)

    return self.model.predict(X)

Because BaseCombiner.predict() delegates to:

self.combine(X)

both of these are equivalent:

combiner.combine(P_test)

and:

combiner.predict(P_test)

docs.title: Direct example
docs.text:
import numpy as np

from kfc_procedure.core.combiner.regression import (
    WeightedMeanCombiner,
)


P_train = np.array([
    [10.0, 10.5,  9.8],
    [12.0, 11.8, 12.3],
    [18.0, 18.4, 17.9],
    [25.0, 24.7, 25.2],
])

y_train = np.array([
    10.2,
    12.1,
    18.3,
    25.0,
])


combiner = WeightedMeanCombiner(
    fit_intercept=False,
)

combiner.fit(
    P_train,
    y_train,
)


P_test = np.array([
    [14.0, 14.2, 13.9],
    [20.0, 19.8, 20.3],
])

y_pred = combiner.predict(
    P_test
)

print(
    y_pred
)

docs.title: Inspect the learned coefficients
docs.text:
The fitted scikit-learn model is available at:

combiner.model

The learned coefficients are:

combiner.model.coef_

For example:

print(
    combiner.model.coef_
)

If there are three prediction columns, the shape is typically:

(3,)

docs.title: Inspect the intercept
docs.text:
print(
    combiner.model.intercept_
)

With:

fit_intercept=False

scikit-learn's fitted intercept is effectively zero.

With:

fit_intercept=True

the model estimates an intercept from the training data.

docs.title: Interpreting coefficients
docs.text:
Suppose the F-Step column order is:

euclidean
gkl
logistic

and the learned coefficients are:

[
    0.50,
    -0.20,
    0.90,
]

With no intercept, the learned aggregation rule is:

\[ \widehat y = 0.50p_{\text{euclidean}} - 0.20p_{\text{gkl}} + 0.90p_{\text{logistic}}. \]

This example shows why the implementation should not be interpreted as a convex average.

docs.title: KFC prediction-column order
docs.text:
The F-Step prediction matrix is ordered according to:

model.fstep_.models_

You can inspect the column names with:

divergence_names = list(
    model.fstep_.models_.keys()
)

print(
    divergence_names
)

Then pair them with the learned coefficients:

weights = model.cstep_.strategy_.model.coef_

for name, weight in zip(
    divergence_names,
    weights,
):
    print(
        name,
        weight,
    )

This is the recommended way to interpret which divergence-specific predictions receive positive or negative linear coefficients.

docs.title: Using an intercept
docs.text:
To fit an intercept:

combiner = WeightedMeanCombiner(
    fit_intercept=True,
)

Then the model is:

\[ \widehat y = b + Xw. \]

Inspect:

print(
    combiner.model.intercept_
)

and:

print(
    combiner.model.coef_
)

docs.title: KFC integration
docs.text:
Conceptually, the registry name is:

weighted_mean

and the intended KFC configuration is:

from kfc_procedure import KFCRegressor

model = KFCRegressor(
    divergences=[
        "euclidean",
        "gkl",
    ],
    local_model="ridge",
    combiner="weighted_mean",
    combiner_params={
        "fit_intercept": False,
    },
)

However, the current C-Step implementation introduces an important constructor compatibility issue.

docs.title: Current C-Step random_state issue
docs.text:
When C-Step resolves a string combiner, the source does:

params = dict(
    self.combiner_params
)

if "random_state" not in params:
    params["random_state"] = self.random_state

and then:

CombinerFactory.create(
    name,
    **params
)

That means a string-based weighted_mean configuration is constructed conceptually as:

WeightedMeanCombiner(
    fit_intercept=False,
    random_state=...,
)

But the actual constructor is only:

def __init__(
    self,
    fit_intercept=False,
):
    ...

It does not accept:

random_state

docs.title: Result
docs.text:
The current string-based KFC path can raise:

TypeError:
WeightedMeanCombiner.__init__() got an unexpected keyword argument 'random_state'

This can happen even if the forwarded value is:

None

because the unsupported keyword is still present.

Current source limitation

With the current source version, weighted_mean is affected by C-Step's unconditional random_state parameter injection.

This is an implementation issue in C-Step parameter forwarding, not an issue with WeightedMeanCombiner itself.

docs.title: Current workaround
docs.text:
Pass a pre-instantiated combiner object instead of the string name.

from kfc_procedure import KFCRegressor

from kfc_procedure.core.combiner.regression import (
    WeightedMeanCombiner,
)


model = KFCRegressor(
    divergences=[
        "euclidean",
        "gkl",
    ],
    local_model="ridge",
    combiner=WeightedMeanCombiner(
        fit_intercept=False,
    ),
    random_state=42,
)

C-Step checks:

if not isinstance(
    self.combiner,
    str,
):
    return self.combiner

so the already-created object is used directly and the unsupported random_state keyword is not injected into its constructor.

docs.title: How KFC trains weighted mean
docs.text:
KFC internally separates the provided training data into two subsets:

D_k
D_l

The K-Step and F-Step are fitted using:

D_k

Then:

D_l

is passed through those fitted stages to create:

P_l

The C-Step then fits:

WeightedMeanCombiner.fit(
    P_l,
    y_l,
)

Conceptually:

flowchart LR
    DK["Dₖ"]
    K["K-Step"]
    F["F-Step"]

    DL["Dₗ"]
    P["Prediction matrix Pₗ"]
    W["WeightedMeanCombiner"]
    Y["Learned linear combiner"]

    DK --> K --> F
    DL --> P
    F --> P
    P --> W
    DL --> W
    W --> Y

The weighted combiner is therefore trained on divergence-level predictions generated for the internal aggregation subset.

docs.title: Reconstruct the C-Step input
docs.text:
After fitting:

clusters = model.kstep_.predict(
    X_test
)

P_test = model.fstep_.predict(
    X_test,
    clusters,
)

print(
    P_test.shape
)

Then:

y_pred = model.cstep_.predict(
    P_test
)

uses the fitted weighted linear model.

docs.title: Inspect the fitted KFC combiner
docs.text:
After fitting:

strategy = model.cstep_.strategy_

Then:

print(
    type(strategy).__name__
)

should be:

WeightedMeanCombiner

when that strategy is used.

The internal linear regression model is:

strategy.model

docs.title: Inspect KFC coefficients
docs.text:
weights = strategy.model.coef_

print(
    weights
)

Map the coefficients to divergence names:

divergence_names = list(
    model.fstep_.models_.keys()
)

for name, weight in zip(
    divergence_names,
    weights,
):
    print(
        f"{name}: {weight}"
    )

docs.title: Inspect the KFC intercept
docs.text:
print(
    strategy.model.intercept_
)

Its interpretation depends on:

fit_intercept

used when creating the combiner.

docs.title: Example coefficient table
docs.text:
import pandas as pd

divergence_names = list(
    model.fstep_.models_.keys()
)

weights = model.cstep_.strategy_.model.coef_

table = pd.DataFrame({
    "divergence": divergence_names,
    "coefficient": weights,
})

print(
    table
)

Conceptually:

    divergence    coefficient
0   euclidean        0.62
1   gkl              0.18
2   logistic        -0.11
3   is               0.44

Again, these are OLS coefficients, not normalized ensemble probabilities or convex weights.

docs.title: Weighted mean vs ordinary mean
docs.text:
MeanCombiner uses:

\[ \widehat y = \frac{1}{K} \sum_k X_k. \]

Every column contributes equally.

WeightedMeanCombiner instead learns:

\[ \widehat y = Xw \]

or:

\[ \widehat y = b+Xw. \]

So the coefficient assigned to each column is learned from data.

docs.title: Weighted mean vs stacking regressor
docs.text:
Both use supervised C-Step fitting.

The default implementations differ as follows:

Property Weighted Mean Stacking Regressor Internal model LinearRegression default LinearRegression Default intercept False sklearn default, normally True Custom meta-model No Yes Fitted estimator location model meta_model_ Clones configured estimator No Yes Purpose OLS coefficient combiner general meta-regression abstraction

With their defaults, both are linear, but they are not configured identically.

For more detail, see:

Stacking

docs.title: Weighted mean vs GradientCOBRA
docs.text:
WeightedMeanCombiner learns one global linear relationship:

\[ \widehat y = Xw+b. \]

GradientCOBRACombiner instead passes the F-Step matrix into a kernel-based prediction-space aggregation procedure.

So their aggregation mechanisms are structurally different:

weighted_mean
    prediction matrix
        ↓
    global OLS fit
        ↓
    final value

versus:

gradientcobra
    prediction matrix
        ↓
    distance / kernel consensus
        ↓
    local weighted aggregation
        ↓
    final value

For the algorithmic details, see:

GradientCOBRA

docs.title: Weighted mean with one divergence
docs.text:
If KFC uses only:

divergences=[
    "euclidean"
]

then the prediction matrix has shape:

(n_samples, 1)

Weighted mean still works as a linear calibration model:

\[ \widehat y = wp \]

or with an intercept:

\[ \widehat y = b+wp. \]

So even with one divergence, the learned mapping can rescale or shift the single F-Step prediction column.

docs.title: Weighted mean with several divergences
docs.text:
With:

divergences=[
    "euclidean",
    "gkl",
    "logistic",
    "is",
]

the combiner learns four coefficients:

\[ w = ( w_{\text{euclidean}}, w_{\text{gkl}}, w_{\text{logistic}}, w_{\text{is}} ). \]

The source does not perform feature selection or regularization inside this combiner.

All behavior comes from standard LinearRegression.

docs.title: Multicollinearity
docs.text:
Because WeightedMeanCombiner delegates directly to sklearn.linear_model.LinearRegression, the source itself adds no special handling for strongly correlated prediction columns.

For example, two divergences may produce very similar F-Step predictions.

The current combiner does not:

regularize coefficients
drop duplicate columns
normalize weights
enforce sparsity

Any numerical behavior in such cases comes from the underlying LinearRegression implementation.

docs.title: No internal cross-validation
docs.text:
WeightedMeanCombiner does not perform cross-validation.

Its complete fitting logic is:

self.model.fit(
    X,
    y,
)

There is no internal search over:

fit_intercept
regularization strength
subset of columns
weight constraints

If you need a more flexible learned C-Step, use a custom stacking meta-model or a COBRA strategy.

docs.title: No normalization inside the combiner
docs.text:
The source does not normalize or standardize the prediction columns before calling:

LinearRegression.fit()

The F-Step prediction matrix is used as supplied.

So if prediction columns have different numerical behavior, the current combiner itself does not rescale them first.

docs.title: No explicit finite-value validation
docs.text:
WeightedMeanCombiner.fit() explicitly validates only:

X is two-dimensional

It does not manually check:

NaN
infinity
X/y sample mismatch

Those errors, when relevant, are left to scikit-learn's LinearRegression.

A useful upstream check is:

import numpy as np

print(
    np.isfinite(
        P_train
    ).all()
)

docs.title: Fit-before-predict behavior
docs.text:
The combiner itself does not maintain its own _is_fitted flag.

It relies on the wrapped scikit-learn model.

If:

combiner.predict(X)

is called before:

combiner.fit(X, y)

then LinearRegression.predict() is responsible for reporting that the model is not fitted.

docs.title: Direct use outside KFC
docs.text:
WeightedMeanCombiner can aggregate predictions from any regression models, not only KFC divergence families.

For example:

P_train = np.column_stack([
    pred_model_a_train,
    pred_model_b_train,
    pred_model_c_train,
])

P_test = np.column_stack([
    pred_model_a_test,
    pred_model_b_test,
    pred_model_c_test,
])

combiner = WeightedMeanCombiner(
    fit_intercept=False,
)

combiner.fit(
    P_train,
    y_train,
)

final_prediction = combiner.predict(
    P_test
)

The class only assumes that X is a two-dimensional prediction matrix.

docs.title: Custom constrained weighting
docs.text:
The current implementation does not provide constrained weights.

If you need:

\[ w_k\geq0 \]

and:

\[ \sum_kw_k=1, \]

that behavior is not supported by WeightedMeanCombiner as currently written.

A custom BaseCombiner implementation would be needed for those constraints.

For example, the custom combiner would have to solve an explicitly constrained optimization problem rather than using ordinary LinearRegression.

docs.title: 1. Inspect matrix shape
docs.text:
print(
    P_train.shape
)

Expected:

(n_samples, n_prediction_columns)

docs.title: 2. Check finite values
docs.text:
print(
    np.isfinite(
        P_train
    ).all()
)

docs.title: 3. Inspect fitted coefficients
docs.text:
strategy = model.cstep_.strategy_

print(
    strategy.model.coef_
)

docs.title: 4. Inspect intercept
docs.text:
print(
    strategy.model.intercept_
)

docs.title: 5. Inspect divergence order
docs.text:
print(
    list(
        model.fstep_.models_.keys()
    )
)

docs.title: 6. Check the current constructor error
docs.text:
If KFC raises:

unexpected keyword argument 'random_state'

while using:

combiner="weighted_mean"

use:

combiner=WeightedMeanCombiner(...)

instead of the string path with the current source version.

docs.title: Quick reference
docs.text: Property Current behavior Registry name weighted_mean Task regression Internal model LinearRegression Default fit_intercept False Requires target in fit() Yes Input requirement 2D prediction matrix Weight positivity enforced No Sum-to-one enforced No Internal normalization No Internal cross-validation No Regularization No Learned coefficients model.coef_ Learned intercept model.intercept_ Current string KFC path affected by C-Step random_state injection

docs.title: Mental model
docs.text:
Weighted mean learns one global OLS coefficient for each F-Step prediction column.

\[ \boxed{ \begin{bmatrix} p_1(x) & p_2(x) & \cdots & p_K(x) \end{bmatrix} \rightarrow \text{LinearRegression} \rightarrow \widehat y(x) } \]

Despite the class name, the current source implements unconstrained linear regression rather than a normalized weighted average.

docs.title: Base Estimators
docs.text:
The base estimator layer provides the predictive models used by the F-Step of the KFC Procedure.

The F-Step does not hard-code one regression model or one classifier. Instead, it resolves local learners through a registry:

LocalModelFactory

and trains one model inside every divergence-specific cluster.

\[ \boxed{ \text{cluster data} \rightarrow \text{local estimator} \rightarrow \text{local prediction} } \]

The main implementation lives in:

kfc_procedure/core/ml/
├── base.py
├── sklearn.py
└── __init__.py

docs.title: Main components
docs.text:
The estimator layer contains three important pieces.

  • BaseLocalModel

    Abstract interface used by F-Step local models.

    Requires:

    fit()
predict()

  • LocalModelFactory

    Registry and factory used to resolve estimator names.

    Models are categorized as:

    regression
classification

  • SklearnLocalModel

    Adapter that wraps scikit-learn estimators so they can be used by the F-Step.

docs.title: BaseLocalModel
docs.text:
All local-model implementations inherit from:

BaseLocalModel

which itself inherits:

sklearn.base.BaseEstimator

and ABC.

The abstract interface is:

class BaseLocalModel(BaseEstimator, ABC):

    @abstractmethod
    def fit(self, X, y):
        ...

    @abstractmethod
    def predict(self, X):
        ...

    def predict_proba(self, X):
        raise NotImplementedError

The base class is intentionally task-agnostic.

Task separation is handled by the factory registry.

docs.title: Required methods
docs.text:
A local model must implement:

fit(X, y)

and:

predict(X)

The F-Step relies on exactly these methods when training and generating the prediction matrix consumed by the C-Step.

docs.title: Optional probability method
docs.text:
The base class also defines:

predict_proba(X)

but its default behavior is:

raise NotImplementedError

So probability prediction is optional at the local-model level.

The current F-Step itself does not expose a predict_proba() method, so end-to-end KFC classification probabilities are not currently available even when a local classifier supports probabilities.

docs.title: LocalModelFactory
docs.text:
The registry used by F-Step is:

from kfc_procedure.core.ml import LocalModelFactory

It subclasses the package's general-purpose:

BaseFactory

and keeps its own independent registry.

The class documentation defines the categories:

regression
classification
multitask

although the current built-in registrations primarily use:

regression
classification

docs.title: Why use a registry?
docs.text:
Instead of requiring users to instantiate every estimator manually, KFC can resolve a model from a string:

local_model="ridge"

or:

local_model="logistic_regression"

F-Step then asks the factory to create the matching implementation.

Conceptually:

"ridge"
   │
   ▼
LocalModelFactory
   │
   ▼
SklearnLocalModel(Ridge)
   │
   ▼
fit on one cluster

docs.title: Automatic scikit-learn registration
docs.text:
When this module is imported:

from kfc_procedure.core.ml import ...

the package automatically calls:

register_all_sklearn_models()

The registration function uses:

sklearn.utils.all_estimators()

to discover available scikit-learn estimators.

It keeps estimator classes that:

have fit()
and inherit ClassifierMixin or RegressorMixin

Those estimators are then registered automatically with LocalModelFactory.

docs.title: Registration categories
docs.text:
A discovered estimator is registered as:

classification

if it subclasses:

ClassifierMixin

and otherwise as:

regression

if it subclasses:

RegressorMixin

This category information is later used by F-Step to prevent task mismatch.

docs.title: Estimator names
docs.text:
Scikit-learn class names are converted to lower-case snake case.

The conversion is performed by:

clean_sklearn_name()

Examples:

Scikit-learn class Registry name LinearRegression linear_regression LogisticRegression logistic_regression RandomForestRegressor random_forest_regressor RandomForestClassifier random_forest_classifier KNeighborsRegressor k_neighbors_regressor KNeighborsClassifier k_neighbors_classifier DecisionTreeClassifier decision_tree_classifier RidgeCV ridge_cv LassoCV lasso_cv SVC svc SVR svr

All-uppercase names are simply lowercased.

For example:

SVC -> svc
SVR -> svr

docs.title: The exact available model list depends on scikit-learn
docs.text:
Because KFC discovers estimators dynamically with:

all_estimators()

the complete set of model names depends on the installed scikit-learn version.

For that reason, application code and documentation should not rely on a permanently fixed exhaustive list.

Instead, inspect the registry in the installed environment.

docs.title: List all registered local models
docs.text:
from kfc_procedure.core.ml import (
    LocalModelFactory,
)

print(
    LocalModelFactory.available()
)

This returns a sorted list of all registered names and aliases.

docs.title: List regression models
docs.text:
print(
    LocalModelFactory.available_by_category(
        "regression"
    )
)

docs.title: List classification models
docs.text:
print(
    LocalModelFactory.available_by_category(
        "classification"
    )
)

This is the recommended way to discover the models actually available in the installed package.

docs.title: Common regression estimators
docs.text:
The dynamically registered estimator set commonly includes names such as:

linear_regression
ridge
ridge_cv
lasso
lasso_cv
elastic_net
elastic_net_cv
decision_tree_regressor
random_forest_regressor
extra_trees_regressor
gradient_boosting_regressor
hist_gradient_boosting_regressor
k_neighbors_regressor
svr
dummy_regressor

Note

This is an illustrative subset.

The exact available names should be obtained from:

LocalModelFactory.available_by_category(
    "regression"
)

docs.title: Common classification estimators
docs.text:
Typical dynamically registered names include:

logistic_regression
decision_tree_classifier
random_forest_classifier
extra_trees_classifier
gradient_boosting_classifier
hist_gradient_boosting_classifier
k_neighbors_classifier
svc
linear_svc
gaussian_nb
dummy_classifier

Again, use the registry to inspect the actual installed set.

docs.title: Built-in MeanRegressor
docs.text:
In addition to dynamically registered scikit-learn models, the source explicitly registers:

mean_regressor
dummy_mean

as aliases for:

MeanRegressor

The registration is:

@LocalModelFactory.register(
    "mean_regressor",
    "dummy_mean",
    categories={"regression"},
)

The model wraps:

DummyRegressor(
    strategy="mean"
)

docs.title: Mean-regressor behavior
docs.text:
Its implementation is:

class MeanRegressor(BaseLocalModel):

    def __init__(self):
        self.estimator = DummyRegressor(
            strategy="mean"
        )

    def fit(self, X, y):
        self.estimator.fit(
            X,
            y,
        )
        return self

    def predict(self, X):
        return np.asarray(
            self.estimator.predict(X),
            dtype=float,
        )

So each local cluster predicts the mean target learned from that cluster.

docs.title: Current MeanRegressor integration issue
docs.text:
The current F-Step automatically injects:

random_state=self.random_state

when a local model is resolved from a string.

However:

MeanRegressor.__init__()

currently accepts no parameters.

Therefore a string-based configuration such as:

local_model="mean_regressor"

can receive an unsupported random_state keyword when created by F-Step.

Current source behavior

In this source version, mean_regressor / dummy_mean may raise a constructor TypeError when selected through F-Step.

This is an implementation issue, not a conceptual limitation of a cluster-wise mean predictor.

docs.title: SklearnLocalModel
docs.text:
Scikit-learn estimators are not registered directly.

Instead, each dynamically registered name points to a small builder that returns:

SklearnLocalModel(
    model_cls,
    **kwargs,
)

This adapter gives scikit-learn models the BaseLocalModel interface expected by F-Step.

docs.title: Constructor
docs.text:
The adapter receives:

model_cls

and arbitrary keyword arguments:

SklearnLocalModel(
    model_cls,
    **kwargs,
)

It then inspects:

model_cls.__init__

using:

inspect.signature()

and retains only keyword arguments that are explicitly present in the constructor signature.

docs.title: Parameter filtering
docs.text:
The implementation performs:

valid_kwargs = {
    key: value
    for key, value in kwargs.items()
    if key in signature.parameters
}

and then:

self.model = model_cls(
    **valid_kwargs
)

This has an important user-facing consequence.

Unknown parameters are silently removed instead of raising an error at this adapter layer.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Suppose:

local_model_params={
    "alpha": 2.0,
    "not_a_real_parameter": 99,
}

and the selected estimator only accepts alpha.

The adapter keeps:

alpha=2.0

and discards:

not_a_real_parameter

Check parameter spelling

A typo in a scikit-learn constructor parameter can therefore be silently ignored.

Inspect the fitted local estimator's parameters if configuration accuracy matters.

docs.title: Inspect estimator parameters
docs.text:
After KFC has fitted local models, retrieve one:

local_model = model.fstep_.models_[
    "euclidean"
]["m0"]["model"]

Then:

print(
    local_model.get_params()
)

For SklearnLocalModel, get_params() delegates directly to:

self.model.get_params()

docs.title: Change parameters with set_params()
docs.text:
The adapter also delegates:

set_params(...)

to the underlying scikit-learn estimator.

local_model.set_params(
    alpha=2.0
)

This matches the standard scikit-learn parameter API.

docs.title: Access the wrapped estimator
docs.text:
The underlying estimator is stored as:

local_model.model

Example:

wrapped = model.fstep_.models_[
    "euclidean"
]["m0"]["model"]

print(
    wrapped.model
)

You can then inspect estimator-specific fitted state:

print(
    wrapped.model.coef_
)

when the selected estimator defines that attribute.

docs.title: Probability capability
docs.text:
During initialization, SklearnLocalModel records whether the wrapped estimator exposes:

predict_proba

with:

self._has_proba = hasattr(
    self.model,
    "predict_proba",
)

Then:

local_model.predict_proba(X)

delegates to the wrapped estimator when available.

Otherwise it raises:

<EstimatorName> does not support predict_proba

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
A model such as logistic regression normally supports:

predict_proba()

while some classifiers do not.

The adapter handles this capability check dynamically.

Important

This local capability does not currently make KFCClassifier.predict_proba() functional, because the current FStep itself has no predict_proba() method.

docs.title: random_state handling
docs.text:
The F-Step resolves string models with:

params = dict(
    self.local_model_params
)

if "random_state" not in params:
    params["random_state"] = self.random_state

Therefore the top-level KFC seed is attempted for every string-based local model.

For scikit-learn-backed estimators, the adapter filters it out when the constructor does not accept random_state.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
model = KFCRegressor(
    divergences=["euclidean"],
    local_model="random_forest_regressor",
    local_model_params={
        "n_estimators": 300,
    },
    combiner="gradientcobra",
    random_state=42,
)

F-Step creates each random forest using the equivalent of:

RandomForestRegressor(
    n_estimators=300,
    random_state=42,
)

docs.title: Local seed overrides top-level seed
docs.text:
If you explicitly pass:

local_model_params={
    "random_state": 123,
}

the F-Step does not replace it.

So:

local_model_params["random_state"]

takes precedence over:

KFC random_state

docs.title: Task validation
docs.text:
Before creating a string-based local model, F-Step checks:

LocalModelFactory.supports(
    name,
    self.task,
)

This prevents incompatible estimator categories.

docs.title: Regression mismatch example
docs.text:
This is invalid:

KFCRegressor(
    divergences=["euclidean"],
    local_model="logistic_regression",
    combiner="gradientcobra",
)

because:

logistic_regression

is registered as:

classification

docs.title: Classification mismatch example
docs.text:
This is invalid:

KFCClassifier(
    divergences=["euclidean"],
    local_model="ridge",
    combiner="combined_classifier",
)

because:

ridge

is registered as:

regression

docs.title: Check whether a model supports a task
docs.text:
from kfc_procedure.core.ml import (
    LocalModelFactory,
)

print(
    LocalModelFactory.supports(
        "ridge",
        "regression",
    )
)

Expected:

True

For:

print(
    LocalModelFactory.supports(
        "ridge",
        "classification",
    )
)

expected:

False

docs.title: Check whether a model exists
docs.text:
print(
    LocalModelFactory.contains(
        "random_forest_regressor"
    )
)

This returns a Boolean rather than raising for invalid input names.

docs.title: Inspect registry metadata
docs.text:
The underlying factory provides:

LocalModelFactory.info(name)

Example:

info = LocalModelFactory.info(
    "ridge"
)

print(info)

The result contains:

name
class
module
categories
metadata

For dynamically registered scikit-learn estimators, the registered target is the builder function created by the registration loop.

docs.title: Registry normalization
docs.text:
BaseFactory normalizes registration names by:

stripping surrounding whitespace
converting to lowercase

So lookups are case-insensitive with respect to registry normalization.

Conceptually:

LocalModelFactory.contains(
    "RIDGE"
)

resolves the normalized key:

ridge

docs.title: Registry aliases
docs.text:
The factory can register multiple names for the same target.

For example:

mean_regressor
dummy_mean

refer to the same built-in MeanRegressor class.

The general factory also provides:

find_by_class(...)

to retrieve aliases registered for a target class.

docs.title: Registry categories
docs.text:
Inspect all categories:

print(
    LocalModelFactory.available_categories()
)

For the current local-model registry, the important categories are:

regression
classification

docs.title: F-Step creates one estimator per cluster
docs.text:
When local_model is a string, F-Step calls:

LocalModelFactory.create(...)

inside the loop over divergence/cluster pairs.

Therefore each cluster receives a new local-model instance.

This is an important property.

For:

divergences=[
    "euclidean",
    "gkl",
]

n_clusters=3

the F-Step can create:

euclidean / cluster 0 -> new estimator
euclidean / cluster 1 -> new estimator
euclidean / cluster 2 -> new estimator

gkl / cluster 0       -> new estimator
gkl / cluster 1       -> new estimator
gkl / cluster 2       -> new estimator

The estimators have the same class and constructor configuration but learn independently from different subsets.

docs.title: One model type across all clusters
docs.text:
The current F-Step accepts one global:

local_model

and one global:

local_model_params

Therefore you cannot currently configure:

Ridge for Euclidean clusters
RandomForest for GKL clusters
SVR for Logistic clusters

within one F-Step instance.

All divergence/cluster combinations use the same estimator type and parameter configuration.

docs.title: Pre-instantiated estimator objects
docs.text:
F-Step also accepts a non-string local model object:

local_model=my_model

The relevant source logic is:

if not isinstance(
    self.local_model,
    str,
):
    return self.local_model

This means the exact same object instance is returned for every cluster.

docs.title: Important reuse behavior
docs.text:
Suppose:

my_model = MyEstimator()

model = KFCRegressor(
    divergences=["euclidean"],
    local_model=my_model,
    combiner="gradientcobra",
)

During F-Step fitting, the same object can be fitted repeatedly:

cluster 0 -> my_model.fit(...)
cluster 1 -> same my_model.fit(...)
cluster 2 -> same my_model.fit(...)

The current F-Step does not clone the object.

Prefer registered string estimators

For independent cluster models, use a registered string name.

Pre-instantiated local-model objects are reused rather than cloned in the current implementation.

docs.title: Custom local estimator
docs.text:
A custom estimator can subclass:

BaseLocalModel

and implement:

fit()
predict()

For example:

import numpy as np

from kfc_procedure.core.ml import (
    BaseLocalModel,
)


class MedianRegressor(
    BaseLocalModel
):

    def fit(
        self,
        X,
        y,
    ):
        self.value_ = float(
            np.median(y)
        )
        return self

    def predict(
        self,
        X,
    ):
        return np.full(
            len(X),
            self.value_,
            dtype=float,
        )

docs.title: Register a custom estimator
docs.text:
Register it with:

LocalModelFactory

using a task category.

from kfc_procedure.core.ml import (
    LocalModelFactory,
)


@LocalModelFactory.register(
    "median_regressor",
    categories={"regression"},
)
class MedianRegressor(
    BaseLocalModel
):
    ...

Then use:

model = KFCRegressor(
    divergences=["euclidean"],
    local_model="median_regressor",
    combiner="gradientcobra",
)

docs.title: Custom constructor compatibility
docs.text:
Remember that F-Step adds:

random_state=...

to every string-based local-model constructor unless it is already present in local_model_params.

Therefore a directly registered custom estimator should normally support:

def __init__(
    self,
    random_state=None,
    ...
):
    ...

or accept arbitrary keyword arguments.

Otherwise factory creation can fail with:

unexpected keyword argument 'random_state'

The scikit-learn adapter avoids this problem by filtering unsupported kwargs, but directly registered custom classes do not receive that filtering automatically.

docs.title: Register multiple aliases
docs.text:
The factory supports multiple registration names:

@LocalModelFactory.register(
    "median_regressor",
    "median",
    categories={"regression"},
)
class MedianRegressor(
    BaseLocalModel
):
    ...

Then both names create the same class.

docs.title: Duplicate-name protection
docs.text:
BaseFactory.register() normalizes names and checks for conflicts before registration.

Attempting to register a name that already exists raises:

KeyError

This protects the estimator registry from silent replacement.

docs.title: Registration names are normalized
docs.text:
The factory:

  1. strips surrounding whitespace;
  2. converts names to lower case;
  3. rejects empty names;
  4. rejects duplicates in the same registration call.

So:

"  MyModel  "

becomes:

mymodel

docs.title: Creating an estimator directly from the factory
docs.text:
Although normal KFC users let F-Step do this, you can create a model directly.

from kfc_procedure.core.ml import (
    LocalModelFactory,
)

model = LocalModelFactory.create(
    "ridge",
    alpha=2.0,
)

For a dynamically registered scikit-learn estimator, this returns a SklearnLocalModel wrapper.

Then:

model.fit(
    X_train,
    y_train,
)

prediction = model.predict(
    X_test,
)

docs.title: Inspect the created wrapper
docs.text:
local_model = LocalModelFactory.create(
    "ridge",
    alpha=2.0,
)

print(
    type(local_model).__name__
)

The wrapper type is:

SklearnLocalModel

The underlying estimator can be accessed through:

print(
    local_model.model
)

docs.title: Example: regression estimator
docs.text:
from kfc_procedure.core.ml import (
    LocalModelFactory,
)

ridge = LocalModelFactory.create(
    "ridge",
    alpha=1.5,
)

ridge.fit(
    X_train,
    y_train,
)

y_pred = ridge.predict(
    X_test,
)

docs.title: Example: classification estimator
docs.text:
logit = LocalModelFactory.create(
    "logistic_regression",
    C=1.0,
    max_iter=1000,
)

logit.fit(
    X_train,
    y_train,
)

y_pred = logit.predict(
    X_test,
)

If supported:

proba = logit.predict_proba(
    X_test,
)

docs.title: Estimator parameters in KFC
docs.text:
Use:

local_model_params

to configure a string-based estimator.

Regression:

model = KFCRegressor(
    divergences=["euclidean"],
    local_model="random_forest_regressor",
    local_model_params={
        "n_estimators": 300,
        "max_depth": 8,
        "min_samples_leaf": 3,
    },
    combiner="gradientcobra",
    random_state=42,
)

Classification:

model = KFCClassifier(
    divergences=["euclidean"],
    local_model="logistic_regression",
    local_model_params={
        "C": 1.0,
        "max_iter": 1000,
        "class_weight": "balanced",
    },
    combiner="combined_classifier",
    random_state=42,
)

For more detail, see:

Estimator Parameters

docs.title: Choosing a regression estimator
docs.text:
The source does not prescribe one estimator as universally best.

The F-Step architecture is designed so that a local model can be selected according to the application.

A practical code-oriented interpretation is:

  • Linear models

    Examples:

    linear_regression
ridge
lasso

    Useful when relationships inside clusters are approximately simple.

  • Tree models

    Examples:

    decision_tree_regressor
random_forest_regressor

    Useful when local relationships remain nonlinear.

  • Neighborhood models

    Example:

    k_neighbors_regressor

  • Kernel / margin models

    Example:

    svr

These are usage categories, not package-imposed rankings.

docs.title: Choosing a classification estimator
docs.text:
Likewise, classification can use any registered classifier compatible with the cluster-level target distribution.

Common choices include:

logistic_regression
decision_tree_classifier
random_forest_classifier
k_neighbors_classifier
svc

Remember that some classifiers cannot fit when a local cluster contains only one class.

docs.title: Small-cluster behavior
docs.text:
Every F-Step model is trained only on its assigned cluster.

Therefore the effective sample size can be much smaller than the full training sample.

If:

n_clusters

is large, local estimators may receive very few observations.

This can cause:

  • unstable regression models;
  • one-class classification clusters;
  • neighbor-based models with too few samples;
  • estimator-specific validation errors.

The F-Step catches ValueError raised during local-model fitting and rethrows it with divergence and cluster information.

docs.title: F-Step error message
docs.text:
The source wraps fitting errors as:

[FSTEP ERROR] divergence='...', cluster=... failed.
Reason: ...
Hint: cluster contains invalid label distribution.

The hint is always included, even if the original ValueError is not related to classification.

Inspect the underlying Reason: text for the actual estimator failure.

docs.title: Scikit-learn estimator version sensitivity
docs.text:
Because registration is dynamic:

all_estimators()

the exact local-model registry can change when the installed scikit-learn version changes.

This affects:

  • available estimator names;
  • estimator constructor parameters;
  • default values;
  • supported capabilities such as predict_proba().
