The current top-level KFC probability pipeline still has a separate F-Step limitation described in the classification guide.

docs.title: Parameters are constructor parameters
docs.text:
local_model_params is forwarded when the local model is created.

It is not applied after fitting.

Conceptually:

LocalModelFactory.create(
    name,
    **local_model_params,
)

happens before:

model.fit(
    X_cluster,
    y_cluster,
)

So values in local_model_params should match the selected estimator's constructor arguments.

docs.title: Fit-time arguments are not supported separately
docs.text:
The current F-Step always calls:

model.fit(
    Xc,
    yc,
)

with only two arguments.

There is no current top-level F-Step parameter for passing extra fit-time arguments such as:

sample_weight
callbacks
eval_set

to each local estimator.

Current API scope

local_model_params configures constructors only.

It is not a general fit() keyword dictionary.

docs.title: One parameter dictionary for all local fits
docs.text:
Suppose:

local_model="random_forest_regressor"

local_model_params={
    "n_estimators": 300,
    "max_depth": 8,
}

Every cluster receives the same configuration.

The current source does not support:

cluster 0 -> max_depth=4
cluster 1 -> max_depth=8
cluster 2 -> max_depth=None

nor:

Euclidean -> Ridge(alpha=1)
GKL       -> Ridge(alpha=5)

inside one F-Step.

If you require those behaviors, the F-Step would need to be extended.

docs.title: Task categories still apply
docs.text:
Changing parameters does not change the estimator's registered task category.

For example:

local_model="ridge"

remains a regression estimator regardless of its parameter values.

F-Step validates:

LocalModelFactory.supports(
    name,
    task,
)

before model construction.

So parameter customization cannot make a regression model valid for classification or vice versa.

docs.title: Discover the selected estimator
docs.text:
Because KFC auto-registers scikit-learn models, the exact available set can depend on the installed scikit-learn version.

Check whether a model exists:

from kfc_procedure.core.ml import (
    LocalModelFactory,
)

print(
    LocalModelFactory.contains(
        "hist_gradient_boosting_regressor"
    )
)

docs.title: List available regression estimators
docs.text:
print(
    LocalModelFactory.available_by_category(
        "regression"
    )
)

docs.title: List available classifiers
docs.text:
print(
    LocalModelFactory.available_by_category(
        "classification"
    )
)

This should be done before assuming a particular estimator name is available in every environment.

docs.title: Inspect registry metadata
docs.text:
info = LocalModelFactory.info(
    "ridge"
)

print(
    info
)

The factory metadata identifies:

name
class
module
categories
metadata

For dynamically registered scikit-learn estimators, the registered target is the builder function created during automatic registration.

docs.title: Direct factory creation
docs.text:
You can test a parameter configuration without running the full KFC pipeline.

from kfc_procedure.core.ml import (
    LocalModelFactory,
)

local = LocalModelFactory.create(
    "random_forest_regressor",
    n_estimators=300,
    max_depth=8,
    random_state=42,
)

print(
    local.get_params()
)

This is useful for validating which parameters survive the adapter filtering.

docs.title: Check a suspected typo
docs.text:
local = LocalModelFactory.create(
    "random_forest_regressor",
    n_estimator=300,
    random_state=42,
)

params = local.get_params()

print(
    "n_estimator" in params
)

print(
    params["n_estimators"]
)

The typo is not retained.

The underlying estimator uses its own default for n_estimators.

docs.title: Parameter changes after creation
docs.text:
SklearnLocalModel exposes:

set_params(...)

and delegates directly to the wrapped estimator.

Example:

local = LocalModelFactory.create(
    "ridge",
    alpha=1.0,
)

local.set_params(
    alpha=3.0,
)

Then:

print(
    local.get_params()["alpha"]
)

returns:

3.0

docs.title: Changing fitted KFC local models
docs.text:
You can technically call:

set_params()

on a local model extracted from:

model.fstep_.models_

but changing estimator parameters does not automatically refit that local model or the rest of the KFC pipeline.

For example:

local_model.set_params(
    alpha=3.0
)

does not retrain it.

To obtain a coherent KFC model, update the top-level configuration and run:

model.fit(...)

again.

docs.title: Inspect all fitted local-model parameters
docs.text:
You can audit every cluster model after training.

for divergence, models in model.fstep_.models_.items():
    print(
        "\n",
        divergence,
    )

    for model_name, metadata in models.items():
        local = metadata["model"]

        print(
            model_name,
            "cluster=",
            metadata["cluster"],
        )

        if hasattr(
            local,
            "get_params",
        ):
            print(
                local.get_params()
            )

This is useful when verifying reproducibility.

docs.title: Compare requested and effective parameters
docs.text:
A simple audit pattern is:

requested = {
    "n_estimators": 300,
    "max_depth": 8,
    "random_state": 42,
}

local = LocalModelFactory.create(
    "random_forest_regressor",
    **requested,
)

effective = local.get_params()

for key, value in requested.items():
    print(
        key,
        "requested=",
        value,
        "effective=",
        effective.get(
            key,
            "<filtered>",
        ),
    )

docs.title: Parameter compatibility depends on the installed estimator version
docs.text:
Because the adapter examines the actual constructor signature:

inspect.signature(
    model_cls.__init__
)

a parameter is retained only if the installed estimator version declares it.

This means behavior can change when scikit-learn changes estimator signatures.

For reproducible production use, pin the scikit-learn version together with the KFC package version.

docs.title: Directly registered custom models behave differently
docs.text:
The filtering described above belongs specifically to:

SklearnLocalModel

A custom model registered directly with:

LocalModelFactory.register(...)

receives factory keyword arguments directly.

For example:

@LocalModelFactory.register(
    "my_model",
    categories={"regression"},
)
class MyModel(BaseLocalModel):

    def __init__(
        self,
        scale=1.0,
        random_state=None,
    ):
        ...

F-Step can create:

MyModel(
    scale=2.0,
    random_state=42,
)

docs.title: Unsupported custom-model kwargs are not filtered automatically
docs.text:
If your directly registered custom constructor is:

def __init__(
    self,
    scale=1.0,
):
    ...

but F-Step creates it with:

random_state=42

then normal Python constructor behavior applies and a TypeError can be raised.

The factory itself forwards arguments directly:

target_cls(
    *args,
    **kwargs,
)

It does not inspect or remove unsupported keywords.

docs.title: Recommended custom-model constructor pattern
docs.text:
Because F-Step injects random_state, a direct custom local estimator should usually accept it:

class MyRegressor(
    BaseLocalModel
):

    def __init__(
        self,
        scale=1.0,
        random_state=None,
    ):
        self.scale = scale
        self.random_state = random_state

Then:

model = KFCRegressor(
    divergences=["euclidean"],
    local_model="my_regressor",
    local_model_params={
        "scale": 2.0,
    },
    combiner="gradientcobra",
    random_state=42,
)

works with the F-Step parameter path.

docs.title: Current mean_regressor issue
docs.text:
The built-in MeanRegressor constructor is currently:

def __init__(
    self,
) -> None:
    ...

It does not accept:

random_state

But F-Step injects that key for every string model.

Because MeanRegressor is directly registered rather than wrapped in SklearnLocalModel, unsupported arguments are not filtered.

Therefore:

local_model="mean_regressor"

or:

local_model="dummy_mean"

can fail during factory construction in the current source version.

Implementation-specific issue

The problem is parameter forwarding, not the behavior of DummyRegressor(strategy="mean") itself.

docs.title: Nested estimator parameters
docs.text:
Some scikit-learn estimators can expose nested parameters through:

get_params(
    deep=True
)

and standard scikit-learn set_params() can use names such as:

component__parameter

However, the KFC SklearnLocalModel constructor filtering step compares local_model_params only with the selected estimator's direct __init__() signature.

Therefore arbitrary nested __ parameters are not a general constructor-time mechanism provided by the current KFC adapter.

Use the selected estimator's documented direct constructor arguments, or provide a custom registered wrapper if you need a more specialized composite estimator configuration.

docs.title: Parameter tuning
docs.text:
The F-Step does not perform local-estimator hyperparameter search.

For example:

local_model="ridge"
local_model_params={
    "alpha": 1.0,
}

uses exactly that constructor configuration for every cluster.

KFC does not automatically compare:

alpha=0.1
alpha=1.0
alpha=10.0

for the F-Step.

docs.title: Use estimators that tune themselves
docs.text:
Because scikit-learn estimators are registered dynamically, estimators with built-in tuning APIs can be selected when available.

For example:

local_model="ridge_cv"

or:

local_model="lasso_cv"

can perform their own internal estimator-specific tuning when fitted.

Their accepted constructor parameters still follow the installed scikit-learn class signature.

docs.title: External tuning
docs.text:
You can also treat KFC constructor settings as ordinary estimator hyperparameters and evaluate different complete KFC configurations outside the F-Step.

The source itself does not provide a dedicated search utility for local_model_params.

docs.title: Wrong parameter name
docs.text:
local_model_params={
    "n_estimator": 300,
}

instead of:

local_model_params={
    "n_estimators": 300,
}

may be silently ignored by SklearnLocalModel.

docs.title: Passing fit-time options as constructor parameters
docs.text:
local_model_params={
    "sample_weight": weights,
}

does not make F-Step call:

fit(
    X,
    y,
    sample_weight=weights,
)

The current F-Step always calls:

fit(
    Xc,
    yc,
)

docs.title: Assuming parameters differ by cluster
docs.text: One local_model_params dictionary applies to all local model instances.

docs.title: Assuming top-level random_state always controls randomness
docs.text:
It is forwarded only when:

"random_state"

is absent from local_model_params.

Also, estimators without a random_state constructor parameter simply discard the injected value through the scikit-learn adapter.

docs.title: Assuming accepted parameters are stable across scikit-learn versions
docs.text:
The adapter uses the constructor signature present in the installed environment.

Pin dependencies when exact configuration behavior matters.

docs.title: 1. Inspect requested parameters
docs.text:
print(
    model.local_model_params
)

docs.title: 2. Inspect one fitted local model
docs.text:
local = model.fstep_.models_[
    "euclidean"
]["m0"]["model"]

print(
    local
)

docs.title: 3. Inspect effective parameters
docs.text:
print(
    local.get_params()
)

docs.title: 4. Inspect the wrapped estimator
docs.text:
print(
    local.model
)

for a SklearnLocalModel.

docs.title: 5. Compare all cluster configurations
docs.text:
for divergence, models in model.fstep_.models_.items():
    for name, metadata in models.items():
        local = metadata["model"]

        print(
            divergence,
            name,
            local.get_params()
            if hasattr(
                local,
                "get_params",
            )
            else "<no get_params>",
        )

docs.title: Quick reference
docs.text: Question Current behavior Where do local parameters go? estimator constructor Same parameters for every cluster? Yes Same parameters for every divergence? Yes Is random_state added automatically? Yes, if absent Are unsupported sklearn kwargs rejected? No, silently filtered Are unsupported custom-model kwargs filtered? No Are fit-time kwargs supported? No Are local parameters tuned automatically? No Can fitted sklearn parameters be inspected? Yes, via get_params() Can the wrapped estimator be inspected? Yes, via .model Are object local models cloned? No

docs.title: Mental model
docs.text:
local_model_params describes how every cluster-local estimator is constructed; F-Step then creates one independently fitted instance per cluster when the model is selected by registry name.

\[ \boxed{ \text{local_model_params} \rightarrow \text{constructor filtering} \rightarrow \text{new estimator} \rightarrow \text{cluster-specific fit} } \]

docs.title: KFC Classification
docs.text:
This guide shows how to use KFCClassifier for classification tasks.

KFCClassifier applies the complete KFC pipeline:

\[ \boxed{ \text{K-Step} \rightarrow \text{F-Step} \rightarrow \text{C-Step} } \]

for discrete class labels.

Use it when the input space may contain unknown groups whose class boundaries are better modeled locally than by one global classifier.

docs.title: Basic example
docs.text:
from kfc_procedure import KFCClassifier

model = KFCClassifier(
    divergences=["euclidean"],
    local_model="logistic_regression",
    combiner="majority_vote",
    n_clusters=3,
    random_state=42,
)

model.fit(X_train, y_train)

y_pred = model.predict(X_test)

This configuration:

  1. splits the training data into two internal subsets;
  2. clusters the K/F subset using squared-Euclidean Bregman K-means;
  3. fits one logistic regression classifier inside each cluster;
  4. obtains one class prediction per divergence;
  5. combines those predictions with majority voting.

docs.title: Classification workflow
docs.text:
Calling

model.fit(X, y)

first creates the internal K/F and C-Step subsets.

For classification, the current implementation uses a stratified split:

X_k, X_l, y_k, y_l = train_test_split(
    X,
    y,
    test_size=0.5,
    random_state=random_state,
    stratify=y,
)

Therefore the two internal subsets aim to preserve the overall class distribution.

flowchart LR
    D["Training data<br/>X, y"]
    S["Stratified 50 / 50 split"]

    DK["Dₖ"]
    DL["Dₗ"]

    K["K-Step<br/>Bregman clustering"]
    F["F-Step<br/>local classifiers"]
    P["Class-prediction matrix Pₗ"]
    C["Classification combiner"]
    Y["Final class"]

    D --> S
    S --> DK
    S --> DL

    DK --> K --> F
    F --> P
    DL --> P

    P --> C --> Y

  • \(D_k\)

    Used by K-Step and F-Step.

    Clustering models and cluster-local classifiers are fitted here.

  • \(D_l\)

    Passed through the fitted K-Step and F-Step.

    Its class-prediction matrix is used to fit or calibrate the C-Step.

Stratification requirement

Because KFCClassifier uses stratify=y, every class needs enough observations for scikit-learn to create the 50/50 split.

Extremely rare classes can cause train_test_split to fail before KFC reaches the K-Step.

docs.title: What the F-Step produces
docs.text:
Assume three divergences are configured:

divergences=[
    "euclidean",
    "gkl",
    "logistic",
]

For each observation, the F-Step produces one class label from each divergence-specific local-classifier family.

For example:

              euclidean      gkl      logistic
sample 1          0           0           1
sample 2          1           1           1
sample 3          2           1           2

Mathematically,

\[ P = \begin{bmatrix} m^{(1)}(x_1) & \cdots & m^{(M)}(x_1) \\ \vdots & & \vdots \\ m^{(1)}(x_n) & \cdots & m^{(M)}(x_n) \end{bmatrix}, \]

where every entry is a predicted class label.

The C-Step then applies

\[ P\longrightarrow \widehat y. \]

docs.title: Choose the divergences
docs.text:
The built-in divergence names are:

Name Geometry Required input domain euclidean Squared Euclidean real-valued inputs gkl Generalized Kullback–Leibler strictly positive inputs logistic Logistic Bregman divergence values strictly between 0 and 1 is Itakura–Saito strictly positive inputs

For arbitrary real-valued features, start with:

model = KFCClassifier(
    divergences=["euclidean"],
    local_model="logistic_regression",
    combiner="majority_vote",
    random_state=42,
)

For several clustering views:

model = KFCClassifier(
    divergences=[
        "euclidean",
        "gkl",
        "logistic",
        "is",
    ],
    local_model="logistic_regression",
    combiner="majority_vote",
    random_state=42,
)

Domain validation

The package does not automatically transform feature values for the selected divergence.

If all four built-in divergences are used, scale the features to a strict subset of \((0,1)\).

docs.title: Preparing features for several divergences
docs.text:
A practical preprocessing strategy is:

from sklearn.preprocessing import MinMaxScaler

eps = 1e-6

scaler = MinMaxScaler(
    feature_range=(eps, 1.0 - eps),
)

X_train_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X_train)
X_test_scaled = scaler.transform(X_test)

Then:

model = KFCClassifier(
    divergences=[
        "euclidean",
        "gkl",
        "logistic",
        "is",
    ],
    local_model="logistic_regression",
    combiner="majority_vote",
    n_clusters=3,
    random_state=42,
)

model.fit(
    X_train_scaled,
    y_train,
)

y_pred = model.predict(
    X_test_scaled,
)

docs.title: Choose the local classifier
docs.text:
local_model controls the classifier fitted inside every non-empty cluster.

Because KFCClassifier fixes

task="classification"

only models registered in the classification category are accepted.

Common examples include:

logistic_regression
decision_tree_classifier
random_forest_classifier
k_neighbors_classifier
svc

The package also auto-registers compatible scikit-learn classifiers using snake-case estimator names.

docs.title: Logistic regression
docs.text:
model = KFCClassifier(
    divergences=["euclidean"],
    local_model="logistic_regression",
    local_model_params={
        "max_iter": 1000,
        "C": 1.0,
    },
    combiner="majority_vote",
    random_state=42,
)

docs.title: Decision tree
docs.text:
model = KFCClassifier(
    divergences=["euclidean"],
    local_model="decision_tree_classifier",
    local_model_params={
        "max_depth": 6,
    },
    combiner="majority_vote",
    random_state=42,
)

docs.title: Random forest
docs.text:
model = KFCClassifier(
    divergences=["euclidean"],
    local_model="random_forest_classifier",
    local_model_params={
        "n_estimators": 300,
        "max_depth": 8,
    },
    combiner="majority_vote",
    random_state=42,
)

When a selected local classifier accepts random_state, KFC forwards the top-level value unless it is already supplied inside local_model_params.

docs.title: Support vector classifier
docs.text:
model = KFCClassifier(
    divergences=["euclidean"],
    local_model="svc",
    local_model_params={
        "C": 1.0,
        "kernel": "rbf",
    },
    combiner="majority_vote",
    random_state=42,
)

For ordinary predict() usage, probability=True is not required.

docs.title: How many local classifiers are fitted?
docs.text:
With \(M\) divergences and \(K\) clusters, KFC normally fits up to

\[ M\times K \]

local classifiers.

For example:

divergences=[
    "euclidean",
    "gkl",
    "logistic",
    "is",
]

n_clusters=3

can produce up to

\[ 4\times3=12 \]

local classifiers.

Each classifier is trained only on the observations assigned to its own divergence-specific cluster.

docs.title: The single-class cluster problem
docs.text:
Classification introduces an important issue that is less common in regression.

A cluster can contain observations from only one class.

For example:

cluster 0 -> labels [0, 0, 0, 0, 0]

Many classifiers, including logistic regression, require at least two classes during fit().

The F-Step catches the resulting ValueError and raises a more informative message containing:

[FSTEP ERROR]
divergence='...'
cluster=...
Reason: ...
Hint: cluster contains invalid label distribution.

Possible remedies include:

  • reduce n_clusters;
  • use more training data;
  • use a different divergence;
  • use a local classifier compatible with the cluster;
  • inspect class imbalance before fitting.

docs.title: Choose a classification combiner
docs.text:
The current source registers three classification combiners:

majority_vote
stacking_classifier
combined_classifier

docs.title: majority_vote
docs.text:
majority_vote is a stateless hard-voting combiner.

For every row of the F-Step prediction matrix, it selects the most frequent class label.

If

Euclidean -> 1
GKL       -> 1
Logistic  -> 0
IS        -> 1

the final prediction is:

1

Example:

model = KFCClassifier(
    divergences=[
        "euclidean",
        "gkl",
        "logistic",
        "is",
    ],
    local_model="logistic_regression",
    combiner="majority_vote",
    random_state=42,
)

The underlying implementation uses:

Counter(row).most_common(1)[0][0]

for each sample.

Ties

The current implementation relies on Python Counter.most_common().

No additional domain-specific tie-breaking rule is implemented by MajorityVoteCombiner.

docs.title: stacking_classifier
docs.text:
stacking_classifier learns a meta-classifier from the divergence prediction matrix.

By default it uses:

LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)

Example:

model = KFCClassifier(
    divergences=[
        "euclidean",
        "gkl",
        "logistic",
    ],
    local_model="decision_tree_classifier",
    combiner="stacking_classifier",
    random_state=42,
)

The meta-classifier sees samples like:

[0, 0, 1]
[1, 1, 1]
[2, 1, 2]

and learns how those divergence-level class patterns relate to the true labels.

docs.title: Custom meta-classifier
docs.text:
You can supply a custom estimator instance:

from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier

model = KFCClassifier(
    divergences=[
        "euclidean",
        "gkl",
    ],
    local_model="logistic_regression",
    combiner="stacking_classifier",
    combiner_params={
        "meta_model": RandomForestClassifier(
            n_estimators=200,
            random_state=42,
        ),
    },
    random_state=42,
)

The combiner clones the supplied meta_model before fitting it.

docs.title: combined_classifier
docs.text:
combined_classifier wraps the package's prediction-space CombinedClassifier.

Instead of performing direct majority voting, it compares the entire vector of divergence-specific class predictions with prediction vectors from the aggregation sample.

Example:

model = KFCClassifier(
    divergences=[
        "euclidean",
        "gkl",
        "logistic",
        "is",
    ],
    local_model="logistic_regression",
    combiner="combined_classifier",
    combiner_params={
        "distance": "hamming",
        "kernel": "rbf",
        "bandwidth_list": [
            0.01,
            0.1,
            0.5,
            1.0,
            2.0,
        ],
        "random_state": 42,
    },
    random_state=42,
)

Internally, the KFC wrapper calls:

self.cobra.fit(
    X,
    y,
    as_predictions=True,
)

so the F-Step prediction matrix is treated directly as prediction-space data.

For a complete explanation, see:

CombinedClassifier

docs.title: Comparing classification combiners
docs.text:
Combiner Learns parameters? Main idea majority_vote No most common divergence-level label stacking_classifier Yes meta-classifier over prediction patterns combined_classifier Yes kernel consensus in prediction space

A practical sequence is to begin with majority_vote and then compare it with the learned combiners.

docs.title: Full binary-classification example
docs.text:
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.preprocessing import MinMaxScaler

from kfc_procedure import KFCClassifier


# Create data
X, y = make_classification(
    n_samples=1500,
    n_features=10,
    n_informative=7,
    n_redundant=1,
    n_classes=2,
    random_state=42,
)


# Outer train/test split
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X,
    y,
    test_size=0.2,
    stratify=y,
    random_state=42,
)


# Scale for all built-in Bregman divergences
eps = 1e-6

scaler = MinMaxScaler(
    feature_range=(eps, 1.0 - eps),
)

X_train = scaler.fit_transform(X_train)
X_test = scaler.transform(X_test)


# Configure KFC
model = KFCClassifier(
    divergences=[
        "euclidean",
        "gkl",
        "logistic",
        "is",
    ],
    local_model="logistic_regression",
    local_model_params={
        "max_iter": 1000,
    },
    combiner="majority_vote",
    n_clusters=3,
    max_iter=300,
    tol=1e-4,
    random_state=42,
)


# Fit
model.fit(
    X_train,
    y_train,
)


# Predict
y_pred = model.predict(X_test)


# Evaluate
accuracy = accuracy_score(
    y_test,
    y_pred,
)

print("Accuracy:", accuracy)

docs.title: Multiclass example
docs.text:
KFC's classification pipeline is not restricted by its own API to binary labels.

For example:

X, y = make_classification(
    n_samples=1800,
    n_features=12,
    n_informative=8,
    n_classes=3,
    n_clusters_per_class=1,
    random_state=42,
)

Then:

model = KFCClassifier(
    divergences=["euclidean"],
    local_model="random_forest_classifier",
    combiner="majority_vote",
    n_clusters=3,
    random_state=42,
)

model.fit(
    X_train,
    y_train,
)

y_pred = model.predict(X_test)

Whether a particular local model or combiner supports a given multiclass problem depends on that underlying component.

docs.title: Example with stacking
docs.text:
model = KFCClassifier(
    divergences=[
        "euclidean",
        "gkl",
        "logistic",
        "is",
    ],
    local_model="decision_tree_classifier",
    local_model_params={
        "max_depth": 5,
    },
    combiner="stacking_classifier",
    n_clusters=3,
    random_state=42,
)

model.fit(
    X_train,
    y_train,
)

y_pred = model.predict(X_test)

docs.title: Example with CombinedClassifier
docs.text:
import numpy as np

model = KFCClassifier(
    divergences=[
        "euclidean",
        "gkl",
        "logistic",
        "is",
    ],
    local_model="logistic_regression",
    local_model_params={
        "max_iter": 1000,
    },
    combiner="combined_classifier",
    combiner_params={
        "distance": "hamming",
        "kernel": "rbf",
        "bandwidth_list": np.linspace(
            0.01,
            3.0,
            40,
        ),
        "n_cv": 5,
        "random_state": 42,
    },
    n_clusters=3,
    random_state=42,
)

model.fit(
    X_train,
    y_train,
)

y_pred = model.predict(X_test)

docs.title: Prediction workflow
docs.text:
After fitting:

y_pred = model.predict(X_new)

runs:

flowchart LR
    X["New samples"]

    K1["Cluster under<br/>divergence 1"]
    K2["Cluster under<br/>divergence 2"]
    KM["Other divergences"]

    F1["Local classifier"]
    F2["Local classifier"]
    FM["Local classifier"]

    P["Class-prediction matrix"]
    C["Classification combiner"]
    Y["Final class"]

    X --> K1 --> F1 --> P
    X --> K2 --> F2 --> P
    X --> KM --> FM --> P

    P --> C --> Y

For each divergence:

  1. K-Step assigns each new observation to the closest fitted cluster.
  2. F-Step selects the classifier fitted in that cluster.
  3. The local classifier predicts a class label.
  4. All divergence-level labels are stacked into a row.
  5. C-Step converts that row into the final class prediction.

docs.title: Inspect divergence-level class predictions
docs.text:
You can inspect the matrix sent to the C-Step.

clusters = model.kstep_.predict(X_test)

P_test = model.fstep_.predict(
    X_test,
    clusters,
)

print(P_test.shape)
print(P_test[:5])

With four divergences:

P_test.shape == (n_test, 4)

For example:

[[0, 0, 1, 0],
 [1, 1, 1, 1],
 [0, 1, 0, 0]]

docs.title: Inspect the local classifiers
docs.text:
The fitted local models are stored in:

model.fstep_.models_

Example:

for divergence, models in model.fstep_.models_.items():
    print(divergence)

    for model_name, metadata in models.items():
        print(
            model_name,
            "cluster=",
            metadata["cluster"],
            "classifier=",
            type(metadata["model"]).__name__,
        )

Each stored entry contains:

divergence
cluster
model

docs.title: Inspect cluster class distributions
docs.text:
Because single-class clusters can cause local-model failures, it can be useful to inspect the K-Step assignments on the internal training subset.

The fitted K-Step stores:

model.kstep_.clusters_

The public KFCClassifier object does not currently retain y_k as a fitted attribute, so exact internal class distributions are not directly exposed after fit().

For deeper diagnostics, reproduce the same split externally or inspect the K-Step and F-Step during development.

docs.title: Inspect the C-Step
docs.text:
The fitted combiner is available as:

strategy = model.cstep_.strategy_

For majority voting:

print(type(strategy).__name__)

For stacking:

print(strategy.meta_model_)

For CombinedClassifier:

print(strategy.cobra)
print(strategy.cobra.bandwidth_)

when the inner model exposes those fitted attributes.

docs.title: Classification metrics
docs.text:
KFCClassifier returns predicted labels through:

model.predict(X)

Evaluate them with ordinary classification metrics.

docs.title: Accuracy
docs.text:
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score

accuracy = accuracy_score(
    y_test,
    y_pred,
)

docs.title: Balanced accuracy
docs.text:
from sklearn.metrics import balanced_accuracy_score

score = balanced_accuracy_score(
    y_test,
    y_pred,
)

docs.title: F1 score
docs.text:
from sklearn.metrics import f1_score

f1 = f1_score(
    y_test,
    y_pred,
)

For multiclass classification:

f1 = f1_score(
    y_test,
    y_pred,
    average="macro",
)

docs.title: Confusion matrix
docs.text:
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix

cm = confusion_matrix(
    y_test,
    y_pred,
)

docs.title: About predict_proba()
docs.text:
KFCClassifier defines:

model.predict_proba(X)

in kfc.py.

However, the current F-Step implementation only defines:

predict(...)

and does not define:

predict_proba(...)

Yet the top-level probability path attempts to call:

self.fstep_.predict_proba(
    X,
    clusters,
)

Therefore the full KFCClassifier.predict_proba() path is currently incomplete.

Current source limitation

Use:

model.predict(X)

for the current version.

Do not rely on top-level KFCClassifier.predict_proba() until probability propagation is implemented in FStep.

docs.title: Probability support in the combiners
docs.text: The C-Step itself has a predict_proba() method, but support depends on the chosen combiner.

docs.title: majority_vote
docs.text: MajorityVoteCombiner does not implement predict_proba().

docs.title: stacking_classifier
docs.text: The current StackingClassifierCombiner uses a classifier that may itself support probabilities, but the combiner class does not expose its own predict_proba() method.

docs.title: combined_classifier
docs.text:
CobraClassifierCombiner explicitly implements:

predict_proba(...)

and delegates to the wrapped CombinedClassifier.

However, because top-level KFCClassifier.predict_proba() currently fails earlier at F-Step, this C-Step capability is not yet sufficient to provide end-to-end probabilities.

docs.title: Class labels
docs.text:
The KFC classification pipeline works with the labels produced by the chosen local classifiers.

For example, labels may be:

0, 1

or:

"class_a", "class_b"

provided that the selected local estimators and C-Step combiner support them.

MajorityVoteCombiner stores the output in an object-dtype NumPy array, so it can accommodate non-numeric labels.

docs.title: Choosing n_clusters
docs.text:
n_clusters applies independently to each divergence.

model = KFCClassifier(
    divergences=["euclidean"],
    local_model="logistic_regression",
    combiner="majority_vote",
    n_clusters=4,
)

For classification, increasing the number of clusters introduces a special trade-off:

more clusters
    ↓
more localized class boundaries
    ↓
fewer observations per local classifier
    ↓
higher chance of single-class clusters

So classification often requires more care with n_clusters than regression.

docs.title: Class imbalance
docs.text:
KFC's internal train/aggregation split is stratified, but the Bregman clustering itself is unsupervised.

Therefore stratification does not guarantee balanced class distributions inside individual clusters.

A globally balanced dataset can still produce:

cluster 0 -> mostly class 0
cluster 1 -> mixed
cluster 2 -> only class 1

Possible approaches include:

  • reducing n_clusters;
  • using more observations;
  • using local classifiers with suitable class-weight options;
  • choosing a different divergence set;
  • evaluating per-class metrics instead of accuracy alone.

For example:

model = KFCClassifier(
    divergences=["euclidean"],
    local_model="logistic_regression",
    local_model_params={
        "max_iter": 1000,
        "class_weight": "balanced",
    },
    combiner="majority_vote",
    n_clusters=3,
    random_state=42,
)

class_weight="balanced" can help with imbalance inside clusters containing multiple classes, but it cannot make a classifier fit a cluster that contains only one class.

docs.title: Reproducibility
docs.text:
Set:

random_state=42

to control:

  • the internal stratified split;
  • Bregman K-means initialization;
  • compatible local classifiers;
  • compatible C-Step components.
model = KFCClassifier(
    divergences=["euclidean"],
    local_model="random_forest_classifier",
    local_model_params={
        "n_estimators": 300,
    },
    combiner="majority_vote",
    random_state=42,
)

A component that does not expose a random_state constructor argument simply ignores the forwarded value through the package's estimator adapter.

docs.title: Rare class causes internal split failure
docs.text:
Because the internal split uses:

stratify=y

classes with too few observations can make train_test_split fail.

Add more samples, merge unsuitable rare classes when scientifically appropriate, or prepare a dataset with sufficient class support before fitting KFC.

docs.title: Local classifier receives one class
docs.text:
This is one of the most common KFC classification failures.

Example:

ValueError:
[FSTEP ERROR] divergence='euclidean', cluster=2 failed.
...
Hint: cluster contains invalid label distribution.

Try reducing n_clusters first.

docs.title: Invalid classifier name
docs.text:
If local_model is not registered:

local_model="my_unknown_classifier"

F-Step raises an error listing the currently available models.

docs.title: Regression model supplied to classifier
docs.text:
For example:

KFCClassifier(
    ...,
    local_model="ridge",
)

is invalid because ridge is registered for regression.

docs.title: Regression combiner supplied to classifier
docs.text:
For example:

combiner="mean"

is invalid for classification.

Use one of:

majority_vote
stacking_classifier
combined_classifier

docs.title: Divergence domain violation
docs.text:
For example:

divergences=["logistic"]

with values outside \((0,1)\) is invalid.

Scale or otherwise transform the data before fitting.

docs.title: A practical progression
docs.text:
For a new classification problem, start simple:

1. Euclidean
   + logistic_regression
   + majority_vote
            ↓
2. Euclidean
   + decision_tree_classifier
   + majority_vote
            ↓
3. Several divergences
   + logistic_regression
   + majority_vote
            ↓
4. Compare stacking_classifier
            ↓
5. Compare combined_classifier

This sequence makes it easier to isolate whether changes in performance come from clustering, local modeling, or consensus aggregation.

docs.title: Recommended starter configuration
docs.text:
For arbitrary real-valued features:

model = KFCClassifier(
    divergences=["euclidean"],
    local_model="logistic_regression",
    local_model_params={
        "max_iter": 1000,
    },
    combiner="majority_vote",
    n_clusters=3,
    random_state=42,
)

For features already scaled into \((0,1)\):

model = KFCClassifier(
    divergences=[
        "euclidean",
        "gkl",
        "logistic",
        "is",
    ],
    local_model="logistic_regression",
    local_model_params={
        "max_iter": 1000,
    },
    combiner="majority_vote",
    n_clusters=3,
    random_state=42,
)

For prediction-space consensus:

model = KFCClassifier(
    divergences=[
        "euclidean",
        "gkl",
        "logistic",
        "is",
    ],
    local_model="logistic_regression",
    combiner="combined_classifier",
    combiner_params={
        "distance": "hamming",
        "kernel": "rbf",
    },
    n_clusters=3,
    random_state=42,
)

docs.title: Configure C-Step
docs.text:
The C-Step is the final aggregation stage of the KFC Procedure.

It receives the prediction matrix created by the F-Step and converts the divergence-specific predictions into one final regression value or class label.

\[ \boxed{ \text{F-Step prediction matrix} \rightarrow \text{combiner} \rightarrow \text{final prediction} } \]

The implementation is provided by:

from kfc_procedure.core.steps import CStep

Most users configure it through:

KFCRegressor(...)
KFCClassifier(...)

using:

combiner
combiner_params
random_state

docs.title: What the C-Step receives
docs.text:
If the K-Step uses \(M\) divergences, the F-Step creates a matrix with one prediction column per divergence:

\[ P \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times M}. \]

For regression, a row might look like:

[12.4, 11.9, 12.8, 12.2]

For classification:

[0, 0, 1, 0]

The C-Step applies an aggregation function

\[ g(P)\rightarrow \widehat y. \]

The C-Step does not access the original feature matrix, K-Step centroids, or local F-Step models directly. It only sees the F-Step prediction matrix and, during fitting, the target vector.

docs.title: Where C-Step sits in KFC
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    K["K-Step<br/>cluster assignments"]
    F["F-Step<br/>local predictions"]

    P["Prediction matrix<br/>P"]

    C["C-Step<br/>combiner"]

    Y["Final output"]

    K --> F --> P --> C --> Y

During training, KFCProcedure.fit() constructs the C-Step with:

self.cstep_ = CStep(
    combiner=self.combiner,
    combiner_params=self.combiner_params,
    task=self.task,
    random_state=self.random_state,
)

self.cstep_.fit(
    P_l,
    y_l,
)

where P_l is the F-Step prediction matrix for the held-out aggregation subset.

docs.title: Direct C-Step API
docs.text:
The constructor is:

CStep(
    combiner,
    combiner_params=None,
    task="regression",
    random_state=None,
)

The main methods are:

fit(X, y)
predict(X)
predict_proba(X)

where X is a prediction matrix, not the original feature matrix.

docs.title: Combiner registry
docs.text:
String-based combiners are resolved through:

CombinerFactory

The current source registers the following names.

docs.title: Regression
docs.text: Name Implementation mean MeanCombiner weighted_mean WeightedMeanCombiner stacking_regressor StackingRegressorCombiner gradientcobra GradientCOBRACombiner mixcobra MixCOBRACombiner

docs.title: Classification
docs.text:
Name Implementation majority_vote MajorityVoteCombiner stacking_classifier StackingClassifierCombiner combined_classifier CobraClassifierCombiner

The registry also stores a task category, so C-Step validates whether the selected combiner is compatible with regression or classification.

docs.title: Task validation
docs.text:
For a string combiner, C-Step first checks:

CombinerFactory.contains(name)

and then:

CombinerFactory.supports(
    name,
    self.task,
)

Therefore:

CStep(
    combiner="mean",
    task="classification",
)

is invalid.

Likewise:

CStep(
    combiner="majority_vote",
    task="regression",
)

is invalid.

The error includes the available names for the selected task.

docs.title: Regression combiners
docs.text: The regression C-Step can use five built-in strategies.

docs.title: mean
docs.text:
MeanCombiner computes the row-wise arithmetic mean.

For a prediction row

\[ (p_1,\ldots,p_M), \]

the final prediction is

\[ \widehat y = \frac{1}{M} \sum_{m=1}^{M}p_m. \]

The implementation is:

return np.mean(
    X,
    axis=1,
)

and fit() is stateless:

def fit(self, X, y=None):
    return self

docs.title: Direct use
docs.text:
from kfc_procedure.core.combiner.regression import (
    MeanCombiner,
)

combiner = MeanCombiner()

combiner.fit(P_train, y_train)

y_pred = combiner.predict(P_test)

The combiner validates that the input is two-dimensional.

docs.title: weighted_mean
docs.text:
WeightedMeanCombiner learns a linear model over the divergence prediction columns.

The model is:

\[ y \approx Pw. \]

It uses:

LinearRegression(
    fit_intercept=fit_intercept,
)

with:

fit_intercept=False

by default.

docs.title: Direct use
docs.text:
from kfc_procedure.core.combiner.regression import (
    WeightedMeanCombiner,
)

combiner = WeightedMeanCombiner(
    fit_intercept=False,
)

combiner.fit(
    P_train,
    y_train,
)

y_pred = combiner.predict(P_test)

docs.title: Inspect learned coefficients
docs.text:
print(
    combiner.model.coef_
)

print(
    combiner.model.intercept_
)

Note

Despite the name weighted_mean, the implementation does not constrain the coefficients to be positive or to sum to one.

It is ordinary linear regression over the F-Step prediction columns.

docs.title: stacking_regressor
docs.text:
StackingRegressorCombiner learns a meta-regressor.

Its default meta-model is:

LinearRegression()

During fitting, the source clones the supplied meta-model:

self.meta_model_ = clone(
    self.meta_model
)

and then fits it on the prediction matrix.

docs.title: Direct use
docs.text:
from kfc_procedure.core.combiner.regression import (
    StackingRegressorCombiner,
)

combiner = StackingRegressorCombiner()

combiner.fit(
    P_train,
    y_train,
)

y_pred = combiner.predict(P_test)

docs.title: Custom meta-model
docs.text:
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor

combiner = StackingRegressorCombiner(
    meta_model=RandomForestRegressor(
        n_estimators=200,
        random_state=42,
    )
)

The fitted clone is available as:

combiner.meta_model_

docs.title: gradientcobra
docs.text:
GradientCOBRACombiner wraps:

GradientCOBRA

The constructor forwards all keyword arguments to the wrapped estimator:

self.cobra = GradientCOBRA(
    **cobra_params
)

During fitting:

self.cobra.fit(
    X,
    y,
    as_predictions=True,
)

Therefore the F-Step prediction matrix is treated directly as GradientCOBRA's prediction-space representation.

docs.title: KFC example
docs.text:
from kfc_procedure import KFCRegressor

model = KFCRegressor(
    divergences=["euclidean"],
    local_model="ridge",
    combiner="gradientcobra",
    combiner_params={
        "kernel": "rbf",
        "distance": "euclidean",
        "bandwidth_list": [
            0.01,
            0.1,
            0.5,
            1.0,
            2.0,
        ],
    },
    random_state=42,
)

model.fit(
    X_train,
    y_train,
)

Because GradientCOBRACombiner.__init__() accepts arbitrary keyword arguments, the random_state forwarded by C-Step is accepted by this combiner.

For the algorithm itself, see:

GradientCOBRA

docs.title: mixcobra
docs.text:
MixCOBRACombiner wraps:

MixCOBRARegressor

and fits it with:

self.cobra.fit(
    X,
    y,
    as_predictions=True,
)

docs.title: KFC example
docs.text:
model = KFCRegressor(
    divergences=["euclidean"],
    local_model="ridge",
    combiner="mixcobra",
    combiner_params={
        "kernel": "rbf",
        "distance": "euclidean",
    },
    random_state=42,
)

model.fit(
    X_train,
    y_train,
)

The wrapper accepts arbitrary COBRA parameters through:

**cobra_params

For the standalone algorithm, see:

MixCOBRA

KFC integration

Inside the KFC C-Step, MixCOBRA receives only the F-Step prediction matrix through as_predictions=True.

It does not receive the original KFC feature matrix as a separate input-space component.

docs.title: Classification combiners
docs.text: The classification C-Step currently provides three built-in strategies.

docs.title: majority_vote
docs.text:
MajorityVoteCombiner performs hard voting across each row of the prediction matrix.

For example:

[1, 1, 0, 1]

produces:

1

The implementation uses:

Counter(
    row
).most_common(1)[0][0]

for every sample.

docs.title: Direct use
docs.text:
from kfc_procedure.core.combiner.classification import (
    MajorityVoteCombiner,
)

combiner = MajorityVoteCombiner()

combiner.fit(
    P_train,
    y_train,
)

y_pred = combiner.predict(P_test)

fit() is stateless.

docs.title: Tie behavior
docs.text:
The source does not implement a separate tie-breaking strategy.

Tie behavior is inherited from:

collections.Counter.most_common()

and the ordering of labels in the row.

docs.title: stacking_classifier
docs.text:
StackingClassifierCombiner learns a meta-classifier over the F-Step prediction matrix.

The default is:

LogisticRegression(
    max_iter=1000,
)

During fitting, the meta-model is cloned:

self.meta_model_ = clone(
    self.meta_model
)

docs.title: Direct use
docs.text:
from kfc_procedure.core.combiner.classification import (
    StackingClassifierCombiner,
)

combiner = StackingClassifierCombiner()

combiner.fit(
    P_train,
    y_train,
)

y_pred = combiner.predict(P_test)

docs.title: Custom meta-classifier
docs.text:
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier

combiner = StackingClassifierCombiner(
    meta_model=RandomForestClassifier(
        n_estimators=200,
        random_state=42,
    )
)

The fitted model is stored in:

combiner.meta_model_

docs.title: combined_classifier
docs.text:
CobraClassifierCombiner wraps:

CombinedClassifier

and fits it with:

self.cobra.fit(
    X,
    y,
    as_predictions=True,
)

so the F-Step output is interpreted directly as prediction-space data.

docs.title: KFC example
docs.text:
from kfc_procedure import KFCClassifier

model = KFCClassifier(
    divergences=["euclidean"],
    local_model="logistic_regression",
    combiner="combined_classifier",
    combiner_params={
        "distance": "hamming",
        "kernel": "rbf",
        "bandwidth_list": [
            0.01,
            0.1,
            0.5,
            1.0,
        ],
    },
    random_state=42,
)

model.fit(
    X_train,
    y_train,
)

The wrapper also implements:

predict_proba(...)

by delegating to:

self.cobra.predict_proba(X)

For the algorithm itself, see:

CombinedClassifier

docs.title: Current random_state constructor issue
docs.text:
The current C-Step source automatically injects:

random_state=self.random_state

into every string-based combiner unless the key already exists in combiner_params.

The relevant logic is:

params = dict(
    self.combiner_params
)

if "random_state" not in params:
    params["random_state"] = self.random_state

return CombinerFactory.create(
    name,
    **params,
)

CombinerFactory.create() forwards these keyword arguments directly to the registered class constructor.

This creates an important compatibility issue.

The following built-in constructors do not accept random_state:

MeanCombiner
WeightedMeanCombiner
StackingRegressorCombiner
MajorityVoteCombiner
StackingClassifierCombiner

Therefore, in the current source version, selecting these combiners by string through CStep can raise a TypeError, even when the top-level random_state is None.

For example, conceptually:

CStep(
    combiner="mean",
    task="regression",
)

builds the equivalent of:

MeanCombiner(
    random_state=None,
)

but MeanCombiner.__init__() does not accept that argument.

Current source limitation

String-based use of mean, weighted_mean, stacking_regressor, majority_vote, and stacking_classifier is currently affected by this constructor mismatch.

The COBRA wrappers are not affected because their constructors accept arbitrary keyword arguments:

GradientCOBRACombiner(**cobra_params)
MixCOBRACombiner(**cobra_params)
CobraClassifierCombiner(**cobra_params)

docs.title: Workaround: pass a combiner instance
docs.text:
C-Step does not rebuild a combiner when combiner is already an object:

if not isinstance(
    self.combiner,
    str,
):
    return self.combiner

Therefore a direct combiner instance avoids the automatic random_state injection.

docs.title: Mean
docs.text:
from kfc_procedure import KFCRegressor
from kfc_procedure.core.combiner.regression import (
    MeanCombiner,
)

model = KFCRegressor(
    divergences=["euclidean"],
    local_model="ridge",
    combiner=MeanCombiner(),
    random_state=42,
)

docs.title: Weighted mean
docs.text:
from kfc_procedure.core.combiner.regression import (
    WeightedMeanCombiner,
)

model = KFCRegressor(
    divergences=["euclidean"],
    local_model="ridge",
    combiner=WeightedMeanCombiner(
        fit_intercept=False,
    ),
    random_state=42,
)

docs.title: Stacking regression
docs.text:
from kfc_procedure.core.combiner.regression import (
    StackingRegressorCombiner,
)

model = KFCRegressor(
    divergences=["euclidean"],
    local_model="ridge",
    combiner=StackingRegressorCombiner(),
    random_state=42,
)

docs.title: Majority vote
docs.text:
from kfc_procedure.core.combiner.classification import (
    MajorityVoteCombiner,
)

model = KFCClassifier(
    divergences=["euclidean"],
    local_model="logistic_regression",
    combiner=MajorityVoteCombiner(),
    random_state=42,
)

docs.title: Stacking classification
docs.text:
from kfc_procedure.core.combiner.classification import (
    StackingClassifierCombiner,
)

model = KFCClassifier(
    divergences=["euclidean"],
    local_model="logistic_regression",
    combiner=StackingClassifierCombiner(),
    random_state=42,
)

Note

This workaround reflects the current implementation. It is not a conceptual requirement of the KFC algorithm.

docs.title: Pre-instantiated combiner behavior
docs.text:
Unlike the current F-Step behavior for local model objects, using a pre-instantiated C-Step combiner is generally appropriate because C-Step needs only one combiner object.

There is no need to clone a combiner per divergence or cluster.

C-Step simply stores it as:

self.strategy_

and fits it once.

docs.title: combiner_params
docs.text:
For a string-based combiner, constructor options are passed using:

combiner_params

For example, COBRA configuration can be supplied as:

model = KFCRegressor(
    divergences=["euclidean"],
    local_model="ridge",
    combiner="gradientcobra",
    combiner_params={
        "kernel": "rbf",
        "distance": "euclidean",
        "n_cv": 5,
    },
)

C-Step copies the dictionary before modifying it:

params = dict(
    self.combiner_params
)

so the original user dictionary is not changed by _build_combiner().

docs.title: Fitting behavior
docs.text:
C-Step fitting is simple:

self.strategy_ = self._build_combiner()

self.strategy_.fit(
    X,
    y,
)

There is no additional preprocessing, validation, cross-validation, or reshaping in CStep itself.

Those behaviors belong to the selected combiner.

docs.title: Stateless vs learned combiners
docs.text:
• Stateless

    mean

    majority_vote

    Their fit() methods simply return self.

  • Learned

    weighted_mean

    stacking_regressor

    stacking_classifier

    gradientcobra

    mixcobra

    combined_classifier

    These estimate parameters or fit a secondary model from X and y.

docs.title: Prediction behavior
docs.text:
C-Step prediction checks that:

strategy_

has been created by fit():

check_is_fitted(
    self,
    "strategy_",
)

and then delegates directly:

return self.strategy_.predict(X)

BaseCombiner.predict() itself calls:

self.combine(X)

unless a subclass provides different behavior.

docs.title: predict_proba()
docs.text:
C-Step allows probability prediction only when:

task == "classification"

Otherwise:

raise AttributeError(
    "predict_proba only available for classification"
)

For classification, it then checks whether the strategy has a predict_proba attribute.

docs.title: Important abstract-interface detail
docs.text:
BaseCombiner does not define:

predict_proba()

so only subclasses that explicitly implement it expose probability prediction.

Among the current built-in C-Step combiners:

Combiner predict_proba() majority_vote No stacking_classifier No combined_classifier Yes

CobraClassifierCombiner implements:

def predict_proba(self, X):
    return self.cobra.predict_proba(X)

docs.title: Top-level KFC probability limitation
docs.text:
Even though combined_classifier supports C-Step probabilities, the complete KFCClassifier.predict_proba() path is currently incomplete.

The top-level implementation calls:

P = self.fstep_.predict_proba(
    X,
    clusters,
)

but the current FStep source does not define predict_proba().

Therefore:

KFCClassifier.predict_proba(...)

is not currently functional end-to-end.

Warning

This is an F-Step limitation, not a limitation of CobraClassifierCombiner.predict_proba() itself.

docs.title: Inspect the fitted C-Step
docs.text:
After fitting a KFC estimator:

cstep = model.cstep_

The selected fitted combiner is:

cstep.strategy_

Inspect its type:

print(
    type(
        cstep.strategy_
    ).__name__
)

docs.title: Inspect weighted mean
docs.text:
strategy = model.cstep_.strategy_

print(
    strategy.model.coef_
)

print(
    strategy.model.intercept_
)

docs.title: Inspect regression stacking
docs.text:
strategy = model.cstep_.strategy_

print(
    strategy.meta_model_
)

docs.title: Inspect classification stacking
docs.text:
strategy = model.cstep_.strategy_

print(
    strategy.meta_model_

docs.title: Inspect COBRA wrappers
docs.text:
For:

gradientcobra
mixcobra
combined_classifier

the wrapped estimator is:

strategy.cobra

For example:

cobra = model.cstep_.strategy_.cobra

print(
    cobra
)

For GradientCOBRA or CombinedClassifier, fitted hyperparameters may include:

print(
    cobra.bandwidth_
)

when available after fitting.

docs.title: Inspect available combiners
docs.text:
Use the factory directly:

from kfc_procedure.core.combiner import (
    CombinerFactory,
)

print(
    CombinerFactory.available()
)

Regression only:

print(
    CombinerFactory.available_by_category(
        "regression"
    )
)

Classification only:

print(
    CombinerFactory.available_by_category(
        "classification"
    )
)

This reflects the actual registry loaded by the installed package.

docs.title: Custom combiner
docs.text:
A custom C-Step strategy should subclass:

BaseCombiner

and implement:

fit(...)
combine(...)

A minimal regression example:

import numpy as np

from kfc_procedure.core.combiner.base import (
    BaseCombiner,
)


class MedianCombiner(BaseCombiner):

    def fit(
        self,
        X,
        y=None,
    ):
        return self

    def combine(
        self,
        X,
    ):
        X = np.asarray(X)

        return np.median(
            X,
            axis=1,
        )

Use the object directly:

model = KFCRegressor(
    divergences=["euclidean"],
    local_model="ridge",
    combiner=MedianCombiner(),
)

This avoids factory registration entirely.

docs.title: Register a custom combiner
docs.text:
To select it by name, register the class with:

CombinerFactory

Example:

from kfc_procedure.core.combiner import (
    CombinerFactory,
)


@CombinerFactory.register(
    "median",
    categories={"regression"},
)
class MedianCombiner(BaseCombiner):
    ...

Then:

model = KFCRegressor(
    divergences=["euclidean"],
    local_model="ridge",
    combiner="median",
)

Constructor compatibility

In the current C-Step implementation, every string-based combiner receives a random_state keyword.

A custom registered combiner should therefore either accept:

random_state=None

or accept arbitrary keyword arguments.

Otherwise it is subject to the same constructor mismatch described above.

docs.title: Custom classification probabilities
docs.text:
A custom classification combiner can additionally implement:

predict_proba(...)

For example:

class MyClassifierCombiner(BaseCombiner):

    def fit(
        self,
        X,
        y,
    ):
        ...
        return self

    def combine(
        self,
        X,
    ):
        ...

    def predict_proba(
        self,
        X,
    ):
        ...

Then CStep.predict_proba() can delegate to it when:

task="classification"

The current top-level KFC probability path still requires F-Step probability support before this can work end-to-end.

docs.title: Choosing a regression combiner
docs.text:
A useful interpretation is:

Combiner Behavior mean treat all divergence predictions equally weighted_mean learn a linear coefficient for each divergence column stacking_regressor learn a customizable meta-regression function gradientcobra use prediction-space kernel consensus mixcobra use the MixCOBRA wrapper on F-Step predictions

For the current source version, remember the constructor issue affecting the first three when selected by string.

docs.title: Choosing a classification combiner
docs.text:
Combiner Behavior majority_vote hard vote over divergence predictions stacking_classifier learn a meta-classifier combined_classifier prediction-space kernel consensus

Again, the current string-based majority_vote and stacking_classifier paths receive an unsupported random_state argument. Passing combiner instances avoids that issue.

docs.title: Regression with a combiner instance
docs.text:
from kfc_procedure.core.steps import CStep
from kfc_procedure.core.combiner.regression import (
    WeightedMeanCombiner,
)

cstep = CStep(
    combiner=WeightedMeanCombiner(
        fit_intercept=False,
    ),
    task="regression",
)

cstep.fit(
    P_train,
    y_train,
)

y_pred = cstep.predict(P_test)

docs.title: Classification with a combiner instance
docs.text:
from kfc_procedure.core.steps import CStep
from kfc_procedure.core.combiner.classification import (
    MajorityVoteCombiner,
)

cstep = CStep(
    combiner=MajorityVoteCombiner(),
    task="classification",
)

cstep.fit(
    P_train,
    y_train,
)

y_pred = cstep.predict(P_test)

docs.title: Regression with GradientCOBRA by name
docs.text:
cstep = CStep(
    combiner="gradientcobra",
    combiner_params={
        "kernel": "rbf",
        "distance": "euclidean",
        "bandwidth_list": [
            0.01,
            0.1,
            1.0,
        ],
    },
    task="regression",
    random_state=42,
)

cstep.fit(
    P_train,
    y_train,
)

y_pred = cstep.predict(P_test)

This works with the current constructor architecture because GradientCOBRACombiner accepts arbitrary **cobra_params.

docs.title: 5. Check for constructor errors
docs.text:
If you see an error similar to:

TypeError:
... got an unexpected keyword argument 'random_state'

and you are using:

mean
weighted_mean
stacking_regressor
majority_vote
stacking_classifier

the error is caused by the current C-Step random_state injection.

Pass a pre-instantiated combiner object as the workaround.

docs.title: 6. Check C-Step input values
docs.text:
If an upstream F-Step prediction matrix contains missing values, the learned combiner may fail or propagate them.

Inspect:

P = model.fstep_.predict(
    X_test,
    model.kstep_.predict(
        X_test
    ),
)

print(P)

For numeric regression output:

print(
    np.isfinite(P).all()
)

docs.title: Current source limitations
docs.text: Area Current behavior string combiner parameter forwarding always injects random_state simple built-in combiner constructors several do not accept random_state stateless combiners still pass through fit() weighted mean constraints no positivity or sum-to-one constraints stacking probabilities classifier wrapper does not expose predict_proba() KFC end-to-end probabilities blocked by missing F-Step predict_proba() custom string combiners should accept random_state pre-instantiated C-Step combiner used directly without factory reconstruction

docs.title: Mental model
docs.text:
K-Step creates several geometric views, F-Step turns each view into a prediction, and C-Step decides how those predictions should become one output.

\[ \boxed{ \begin{bmatrix} p_1(x) & p_2(x) & \cdots & p_M(x) \end{bmatrix} \rightarrow g \rightarrow \widehat y(x) } \]

For simple combiners, \(g\) is a deterministic rule.

For learned combiners, \(g\) is fitted on the held-out F-Step prediction matrix and target values.

docs.title: Configure F-Step
docs.text:
The F-Step is the local supervised-learning stage of the KFC Procedure.

It receives the divergence-specific cluster assignments created by the K-Step and fits one predictive model inside every non-empty cluster.

\[ \boxed{ \text{K-Step clusters} \rightarrow \text{cluster-specific supervised models} \rightarrow \text{prediction matrix} } \]

The implementation is provided by:

from kfc_procedure.core.steps import FStep

Most users configure the F-Step indirectly through:

KFCRegressor(...)
KFCClassifier(...)

using:

local_model
local_model_params
task
random_state

docs.title: Core idea
docs.text:
Suppose the K-Step creates a partition for divergence \(d\):

\[ C_d = \{C_{d,1},C_{d,2},\ldots,C_{d,K}\}. \]

The F-Step fits one local model for every non-empty cluster:

\[ f_{d,k} : X_{C_{d,k}} \rightarrow y_{C_{d,k}}. \]

With several divergences, the complete collection is

\[ \mathcal{M} = \{ f_{d,k} \}. \]

Each divergence therefore gets its own set of cluster-local models.

docs.title: Where F-Step sits in KFC
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    X["Training data"]
    K["K-Step<br/>cluster assignments"]

    F1["Local model<br/>divergence 1 / cluster 1"]
    F2["Local model<br/>divergence 1 / cluster 2"]
    F3["Local model<br/>divergence 2 / cluster 1"]
    FM["..."]

    P["Prediction matrix"]
    C["C-Step"]

    X --> K
    K --> F1
    K --> F2
    K --> F3
    K --> FM

    F1 --> P
    F2 --> P
    F3 --> P
    FM --> P

    P --> C

The F-Step does not combine models itself.

Its job is to generate one prediction column per divergence. The C-Step performs the final aggregation.

docs.title: Basic regression configuration
docs.text:
from kfc_procedure import KFCRegressor

model = KFCRegressor(
    divergences=["euclidean"],
    local_model="ridge",
    combiner="mean",
    n_clusters=3,
    random_state=42,
)

The F-Step is created internally as:

FStep(
    local_model="ridge",
    local_model_params={},
    task="regression",
    random_state=42,
)

docs.title: Basic classification configuration
docs.text:
from kfc_procedure import KFCClassifier

model = KFCClassifier(
    divergences=["euclidean"],
    local_model="logistic_regression",
    combiner="majority_vote",
    n_clusters=3,
    random_state=42,
)

Internally:

FStep(
    local_model="logistic_regression",
    local_model_params={},
    task="classification",
    random_state=42,
)

docs.title: F-Step inputs
docs.text:
The direct API is:

fstep.fit(
    X,
    y,
    clusters,
)

where:

X
    feature matrix

y
    regression targets or class labels

clusters
    dictionary of cluster assignments from K-Step

A typical cluster dictionary looks like:

{
    "euclidean": np.array([0, 1, 1, 0, 2, ...]),
    "gkl": np.array([1, 1, 0, 2, 2, ...]),
}

Every cluster array must correspond row-for-row with X and y.

docs.title: How fitting works
docs.text:
The source implementation loops over:

for div_name, cluster_ids in clusters.items():
    for k in np.unique(cluster_ids):
        ...

For every divergence and every observed cluster ID, it:

  1. selects the rows belonging to that cluster;
  2. creates or resolves the configured local model;
  3. fits the model on the cluster-specific subset;
  4. stores the fitted model in models_.

Conceptually:

divergence = euclidean

cluster 0
X[cluster == 0], y[cluster == 0]
            │
            ▼
       local model 0

cluster 1
X[cluster == 1], y[cluster == 1]
            │
            ▼
       local model 1

cluster 2
X[cluster == 2], y[cluster == 2]
            │
            ▼
       local model 2

The same process is repeated independently for every divergence.

docs.title: Fitted model structure
docs.text:
After fitting:

fstep.models_

is a nested dictionary.

Its actual structure is:

{
    "euclidean": {
        "m0": {
            "divergence": "euclidean",
            "cluster": 0,
            "model": fitted_model,
        },
        "m1": {
            "divergence": "euclidean",
            "cluster": 1,
            "model": fitted_model,
        },
    },
    "gkl": {
        "m0": {
            "divergence": "gkl",
            "cluster": 0,
            "model": fitted_model,
        },
    },
}

Storage format

The implementation documentation describes models_[divergence][cluster], but the current source actually stores the second-level keys as strings:

m0
m1
m2
...

The numeric cluster ID is stored inside:

metadata["cluster"]

docs.title: Inspect fitted local models
docs.text:
After fitting a complete KFC estimator:

fstep = model.fstep_

Inspect the available divergence model sets:

print(
    fstep.models_.keys()
)

Inspect every local model:

for divergence, models in fstep.models_.items():
    print(divergence)

    for model_name, metadata in models.items():
        print(
            model_name,
            "cluster=",
            metadata["cluster"],
            "model=",
            type(metadata["model"]).__name__,
        )

docs.title: Number of local models
docs.text:
If the K-Step uses:

  • \(M\) divergences;
  • \(K\) clusters per divergence;

then the F-Step can fit up to

\[ M\times K \]

models.

For example:

divergences=[
    "euclidean",
    "gkl",
    "logistic",
    "is",
]

n_clusters=3

normally produces up to:

\[ 4\times3=12 \]

local models.

Only cluster IDs that actually occur in the supplied cluster assignments are fitted.

docs.title: Empty clusters
docs.text:
The F-Step contains:

if np.sum(idx) == 0:
    continue

so an empty cluster is skipped.

In normal KFC usage, the K-Step itself reinitializes empty centroids during clustering, so the training assignments will generally contain only cluster IDs represented by observations.

The F-Step does not create a fallback model for an empty cluster.

docs.title: Choosing a local model
docs.text:
local_model can currently be:

a registered string name

or:

a pre-instantiated BaseLocalModel-compatible object

String-based models are resolved through:

LocalModelFactory

docs.title: String-based local models
docs.text:
String names are normalized to lower case:

name = self.local_model.lower()

The F-Step checks:

LocalModelFactory.contains(name)

and then validates that the model supports the current task:

LocalModelFactory.supports(
    name,
    self.task,
)

This prevents a classifier from being used in regression and vice versa.

docs.title: Regression model example
docs.text:
model = KFCRegressor(
    divergences=["euclidean"],
    local_model="ridge",
    combiner="mean",
)

docs.title: Classification model example
docs.text:
model = KFCClassifier(
    divergences=["euclidean"],
    local_model="logistic_regression",
    combiner="majority_vote",
)

docs.title: Automatic scikit-learn registration
docs.text:
The package dynamically discovers scikit-learn estimators with:

sklearn.utils.all_estimators()

It selects classes that are:

ClassifierMixin

or:

RegressorMixin

and registers them in LocalModelFactory.

The estimator class name is converted to snake case.

For example:

LinearRegression
    -> linear_regression

LogisticRegression
    -> logistic_regression

RandomForestRegressor
    -> random_forest_regressor

RandomForestClassifier
    -> random_forest_classifier

KNeighborsRegressor
    -> k_neighbors_regressor

KNeighborsClassifier
    -> k_neighbors_classifier

This means the available local-model set depends partly on the installed scikit-learn version.

docs.title: Inspect available model names
docs.text:
You can query the registry directly.

from kfc_procedure.core.ml.base import LocalModelFactory

print(
    LocalModelFactory.available_by_category(
        "regression"
    )
)

For classification:

print(
    LocalModelFactory.available_by_category(
        "classification"
    )
)

This is more reliable than maintaining a hard-coded list in application code.

docs.title: Configure model parameters
docs.text:
Use:

local_model_params

to pass constructor parameters to a string-based model.

docs.title: Ridge
docs.text:
model = KFCRegressor(
    divergences=["euclidean"],
    local_model="ridge",
    local_model_params={
        "alpha": 2.0,
    },
    combiner="mean",
)

docs.title: Random forest regression
docs.text:
model = KFCRegressor(
    divergences=["euclidean"],
    local_model="random_forest_regressor",
    local_model_params={
        "n_estimators": 300,
        "max_depth": 8,
        "min_samples_leaf": 3,
    },
    combiner="mean",
    random_state=42,
)

docs.title: Logistic regression
docs.text:
model = KFCClassifier(
    divergences=["euclidean"],
    local_model="logistic_regression",
    local_model_params={
        "C": 1.0,
        "max_iter": 1000,
    },
    combiner="majority_vote",
    random_state=42,
)

docs.title: How unsupported parameters are handled
docs.text:
String-based scikit-learn models are wrapped by:

SklearnLocalModel

Before constructing the estimator, the adapter inspects:

model_cls.__init__

and keeps only keyword arguments that appear in that constructor signature.

Conceptually:

valid_kwargs = {
    key: value
    for key, value in kwargs.items()
    if key in signature.parameters
}

Therefore unknown constructor arguments are silently discarded by the current adapter rather than raising an error.

Parameter typo behavior

A misspelled parameter can be silently ignored.

For example, if an estimator expects:

n_estimators

and you write:

n_estimator

the wrapper may drop the misspelled argument.

Check the fitted estimator's parameters when configuration correctness is important.

docs.title: Inspect the actual estimator parameters
docs.text:
The wrapper implements:

get_params()

by delegating to the underlying scikit-learn model.

Example:

metadata = next(
    iter(
        model.fstep_.models_["euclidean"].values()
    )
)

local_model = metadata["model"]

print(
    local_model.get_params()
)

For scikit-learn-backed models, this returns the wrapped estimator's fitted configuration.

docs.title: random_state
docs.text:
For string-based models, F-Step copies:

local_model_params

and then adds:

random_state=self.random_state

if the parameter is not already present.

Therefore:

model = KFCRegressor(
    ...,
    random_state=42,
)

attempts to pass:

random_state=42

to every local model.

The SklearnLocalModel adapter removes it automatically for estimator classes whose constructor does not accept random_state.

If you specify a local value explicitly:

local_model_params={
    "random_state": 123,
}

that value takes precedence over the top-level KFC seed.

docs.title: Same model type in every cluster
docs.text:
local_model and local_model_params are global F-Step settings.

Therefore all clusters use the same model class and parameter configuration.

For example:

local_model="ridge"

local_model_params={
    "alpha": 2.0,
}

means:

Euclidean / cluster 0 -> Ridge(alpha=2)
Euclidean / cluster 1 -> Ridge(alpha=2)
Euclidean / cluster 2 -> Ridge(alpha=2)

GKL / cluster 0       -> Ridge(alpha=2)
GKL / cluster 1       -> Ridge(alpha=2)
GKL / cluster 2       -> Ridge(alpha=2)

The current FStep API does not provide different model types or parameter sets per divergence or per cluster.

docs.title: Independent instances for string models
docs.text:
When local_model is a string, _resolve() calls:

LocalModelFactory.create(...)

for every cluster.

Therefore each cluster receives a newly created local-model object.

This is the recommended way to configure F-Step.

docs.title: Prediction
docs.text:
After fitting, call:

predictions = fstep.predict(
    X,
    clusters,
)

The F-Step creates one output column for every divergence.

For each divergence:

pred = np.full(
    X.shape[0],
    np.nan,
)

It then routes each observation to the local model corresponding to its predicted cluster ID.

docs.title: Routing logic
docs.text:
For one local model:

k = metadata["cluster"]

idx = cluster_ids == k

pred[idx] = model.predict(
    X[idx]
)

Conceptually:

new observation
      │
      ▼
K-Step cluster ID
      │
      ▼
look up local model
      │
      ▼
model.predict(...)

This happens independently for every divergence.

docs.title: Prediction matrix shape
docs.text:
The returned matrix has shape:

(n_samples, n_divergences)

For four divergences:

(n_samples, 4)

Example regression output:

[[12.5, 13.1, 12.8, 12.4],
 [21.7, 20.9, 21.2, 22.0],
 [ 8.3,  8.0,  8.5,  8.2]]

Example classification output:

[[0, 0, 1, 0],
 [1, 1, 1, 1],
 [2, 1, 2, 2]]

The matrix is consumed directly by C-Step.

docs.title: Column order
docs.text:
predict() iterates over:

self.models_.items()

so the output columns follow the insertion order of the divergence entries in models_.

Those entries were created from the clusters dictionary supplied during fit().

In normal KFC use, that dictionary comes from K-Step and follows the divergence order used there.

If using FStep directly, keep cluster dictionaries consistent between fitting and prediction.

docs.title: Missing predictions and NaN
docs.text:
For each divergence, the prediction vector begins filled with:

np.nan

Only observations whose cluster ID matches one of the stored local models are filled.

Therefore NaN can remain if prediction-time cluster IDs do not correspond to a stored model.

This should not normally happen when K-Step and F-Step come from the same fitted KFC pipeline.

If it does happen, inspect:

model.kstep_.clusters_
model.fstep_.models_

and:

model.kstep_.predict(X)

to check cluster IDs.

docs.title: Direct F-Step example
docs.text:
You can use FStep directly.

import numpy as np

from kfc_procedure.core.steps import FStep


X = np.array([
    [0.0],
    [0.2],
    [0.8],
    [1.0],
])

y = np.array([
    0.0,
    0.2,
    0.8,
    1.0,
])

clusters = {
    "euclidean": np.array([
        0,
        0,
        1,
        1,
    ]),
}

fstep = FStep(
    local_model="linear_regression",
    task="regression",
)

fstep.fit(
    X,
    y,
    clusters,
)

P = fstep.predict(
    X,
    clusters,
)

print(P)

With one divergence:

P.shape == (4, 1)

docs.title: Classification-specific behavior
docs.text:
Classification requires particular attention because a cluster can contain only one class.

Suppose:

cluster 0 -> [0, 0, 0, 0]
cluster 1 -> [0, 1, 0, 1]

A model such as logistic regression cannot be fitted on cluster 0 because it contains only one target class.

docs.title: F-Step error wrapping
docs.text:
The source wraps any ValueError raised during local-model fitting:

try:
    model.fit(Xc, yc)

except ValueError as e:
    raise ValueError(
        "[FSTEP ERROR] ..."
    ) from e

The resulting message includes:

divergence
cluster ID
original error reason
hint about invalid label distribution

Example structure:

[FSTEP ERROR] divergence='euclidean', cluster=2 failed.
Reason: ...
Hint: cluster contains invalid label distribution.

Note

The same wrapper is applied to regression and classification.

The hint always mentions label distribution even when the underlying ValueError has a different cause.

docs.title: Reducing single-class cluster risk
docs.text:
For classification, increasing n_clusters produces smaller local datasets.

more clusters
     ↓
fewer samples per cluster
     ↓
higher probability of a single-class cluster

If a local classifier fails, try:

reduce n_clusters
use more training data
change divergence
choose another local classifier
inspect class imbalance

docs.title: Class weights
docs.text:
If the selected classifier supports class_weight, pass it through local_model_params.

model = KFCClassifier(
    divergences=["euclidean"],
    local_model="logistic_regression",
    local_model_params={
        "max_iter": 1000,
        "class_weight": "balanced",
    },
    combiner="majority_vote",
    n_clusters=3,
    random_state=42,
)

This can help imbalanced multi-class clusters, but it does not solve a cluster containing only one class.

docs.title: predict_proba() support
docs.text:
The local-model abstraction defines:

BaseLocalModel.predict_proba(...)

and SklearnLocalModel can delegate to an underlying estimator when that estimator supports:

predict_proba

For example, the wrapper records:

self._has_proba = hasattr(
    self.model,
    "predict_proba",
)

and then calls:

self.model.predict_proba(X)

when available.

However, the current FStep class does not implement a predict_proba() method.

It only implements:

fit(...)
predict(...)

Therefore probability-capable local classifiers cannot currently be combined through a top-level F-Step probability matrix.

Current KFC limitation

KFCClassifier.predict_proba() attempts to use self.fstep_.predict_proba(...), but that method is absent from the current FStep implementation.

End-to-end KFC probabilities are therefore not functional in this source version.

docs.title: Custom local models
docs.text:
The abstract local-model interface is:

BaseLocalModel

A custom model should implement:

fit(...)
predict(...)

and optionally:

predict_proba(...)

for classification.

A minimal regression example:

import numpy as np

from kfc_procedure.core.ml.base import BaseLocalModel


class ConstantRegressor(BaseLocalModel):

    def fit(self, X, y):
        self.value_ = float(
            np.mean(y)
        )
        return self

    def predict(self, X):
        return np.full(
            len(X),
            self.value_,
            dtype=float,
        )

docs.title: Register a custom local model
docs.text:
Register a model with:

LocalModelFactory

Example:

from kfc_procedure.core.ml.base import (
    BaseLocalModel,
    LocalModelFactory,
)


@LocalModelFactory.register(
    "constant_regressor",
    categories={"regression"},
)
class ConstantRegressor(BaseLocalModel):
    ...

Then:

model = KFCRegressor(
    divergences=["euclidean"],
    local_model="constant_regressor",
    combiner="mean",
)

docs.title: Constructor compatibility with F-Step
docs.text:
For string-based models, F-Step automatically injects:

random_state=...

unless it already exists in local_model_params.

Unlike the scikit-learn adapter, a directly registered custom class receives all arguments directly from the factory.

Therefore a custom registered model should either:

def __init__(
    self,
    random_state=None,
    ...
):
    ...

or otherwise accept the kwargs that F-Step will supply.

This is important for custom registry entries.

docs.title: Important behavior of pre-instantiated model objects
docs.text:
FStep accepts a non-string object through:

local_model=some_model

but the current implementation resolves it as:

if not isinstance(
    self.local_model,
    str,
):
    return self.local_model

That means it returns the same object instance for every cluster.

It does not call:

sklearn.base.clone(...)

and it does not create a copy.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
Suppose:

custom_model = MyLocalModel()

fstep = FStep(
    local_model=custom_model,
)

During fitting:

cluster 0 -> custom_model.fit(...)
